Part II · Constructing the arithmetic inputs›Ch. 8 · Supplying the arithmetic hypotheses›§8.1 From Galois representations to window data

The arithmetic estimate uses many fields and many primes. To control their total contribution, the proof bounds the lengths of cohomology groups on carefully chosen intervals. This is where one must keep track of which parameters have already been fixed when a field or window is chosen.

What length measures · The allowance per measurement · The three contributions · Tower generators · Descent · Selecting the interval · The degree-two bound · Detecting cycles · Counting faces · The plus bound · Trace congruences · The minus bound · The Frobenius test · Choosing both primes · The final window

8.1From Galois representations to window data

Over a CM field E, the row hypothesis applies to a regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representation of positive rank a. A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. In this setting a polarization relates a representation to a twist of its conjugate dual. For each allowed ℓ-adic coefficient realization, the conclusion gives a representation of the absolute Galois group on an a-dimensional ℓ-adic vector space, a weight and Hodge–Tate weight data. Its hypotheses include continuity, semisimplicity and prescribed local compatibility. The local theory uses both places above ℓ and places away from ℓ. The window construction uses this row directly and to obtain its open-image input, together with the base-change theorem.

The separate chapter on the two theta lifts explains the Galois input. For the derivative estimate used on the geometric side, see the factorial gain and the mixed-coordinate correction. The estimate on cohomology below has different indices and quantifiers.

8.2What the good arithmetic window controls

One can first think of a degree-one cohomology class as a way of assigning a value to each symmetry. A cocycle satisfies c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h). Two choices give the same class if they differ by g ↦ g·a − a. For the group of order two acting trivially on ℤ/4, the choice at its generator must double to zero. The two possibilities 0 and 2 give exactly two classes. In the arithmetic problem the group is a Galois group, the action includes a twist and one retains classes whose restrictions vanish at the specified places. This is the reason a kernel of a restriction map occurs below.

We measure a finite ℤℓ-module by its length. Filter it until each successive quotient has order ℓ. If there are d quotients, its order is ℓd. Both ℤ/ℓ² and (ℤ/ℓ)² have length two, although they require different numbers of generators. Later the tower estimate uses both quantities. Over a coefficient ring with residue field of size ℓf, each quotient instead contributes f to the base-ℓ logarithm of the order.

Fix a number field E and a rational prime ℓ. The coefficient module here is the discrete quotient ℚℓ/ℤℓ. A Tate twist changes the scalar by which Galois acts. If the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character is χcyc, the action on this quotient uses χcyc−j for the integer j in the window sum. With this action the cocycle rule above becomes c(gh) = c(g) + χcyc(g)−jc(h). Vanishing on restriction means the restricted cocycle becomes a coboundary.

Let S consist of the finite places above ℓ. Take the Galois group of the maximal extension unramified at every finite place outside S. One chooses a place of the algebraic closure above each member and restricts to the corresponding decomposition group. Write hℓ,j for the ℤℓ-module length of the subgroup of locally trivial degree-one classes. The related degree-two group has coefficients ℤℓ(j + 1). Thus the locally trivial subgroup within degree one is the intersection of the kernels of those local restriction maps.

Given t and B, the cohomological estimate requires finiteness of every hℓ,j for 1 ≤ j < t, for all allowed choices of closure and local data. For every finite set P of rational primes it also requires

∑ℓ ∈ P (log ℓ) ∑1 ≤ j < t hℓ,j ≤ B.

The field varies with a primitive character ψ, the height in a cyclotomic tower, and two auxiliary primes q,d. In a cyclotomic field containing the relevant roots of unity, the subgroup fixing E consists of the automorphisms whose exponents satisfy four conditions. These are congruence to ±1 modulo 2e+2, ψ(a) = 1, and two quadratic-symbol conditions at q and d. For a fixed ψ and 0 < ε < 1/52, choose any integer function e(x) satisfying x2+8ε ≤ 2e(x) ≤ 2x2+8ε for all x ≥ 1. The cohomological window theorem gives J ≥ 1 and a threshold X0. For every X beyond it and every admissible pair (q,d) at scale X1/J, there is Y ≥ X1/J with Y² ≤ X. Throughout [Y,Y²], every such field satisfies the length bound for t = ⌊x401⌋ and B = exp(xε/2). An admissible pair must obey the prime, congruence, divisibility and logarithmic size conditions of the prime-pair theorem.

8.3Splitting the obstruction by the action of conjugation

There is a different estimate for each of three parts of the cohomological sum. To see where they come from, fix a CM field in the construction, a twist index j and an odd prime ℓ. Complex conjugation on the CM field induces a linear involution c on the degree-one cohomology. Its action preserves the locally trivial subgroup. Put s = (−1)j. Because 2 is a unit in ℤℓ, every locally trivial class v has a decomposition

v = ½(v + scv) + ½(v − scv).

Applying c to the first summand multiplies it by s, and applying it to the second multiplies it by −s. Both still lie in the subgroup. A vector in both eigenspaces satisfies 2sv = 0, hence vanishes. The sum is direct, so the full module length equals the sum of its two eigenspace lengths. Here “plus” means eigenvalue (−1)j; for odd j this is the −1 eigenspace. At ℓ = 2 the projectors involve a forbidden division, and the full module is estimated separately.

On the joint window there are bounds B2 on the sum of full lengths at ℓ = 2, and B+ and B− on the logarithmically weighted odd-prime sums of the two corresponding lengths. Each comes with finiteness for its twists and primes. Length additivity gives finiteness of the full group at odd primes as well. For any finite prime set, split off 2 if present, and add the two odd-prime inequalities term by term. This proves the bound B2 log 2 + B+ + B−. It explains why the factor log 2 appears only on the first term.

8.4Putting the three estimates on one interval

Existence of two arbitrarily distant intervals separately would give no control of their intersection. The cyclotomic construction supplies a window with a bound at 2 and bounds on certain layers of auxiliary prime towers. The plus estimate is proved on every window satisfying this condition, once the same prime pair is large enough. Choose the maximum of the two thresholds for X, and an upper bound for the finitely many forbidden-size parameters for the two primes. An interval supplied by the first theorem then satisfies the second theorem with the same endpoints, field and tower level. The minus estimate applies to the composite CM field without any further window choice.

Write NE for the conductor of the field, t for the twist cutoff and u = NEt. On the accepted window u ≥ 1 and log u ≤ 2xε/4. Indeed NE ≤ 2e+2Nψqd. Taking logarithms, the page bound and t ≤ x401 contribute at most a fixed constant plus a constant times log x; the pair satisfies log(qd) ≤ xε/4. The first terms are eventually absorbed in a second xε/4. With constants C,K fixed before x, the three bounds take the form

B2 = exp(x4ε/5),   B− ≤ K exp(8xε/4),
B+ = uC + C exp(x4ε/5).

For u ≥ 1, uC ≤ exp(2|C|xε/4). Every exponent on the right of the displayed estimates is o(xε) for fixed ε > 0. Beyond a common threshold each exponential is at most exp(xε/4), and the sum of the fixed nonnegative prefactors, including log 2 and absolute values for constants, is itself at most exp(xε/4). Their product proves the required exp(xε/2). This comparison is uniform over fields obeying the conductor bound.

The tower estimate uses a bound on degree-two cohomology, Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness, local Tate duality and the Ferrero–Washington theorem. The plus contribution also uses separate representation counts. The following argument explains how the number of generators of a tower module controls the choice of the common interval.

8.5What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof

A generator bound limits how many independent ℓ-adic directions can contribute to the growth of a cohomology group. The argument starts with the ideal class groups of the number fields in the finite layers of a cyclotomic tower, passes to a single module for the infinite tower, and then recovers the length at any chosen finite layer as a quotient of that module. The class group of a number field is the group of its nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal ideals.

Write Cl(L) for the ideal class group of a number field L, written additively. The number of independent characters of order ℓ depends on Cl(L)/ℓCl(L). For an abelian extension K/ℚ containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity at ℓ = 2, the cyclotomic rank bound of Ferrero and Washington gives a single integer r such that

|Cl(K(μℓⁿ))/ℓCl(K(μℓⁿ))| ≤ ℓr   for every n ≥ 0.

Here μℓⁿ denotes the roots of unity of order dividing ℓn. The constant can depend on ℓ and K. The following construction gives one such bound.

First work in the full cyclotomic fields L = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) for fixed f > 1 prime to ℓ. Let C = Cl(L), let J be complex conjugation, and write E = (1 − J)C. The character comparison below supplies a bound B0 for the index of ℓC + (1 − γ)C, for its chosen Galois element γ. It also supplies N and n0, independent of n, such that in the integral group ring (γ − 1)N belongs to the ideal generated by θ, 1 + J and ℓ for n ≥ n0. Here θ is the integral half-sum, whose coefficients use one representative from each pair of opposite residues. The integral annihilator on ideal classes gives θ(1 − J)C = 0. Take the smoothing integer 2fℓ + 1.

Put T = 1 − γ. Multiply the relation by 1 − J. The θ term kills the class group, the 1 + J term disappears because J² = 1, and the last term has image inside ℓE. Hence TN kills V = E/ℓE. Each quotient TaV/Ta+1V is an image of V/TV. The map 1 − J in turn sends C/(ℓC + TC) onto V/TV. Multiplying the at most N quotient sizes gives |V| ≤ B0N. On the finite group E, the kernel and cokernel of multiplication by ℓ have the same order, so the same bound holds for |E[ℓ]|.

At odd ℓ a reflection inequality bounds |C/(ℓC + E)| by ℓ times the number of ℓ-torsion elements on which conjugation acts by −1. Each such element x lies in E, since (1 − J)(((ℓ + 1)/2)x) = x, with the integer scalar (ℓ + 1)/2. The remaining factor |(ℓC + E)/ℓC| is at most |E/ℓE|. The resulting bound is ℓB02N. At ℓ = 2 put C− = ker(1 + J). The separate sign estimate gives [C−∶E] ≤ (2φ(4f))N, where φ is Euler’s totient. On C[2], the map 1 − J has image in E[2] and kernel in C−[2]. The latter has order at most [C−∶E] |E[2]|. Squaring gives the uniform allowance ([C−∶E] |E[2]|)².

To transfer either bound, denoted by B, to the abelian field K, use its inclusion in a cyclotomic field. The embedding lemma chooses f,D before n. For every K′ = K(μℓⁿ) it produces a full cyclotomic field L of conductor fℓm, with m ≥ n0 and [L∶K′] ≤ Dℓn₀. Restrict the unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters from K′ to L. The size of the restriction kernel is bounded by the subgroup index [L∶K′], and the Artin character comparison bounds its image by the number of class-group characters of L. Thus |Cl(K′)/ℓCl(K′)| ≤ Dℓn₀B. The written proof chooses this integer itself for r, since it is at most ℓr. The arithmetic inputs to this derivation include the group-ring relation, the uniform ambiguous-class index, Stickelberger annihilation, reflection and the sign estimate at 2. Their statements have the pinned suppliers above.

8.6Which part of the class group has a uniform bound?

Fix a prime ℓ and a number field F containing a primitive ℓth root of unity. In a layer K = F(μℓn), assume K is totally complex and Gal(K/F) is generated by τ. Write C = Cl(𝒪K) additively. The first input to the uniform class-rank estimate controls the largest quotient of C killed by ℓ on which τ acts trivially. The term coinvariants describes this last condition. Define BF to be the number of continuous characters GF → 𝔽ℓ unramified at every finite place away from ℓ. Ramification above ℓ is allowed. Kummer theory makes this number finite, independently of the layer.

Q = C/(ℓC + (1 − τ)C),   [C ∶ ℓC + (1 − τ)C] = |Q| ≤ BF.

Why can the base field bound this index? A character of Q is determined by its composite with C ↠ Q. That composite is fixed by τ and therefore by its powers. As Q is a finite 𝔽ℓ-vector space, it has as many characters as elements. By the Hilbert class field comparison, pulling class characters back to U = GK identifies the invariant ones with a finite space E of characters on U. They vanish on all finite inertia in U and are invariant under conjugation by G = GF. The total-complexity hypothesis on K supplies the archimedean hypothesis for this identification, including at ℓ = 2.

Intersect the kernels of all characters in E inside U, and call the intersection N. It is open since E is finite and U is open. Since G is profinite and N is normal by conjugation invariance, G/N is a finite group. Every commutator gug−1u−1 belongs to N, so U/N is central in G/N. The quotient G/U is cyclic. Each element of G/N is therefore a power of one lift times a central element, so G/N is abelian. Every character in E factors through U/N, and every character of U/N satisfies the same invariance and inertia conditions.

For any finite abelian ℓ-primary or mixed-order group D, |Hom(D,𝔽ℓ)| equals |D[ℓ]|. The inclusion of the subgroups killed by ℓ in U/N and G/N now bounds the number of characters of the first group by that of the second. Pullback from G/N to G is injective. Every inertia group away from ℓ fixes the cyclotomic layer and hence lies in U. All its elements lie in N by the definition of E. The pulled-back characters are consequently among the BF allowed characters. This proves the index bound. The distinction between counting and extending is visible for 3ℤ/9 ⊂ ℤ/9. Each group has three 𝔽₃-valued characters, and all three characters of ℤ/9 restrict to zero on 3ℤ/9.

Where does the exponent come from? For conductor M = fℓn with (f,ℓ) = 1, put a = 1 for odd ℓ and a = 2 for ℓ = 2. Take the fixed base F = ℚ(μfℓa) and varying K = ℚ(μM), n ≥ 2. In the units modulo M, γ = 1 + fℓa generates the kernel of reduction to conductor fℓa. Its subgroup has index φ(fℓa), where φ is Euler’s totient. The archive acts on ideal classes by the inverse automorphism, so it uses the relative generator τ corresponding to γ−1. This provides one BF for all these layers.

Suppose now f > 1, write J for complex conjugation, and let Θ be the integral Stickelberger element used in this calculation, with auxiliary integer c = 2fℓ + 1. Two further results enter. Integral Stickelberger annihilation makes Θ(1 − J) act as zero on C. Separately, nonvanishing of the twisted, projected Θ in characteristic ℓ supplies a depth n₀ and one exponent N such that (γ − 1)N belongs to the group-ring ideal (Θ, 1 + J, ℓ) for every n ≥ n₀. The tested characters satisfy χ(−1) = −1, a condition which in characteristic two reads χ(−1) = 1. These two inputs give the first inequality below, and the ambiguous-class estimate gives the second.

|(1 − J)C ∩ C[ℓ]| ≤ |Q|N ≤ BFN.

At odd primes reflection then bounds |C/ℓC| by ℓ(BFN)². At 2 the proof inserts the bound from real-unit signatures and obtains ((2φ(4f))NBFN)². These are the eventual cyclic-layer estimates used to bound the original abelian tower.

How does the minus class count control the plus classes?

Let K be a CM field containing a primitive ℓth root of unity ζ, with ℓ an odd prime. Write C = Cl(K) additively, let J be complex conjugation, and put E = (1 − J)C. The tower estimate bounds the number of elements in E[ℓ], where brackets denote the subgroup killed by ℓ. To see which classes still need to be counted, first divide C/ℓC by the image of E. In the resulting vector space Q = C/(ℓC + E), each class coincides with its conjugate. In fact Q identifies with the plus eigenspace of C/ℓC by sending a representative x to (x + Jx)/2. The division takes place in 𝔽ℓ.

Odd-prime reflection. Let C[ℓ]− consist of the classes y with ℓy = 0 and Jy = −y. Then

|Q| ≤ ℓ · |C[ℓ]−|.

Count the linear maps χ from Q to 𝔽ℓ. Choosing their values on a basis shows that there are |Q| of them. By Artin reciprocity each gives a character of the absolute Galois group of K unramified at every finite prime. These characters satisfy χ(c⁻¹gc) = χ(g), where c is any lift of J to the algebraic closure. Indeed the Artin map carries conjugate primes to conjugate Frobenius elements and χ has the same value on a class and its conjugate.

Fix ζ for the rest of the argument. For each character choose a nonzero β satisfying g(β)/β = ζχ(g). For a nonzero χ, let L/K be the cyclic extension fixed by its kernel. A generator acts by a scalar ζχ(g) of norm one, so Hilbert’s Theorem 90 gives such a β in that extension. For the zero character take β = 1. Then a = βℓ lies in K×. At every finite prime the extension is unramified. Its normalized integer valuation therefore restricts to the normalized valuation on K. Evaluating βℓ gives ℓ ∣ ord𝔭(a) at every prime 𝔭. The fractional ideal (a) is consequently the ℓth power of a unique fractional ideal 𝔞.

Send χ to the class [𝔞]. A different choice of β differs by a factor from K×, so 𝔞 changes only by a principal ideal. Products of radicals give sums of characters, making this a homomorphism. Its image is killed by ℓ. To find its sign, apply g to βc(β). The factor from β is ζχ(g). The factor from c(β) is c(ζχ(c⁻¹gc)) = ζ−χ(g), because conjugation inverts ζ. Their product is 1, so d = βc(β) lies in K× and a · J(a) = dℓ. Taking the unique ideal ℓth root gives 𝔞J(𝔞) = (d), hence J[𝔞] = −[𝔞]. This is where a plus character produces a minus ideal class.

Where does the extra factor ℓ come from?

Suppose [𝔞] = 0. Taking a generator b of 𝔞 gives a = u bℓ with u a unit of K. The relation a · J(a) = dℓ implies that u · J(u) is an ℓth power in K. Also u/J(u) is an algebraic integer with absolute value one at every complex embedding. By Kronecker’s theorem it is a root of unity. Thus u² = (u/J(u)) · u · J(u) is represented by a root of unity modulo ℓth powers. Since ℓ is odd, raising this equality to the power (ℓ + 1)/2 shows that u itself has that property.

Finally, the class of a modulo ℓth powers determines χ. If two such classes coincide, the quotient of the two radicals, after division by an element of K×, is an ℓth root of unity and therefore belongs to K. The two characters agree. The kernel thus injects into the image of the roots of unity in K×/(K×)ℓ. The roots of unity in a number field form a finite group. Under a complex embedding they are contained in the cyclic group of roots of Xm − 1, where m is their number, so they form a cyclic group themselves. Its quotient by ℓth powers has at most ℓ elements. Multiplying this kernel bound by the size of the minus subgroup containing the image proves the reflection inequality.

Lean correspondence

The theorem reflOdd applies reflect over the base field itself and with local modulus one. The argument on this page specializes the kernel count to roots of unity modulo ℓth powers. The general construction passes through the finite-order radicals counted in reflRoot.

Why is the bound squared in the tower?

If y belongs to C[ℓ]−, then (1 − J)((ℓ + 1)y/2) = (ℓ + 1)y = y. Here (ℓ + 1)/2 is an ordinary integer. Thus each such y belongs to E[ℓ]. The map C/ℓC → Q has kernel E/(E ∩ ℓC). This kernel is a quotient of E/ℓE, which has size |E[ℓ]| by counting the kernel and image of multiplication by ℓ on the finite group E. Hence

|C/ℓC| = |E/(E ∩ ℓC)| · |Q| ≤ ℓ · |E[ℓ]|².

The two copies of |E[ℓ]| have different origins. One counts what was lost in forming the quotient Q. The other bounds the possible images of characters of Q under reflection. For a check of this multiplication, take ℓ = 3 and the abstract group C = ℤ/9 ⊕ (ℤ/3)², with J negating the first coordinate and fixing the other two. Here E is the entire first factor, |E[3]| = 3, and |Q| = 9. Multiplication by 3 on C has image of size 3, so |C/3C| = 81/3 = 27, exactly 3 · 3². For n ≥ 1 in the cyclotomic tower, the layer K = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) contains the primitive ℓth root ζfℓⁿfℓⁿ⁻¹. The uniform bound |E[ℓ]| ≤ BFN now gives ℓBF2N.

Fixed classes and coinvariants in two dimensions

Let C = 𝔽₃² and τ(x,y) = (x + y, y), an automorphism of order three. Its fixed vectors form the first coordinate line. Since (1 − τ)(x,y) = (−y,0), this entire line maps to zero in Q. The second coordinate induces Q ≃ 𝔽₃. Both groups have three elements, but the projection kills every fixed vector. The three invariant characters are exactly (x,y) ↦ by, one for each b ∈ 𝔽₃.

For an arithmetic check of the two indices, take ℓ = 3, f = 2 and n = 2. The units mod 18 form a group of order six. The powers of γ = 7 are 1, 7, 13, so their subgroup has index two and the relative class action uses 13. The field ℚ(μ₁₈) = ℚ(μ₉) has absolute discriminant 3⁹. Its Minkowski bound is (4/π)³(6!/6⁶)√(3⁹) < 4.47. The prime 2 has order six mod 9, so the prime above it has norm 64. The sole prime above 3 is generated by 1 − ζ₉. Every class thus has a principal representative of norm at most four. Here the class-group index |Q| is one. Over the base ℚ(μ₃), Kummer theory also gives BF = 9. Its Eisenstein integers are principal, so every cube class unramified away from 3 has a representative which is a unit times a power of 1 − ζ₃. Conversely these representatives are units away from 3, where the cube-root polynomial has separable reduction. The six roots of unity supply three classes modulo cubes and the exponent at the sole prime above 3 supplies three more choices, giving 3 · 3.

Why a Stickelberger coefficient survives reduction modulo ℓ

The class-group argument needs one depth at which every allowed character leaves a nonzero coefficient. Fix a prime ℓ, an integer f ≥ 1 coprime to ℓ and an odd integer c > 1 coprime to fℓ. In the selected cyclotomic tower f > 1 and c = 2fℓ + 1. At level n put M = fℓn. For a residue s modulo M, let ⟨s⟩ be its representative between 0 and M−1. Each unit supplies a basis element [s] of the group ring. The integral relation uses just one unit from each pair {s,−s}.

g(s) = ⌊c⟨c−1s⟩/M⌋ − (c−1)/2,   Θ = ∑s unit, 2⟨s⟩<M g(s)[s].

For odd ℓ let W be the group of (ℓ−1)st roots of unity in ℤℓ. For ℓ = 2 take W = {1,−1}. At depth d ≤ n, the map πd reduces a unit modulo ℓd and then takes its coset modulo the image of W. Twisting by a character χ sends [s] to χ(s)[πd(s)]. The theorem gives one d ≥ 2 depending on ℓ, f and c. For every n ≥ d, every field k of characteristic ℓ and every character χ of the units modulo M into k× with χ(−1) = −1, the twisted image of Θ has a nonzero coefficient at depth d. The coset carrying that coefficient may vary.

Convert the coefficients into a difference. Extend χ by zero on nonunits, calling the extension Ψ. Sum g(s)Ψ(s) over all residues s above y modulo ℓd and call the result α(y). Choose one ℓ-adic root r from each pair {r,−r} in W, forming a set R. On units, both g and χ change sign under negation, so their product has the same value at both representatives. The lower-half sum defining Θ can therefore use the representatives selected by R in each quotient fibre. Reduction is injective on W at depth d ≥ 2, and on nonunit fibres α vanishes. Thus vanishing of the twisted image would imply ∑r∈R α(r−1y) = 0 for every y, with r reduced modulo ℓd. This argument chooses representatives directly, which is essential in characteristic two.

The function Ψ has additive period fℓ. Adding fℓ preserves the prime divisors shared with M. On a unit s it amounts to multiplying by 1 + fℓ/s, a unit of ℓ-power order. Its character value is 1 because in characteristic ℓ the only ℓ-power root of unity in a field is 1. Set B = cfℓ. Subtracting c from s lowers the residue ⟨c−1s⟩ by one, with wraparound at zero. The floor difference counts the integers 0 ≤ j < c congruent to s, with a correction −c at zero. Add fℓ such consecutive differences. The corrections now occur at the multiples of c. Periodicity lets Ψ weight the result, and summing over the fibres gives a formula at the chosen depth.

α(y) − α(y−B) = ∑0≤j<B, j≡y mod ℓd P(j),   P(j) = Ψ(j)(1 − c·1c∣j).

In particular P(1) = 1, because Ψ(1) = 1 and c > 1. The issue is whether different directions r and different indices j can hide that coefficient after reduction.

Sinnott’s separation argument. Write Xv for a formal translation by an additive residue v, so multiplication adds exponents. At finite level put Ar = ∑y α(y)Xry and Pr = ∑j<B P(j)Xjr. The difference equation says Pr = (1−XBr)Ar. The putative vanishing says ∑r Ar = 0. Multiplying by the product of all the differences eliminates the functions Ar.

∑r∈R Pr ∏u∈R, u≠r (1−XBu) = 0.

Write the same expression with exponents in the additive group ℤℓ before reduction. Only finitely many exponents can occur. They have the form jr + ∑u∈S Bu for 0 ≤ j < B and a subset S of R. This finite list is known before the coefficient field or character is chosen. Any two distinct ℓ-adic integers differ at some finite depth. Taking the maximum of these depths over the list and increasing it to at least two makes reduction injective on the list. Hence the displayed identity also holds with exponents in ℤℓ.

Fix one direction r₀ and take exponents modulo the additive subgroup ℤ·Br₀. Every summand except the one indexed by r₀ contains the zero factor 1−XBr₀. For every other u, the image of Bu has infinite order. Indeed, a nonzero integer relation between u and r₀ would make their ratio a rational root of unity and hence ±1, excluded by the choice of representatives. Multiplication by 1−XBu is then injective on finite sums. Any nonzero coefficient fixed by this translation would repeat at infinitely many exponents. Cancel these factors. The exponents jr₀ for 0 ≤ j < B remain distinct modulo ℤ·Br₀, so every P(j) vanishes. This contradicts P(1) = 1.

A failed shallow test at 2. Take ℓ = 2, f = 3 and c = 13. Every character here satisfies the sign condition. Indeed χ(−1)² = 1, so (χ(−1)−1)² = 0 in the characteristic-two field and χ(−1) = 1 = −1. At n = d = 2, M = 12 and the units in the lower half are 1 and 5. Since 13 ≡ 1 modulo 12, the coefficients are ⌊13/12⌋−6 = −5 and ⌊65/12⌋−6 = −1. Both represent the same coset modulo 4 after quotienting by {±1}. The trivial character gives −6 = 0 in 𝔽₂. The theorem allows this cancellation at a shallow depth.

For these same parameters the general argument gives d = 7. We will then calculate the first working depth directly. There is just one direction, which we may choose as 1, and B = 78 < 128. If all projected coefficients vanished, α would vanish everywhere. At y = 1 the difference equation instead gives α(1)−α(51) = P(1) = 1. This works for every input level n ≥ 7. As a numerical check at n = 7 and χ trivial, the units above 1 are 1 and 257 with coefficients 5 and 0. The units above 51 are 179 and 307 with coefficients 0 and 4. The two fibre sums are therefore 1 and 0 in 𝔽₂. The finite fibre calculation lets you compare cancellations at different levels.

For this example the first depth that works at all later levels is actually 3. Every character in characteristic two is trivial here: the unit group modulo 3·2n has order a power of two, and in a field of characteristic two an element of 2-power order equals 1. At M = 24 the lower-half representatives 1, 5, 7, 11 have coefficients 1, 3, 4, 6. The two cosets modulo 8 are {±1} and {±3}. Their respective sums are 1 + 4 = 5 and 3 + 6 = 9, both odd.

Why does this persist when the modulus doubles? Write gM for the coefficient at modulus M. The two lifts of any unit s have preimages under multiplication by 13 of the form t and t + M. The identity ⌊x⌋ + ⌊x + 13/2⌋ = ⌊2x⌋ + 6, with x = 13t/(2M), gives g2M(s) + g2M(s + M) = gM(s). Thus the sum on each individual fibre y modulo 8 is preserved exactly. The projected sum instead chooses the lower-half member of each pair {s, −s} above {y, −y}. Replacing it by the member above y preserves its parity because gM(−s) = −gM(s). Hence the projected sums stay odd for every n ≥ 3. The calculation modulo 12 already excluded depth 2.

How does a surviving coefficient bound a power of γ − 1?

The nonvanishing theorem detects a twisted sum at one fixed projection depth d, however far up the tower the source lies. The class-group bound needs an integral ideal membership with a single exponent at all those levels. The bridge between them is a polynomial in one nilpotent variable.

Read the order of vanishing in the cyclic direction. At level n let G be the units modulo fℓn. Write [g] for the basis element of its group algebra and set T = [γ]−1. Work over an algebraic closure k of 𝔽ℓ. The proof constructs a homomorphism p from G into the cyclic subgroup generated by γ. It preserves the shallow projection π, sends complex conjugation J to 1, and γ has order dividing ℓn. Consequently Tℓn = [γℓn]−1 = 0. For an odd character χ the twist Φ formed with p is a polynomial in T, since every [p(g)] is a nonnegative power of 1+T. The map induced by π takes Φ to the known nonzero twist and sends Tℓd to zero.

Choose a polynomial representing Φ and factor out its lowest nonzero power, writing Φ = Tru(T) with u(0) ≠ 0. The polynomial u(T) has an inverse. After division by its constant term it is one plus a nilpotent, whose inverse is a finite geometric sum. If r ≥ ℓd, the image of Φ in the shallow quotient would vanish. Thus Φ divides the required power, with multiplier Tℓd−ru(T)−1.

A detectable coefficient which has no inverse

In the group algebra of a cyclic group of order eight over 𝔽₂, write T = [γ]−1. The elements 1, T, …, T⁷ form a basis and T⁸ = 0. Project to the cyclic group of order four, where T⁴ = 0. The element Φ = T³(1+T) has nonzero image T³. It has no inverse in the original ring, but it divides T⁴. Multiplying Φ by T(1+T)⁷ gives T⁴ because (1+T)⁸ = 1. This is a check of the polynomial step.

Recover the untwisted relation. The part discarded by p has exponent dividing φ(fℓe) = ℓam with ℓ ∤ m. Here e is 1 at odd ℓ and 2 at ℓ = 2. Raising g/p(g) to ℓa defines a homomorphism b with image D of order prime to ℓ. In the algebra k[G]/(Θ,1+[J]), split the action of D into characters. For an eigenvector v ≠ 0 of character ψ, take χ satisfying χ(g)ℓa = ψ(b(g)), using inverse Frobenius in k. As [J] acts by −1 and p(J)=1, this χ satisfies χ(J)=−1, precisely the required sign.

Taking the ℓa-th power of the coefficient sum for Θ raises each term to that power in characteristic ℓ. On an eigenvector the one-term identity is [g]ℓav = [p(g)]ℓaψ(b(g))v. Thus the result on v equals the ℓa-th power of the cyclic twist Φ acting on v. Since Θ itself is zero in this quotient, that power of Φ kills v. Raising its divisibility relation to the same power shows that Tℓd+a kills v. Character orthogonality recovers the identity. Summing the character projectors before normalization gives |D| times 1, and |D| is invertible in k. Hence this power of T is itself zero in the quotient.

Lift back to ℤ. Put N = ℓd+a. Write the relation over k as TN = uΘ + v(1+[J]). Choose an 𝔽ℓ-linear map k → 𝔽ℓ fixing 1. Apply it to every coefficient of the equation. Linearity suffices because the factors Θ and 1+[J] have integral coefficients. Lift the two multipliers from 𝔽ℓ to ℤ. Every coefficient of the remaining difference is divisible by ℓ, giving the third generator of the ideal. Both d and a were fixed before the source level n.

([γ]−1)N ∈ (Θ, 1+[J], ℓ) ⊂ ℤ[G]   for every n ≥ d.

To use this relation, put V = (1−J)Cl(L)/ℓ(1−J)Cl(L). The integral class annihilator makes Θ act by zero there, (1+J)(1−J) = 0, and reduction kills ℓ. Hence the operator T = [γ]−1 satisfies TNV = 0. Multiplication by Ta maps V/TV onto each successive quotient TaV/Ta+1V. A bound B for the first quotient thus gives |V| ≤ BN. This is where the uniform exponent enters the class-group estimate.

In the dyadic example, f = 3 gives φ(3·4) = 4 and a = 2. Taking the sufficient depth d = 7 from the difference calculation gives N = 2⁹ = 512 for every n ≥ 7. The calculation modulo 8 tests a single character at a smaller depth. The exponent 512 uses a depth that works for every allowed character in every later layer.

Which integral element kills the ideal classes?

Fix M > 2, let L = ℚ(ζM), and write C = Cl(L) additively. A class is zero when an ideal representing it is principal. For a unit t modulo M, let σt send ζM to ζMt. Write et = σt−1, so et sends the class of an ideal to the class of the ideal obtained by applying σt−1. In particular J = e−1 acts by complex conjugation. Write ⟨t⟩ for the representative in {0, …, M−1}.

Stickelberger’s annihilation theorem. In the rational group ring of G = Gal(L/ℚ) put ϑ = ∑t(⟨t⟩/M)et, summing over the units. If β ∈ ℤ[G] and βϑ has integer coefficients, then (βϑ)C = 0. In ideal language the product of the Galois translates, raised to those integer coefficients, is a principal fractional ideal. C. S. Yogananda, Stickelberger Revisited, p. 151, opening theorem and proof[252].

Take an odd positive integer c coprime to M and put k = (c−1)/2. For each unit t, set u = ⟨c−1t⟩. Division with remainder gives cu = M⌊cu/M⌋ + ⟨t⟩. Thus the coefficient g(t) = ⌊cu/M⌋ − k is an integer. Replacing t by −t replaces u by M−u and the quotient by c−1−⌊cu/M⌋. Hence g(−t) = −g(t). The half-sum θ used in the tower takes g(t)et once per pair, on the side 2⟨t⟩ < M. Multiplication by 1−J restores the other coefficients with opposite signs.

θ(1−J) = ∑t g(t)et = [c ec − (k+1) − kJ] ϑ.

To check the last equality, multiply its coefficient at et by M. The three terms give cu − (k+1)⟨t⟩ − k(M−⟨t⟩) = M g(t). The bracket therefore supplies precisely the integral multiple required by the theorem.

Why does a carry give a principal ideal?

Here is the ideal calculation behind this particular annihilator. Take any class x. Artin reciprocity for the Hilbert class field and Chebotarev’s theorem give a prime ideal 𝔭 in this class of rational prime norm p, with p coprime to M. Since L/ℚ is Galois and 𝔭 has residue degree one, p splits completely. The distinct ideals et𝔭 therefore multiply to (p).

For residues a, b let εt(a,b) equal 1 when ⟨at⟩ + ⟨bt⟩ ≥ M and 0 otherwise. For a, b, a+b all nonzero, the finite-field Jacobi sum attached to the two character powers divides p. Testing a value at et𝔭 amounts to applying σt and then reducing at 𝔭. Since σt raises the character values to the tth power, the two exponents become at and bt. The Jacobi sum vanishes on reduction at precisely the conjugate primes with εt = 0. The factorization of (p) is square-free, so the complementary product, over the primes with a carry, is the ideal generated by p divided by this Jacobi sum. For a = 0 or b = 0 the carry product is empty. For a+b = 0 with both nonzero it is (p). In all cases ∑t εt(a,b)etx = 0. Residue test for the Jacobi sum · Why the Jacobi sum divides the prime.

Adding ⟨t⟩ to itself h times produces ⌊h⟨t⟩/M⌋ carries. Indeed, increasing h by one increases the floor by εt(h,1). The carry relations show that Fh = ∑t⌊h⟨t⟩/M⌋et kills x. Also (∑tet)x = 0 because the product of all the conjugate prime ideals is (p). Reindexing the coefficient of Fc gives θ(1−J) = ecFc − k∑tet. Both summands kill x. Since the prime could be chosen in every class, this proves the required action on C.

How does the integral relation meet the calculation modulo ℓ?

Set E = (1−J)C. The integral computation gives θE = 0. This statement applies at ℓ = 2 as well, because its proof uses the image of 1−J without dividing by 2. For example, take M = 8 and c = 3. At t = 1,3,5,7 the four coefficients are 0,−1,1,0. The half-sum θ = −e₃ has nonzero reduction modulo 2, and it acts invertibly on C. Its integral annihilation of E therefore implies E = 0 in this example.

In the tower M = fℓⁿ take c = 2fℓ+1, with f > 1 prime to ℓ. The nonzero projected coefficient yields a separate group-ring relation (γ−1)N ∈ (θ, 1+J, ℓ) with N uniform for sufficiently large n. Apply it to E. The first generator acts by zero by integral annihilation. The second acts by zero since (1+J)(1−J) = 0. The third maps E into ℓE. Thus (γ−1)N acts by zero on E/ℓE, the group whose successive layers enter the class-rank bound.

Fundamental equality and Tate cohomology vanishing for cyclic idèle class groups

Why does the vanishing of the minus-one cyclic Tate cohomology group Ĥ−1(G, CL) follow purely from comparing two bounds on the global idèle-class norm index [CK : NL/K(CL)], and why is this single vanishing statement the exact cohomological obstruction behind the cyclic and quadratic Hasse norm theorems? For a cyclic Galois extension L/K of number fields with Galois group G = ⟨σ⟩, the base-change map ι : CK ↪ CL identifies CK with the G-invariant subgroup CLG and sends the idèle-class norm NL/K(CL) onto the cyclic Galois norm image NG(CL), giving an isomorphism CK/NL/K(CL) ≅ Ĥ0(G, CL). Because the Herbrand quotient h(CL) = |Ĥ0(G, CL)| / |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| equals the field degree [L : K] with finite nonzero denominator, the norm index is literally [L : K] times |Ĥ−1(G, CL)|. That immediately yields the first inequality [L : K] ≤ [CK : NL/K(CL)], with equality if and only if |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| = 1. The second inequality supplies the opposite bound [CK : NL/K(CL)] ≤ [L : K], locking the norm index to [L : K] and forcing Ĥ−1(G, CL) to be trivial: every idèle class in CL of norm 1 is a Galois coboundary σ(d)/d.

1. Cyclic Tate cohomology of idèle classes and the class-field axiom. Let K and L be number fields with L/K a finite Galois extension whose Galois group G = Gal(L/K) is cyclic, generated by σ ∈ G. Let 𝕀K and 𝕀L denote the idèle groups of K and L, with idèle class groups CK = 𝕀K/K× and CL = 𝕀L/L×, canonical base-change homomorphism ι : CK → CL, and idèle-class norm NL/K : CL → CK. Viewing CL as a G-module (written additively in cohomology, with multiplicative notation c ↦ σ(c)/c for σ − 1 and c ↦ ∏g∈G g(c) for the cyclic norm NG), define the cyclic Tate cohomology groups Ĥ0(G, CL) = ker(σ − 1)/im(NG) and Ĥ−1(G, CL) = ker(NG)/im(σ − 1), and the Herbrand quotient h(CL) = |Ĥ0(G, CL)| / |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| whenever both groups are finite.

Proposition (Fundamental equality and vanishing of minus-one cyclic Tate cohomology).

(i) The base-change homomorphism induces a group isomorphism CK/NL/K(CL) ≅ Ĥ0(G, CL), so |Ĥ0(G, CL)| = [CK : NL/K(CL)]. From the Herbrand quotient h(CL) = [L : K], both cyclic Tate groups are finite (hence |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| ≠ 0), and

|Ĥ0(G, CL)| = [CK : NL/K(CL)] = [L : K] · |Ĥ−1(G, CL)|,   [L : K] ≤ [CK : NL/K(CL)].

(ii) Combining this first inequality with the second inequality [CK : NL/K(CL)] ≤ [L : K] gives the fundamental equality and the cyclic class-field axiom:

[CK : NL/K(CL)] = [L : K],   |Ĥ0(G, CL)| = [L : K],   |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| = 1.

In particular, Ĥ−1(G, CL) is trivial: every idèle class c ∈ CL with NG(c) = 1 lies in im(σ − 1), that is, c = σ(d)/d for some d ∈ CL.

Proof. For (i), let Φ : CK → Ĥ0(G, CL) send c ∈ CK to the coset of ι(c) modulo im(NG). Since the Galois action on CL fixes the image of ι, σ(ι(c)) = ι(c), so ι(c) ∈ ker(σ − 1) and Φ is a well-defined homomorphism. To see that Φ is surjective, take any coset represented by y ∈ ker(σ − 1); because σ generates G, σ(y) = y implies g(y) = y for every g ∈ G, so Galois descent for idèle classes yields c ∈ CK with ι(c) = y, whence Φ(c) is the given coset. To compute ker(Φ), observe that for every d ∈ CL the cyclic Galois norm satisfies NG(d) = ∏g∈G g(d) = ι(NL/K(d)). Therefore c ∈ ker(Φ) if and only if ι(c) = ι(NL/K(d)) for some d ∈ CL; since ι : CK → CL is injective, this holds if and only if c ∈ NL/K(CL). By the first isomorphism theorem, CK/NL/K(CL) ≅ Ĥ0(G, CL), giving |Ĥ0(G, CL)| = [CK : NL/K(CL)].

Next, the Herbrand quotient of the cyclic G-module CL is well-defined (both Ĥ0(G, CL) and Ĥ−1(G, CL) are finite, so |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| ≥ 1) and satisfies |Ĥ0(G, CL)| / |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| = [L : K] in ℚ. Clearing the nonzero denominator and substituting |Ĥ0(G, CL)| = [CK : NL/K(CL)] gives the exact natural-number identity [CK : NL/K(CL)] = [L : K] · |Ĥ−1(G, CL)|. Because |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| ≥ 1 and [L : K] ≥ 1, this yields both the first inequality [L : K] ≤ [CK : NL/K(CL)] and finiteness of the norm index.

For (ii), the second inequality states that the cardinality of the quotient CK/NL/K(CL) is at most [L : K], so [CK : NL/K(CL)] ≤ [L : K]. Antisymmetry with the first inequality establishes the fundamental equality [CK : NL/K(CL)] = [L : K], and hence |Ĥ0(G, CL)| = [L : K]. Substituting [CK : NL/K(CL)] = [L : K] into [CK : NL/K(CL)] = [L : K] · |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| gives [L : K] · 1 = [L : K] · |Ĥ−1(G, CL)|; cancelling [L : K] > 0 forces |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| = 1. A group of cardinality 1 has only the identity element, so every c ∈ ker(NG) represents 0 in ker(NG)/im(σ − 1) and therefore satisfies c = σ(d)/d for some d ∈ CL.

Role of the Herbrand quotient, origin of the second inequality, and a finite-module contrast

For any finite cyclic group G = ⟨σ⟩ and finite G-module A, the exact sequences for σ − 1 and NG force |Ĥ0(G, A)| = |Ĥ−1(G, A)|, so h(A) = 1. For example, with G = ⟨σ⟩ of order 2 acting on A = ℤ/4ℤ by σ(a) = −a, one has NG(a) = a − a = 0 and (σ − 1)(a) = −2a; hence ker(σ − 1) = {0, 2} and im(NG) = {0} give |Ĥ0| = 2, while ker(NG) = ℤ/4ℤ and im(σ − 1) = {0, 2} give |Ĥ−1| = 2, so h(A) = 2/2 = 1. By contrast, CL is infinite; choosing a large finite set of places S containing all ramified places and generators of Cl(L) expresses CL as the quotient of the S-idèle group 𝕀L,S by the S-unit group 𝒪L,S×, whose Herbrand quotients are respectively ∏v∈S [Lw : Kv] (with w any place of L over v, independent of the choice since L/K is Galois) and (∏v∈S [Lw : Kv])/[L : K] (from Dirichlet’s S-unit lattice). Taking the ratio cancels all local factors and leaves h(CL) = [L : K].

In the second inequality, the cyclic global norm bound [CK : NL/K(CL)] ≤ [L : K] is deduced from the first inequality itself by strong induction on [L : K]: reducing along a prime-index subgroup reduces to prime-degree cyclic extensions, and adjoining primitive p-th roots of unity reduces to Kummer extensions, where the first inequality applied to auxiliary fields yields the upper bound on the norm index.

Cyclic and quadratic Hasse norm theorems and everywhere-local norm criteria for CM ideals

When does being a local norm at every place of a number field K guarantee that an element x ∈ K× is a global norm from an extension L/K, and why does a totally positive generator a of a conjugate ideal product I · c(I) = (a) in a finitely unramified CM extension K/K+ satisfy those local conditions automatically, supplying the global norm step in the dyadic signature injection? For any cyclic Galois extension L/K, the local-to-global passage factors into two clean steps. First, local norms at every finite and infinite place assemble into an idèle j ∈ 𝕀L with NL/K(j) = diag(x), because all but finitely many places are unramified and at every unramified finite place the local norm maps local integer units surjectively onto 𝒪Kv×. Second, the idèle class [j] ∈ CL has cyclic Galois norm 1 because diag(x) is principal; by Tate cohomology vanishing, [j] = [σ(e)/e] for an idèle e ∈ 𝕀L, so (σ(e)/e)−1j is a principal idèle diag(a) with a ∈ L×, and G-invariance of the idèle norm gives NL/K(a) = x. Since every quadratic extension of number fields is cyclic Galois, this applies immediately to any CM extension K/K+. For an ideal I ⊆ 𝒪K with I · c(I) = (a) and a = x ∈ (K+)× totally positive, Dedekind approximation at each finite place v of K+ picks b ∈ I whose norm n = b c(b) differs from x by a v-adic unit t, which is a local norm by unramifiedness; at each infinite place of K+ (necessarily real), total positivity supplies a positive real d-th root whose local norm is x.

1. Cyclic and quadratic local-to-global norm equivalence and CM local norm criteria. Let K and L be number fields with L/K a finite extension, diag : K× ↪ 𝕀K the diagonal embedding, and NL/K : 𝕀L → 𝕀K the idèle norm, whose component at a finite place v (resp. an infinite place v) of K is the product of local field norms Nv : ∏w∣v Lw× → Kv×. Write xv for the image of diag(x) at the place v. For a CM number field K, write K+ for its maximal totally real subfield ([K : K+] = 2) and c for complex conjugation on K (and its restriction to 𝒪K).

Proposition (Cyclic and quadratic Hasse norm theorems and everywhere-local norm criteria in CM extensions).

(i) Suppose L/K is Galois with cyclic Galois group G = Gal(L/K) (in particular, this holds automatically whenever [L : K] = 2). For every x ∈ K× (equivalently, every nonzero x ∈ K),

x ∈ NL/K(L×)   ⟺   diag(x) ∈ NL/K(𝕀L)   ⟺   (∀ v finite, xv ∈ im Nv) ∧ (∀ v infinite, xv ∈ im Nv).

(ii) Let K be a CM number field such that every finite place of K is unramified over K+. Let I ⊆ 𝒪K be a nonzero integral ideal, a ∈ 𝒪K, and x ∈ (K+)× such that a = x in K, I · c(I) = (a), and Re φ(a) > 0 for every complex embedding φ : K → ℂ. Then xv ∈ im Nv at every finite place v and every infinite place v of K+, and consequently

I · c(I) = (a),   a = x ∈ (K+)×,   Re φ(a) > 0 (∀ φ : K → ℂ)   ⟹   ∃ β ∈ K×,   NK/K+(β) = x.

Proof. For the first equivalence in (i), if x = NL/K(a) with a ∈ L×, then diag(x) = NL/K(diag(a)) ∈ NL/K(𝕀L). Conversely, suppose diag(x) = NL/K(j) for some idèle j ∈ 𝕀L, and pick a generator σ of the cyclic group G = Gal(L/K). Let y = [j] ∈ CL be the idèle class of j. Because diag(x) is principal, its idèle class in CK is 1, so the cyclic Galois norm satisfies

NG(y) = ∏g∈G g([j]) = ι(NL/K([j])) = ι([NL/K(j)]) = ι([diag(x)]) = 1.

Thus y ∈ ker(NG). By vanishing of minus-one cyclic Tate cohomology, |Ĥ−1(G, CL)| = 1, so Ĥ−1(G, CL) has only one element and the class of y in ker(NG)/im(σ − 1) is trivial. Hence y = σ(d)/d for some d ∈ CL. Choosing a lift e ∈ 𝕀L with [e] = d gives [j] = [σ(e)/e] in CL = 𝕀L/L×, so there exists a ∈ L× whose diagonal idèle satisfies diag(a) = (σ(e)/e)−1 · j. Applying the idèle norm NL/K, which is invariant under G (so NL/K(σ(e)/e) = NL/K(σ(e))/NL/K(e) = 1), yields

diag(NL/K(a)) = NL/K(diag(a)) = NL/K((σ(e)/e)−1) · NL/K(j) = 1 · diag(x) = diag(x).

Since diag : K× ↪ 𝕀K is injective, NL/K(a) = x. The second equivalence in (i) follows from local-to-idelic norm assembly (detailed below), and when [L : K] = 2 (in characteristic 0), L/K is automatically Galois with cyclic Galois group of order 2.

For (ii), fix first any finite place v of K+ (a nonzero prime ideal of 𝒪K+), choose a prime ideal w of 𝒪K lying over v, and set P = v𝒪K. Then P is nonzero and fixed by complex conjugation c (since c fixes 𝒪K+). By Dedekind approximation in 𝒪K (detailed below), since I · c(I) = (a) and c(P) = P, there exist b, t ∈ 𝒪K such that b c(b) = a t and t ∉ w (for every prime ideal w containing P). Since t ∉ w, we have t ≠ 0, hence b ≠ 0 (as a = x ≠ 0). Because Gal(K/K+) = {1, c}, the element n = NK/K+(b) ∈ (K+)× satisfies n = b c(b) = a t in K, so n x−1 = t in K. Because t ∉ w, its multiplicative w-adic valuation equals 1 (so t is a w-adic unit); as w lies over v with positive ramification index, the multiplicative v-adic valuation of n x−1 is also 1, so (n x−1)v lies in the local integer unit group 𝒪Kv+×. Since w is unramified over v (ramification index 1), the local norm map from the integer units over v surjects onto 𝒪Kv+×, proving (n x−1)v ∈ im Nv. Meanwhile n = NK/K+(b) is a global norm, hence nv ∈ im Nv; multiplying (n x−1)v−1 · nv = xv inside the local norm subgroup shows xv ∈ im Nv.

Next fix any infinite place v of K+, and choose an infinite place W of K lying over v. Because K+ is totally real, v is a real place, giving a canonical ring isomorphism e : Kv+ ≅ ℝ. The complex embedding of W restricts to v (up to complex conjugation), so total positivity Re φ(x) > 0 implies e(xv) > 0 in ℝ. Let d = [KW : Kv+] ∈ {1, 2} be the local archimedean degree (equal to 2 since K is totally complex), and define r = e−1(e(xv)1/d) ∈ Kv+; then rd = xv ≠ 0, so the image of r in KW is nonzero. Setting the component at W equal to r and all other components over v equal to 1 produces an element of ∏W′∣v KW′× whose local norm is NKW/Kv+(r) = rd = xv, proving xv ∈ im Nv. Applying (i) to the quadratic extension K/K+ yields β ∈ K× with NK/K+(β) = x.

Local-to-idelic assembly via unramified unit norms, the Dedekind ideal-approximation step, and a quadratic illustration

For the second equivalence in (i), any idèle norm NL/K(j) = diag(x) restricts at every place v to a local norm. Conversely, suppose xv ∈ im Nv for every finite and infinite place v. Because the different ideal of the finite separable extension L/K is nonzero, it has only finitely many prime factors, so all but finitely many finite places w of L have ramification index 1 over K. At any finite place v of K admitting an unramified place w of L over it, every local unit u ∈ 𝒪Kv× is the local norm of an integer unit y ∈ 𝒪Lw× (placed at w, with 1 at every other place w′ over v), so Nv maps ∏w′∣v 𝒪Lw′× surjectively onto 𝒪Kv×. Because xv ∈ 𝒪Kv× for all but finitely many finite places v, the local preimages over v can be chosen inside the integer units at all but finitely many finite places, assembling into an idèle j ∈ 𝕀L with NL/K(j) = diag(x).

For the Dedekind approximation step in (ii), let R = 𝒪K, with nonzero ideals P, I, nonzero a ∈ R, c(P) = P, and I · c(I) = (a). Since I P ⊆ I and I P ≠ 0 in the Dedekind domain R, there exists b ∈ I such that I P + (b) = I. Because (b) ⊆ I, factorization of ideals gives an integral ideal J with (b) = I J, so I(P + J) = I; cancelling the nonzero ideal I yields P + J = R, and applying the ring automorphism c gives P + c(J) = R. Multiplying (b) = I J by (c(b)) = c(I)c(J) yields (b c(b)) = (I c(I))(J c(J)) = (a)(J c(J)) ⊆ (a), so b c(b) = a t for some t ∈ R. Cancelling (a) ≠ 0 gives (t) = J c(J). If a prime ideal w containing P contained t, then J c(J) ⊆ w would force J ⊆ w or c(J) ⊆ w, contradicting P + J = R or P + c(J) = R; hence t ∉ w.

As a concrete illustration over K+ = ℚ with K = ℚ(i), take x = 5 and I = (2 + i), so I · c(I) = (5). At the real place, x = 5 > 0 has the positive square root r = √5 ∈ ℝ with Nℂ/ℝ(√5) = 5; at every unramified odd prime p ≠ 5, 5 is a p-adic unit and hence a local norm, and at p = 5 (which splits) and p = 2 (where 5 ≡ 1 mod 4), 5 = Nℚ(i)/ℚ(2 + i) is already a global norm. By contrast, x = −5 fails the archimedean positivity condition (Re(−5) < 0) and is not a norm from ℚ(i). In the dyadic cyclotomic layers L = ℚ(ζf 2n) with odd f > 1 and n ≥ 2 used in the dyadic signature injection, L/L+ is unramified at every finite place (including places above 2), so part (ii) supplies the global norm β ∈ L× directly.

How many sign patterns can a dyadic class miss?

Let f > 1 be odd, n ≥ 2, M = f2n and L = ℚ(ζM). Write G = (ℤ/M)× and let J = −1 act by complex conjugation. On the ideal class group C = Cl(𝒪L), use multiplicative notation. Put K = {x ∈ C ∣ x(Jx) = 1} and D = {x/(Jx) ∣ x ∈ C}. Then D ⊆ K. A class in K has trivial product with its conjugate. The index [K : D] measures the additional requirement that the class be a quotient by conjugation. To estimate it, the proof records signs in the maximal real subfield L+.

Give an ideal class a sign at each real embedding. Index the complex embeddings of L by t ∈ G through ζM ↦ exp(2πit/M). For a nonzero real element, record a bit at t, equal to 1 when the embedded value is negative. It has the same bit at −t. Write V for all such even bit patterns, and S for the subgroup consisting of the signatures of units fixed by J. Multiplication adds signatures. In particular the unit −1 supplies the constant pattern of ones.

Represent x ∈ K by an ideal I. The product I·JI is principal, and it admits a real generator a. Indeed, for an initial generator b, the quotient Jb/b is a unit of absolute value 1 at every embedding, hence a root of unity. In this tower the map v ↦ v/(Jv) from units onto roots of unity is surjective. Choose its value to be Jb/b. Then a = bv is fixed by conjugation. Two real generators of the same ideal differ by a real unit, so they determine the same coset of S. Multiplying I by a principal fractional ideal (z) multiplies its product with its conjugate by the totally positive factor zJz. Multiplying I by a fractional ideal of the form A/(JA) leaves that product fixed. These observations explain why signs modulo S measure classes modulo D.

Choose representatives of the two cosets being compared. Suppose their ideals I and I′ have real generators a and a′ for the respective products with their conjugates. If the sign cosets agree, a real unit u has the sign pattern of aa′. Thus aa′u is totally positive and generates the product of (JI)I′ with its conjugate. Here L/L+ is unramified at every finite place. The ideal identity gives local norms there, and positivity gives a local norm at every real place. The quadratic Hasse norm theorem supplies a global norm. Dividing the ideal by the corresponding principal ideal leaves a fractional ideal whose product with its conjugate is one. Its valuations cancel in conjugate pairs, so its class belongs to D. The class of (JI)I′ is x−1x′. This proves the injection of coset sets K/D → V/S.

A real unit provides the needed signature. Choose an odd positive c coprime to M. The tower uses c = 4f+1. Write k = (c−1)/2 and abbreviate ζM to ζ. The sum 1 + ζ + ⋯ + ζc−1 is a unit. The quotient (1−ζc)/(1−ζ) and its inverse are both integral geometric sums, using an inverse of c modulo M for the latter. Multiplication by ζ−k centers the exponents in pairs and makes the unit uc real. For the representative 0 < t < M, summing the geometric progression gives

uc(t) = sin(πct/M)/sin(πt/M),   s(t) = ⌊ct/M⌋ mod 2.

The denominator is positive, and the numerator changes sign at successive integers of ct/M. The half element Θ of the nonvanishing calculation uses the coefficient g(t) = ⌊c⟨c−1t⟩/M⌋ − k, with ⟨·⟩ the least nonnegative residue. Over ℤ, Θ(1−[J]) restores the signed coefficients g(t) on both halves and annihilates the ideal classes. For signatures use the coefficient of Θ(1+[J]) modulo two. It equals g(t) mod 2, hence s(c−1t) − k mod 2. This translated bit pattern belongs to S because a Galois conjugate of a real unit is again a real unit. The constant correction is the signature of (−1)k.

Four real embeddings at conductor 24

Take f = 3, n = 3 and c = 13. Order the pairs ±t by 1, 5, 7, 11. The floors ⌊13t/24⌋ are 0, 2, 3, 5, giving u13 the pattern 0011. Since 13−1 ≡ 13 modulo 24, multiplication by its inverse sends these four pairs to 11, 7, 5, 1. The correction k = 6 is even, so Θ(1+[J]) gives 1100. One can check this directly from the four lower-half coefficients 1, 3, 4, 6. Every translate of 0011 is either 0011 or its complement, since {±1,±5} is an index-two subgroup. Together with −1 these units generate the four signatures 0000, 0011, 1100, 1111. Thus among the 16 even patterns the full unit signature subgroup has index at most four.

Bound the number of missing patterns uniformly in the layer. Map the additive group of ℤ[G] onto V by folding the two coordinates at each conjugate pair, κ(x)(t) = xt + xJt mod 2. Each desired bit can be placed on one member of its pair. Let IS = κ−1(S). Translating a group-ring basis element translates the folded pattern, so IS is an ideal. It contains Θ by the unit calculation, 2 by reduction, and 1+[J] because folding it gives zero. The additive quotient W = ℤ[G]/IS therefore has cardinality [V : S] and exponent dividing two.

Now take n at least the uniform depth and T equal to multiplication by [γ]−1 on W. The integral ideal relation gives TN = 0. In W/TW the basis labels g and γg coincide, leaving at most one binary generator per coset of ⟨γ⟩. This gives |W/TW| ≤ 2[G : ⟨γ⟩]. Each layer TjW/Tj+1W is a quotient of W/TW by applying Tj. Multiplying over N layers bounds |W|. In this tower γ = 1+4f modulo M and [G : ⟨γ⟩] = φ(4f). Consequently

[K : D] ≤ [V : S] ≤ (2φ(4f))N.

Both φ(4f) and N are fixed before the choice of the layer n.

Where the factor enters the class-rank estimate. For the finite group C, |C/C²| = |C[2]| by counting the kernel and image of squaring. Put h = |D ∩ C[2]| and r = [K : D]. On C[2] the map x ↦ x/(Jx) has image of size at most h. Its kernel lies in K ∩ C[2], since a fixed element of order dividing two is its own inverse. Mapping this intersection into K/D costs at most r in the image and h in the kernel. Thus |C/C²| ≤ rh² ≤ (rh)². The ambiguous-class bound with constant BF for F = ℚ(μ4f), together with the integral annihilator Θ(1−[J]), gives h ≤ BFN. Substituting the two estimates gives the dyadic bound used by the cyclotomic theorem.

|C/C²| ≤ ((2φ(4f))N BFN)².

8.7From class-group characters to generators

Let U∞ be the kernel of the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character on the absolute Galois group, and put A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ. For an integer s ≥ 1, let Ds be the group of locally constant homomorphisms U∞ → A vanishing on its intersections with every inertia group and with each decomposition group above a prime dividing s. Define Xs = Homℤℓ(Ds, A). The earlier cokernel calculation uses s = ℓ. The generator proof starts at s = 1.

At the finite field K(μℓⁿ), n ≥ 2, class field theory pulls the class-group characters onto the everywhere unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters. Their number is bounded by the cardinality of Cl/ℓCl, since they factor through that finite vector space and its dual has the same dimension. At infinite level every such character extends to a finite level. The extension theorem first extends the locally constant homomorphism and then enforces the local conditions after moving higher. Compactness of the relevant sets of decomposition and inertia elements makes a single higher level suffice. The images under restriction from successive levels are nested and cover the infinite-level characters. Any ℓr + 1 distinct characters would therefore already occur together at one level, contradicting the finite bound. Adding the decomposition conditions for s can only reduce their number.

Every element of Ds has ℓ-power order. Its domain is compact, so its locally constant image is finite, and every element of A is killed by a power of ℓ. Further, Ds[ℓ] has at most ℓr elements by the character bound and the identification A[ℓ] ≅ ℤ/ℓ. Embed this vector space in Ar using at most r coordinates. Each coordinate extends to all of Ds because A is divisible and hence injective over the principal ideal domain ℤℓ. Their joint map is still injective. Indeed a nonzero kernel element of order ℓk would yield a nonzero kernel element of order ℓ by multiplication by ℓk−1. Any map Ds → A now extends to Ar. Each endomorphism of A is scalar multiplication by an ℓ-adic integer, as seen by its compatible values on the cyclic groups A[ℓk]. The r extended coordinates thus generate Xs. This proves the precise generator conclusion used in the layer bound, a surjection ℤℓr → Xs.

Which ideal-class characters survive the local conditions?

At a finite cyclotomic layer K, the class-group bound counts characters into 𝔽ℓ. The cohomology argument counts characters of a Galois group with prescribed local vanishing. The passage between them uses the ordinary Hilbert class field. The modulus selecting this field is 1. A separate integer N selects the primes where the Galois character must vanish on the entire decomposition group.

From the idèle-class norm to arithmetic Frobenius

Write CK = 𝔸K×/K× and let H be the Hilbert class field in a fixed algebraic closure of K. The norm takes idèle classes of H to idèle classes of K. Its image is represented by idèles whose finite components are units. Every infinite component is allowed, including both signs at a real place. Sending an idèle to its fractional ideal by taking the valuation at each finite place kills precisely those finite-unit idèles before quotienting by principal ideals. Passing to classes gives the ordinary ideal class group.

CK/NH/K(CH) ≃ Cl(𝒪K)   ≃   Gal(H/K).

The class-field existence theorem selects H from this norm subgroup. The reciprocity theorem identifies the displayed quotient with its Galois group. These are the global class field theory inputs used here. To fix the direction, put a uniformizer at a finite prime 𝔭 and 1 at all other places. Its ideal is 𝔭 and its local symbol acts on the residue field upstairs as x ↦ xN𝔭. Thus ArtK([𝔭]) is arithmetic Frobenius. The norm N𝔭 here is the cardinality of the residue field.

In the character calculation the map points from the absolute Galois group GK to Cl(𝒪K). Restrict an automorphism to H and apply ArtK−1 to obtain αK. Every automorphism of H over K extends to the algebraic closure, so this is surjective. Its fibres are open because H/K is finite. At a place over 𝔭, inertia maps to 1 and every arithmetic Frobenius lift maps to [𝔭]. Inertia and Frobenius topologically generate the decomposition group, whose image is therefore exactly the finite cyclic group generated by [𝔭].

Impose the local conditions on a class character

Let N ≥ 1, let S be the finite primes of K dividing N, and take an additive module M over a commutative ring. Assume K is totally complex or M[2] = 0. On the full GK, precomposition with αK gives the following identification. Characters on the right are locally constant group homomorphisms into the additive group of M. The conditions hold for every prolongation of each finite place.

Hom(Cl(𝒪K)/⟨[𝔭] ∣ 𝔭 ∈ S⟩, M) ≃ {φ on GK ∣ φ(I𝔭) = 0 for every finite 𝔭,   φ(D𝔭) = 0 for 𝔭 ∈ S}.

From left to right the two conditions follow from the images of inertia and decomposition. For the converse, the open kernel of φ cuts out a finite abelian extension. Killing finite inertia makes it unramified at every finite place. At a real place, complex conjugation has order at most two, so its image vanishes if M[2] = 0. For a totally complex field there are no real places to check. The resulting extension lies in H by its maximality. Thus φ factors uniquely through αK. Vanishing on each selected decomposition group kills precisely the required prime classes. This converse uses the entire Galois group of K. For a subgroup, restriction still gives the forward inclusion.

When K is normal over a base field and g above the base induces τ on K, conjugation sends a Frobenius at 𝔭 to one at τ𝔭. More generally αK(gug−1) = τ∗αK(u). Thus the coefficient condition φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u) reads θ(τ∗c) = ρ(g)θ(c) on ideal classes. In the degree-one descent, ρ acts on ℚℓ/ℤℓ by χcyc−e. The exponent belongs to the coefficient action. The Artin normalization is the same for every twist.

|Cl(𝒪K)/ℓCl(𝒪K)| ≤ [L∶K] · |Cl(𝒪L)/ℓCl(𝒪L)|.

8.8One generator bound before choosing the two primes

At each odd ℓ the abelian field datum is fixed. The argument above works in any realization of that field and the source takes R = max(1, r) to meet the positivity hypothesis. At 2 the field varies with q,d. Fix the abelian base datum M of degree b, adjoin i with i² = −1, and obtain an exponent g from the class-group bound there. Adjoining the two quadratic fields specified by q and d gives a generator bound uniform in all prime pairs with q ≡ 3 mod 8, d ≡ 7 mod 16 and qd coprime to the modulus of M.

R2 = 4(g + 6b).

Allow ramification at q and then at d in the larger space of mod-2 characters. Their inertia groups can be tested on at most 2b and 4b orbits respectively, by the two congruences. Evaluating on one tame inertia generator per representative gives at most two choices per orbit. Two characters with the same values differ by one from the previous space. Thus the character count is at most 2g+6b. Next pass to the subgroups corresponding to the two quadratic extensions. The index-two estimate at most squares the count at each step. For an index-two subgroup, conjugation by an outside element induces an involution c on its characters. In characteristic 2, (1 + c)² = 0, so the image lies in its kernel, the invariant characters. The source bounds the number of invariants by the old character count. Evaluation on the square of the outside element records the obstruction to extending an invariant character, and the quotient character of the index-two subgroup records this bit after extension. Hence the number of all characters is at most the square of the old count. Two squarings give the displayed exponent. Restoring the unramified and splitting conditions selects a subgroup, so the same bound applies to the two tower modules X1 and X2.

How many independent inertia values can a new ramified prime contribute?

Allow a character with values in 𝔽₂ to ramify at one new odd prime p. Its restriction to inertia at one prolongation of p takes at most one additional bit to record. Conjugate prolongations give the same information when the conjugating element lies in the group on which the character is defined. We therefore need a bound on the number of its orbits of places, uniform even in the infinite cyclotomic tower.

Fix an algebraic closure Ω of ℚ, with absolute Galois group G, and an abelian datum M of degree b and modulus m. Let W be its fixing subgroup in G, of index b. Let K = ker χ₂ fix all roots of unity of 2-power order, and put V = W ∩ K. This is the group used after adjoining i to M and passing up the dyadic tower, since K already fixes i. For each prime in either congruence class below there exists a set of prolongations of the indicated size or smaller. Every prolongation of p is a V-translate of a member of that set.

Number of V-orbits over p ≤ 2b   if p ≡ 3 (mod 8),   ≤ 4b   if p ≡ 7 (mod 16).
Follow one Frobenius through all finite layers

Choose a place A above p and let D be its decomposition group. An arithmetic Frobenius lift g in D sends every root of unity of order prime to p to its pth power. Testing the same g on a primitive root of order 2t at every depth gives χ₂(g) = p in ℤ₂×. The image H = χ₂(D) is closed because D is compact.

Put a = v₂(p² − 1). If p ≡ 3 mod 8, the two factors p − 1 and p + 1 have valuations 1 and 2. If p ≡ 7 mod 16 they have valuations 1 and 3. Thus a is 3 or 4 respectively. Write Pa = 1 + 2aℤ₂. At every t ≥ a, the powers of p² exhaust the principal units modulo 2t. Indeed, squaring a unit congruent to 1 modulo 4 increases the valuation of its difference from 1 by exactly one, since the other factor is congruent to 2 modulo 4. Consequently the order of p² at depth t is 2t−a, the size of that finite principal-unit group. Closedness now puts all of Pa inside H. Also p itself belongs to H and lies outside Pa. Hence H occupies at least two of the φ(2a) principal-unit cosets, and its index is at most φ(2a)/2, namely 2 or 4.

Because K is the kernel of χ₂, the subgroup KD is the preimage of H. Its index in G is bounded by the index of H in ℤ₂×. Intersecting K with W can increase the count by at most [G∶W] = b. Take one representative r per left coset of VD in G and mark the place rA. Every prolongation of p is gA for some g in G. Write g = rvd with v ∈ V and d ∈ D. Then gA = (rvr−1)(rA), with rvr−1 ∈ V. This gives the asserted cover. It works in Ω itself. At each finite layer the fixing group is larger than V, so passing to its orbits can only merge members of the cover. The estimate has no factor depending on the tower depth.

Record one inertia value per orbit

For a subgroup V of an absolute Galois group write C(N) for its locally constant additive 𝔽ℓ-characters unramified outside the primes above N. Suppose p is prime to ℓ, all inertia groups at p lie in V, and a set T of at most k prolongations covers the V-orbits at p. At each B ∈ T, choose an inertia element γB detecting all such characters of that inertia group. Wild inertia has residue characteristic different from ℓ, and the tame quotient has a procyclic ℓ-part. Thus a character vanishing on the chosen element vanishes on the whole inertia group. In the dyadic application the orbit bound holds in both congruence classes for every M. The additional assumption p coprime to 2m ensures the inertia inclusion needed here.

Evaluate φ ∈ C(Np) on the chosen elements to obtain Lφ ∈ 𝔽ℓT. Two characters with the same evaluations have difference vanishing on inertia at each B ∈ T. If A = vB for v ∈ V, then v−1IAv = IB. An additive character on V is constant on such conjugates, so the difference lies in C(N). Choose one character s(y) in each attained evaluation fibre. Recording the values and subtracting that representative gives the injection below. Its image uses only the evaluation vectors that actually occur.

C(Np) ↪ 𝔽ℓT × C(N),   φ ↦ (Lφ, φ − s(Lφ)).

Start with at most 2g unramified characters over the dyadic tower of M(i). For the admissible prime pair q, d the two steps add at most 2b and 4b to the exponent, giving 2g+6b characters when ramification at both primes is allowed. Adjoining the two quadratic fields gives two subgroup changes of index dividing two. Each squares the upper bound. The unramified characters over the new base form a subspace of these characters with allowed ramification. The resulting generator bound is 4(g + 6b). The initial g is chosen for the fixed M(i) before the two prime sizes, the realization of the new field, or its cyclotomic depth are specified.

Why does one inertia value suffice?

At a finite place of residue characteristic p ≠ ℓ, let I be inertia and P its wild subgroup. The orbit count uses one element γ ∈ I per representative place. Every locally constant additive character I → 𝔽ℓ is determined by its value on γ. The choice of γ precedes the choice of character. The reason is that the image of γ generates a dense subgroup of tame inertia I/P, while an ℓ-primary character kills P.

Choosing the same lift at all depths. The archive works with a valuation on an algebraic closure Ω of a number field, prolonged from the given place. For each n, take a root rₙ of rₙn! = p. The map θn(σ) is the class of σ(rₙ)/rₙ modulo the principal units. It has finite cyclic image since the ratio is an n!th root of unity. The kernels decrease as n increases. In compact I, the inverse images of the sets of generators form nested nonempty closed sets, so one γ generates every image. For any σ ∈ I, the powers of γ that match θn(σ) at level n give a second compactness argument. It yields h in the closure of the powers of γ with θn(h−1σ) = 1 for every n.

The proof uses that every nonzero y ∈ Ω is algebraic over ℚ. In an integral polynomial relation for y, at least two nonzero terms attain the largest absolute value, so |y|m = |p|k for some m > 0 and integer k. At a sufficiently divisible factorial level, y thus has the same absolute value as an integer power of rₙ. Their quotient is a unit, on whose residue inertia acts trivially. It follows that h−1σ satisfies |(h−1σ)(y)/y − 1| < 1 for every y ≠ 0. This is exactly the wild condition.

What forces wild inertia into the kernel? For an additive character φ to a discrete ℓ-primary group, local constancy gives a finite field extension whose fixing subgroup intersects I inside ker φ. A positive power of any wild σ fixes that extension. Write the exponent as ℓab, with ℓ ∤ b. A wild automorphism τ that fixes x after k iterations already fixes x whenever p ∤ k. Indeed, if y = τx − x is nonzero, the telescoping sum of τiy for 0 ≤ i < k is zero. Dividing by y and reducing modulo the maximal ideal gives k = 0 in the residue field, a contradiction. Apply this with τ = σb and k = ℓa. Then bφ(σ) = 0, so φ(σ) = 0. If φ(γ) also vanishes, its closed kernel contains P and γ and hence all of I. Applying this to a difference proves injectivity of evaluation.

Homcont(I, A) ↪ A,   φ ↦ φ(γ)   for discrete ℓ-primary A.

For A = 𝔽ℓ this gives at most ℓ choices per representative, precisely the factor used in the count. For A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ the same proof applies because each individual value has ℓ-power order. Each continuous character has finite image by compactness of I, so its image lies in A[ℓr] for some r depending on the character. At fixed r evaluation gives at most ℓr choices.

Two values and four values at the same place

Over ℚ₅ take the extension generated by a primitive 25th root ζ. The polynomial Φ₂₅(1 + X) is Eisenstein at 5, with reduction X²⁰ and constant term 5. Thus π = ζ − 1 is a uniformizer and the extension is totally ramified of degree 20. Its finite inertia group is (ℤ/25)×, with a acting by ζ ↦ ζa. The residue of σa(π)/π is a modulo 5. The wild subgroup is therefore the five elements congruent to 1 modulo 5. The element 7 maps to the generator 2 modulo 5 and satisfies 7² ≡ −1 modulo 25. For this finite inertia quotient, evaluation at 7 gives the two values of 𝔽₂, or the four values 0, ¼, ½, ¾ in ℚ₂/ℤ₂. In both cases the wild subgroup contributes a single possible restriction, the zero character.

Why does adjoining a quadratic field at most double the number of character generators?

Enlarging the field shrinks its Galois group. A character of the smaller group may fail to extend to the larger one. The dyadic argument controls this failure and obtains a square bound on the number of characters, hence a factor of two in their dimension over 𝔽₂.

Let U be an open subgroup of V of index dividing two. Both lie in a topological group Γ. For a subset S of Γ, write C(V) for the locally constant homomorphisms V → 𝔽₂ vanishing on S ∩ V, and define C(U) likewise. Assume v−1Sv = S for every v ∈ V, and S ∩ V ⊆ U. If U = V the count is immediate. Otherwise U is normal in V. Fix an element σ in its other coset, so σ² ∈ U.

What prevents an invariant character from extending?

Conjugation acts on a character by (Jφ)(u) = φ(σ−1uσ). The first condition on S ensures this action preserves C(U). For a fixed character Jφ = φ, put b(φ) = φ(σ²). Every character on V takes value zero on σ², since twice any value in 𝔽₂ is zero. Conversely, if b(φ) = 0, define its extension Eφ to equal φ on U and to take v outside U to φ(vσ). Then Eφ(σ) = 0. In multiplying two outside elements v, w, the sum of their values becomes φ(vσ) + φ(σ−1w) = φ(vw). Here invariance and φ(σ²) = 0 give φ(wσ) = φ(σ−1w). The mixed products use invariance alone. The formula is locally constant on both open cosets and agrees with φ on S ∩ V.

If a fixed character takes value 1 on σ², choose one such character φ₀ once. Otherwise take φ₀ = 0. Each fixed φ now gives a corrected character φ + b(φ)φ₀ that extends by the preceding formula. The quotient character ε of V/U is zero on U and one on the other coset. Since S ∩ V ⊆ U, it belongs to C(V). This allows the obstruction to be recorded in the value at σ.

Θ(φ) = E(φ + b(φ)φ₀) + b(φ)ε,   Θ(φ)(σ) = b(φ).

Restriction of Θ(φ) to U recovers the corrected character. Reading its value at σ recovers the bit needed to undo the correction. Thus the fixed characters inject into C(V) itself, even when some of them cannot extend. This accounts for the factor of two that would appear if the bit were counted independently.

Count the other characters using a square-zero map

Put D = 1 + J on C(U). Conjugating twice is conjugation by σ² inside U, which acts trivially on additive characters of U. Hence J² = 1 and in characteristic two D² = 0. The kernel consists of the fixed characters just counted, and the image is contained in the kernel. The quotient by the kernel is isomorphic to the image. In particular, finiteness of C(V) gives finiteness of both factors below.

|C(U)| = |ker D| · |im D| ≤ |ker D|² ≤ |C(V)|².

In the arithmetic application, S is the union of inertia groups at places away from the primes dividing N. Adjoining the quadratic datum of prime modulus p intersects V with an open subgroup of index dividing two. Conjugation carries inertia to inertia at a conjugate place. Since p divides N, every inertia group still required to vanish is away from p and acts trivially on the pth roots of unity. This gives S ∩ V ⊆ U. Applying the square bound once for each of the two primes in the generator count takes an initial cardinality bound B first to B², then to B⁴.

A fixed character that detects σ². Let V = 𝔽₂² ⋊ ℤ/4 with generator σ of ℤ/4 exchanging the two coordinates. Use the discrete topology and impose vanishing only at the identity. The orbit count gives an upper bound on the number of generators of the dyadic module. One generator can still yield a quotient of infinite length, as ℤ₂/(1−1)ℤ₂ shows. To compute the length at a finite layer, we next determine which ℚℓ/ℤℓ-valued characters of the infinite kernel extend to locally trivial cocycles with the prescribed twist. Dualizing that description gives the quotient whose length is needed.

8.9Why restriction recovers the locally trivial classes

Fix a field F in one of these towers. Let G be its absolute Galois group, χ its cyclotomic character, U = ker χ, and e a nonzero integer. The coefficient module A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ carries the action ρ(g) = χ(g)−e. For a class in degree one, inflate to G and restrict a cocycle z to U. Since U acts trivially, z restricts to an additive character φ, and every coboundary restricts to zero. Conjugation of the cocycle identity gives φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u). Local triviality forces φ to vanish on inertia and on decomposition groups above ℓ, in each case after intersection with U. We will recover exactly the equivariant characters with these vanishing conditions.

For injectivity, suppose φ = 0. The cocycle then factors through the cyclotomic quotient. In our fields this quotient is procyclic. Choose g whose image topologically generates it. The value χ(g)−e − 1 is nonzero. Indeed the cyclotomic degrees over a fixed number field grow without bound, whereas the ℓ-adic roots of a fixed nonzero power are finite. Multiplication by this nonzero scalar is surjective on A, so choose a with (ρ(g) − 1)a = z(g). Subtract its coboundary. The resulting cocycle vanishes on g, hence by the cocycle rule on all its powers, and by continuity on the quotient. This is where the condition e ≠ 0 enters.

For surjectivity let φ be one of the equivariant characters. Write C for the closure of the powers of a lift of a cyclotomic generator. Its compact image surjects onto χ(G), so G = CU. The character φ vanishes on C ∩ U. In group-theoretic terms the pro-ℓ part of the procyclic group C maps onto an infinite pro-ℓ group. That part is ℤℓ, and all its nonzero closed subgroups have finite index. Its kernel is therefore zero. The intersection has only prime-to-ℓ finite quotients, so its continuous characters into ℓ-primary torsion vanish. The code proves this vanishing directly by congruences in finite quotients. We may consequently define

z(cu) = ρ(c)φ(u),   c ∈ C,   u ∈ U.

Two decompositions differ by an element of the intersection, making the formula independent of the choice. Equivariance gives the cocycle identity on multiplying two decompositions. Continuity follows because C × U → G is a continuous surjection of compact Hausdorff spaces, hence a quotient map. Away from ℓ, inertia already lies in the cyclotomic kernel, where φ vanishes. Above ℓ, the restricted cocycle vanishes on the kernel of the local cyclotomic character. Its image on the decomposition group is open in ℤℓ×, and the allowed roots of unity give the same procyclic condition. The preceding generator argument therefore subtracts a local coboundary. Inflation from the group unramified outside ℓ now supplies a locally trivial class, whose restriction is φ.
