How does a character on the infinite kernel extend across the cyclotomic direction?

Let G be the absolute Galois group of a number field F, χ its ℓ-adic cyclotomic character, U = ker χ and A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ with action ρ = χ−e. A character φ on U in the restriction theorem is locally constant, additive on products and satisfies φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u). It vanishes on the intersections of U with finite inertia groups and with decomposition groups over ℓ. We assume e ≠ 0. At odd ℓ the generator condition holds for the cyclotomic image of any number field. At 2 the theorem assumes χ ≡ 1 modulo 4 throughout G, as happens when F contains a primitive fourth root of unity.

What happens if two lifts give the same element? Choose γ lifting a topological generator of χ(G), and write C for the closure of its integer powers. Its image is compact, contains all powers of χ(γ) and hence equals χ(G). Thus G = CU. To define a cocycle vanishing on C and restricting to φ on U, the two prescriptions must agree on C ∩ U. Here is the congruence calculation that forces agreement.

Fix x in this intersection. Local constancy at the identity gives an open subgroup H of G with φ = 0 on H ∩ U. The finite coset space of H gives a positive integer d with γd in H. Write d = ℓab, with ℓ coprime to b. The unit w = χ(γ) has infinite order. The orders of its reductions modulo ℓj therefore contain arbitrarily large powers of ℓ. Indeed each reduced order divides (ℓ − 1)ℓj−1 for j ≥ 1. If their ℓ-parts were bounded by ℓa, every reduction of w(ℓ−1)ℓa would equal 1, forcing the same equality in ℤℓ. Choose j so that wk ≡ 1 modulo ℓj implies ℓa+1 divides k.

A power γk can approximate x simultaneously in the coset xH and in its cyclotomic residue class modulo ℓj. Since χ(x) = 1, we have ℓa ∣ k and hence d ∣ kb. Thus γkb belongs to H. Also x−1γk belongs to H. The elements x and γ commute because x lies in the closure of the powers of γ. Taking the bth power in this last relation gives xb ∈ H ∩ U. Now bφ(x) = 0 and φ(x) has ℓ-power order. Coprimality forces φ(x) = 0. Only the finite coset space of H was needed to choose d.

For two expressions cu = c′u′, the element c′−1c = u′u−1 is in the intersection. It has zero φ-value and acts trivially on A. Consequently the formula below is independent of the expression. Multiplying two expressions gives (cu)(dv) = cd(d−1ud)v. Equivariance of φ gives the displayed cocycle rule. The product map C × U → G is a continuous surjection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, so continuity descends from the formula on the product.

z(cu) = ρ(c)φ(u),   z(gh) = z(g) + ρ(g)z(h).

How do the restrictions survive passage to the unramified quotient? Let S be the places over ℓ and N the closed normal subgroup of G generated by all inertia groups away from S. The cyclotomic character χ, and hence its twist, factors through GS = G/N. In particular, all such inertia groups lie in U and z vanishes there. Inside N the zero set of z is a closed subgroup, since N acts trivially on the coefficients. It is normal in G by the cocycle rule, which gives z(gng−1) = ρ(g)z(n) for n in N. It therefore contains all of N. Now z(gn) = z(g) gives the continuous quotient cocycle.

For a prolongation over a place in S, let D be its decomposition group. The restriction of z kills D ∩ U. Choose a lift γD of a generator of the open local cyclotomic image. Since e ≠ 0, the scalar ρ(γD) − 1 is nonzero. Multiplication by it on A is surjective. Choose a with (ρ(γD) − 1)a = z(γD). Subtracting δa, where δa(d) = ρ(d)a − a, gives zero on the local kernel and on every generator power, hence on D by continuity. The same argument on the global quotient proves injectivity of restriction on H¹.

A different prolongation changes D to gDg−1. For d in D, the cocycle rule gives z(gdg−1) = z(g) + ρ(g)z(d) − ρ(gdg−1)z(g). Substitution of δa gives the new local primitive below. Thus the class descends with its local conditions. Choosing another global cocycle in the same class changes it by a coboundary, whose restriction to U is zero. The tower argument uses injectivity and precisely this description of the image to identify the locally trivial H¹ with its equivariant characters.

z|D = δa   ⇒   z|gDg−1 = δ(ρ(g)a − z(g)).
Two decompositions and a conjugate subgroup in a group of order 54

Use triples (n,k,ε) with coordinates modulo 9, 3 and 2 respectively. Give the first coordinate of a product (n,k,ε)(m,j,η) the value n + 7km modulo 9, and add the other coordinates. This defines a group since 7³ ≡ 1 modulo 9. Take the finite character χ = 4k modulo 9 and let ρ = χ−1 act on ℤ/9. Here U consists of the triples with k = 0 and C is generated by γ = (0,1,1) of order six. Their intersection is generated by γ³ = (0,0,1), which any homomorphism into ℤ/9 kills. The equivariant character φ(n,0,ε) = n extends to z(n,k,ε) = n.

The two expressions γ(8,0,1) and γ⁴(8,0,0) both represent (2,1,0). Each gives 7 · 8 ≡ 2 modulo 9. Multiplying this element by (4,2,1) gives cocycle value 2 + 7 · 4 ≡ 3. Finally z vanishes on C. Conjugate γ by g = (1,0,0) to get (3,1,1). The transported primitive is −z(g) ≡ 8 and its coboundary on this element is (7 − 1) · 8 ≡ 3. This finite model checks extension and change of a local primitive. In the number-field argument the surjectivity of ρ(γD) − 1 uses the divisible module ℚℓ/ℤℓ.

8.10The inverse action and the Tate twist

Return to the base field L0 and one of its cyclotomic layers Lm of relative degree ℓm, embedded in the same algebraic closure. The two fields have the same infinite cyclotomic kernel. Write c for the largest exponent such that L0 contains a primitive ℓcth root. Under the roots-of-unity hypothesis its cyclotomic image is 1 + ℓcℤℓ. The subgroup for the layer has image 1 + ℓc+mℤℓ. Choose γ in the base Galois group lifting a generator of its cyclotomic image. The valuation of χ(γ) − 1 is exactly c, and b = γℓm generates the image for that layer. In these statements “generator” refers to the closure of powers in the cyclotomic image.

On the common character module D = Dℓ the action is (de(g)φ)(u) = χ(g)−eφ(g−1ug). Equivariance says that φ is fixed by the layer group. It suffices to require it fixed by b, equivalently by b−1. Indeed each character is killed by a power of ℓ and its conjugation action is locally constant on a sufficiently high congruence subgroup. Powers of χ(b) meet every needed open coset. Thus the kernel of de(b−1) − 1 is the entire invariant group just identified with Sha.

The linear dual X = Homℤℓ(D, A) carries the contragredient action xe(g)f = f ∘ de(g−1). Consequently its scalar factor is χ(g)+e. Put T = de(b−1) − 1. Restriction X → Hom(ker T, A) is onto by injectivity of A. Its kernel consists exactly of the maps f ∘ T. Indeed a functional vanishing on ker T factors through the image of T and extends from there to D. This identifies the dual of ker T with the cokernel of xe(b) − 1. Duality with A preserves length. For finite length, dualize a composition series and use that the dual of ℤ/ℓ is again ℤ/ℓ. For infinite length, annihilators reverse strict inclusions of submodules since A separates points of their quotients. Arbitrarily long chains therefore persist in the dual.

length Sha¹(Lm, A(−e)) = length [X / ((χ(γ)ex0(γ))ℓm − 1)X].

Here x0 denotes the untwisted dual action. The equality holds for each nonzero integer e and takes values in the extended natural numbers. The window uses e ≥ 1.

As an algebraic check of the signs, take ℓ = 3, D = ℚ3/ℤ3, χ(γ) = 4, and let the untwisted action on D be multiplication by 4 at γ. The untwisted dual action on X = ℤ3 is multiplication by 1/4. For e = 1 the two twisted actions at γ are the identity. At layer zero the whole character group is fixed and the dual cokernel is all of ℤ3, both of infinite length. Using a negative scalar exponent on the dual would instead give 1/16 − 1 = −15/16, which has 3-adic valuation 1. This example tests the algebra underlying the formula. The arithmetic window supplies its own finiteness estimates.

At the reference layer the proof also needs a comparison with degree two. The Tate dual of A(−e) has integral coefficient twist e + 1. Under finite-level Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness and local Tate duality, the two locally trivial groups have equal length. Take a decreasing filtration on the locally trivial degree-two group and an increasing torsion-level filtration on degree one. The former is separated and the latter exhaustive. At all sufficiently high levels the finite quotients of the first and the finite pieces of the second have equal cardinality by finite-level duality and control of localization. Their lengths therefore agree, including the case of unbounded lengths. The degree-two group embeds into full H², giving the upper bound used for the exceptional twists. The numerical bound on full H² remains a separate input.

8.11The cost of one more cyclotomic layer

Fix a rational prime ℓ and a totally complex number field L0 containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root when ℓ = 2. A layer of index m is an extension of L0 obtained by adjoining roots of unity of ℓ-power order and having degree ℓm. Suppose the tower module X admits a surjection ℤℓR → X, where R ≥ 1. Choosing a cyclotomic generator gives an endomorphism γ of X unipotent modulo ℓ and a scalar u with exact valuation vℓ(u − 1) = c ≥ 1, with c ≥ 2 for ℓ = 2. Normalize vℓ(ℓ) = 1 and set vℓ(0) = ∞. The cited descent theorem identifies the locally trivial degree-one length at twist index e ≥ 1 on every layer m with the following cokernel length.

g = ueγ,   hm(e) = lengthℤℓ X / (gℓm − 1)X,
j0 = ⌊logℓ R⌋ + 3,   hm(e) ≤ hj₀(e) + R max(0, m − j0).

To prove the inequality, reduce X modulo ℓ. The quotient is a vector space of dimension at most R over the field with ℓ elements. On it, g − 1 equals γ − 1 and is nilpotent. Its successive images must strictly decrease in dimension until they vanish, so its Rth power vanishes. Put k = ⌊logℓ R⌋ + 1. Since ℓk ≥ R, the characteristic-ℓ binomial identity gives gℓk ≡ 1 modulo ℓ. For any w ≡ 1 modulo ℓ, the sum S = 1 + w + ⋯ + wℓ−1 maps X into ℓX. As wℓ − 1 = S(w − 1), one more power gives congruence to 1 modulo ℓ². It persists at every higher layer.

Now take w ≡ 1 modulo ℓ². For each x, Sx ≡ ℓx modulo ℓ²X. Thus SX ⊆ ℓX and ℓX = SX + ℓ(ℓX). The quotient ℓX/SX is finitely generated and equals its own multiple by the maximal ideal (ℓ). Nakayama’s lemma makes it zero. Hence the cokernel of S has length at most R. For endomorphisms A,B, the sequence coker B → coker(AB) → coker A → 0 is exact, with first map induced by A. Length subadditivity applied to S(w − 1) gives an increase of at most R per layer. Sum from j0. For m below j0, the larger power minus one factors through the smaller, so the smaller-layer quotient has no greater length. This argument also holds for lengths taking the value ∞.

8.12Why only finitely many twists need the second estimate

Write j = j0. Lift γℓj to a matrix M on the free module ℤℓR by choosing a preimage for the image of each generator. Put ae = (uℓj)e. The cokernel of aeM − 1 surjects onto the one defining hj(e). Its length is the valuation of its determinant, which factors over an algebraic closure of ℚℓ as ∏i(aezi − 1), with the R eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.

For a single eigenvalue z, use the ℓ-adic norm |ℓ|ℓ = ℓ−1. The exact level of u gives |ae − af|ℓ = ℓ−j−c|e − f|ℓ. This left-hand side is at most max(|aez − 1|ℓ, |afz − 1|ℓ). For |z|ℓ ≥ 1, subtract the two defects and apply the ultrametric inequality. For |z|ℓ < 1, both defects have norm 1. Consider the closed balls in ℤℓ centered at e of radius ℓj+c|aez − 1|ℓ. The center of a smallest-radius ball in any finite subfamily lies in every ball of that subfamily. Compactness of ℤℓ gives a common point s for all e. Thus vℓ(aez − 1) ≤ j + c + vℓ(s − e). Sum over the eigenvalues, then apply the layer increment. The resulting centers s1, …, sR work for every twist and layer.

hm(e) ≤ ∑i=1R [max(m, j0) + c + vℓ(si − e)].

Fix an integer cutoff Z ≥ 1 and write B = ⌊logℓ Z⌋. Mark an integer 1 ≤ e ≤ Z if |si − e|ℓ < ℓ−B for some i. Two integers in the same such ball differ by a multiple of ℓB+1, while their ordinary distance is less than Z < ℓB+1. They coincide. At most R twists are marked. On the others each valuation vℓ(si − e) is at most B, giving a finite bound at once.

For every unmarked e in [1, Z],   hm(e) ≤ R(max(m, j0) + c + ⌊logℓ Z⌋).

For a marked twist use the other estimate. Poitou–Tate duality and the local finiteness and duality hypotheses identify the degree-one length at j0 with that of a locally trivial degree-two group. The latter embeds into the full degree-two cohomology with coefficients ℤℓ(e + 1). The full group’s length therefore bounds hj₀(e). The growth inequality carries this bound to every m. The degree-two estimate gives finiteness of that full group and bounds the logarithm of its order by exp((2en)CK log(2D)), where n is the field degree over ℚ and D its absolute discriminant. A finite ℤℓ-module of length d has order ℓd, since each composition factor has order ℓ. Thus keeping the exceptional e small controls this second estimate. The odd-prime window proof takes Z = ⌊XCt⌋ and chooses a window where every marked twist in the active range e ≤ xCt satisfies e ≤ xε/(2CK). Here X is the outer real scale, Ct the cutoff exponent and CK ≥ 1 the chosen constant in that estimate. The exceptional twists thus remain in the cohomological sum.

8.13Why finitely many marked twists leave a whole interval

Fix the outer scale X and combine the dyadic marks with the marks for the fixed collection of odd primes. The union has size at most R, fixed before choosing X. Put α = ε/(2CK) and β = Ct, so 0 < α ≤ β. A marked integer e is troublesome only when xα < e ≤ xβ. Above this range it is absent from the sum. Below it we can use the degree-two estimate, since eCK ≤ xε/2. The field degree and discriminant in that estimate still have to be bounded.

Write u = log x, a = (log e)/β and B = β/α. This mark forbids exactly a ≤ u < Ba. A window [Y, Y²] becomes [y, 2y] in this coordinate. Begin with an upper limit U = log X. If each mark satisfies a ≤ U/(2B) or a > U, the entire top interval [U/2, U] is safe. Otherwise choose a mark with U/(2B) < a ≤ U. Lower the upper limit to U/(2B). This mark now lies strictly beyond it, so remove that mark and repeat. In at most R reductions the process stops. Thus one may use the uniform constant J = 2R+2BR, with X1/J ≤ Y and Y² ≤ X. Every marked twist still in the sum is small enough throughout the same interval.

8.14The degree-two bound for an exceptional twist

In the preceding window argument, a marked twist can approach an ℓ-adic root too closely for its valuation to give a uniform estimate. The proof returns to a finite layer, where it bounds a different quantity. Let ℓ be any prime and L a totally complex number field of degree n and absolute discriminant Δ. Assume L contains a primitive ℓth root of unity for odd ℓ, or a primitive fourth root when ℓ = 2. Let S be all finite primes over ℓ and GS the Galois group unramified outside them. The assertion holds for every algebraic closure, every choice of places above S and every compatible descended cyclotomic character.

For every integer e ≥ 1,   H²(GS, ℤℓ(e + 1)) is finite,   log |H²| ≤ KC(e,n,Δ) = exp((2en)C log(2Δ)).

One exponent works simultaneously for all these choices. Tracing three numerical witnesses in the proof gives C = 150. The theorem returned to the window argument quantifies existentially over C. The numerical estimate applies to log order, so a length bound is obtained by dividing by log ℓ.

Enlarging the field to count characters

Write s(L) for the ℤℓ-length of the locally trivial degree-one group with coefficients (ℚℓ/ℤℓ)(−e). In absolute cohomology these classes restrict to zero on decomposition groups over ℓ and on inertia groups elsewhere. The length can initially be infinite. The proof enlarges L to a cyclotomic layer L′ with degree d over L. If c is the largest depth of an ℓ-power root of unity in L′ and r₂ its number of complex places, then 2e + 1 is strictly smaller than both ℓc and r₂. Put n′ = dn and Δ′ = |disc L′|. The costs are

d ≤ (n + 1)(4e + 4),   ℓc ≤ 2n′,   Δ′ ≤ Δd(ℓc)n′,   s(L) ≤ s(L′).

Choose m least with ℓm ≥ 4e + 4 and take the tower layer of relative degree ℓm. The root hypothesis gives ℓ ≤ n + 1. To control the discriminant, choose a primitive root ζ of order N generating the layer. Differentiate the factorization of XN − 1 by its minimal polynomial and evaluate at ζ. The relative different contains N, hence its norm divides Nn′. The tower discriminant formula and N ≤ ℓc give the displayed estimate. For the length comparison, the tower description represents both lengths by quotients of one module. The factorization of gℓm − 1 by g − 1 produces a surjection from the higher quotient to the lower one.

Which bound passes from a cyclotomic layer back to the base field?

Fix a prime ℓ, an integer twist E ≥ 1 and a totally complex number field L containing a primitive ℓth root of unity for odd ℓ, or a primitive fourth root for ℓ = 2. The matrix-group calculation takes place over the integers of a field with sufficiently many complex places. The degree-two argument produces such a field L′ above its original field L. What it brings back to L is an upper bound on a Galois cohomology length. To see which classes enter that comparison, keep three fields in view. The base L is the field of the requested bound, L′ is the fixed layer on which the matrix-group count runs, and F ranges through further cyclotomic layers over L′.

Which cycles enter the count? The matrices and cycles in the count are over 𝒪L′. The odd-degree rank bound controls their evaluations in that field. The quotient map below carries the resulting bound on length down to L. In the real bar complex, a cycle z is primitive if Δ∗z − (ι₁)∗z − (ι₂)∗z is a boundary in the product group. Here Δ is the diagonal and the two inclusions put the identity in the other coordinate.

Apply the filtered rank theorem in odd homological degree m = k + 1, with k even. It bounds the integral rank of a filtered image in that same field by its number of complex places. At the character count, put m = 2E + 1. Data over F provide cycles with ℤ/ℓν coefficients in GLN(𝒪L′). The primitive object here is a family of linear evaluations Φ. It kills boundaries, preserves values under stabilization and multiplies them by d under d-fold block repetition. The counting proof bounds the number of distinct values of ℓ2EΦ on the constructed cycles. The rank and torsion inputs are over L′, with stable size 4E + 6 and adjacent homology degrees 2E + 1 and 2E. This is the entry point of the filtered rank bound.

Lean correspondence

The proposition PV says that in degree k + 1 such cycles bound once the matrix size reaches 2(k + 1) + 4. The name SBig occurs once in the original Lean archive, in the definition of an implication from PV over every totally complex field with k + 1 < r₂ to PV over every totally complex field. The neighbouring statement PVBig assumes k odd, so its cycles have even degree. The definition of the fieldwise implication · The parity in the large-place primitive statement

The map that gives the inequality. Write s(K) for the ℤℓ-length of the absolute, locally trivial degree-one group over K with coefficients (ℚℓ/ℤℓ)(−E). The local conditions impose trivial restriction to decomposition groups above ℓ and to inertia elsewhere. This length takes values in ℕ ∪ {∞}. After fixing an algebraic closure of L, the root-of-unity hypothesis on L supplies a lift γ of a topological generator of its cyclotomic image. The tower descent calculation expresses the two lengths using one ℤℓ-module M and one operator g. The operator on the dual is the untwisted dual action of γ multiplied by the Eth power of its cyclotomic character. In the base field the length is that of M/(g − 1)M. In the layer of relative degree d = ℓa, it is that of M/(gd − 1)M.

gd − 1 = (g − 1)(1 + g + ⋯ + gd−1),   M/(gd − 1)M ↠ M/(g − 1)M.

The identity on representatives gives the surjection because (gd − 1)M is contained in (g − 1)M. Its kernel is (g − 1)M/(gd − 1)M. Length is monotone under quotients, so s(L) ≤ s(L′). The argument first compares the lengths, then uses finiteness of the upper length to conclude finiteness of the lower one. The map acts on the two cokernel models.

Degree three in matrix homology, degree nine in the field tower

Take ℓ = 3, E = 1 and L = ℚ(ζ₃). Its largest depth of a 3-power root is one. The construction selects the least a with 3a ≥ 4E + 4 = 8. Thus a = 2, d = 9 and L′ = ℚ(ζ₂₇). This has degree 18 over ℚ and nine complex places. Both 27 and nine exceed the matrix homology degree three. For instance at depth ν = 4 one can take F = ℚ(ζ₈₁). Raising ζ₈₁ to the 28th power fixes ζ₂₇ and has order three. The coefficient ring for those cycles is ℤ/81 and their matrices are over 𝒪L′.

To compute the quotient map by hand, use the separate rank-one model M = ℤ₃ and let g act by multiplication by 4. Then g − 1 = 3 and g⁹ − 1 = 262143 = 27·9709, with 9709 a 3-adic unit. The projection is reduction ℤ/27 ↠ ℤ/3 and its kernel consists of the nine multiples of 3 modulo 27. The lengths are three upstairs and one downstairs. The arithmetic example supplies the degree nine; the scalar 4 illustrates how the projection acts on representatives.

A count uniform in cyclotomic depth

Above L′ take depth ν ≥ c, write q = ℓν, and let γ generate the cyclic Galois group, acting on a primitive qth root by raising it to 1 + ℓc. Its order is ℓν−c. Put a = (1 + ℓc)e. The finite set counted consists of characters φ of the ideal class group into ℤ/qℤ. On prime ideals their condition is φ(γ−1P) = aφ(P). Vanishing on principal divisors makes the characters descend from the free divisor group to the class group.

Set Tj equal to the order of the torsion subgroup in integral degree-j homology of GL4e+6(𝒪L′). A detection argument attaches cycles to elements with a prescribed twisted principal divisor. Equality of their evaluated cycles makes a ratio of powered twisted norms a qth power at the tested residue fields. Global power detection gives the corresponding equality modulo qth powers of the field. Thus a collection distinguished by those norms injects into the evaluated cycle values. The homological upper bound for the number of values is B = qr₂T2eT2e+1.

Let 𝓧 be the group of equivariant class characters. The independent Selmer count bounds |𝓧| qr₂ by BℓX. Its ℓ-primary kernel estimate uses the identity vℓ(aℓν−c − 1) = ν + vℓ(e). At ℓ = 2 the primitive-fourth-root hypothesis ensures c ≥ 2. A Selmer estimate bounds the ℓ-torsion of the intermediate counting group by at most ℓg elements, where g = 2n′ + ⌊log₂ h(L′)⌋ + 2 and h is the class number. Successive multiplication by ℓ bounds a kernel killed by ℓb+f by ℓ(b+f)g on its ℓ-primary part. Here f = vℓ(e) and b = 2e + (2e + 1)(c + 2e + 1). Cancelling the same positive qr₂ on both sides gives

|𝓧| ≤ T2eT2e+1 ℓX,   X = (b + f)g + c + f.

The right side is independent of ν. To see why this matters, take any finite set of distinct locally trivial classes. Restriction to the infinite cyclotomic level is injective. Each restricted class can be represented at a sufficiently high finite level and killed there by ℓν. A common level works for the whole finite set. An injection into the equivariant characters there bounds its size by the displayed number. An infinite group would contain a finite subset one element larger. Thus s(L′) is finite and ℓs(L′) satisfies the same upper bound.

What the detecting cycles see

Work over the enlarged totally complex field L′ in the degree-two argument. Write e ≥ 1 for the twist and m = 2e + 1. The field enlargement ensured m < ℓc and m < r₂, the number of complex places of L′. At depth ν ≥ c, take the cyclic extension F/L′ containing a primitive root ζ of order q = ℓν. Its generator γ sends ζ to ζκ with κ = 1 + ℓc. Put a = κe. To a nonzero field element α attach the twisted norm

Na(α) = ∏0≤j<ord(γ) γj(α)aʲ.

For the test, α must have a divisor of the form ordP(α) = D(γP) − aD(P) for some integral divisor D. Fix b = 2e + m(c + m). The counting theorem bounds any finite set S of such α whose powered twisted norms Na(α)ℓᵇ are distinct modulo qth powers in F×. Where does such a set arise? Let U be the group of elements α satisfying the divisor condition. Take its quotient W by those elements in the subgroup generated by roots of unity and γ−1(t)/ta for t ∈ F×. This quotient is finite. On a representative α the homomorphism from W sends the class to the powered twisted norm modulo qth powers and roots of unity. Choose one lift for each element of its image. If two powered norms differ by a qth power, their images agree, hence the chosen lifts agree. Bounding |S| now bounds the size of that image. A separate kernel estimate in the character count controls the part lost by this homomorphism.

Where does the filling chain come from?

Put q = ℓν for the prime ℓ and depth ν of the arithmetic test. The construction needs a sum of cycles that bounds, with at least one coefficient invertible modulo q. This lets it isolate one determinant after the other blocks cancel. Both properties follow from a finite calculation before any number field is used. Keep the positive twist e of this chapter.

Write C = ℤ/q additively, and let [a|b] denote a basis vector, the ordered pair of group elements in a degree-two chain. Its boundary is [b] − [a + b] + [a]. In any degree, drop the first entry, merge each successive pair, then drop the last entry, with alternating signs throughout. Define a chain in degree 2e by summing the words

z = ∑j∈Cᵉ [j₁ | 1 | j₂ | 1 | … | je | 1]   with coefficients in ℤ/q.

For e = 1 the first faces give q[1] = 0 and the other faces telescope around the circle. The same two cancellations work in higher degree. Dropping the first entry leaves a word repeated q times. At any interior pair, the merge of ja with 1 gives the same output as the next merge after replacing (ja, ja+1) by (ja + 1, ja+1 − 1). The signs are opposite and the substitution permutes the summation indices. At the last pair only the first shift is needed, since the final face drops the 1. Hence ∂z = 0.

Why one coefficient is a unit

Send each entry a to (a, ta) in D = C × C. Use the 2e + 2 values t = 0,…,2e + 1 and call the resulting cycles zt. The homology group in degree 2e is the cycles modulo boundaries. Why can it be generated by only 2e + 1 elements? Consider projection of a finite group G onto C with kernel K. On the module of functions W from C to A = ℤ/q, the forward difference Δf(j) = f(j + 1) − f(j) has kernel the constants. Its image consists exactly of functions with sum zero. For the converse add successive values starting at zero. The partial sums give a periodic primitive because the whole sum is zero. This proves exactness of 0 → A → W →Δ W →sum A → 0.

Translations permute the entries of W transitively, and the stabilizer of one entry is K. Shapiro’s isomorphism identifies the homology of G with coefficients in W with the homology of K with coefficients in A. Split the displayed sequence at the image of Δ. Each of the two long exact homology sequences bounds the number of generators of a middle term by those needed on either side. In particular, in passing from degree n to degree n + 2 for G, one may add generator bounds for K in degrees n + 1 and n + 2. For G = C, the kernel of the identity projection is trivial, so the positive-degree homology of that kernel vanishes. Degrees zero and one for C need at most one generator each, hence so does every higher degree. For G = D, project onto the first factor. Now K is cyclic, so each two-degree step adds at most two to the bound of one in degree zero. After e steps the bound is 2e + 1.

Lift the 2e + 2 classes to a free abelian group of rank at most 2e + 1 mapping onto this homology. There is a nonzero integer relation upstairs. Divide its coefficients by their common powers of ℓ while they are all divisible. Division preserves the relation in a free abelian group. This precaution matters downstairs. For example, 5 times a generator of ℤ/5 vanishes, while the generator itself survives. Project the resulting relation to homology and reduce its coefficients modulo q = ℓν. At least one coefficient is prime to ℓ and is therefore invertible. Since the relation vanishes in homology, it has a filling w in the next chain group.

∑t=02e+1 ntzt = ∂w,   nt₀ ∈ (ℤ/q)×.

At twist one this argument uses four degree-two cycles and three generators. It supplies both the filling and the inverse coefficient used to normalize the degree-three cycle constructed next.

Turning a determinant into a cycle evaluation

For each α the construction produces a cycle yα of degree m in the group chains of GLn(𝒪L′) with coefficients ℤ/q. Here n may depend on α. A cycle is a chain with zero boundary. The source starts with a relation ∑ ntzt = ∂w among images of a lower-dimensional cyclic-group cycle. It maps the filling w into a lattice stabilizer in two ways and subtracts the two images. Their boundaries are the corresponding difference of the sums. For each t a prism is a chain whose boundary is the difference of the two images of zt in the opposite order. Adding the weighted prisms cancels the boundary term by term. The source transports this cycle into an integral matrix group after multiplying by the inverse of one distinguished unit coefficient nt₀.

At a tested prime of F of residue degree one over ℚ, let k be its residue field. The prime is away from ℓ and the denominators of all the selected cycles. Since k has prime order, the rational integers already map onto it, and so does 𝒪L′. The primitive root still has order q after reduction. The multiplicative group k× is cyclic, so reducing its discrete logarithm modulo q defines an index v with kernel (k×)q. A residue-field functional Φ kills boundaries and adds on direct sums. On a prism in a block with character weight x and gluing matrix g, its value is xev(det g). The lattice construction arranges determinant 1 on the other blocks, so their indices vanish. At the distinguished block, the product over conjugates turns the remaining terms into the explicit evaluation below. A bar denotes reduction to k.

Φ(yα) = De · v(Na(α))   in ℤ/q,   De = ∏0≤j<m, j≠e(κe − κj).

How a residue field reads a determinant

We can now construct the functional Φ used above. Its scalar part takes one input from each of the e pairs in the cyclic word and one from the gluing element. Let k be the finite residue field, let ζ have order q in k×, put r = |k×|/q and fix the additive index v on k× with values in ℤ/q. Choose an integer logarithm L additive modulo qr and normalized by L(ζ) ≡ r modulo qr. To see that the normalization is possible, write ζ = hd for a generator h. Its order gives gcd(d, qr) = r. A Bézout coefficient b satisfies bd ≡ r modulo qr, so multiplying the ordinary discrete logarithm by b gives a suitable L.

u(a,b) = [L(a) + L(b) − L(ab)] / (qr).

This integer is symmetric in its arguments. Compute the sum of the carries for a product of three elements by putting the parentheses on either side. The intermediate logarithm cancels, giving u(a,b) + u(ab,c) = u(b,c) + u(a,bc). Reduce modulo q. On a word of length 2e + 1 take the product of u over its first e consecutive pairs, times v of the last entry. This is a cocycle, a functional vanishing on boundaries. To check it, expand the alternating bar faces. The three faces involving the first pair reduce by the displayed carry identity to the first carry times the boundary test on the remaining word. The induction ends at the additivity of v.

For a weight x let χ(j) = ζxj. Sum one carry u(χ(j),χ(1)) over j modulo q. The sums of L(χ(j)) and L(χ(j + 1)) agree by a cyclic shift. The result is L(χ(1))/r ≡ x modulo q. Inserting g in the cyclic word gives the prism. In this abelian group its terms run over the 2e + 1 positions with alternating signs. Insertion immediately before or after the first entry of any pair gives opposite terms since u is symmetric. Only the last insertion survives. Each pair now sums independently, so the scalar prism reads xev(g).

From one scalar to a matrix

To transfer this scalar test to an invertible matrix on a finite k-vector space V, sum over the lines in V. Choose a scale λ on nonzero vectors with λ(av) = aλ(v). For a line represented by v and a matrix g, record λ(v)/λ(g−1v) and move to the line of g−1v. The scale ratio for two successive matrices is the product of their ratios along this path. Thus merging adjacent entries of a word gives the same result before or after transfer. Dropping the first entry permutes the starting lines. The transfer therefore commutes with the boundary. Changing λ introduces ratios at consecutive endpoints whose change on a cycle is a boundary, so the scalar cocycle gives the same answer. In a one-dimensional space there is just one line, and a scalar matrix a produces the ratio a.

For a direct sum V ⊕ W, project a line with nonzero first component to its line in V. Fixing a representative of that line leaves exactly |W| choices of its second component. Every remaining line lies in W and contributes once. With the scale chosen from the projected component, the ratios are those of the corresponding block. Since q divides |k| − 1, both multiplicities are 1 modulo q. For k = 𝔽₁₁ and two one-dimensional summands the twelve lines split into the eleven [1 : w] and the single [0 : 1]. Each block contributes once modulo 5.

For fixed x, composing two gluing maps adds their prism values. The prism identity gives this equality up to a boundary, which Φ kills. The resulting homomorphism from GL(V) is invariant under a change of basis, and direct sums add their values. For q > 1, conjugating an elementary shear T(c) by a diagonal entry ζ replaces it by T(ζc). Conjugation leaves the value unchanged, so T((ζ − 1)c) has value zero. As ζ − 1 is invertible, every shear has value zero. Elimination reduces the calculation to diagonal matrices. On a diagonal the scalar values add to xev of the product of its entries. We have obtained

Φ(prism on the weight-x block with gluing map g) = xe v(det g)   in ℤ/q.

For q = 1 the target is zero. At a tested prime the lattice construction can now use its prescribed determinants. All blocks with determinant 1 drop out. The normalization by nt₀−1 removes the unit attached to the distinguished block, leaving the twisted norm evaluation.

How one slope carries the prescribed determinant

The relation among cycles singles out a slope t₀ with unit coefficient. How can its gluing map carry one chosen determinant when all the maps must connect the same two lattices? Write C = ℤ/q, q = ℓν, m = 2e + 1 and κ = 1 + ℓc. Let t run from 0 through m. On the coordinates indexed by C², each slope t groups indices (u,v) by the weight u + tv. We seek integer multiplicities η(u,v) whose sums on these fibers have the following values. Write [x] for unit mass at x and P(T) = ∏0≤j<m(T − κj) = ∑ piTi.

πtη = ∑(u,v)∈C² η(u,v) [u + tv],
πtη = 0   (t ≠ t₀),   πt₀η = ∑i=0m pi[κi].

These are equalities of integer sums at each residue. At an unwanted slope s, the two points (0,1) and (s,0) project to the same weight. Multiplying their differences [0,1] − [s,0] over all s ≠ t₀ kills every unwanted projection. Multiplication here adds the point labels, so [x][y] = [x + y]. A final factor supported on the first coordinate adjusts what survives at t₀.

Why can the final factor have integer coefficients?

Put w = ℓc and H = Xw − 1. Substitution X ↦ Xκ sends H to H times a geometric sum congruent to κ modulo H. It fixes every polynomial modulo H. Thus if Hj divides f, then Hj+1 divides f(Xκ) − κjf(X). Apply the m steps to f = X. The result is ∑ piXκi, divisible by Hm. Set X = [1] in the integer group algebra of C. Each nonzero slope difference t₀ − s has absolute value at most m < w. Its ℓ-power part divides w and the remaining factor is invertible modulo q. Consequently [t₀ − s] − [0] divides [w] − [0] by the geometric sum identity. The product of all m differences therefore divides the desired projection, and each translate [s] in [t₀] − [s] = [s]([t₀ − s] − [0]) is invertible. Lift the resulting integer quotient along x ↦ (x,0).

Use the multiplicities to assign divisor η(u,v)D to each coordinate. At an unwanted slope the divisor sum in every weight block vanishes. The lattice isomorphism theorem supplies maps of determinant 1 there. At the selected slope, γ−i sends ζκi back to ζ, collecting all the prescribed weights at weight 1. To identify the determinant there, put a = κe and Pe(T) = P(T)/(T − a) = ∑ biTi. The element β = ∏i γ−i(α)bi has exactly the required divisor. Indeed ordP′(γ−iα) equals ordγiP′(α). By the divisor condition on α, this is D(γi+1P′) − aD(γiP′). Multiplying by bi and summing gives coefficient bi−1 − abi = pi on D(γiP′), taking missing coefficients as zero. The same lattice theorem now realizes β as determinant in the weight-one block and 1 in all the others.

Choose the nonzero denominator B ∈ 𝒪L′ used by the lattice construction. Work in the subgroup of F× defined by ord𝔓(z) = 0 at every finite prime 𝔓 of F outside the divisors of B𝒪F. This subgroup is Galois stable and contains α. At a tested degree-one prime 𝔭 of F away from ℓB, reduce into k = 𝒪F/𝔭 and define f(z) = v(z), where v sends k× to ℤ/q. Write χ(σ) for the exponent by which σ acts on ζ. The surviving conjugate blocks contribute S(β) = ∑σ χ(σ)ef(σβ) after cancellation of the unit coefficient nt₀. In S(γ−iα), substitute σ = τγi. The character weight picks up χ(γ)ie = ai modulo q. Since f sends products to sums, and γ generates the whole Galois group,

S(β) = ∑i biaiS(α) = Pe(a) f(Na(α)) = De v(Na(α))   in ℤ/q.

For a sign check take ℓ = 5, c = 1, ν = 3 and e = 1. Then κ = a = 6 and P1(T) = (T − 1)(T − 36) = T² − 37T + 36. The three translates of α in β contribute respectively 36, −37·6 and 6² times S(α). Their sum is −150 ≡ 100 modulo 125. This coefficient survives the normalization by nt₀−1.

How the determinant reaches an integral matrix group

The interpolation step prescribes a determinant on every block. To use it in group homology, we must construct a map that realizes those numbers and find an integral matrix group carrying the resulting cycle. Start with the number field F in the cyclotomic layer over L′. For a divisor a supported on finitely many prime ideals of 𝒪F, let I(a) be the fractional ideal with ord𝔓(x) ≥ a(𝔓) at every prime, including zero in the ideal. A tuple of divisors defines the lattice Λ(a) = ⊕jI(aj) in FJ. Positive orders require divisibility and negative orders permit denominators.

Take β ∈ F×. A matrix taking Λ(a) onto Λ(b) with determinant β must carry the product of the input ideals to the product of the output ideals by multiplication by β. The proof constructs such a matrix whenever the resulting order equations hold. For a block with no coordinates its determinant must be one.

ord𝔓(β) = ∑j(bj(𝔓) − aj(𝔓))   for every finite prime 𝔓 of F.

In a nonempty block multiply a single coordinate by β. This sets the determinant correctly and leaves the right total divisor for the target lattice. Now move a divisor d from coordinate j to coordinate i with a determinant-one matrix. Repeating this operation fixes one coordinate at a time while a chosen coordinate absorbs the differences. Once all the others agree, equality of the totals fixes the last one.

How can one two-coordinate move work at every prime?

For current divisors ai, aj, write C = I(d) and D = I(ai+d−aj). The proof chooses u ∈ C nonzero and v ∈ D so that uC−1 + vD−1 = 𝒪F. Express 1 in that sum as us − vr with s ∈ C−1, r ∈ D−1. The matrix with rows (u, v) and (r, s) has determinant one. The ideal memberships put the first output in I(ai+d) and the second in I(aj−d). The inverse has rows (s, −v) and (−r, u), giving the reverse inclusions. One pair of fractional ideals thus enforces all the valuation inequalities simultaneously.

Lean correspondence
  • The comaximal ideals and determinant-one matrix
  • Valuation checks in both directions

For example, over ℚ the lattice 2ℤ ⊕ (3/2)ℤ has total order zero at 2 and one at 3, so β = −3 has the required orders. The map (x, y) ↦ (2x+2y, 3x/2) has determinant −3. Every pair (2a, 3b/2) in the target has preimage (b, a−b) in ℤ². The matrix and its inverse preserve ℤ[1/6]². The target of the integral lattice map is the specified fractional lattice.

Apply this construction to the indices J = (ℤ/q)². At each unwanted slope the fiber sums of η vanish, so the specified determinants are all one. At the selected slope a coordinate with weight κh is conjugated by γ−h to have weight one, where γ(ζ) = ζκ. Equal powers of κ modulo q give equal powers of γ, so this choice is consistent. In the regrouped coordinates the divisors at 𝔓 sum to ord𝔓(β) on the weight-one block and zero on every other block. The weight-one block contains the coordinate (1,0). We have therefore realized β and the unit determinants by F-linear block maps. Undoing the conjugations produces an L′-linear map gt on FJ at each slope. On each regrouped block the cyclic action is scalar, so its block map commutes with that action. The prescribed determinants refer to those blocks.

Choose a common nonzero denominator B ∈ 𝒪L′ covering the divisor support and the excluded splitting primes. All the gt preserve the lattice away from B, and each carries the full integral lattice M = (𝒪F)J to the same target. Thus gt−1gt₀ preserves M itself. Together with the diagonal actions and their required conjugates, these relations allow the prism construction to produce a cycle in the subgroup H stabilizing M inside the group integral away from B.

The module M is finite projective over R = 𝒪L′. A finite free module RN therefore admits a surjection s onto M and a section i with si = 1. For h ∈ H let α(h) act on M. The following matrix acts by α(h) on iM and by the identity on ker s. Its inverse is obtained by replacing h by h−1.

λ(h) = iα(h)s + (1−is) ∈ GLN(𝒪L′).

Pushing the cycle along λ gives the ordinary integral matrix cycle. At each tested residue map 𝒪F → k away from B whose restriction to R is onto, its representation on kN is conjugate to the residue action on kGal(F/L′)×J plus an identity action. The additive cycle test gives the same value after this extension. The rank N is chosen before the residue tests and can depend on the integral construction. The later stable-rank comparison handles varying ranks in the homology count.

How one denominator works for every residue test

The stabilized cycle is chosen before its reductions. Each test must identify the reduction of the coefficient module with one copy of the residue field for each Galois automorphism and each coordinate. Here is the field calculation for one coordinate. Let F/L′ be the finite Galois extension in the construction and write G for its Galois group. Given a ring map r from 𝒪F to a finite field k, denote its restriction to 𝒪L′ by r0. Assume r0 is onto. We want to prescribe all entries of the tuple (r(σa))σ∈G and identify its kernel. Which single element may we exclude from every later test?

Start with a basis ui of F over L′ and its dual ui∨ for the pairing (x,y) ↦ Tr(xy). The pairing is nondegenerate because the extension is separable. Clear the denominators in both finite lists with one nonzero integer m. Put ei = m ui∨, fi = m ui and b0 = m². Multiplying trace-dual expansion by m² gives the first identity below. For the second, apply σ and expand the trace as a sum over τ ∈ G. Linear independence of distinct field automorphisms as functions of x identifies the coefficient of τ(x) on both sides.

b0x = ∑i Tr(xfi)ei,   ∑i τ(fi)σ(ei) = b0 δστ.

Suppose r0(b0) ≠ 0. For a prescribed tuple (vτ), lift each scalar ∑τvτr(τfi)/r0(b0) to a coefficient ci in 𝒪L′ using surjectivity of r0. Then a = ∑iciei has exactly the specified tuple by the second identity. Conversely, if every entry for a vanishes, each integral trace Tr(afi) belongs to ker r0. The first identity shows that b0a belongs to (ker r0)𝒪F. In the quotient b0 has an inverse lifted from k, so a belongs to the same ideal. Its elements all have zero tuple since every σ fixes the base. We have obtained the ring isomorphism

𝒪F / (ker r0)𝒪F ≃ ∏σ∈G k.

The trace formula constructs the required coefficients without choosing an integral basis over the base ring. A linear basis over the field and a common denominator suffice.

Prescribe the two conjugate residues in the Gaussian integers

For ℚ(i)/ℚ take the basis (1,i), trace dual (1/2,−i/2), m = 2 and b0 = 4. Reduce at 5 by sending i to 2. The two rows send a + ci to a + 2c and a − 2c. To obtain (0,1), add the equations to get 2a = 1 and subtract them to get 4c = −1 in 𝔽5. Thus a = 3 and c = 1 work. The kernel consists exactly of multiples of 5. At 2 the two readings coincide, and b0 reduces to zero. This shows why the invertibility assumption matters.

The lattice also has a divisor 𝔡 prescribing lower bounds for the orders of its coordinates. Enlarge b0 to B = b0∏𝔓∈supp 𝔡 Norm(𝔓). Each norm lies in its prime ideal and is nonzero. Every prime in the finite support now contains B. Away from B, the prescribed order and the ordinary integrality condition agree. At a prime dividing B, multiplying by B raises the order by at least one. For any vector integral away from B, one large enough power Bn therefore brings all its finitely many coordinates into the prescribed lattice. This works for either lattice transported by a gluing map. After inverting B, the map and its inverse preserve the same module. The fixed B works across the maps and future residue tests, while n can depend on the vector. For any allowed reduction, r0(B) ≠ 0 implies r0(b0) ≠ 0, so the split tuple above is available for the cycle test.

The coefficient De may have positive ℓ-adic valuation. Its residue modulo q divides ℓm(c+m). For each factor, remove the unit power of κ. The binomial expansion κd − 1 = ℓc(d + ℓct) shows that a factor with 0 < d < m has valuation less than c + m, using m < ℓc. Multiplying the resulting divisibilities gives the stated bound. Thus equal scaled evaluations ℓ2eΦ(yα) imply equal indices of the norms raised to ℓb. Their ratio is a qth power in the residue field. As a small example of this last test, 2 generates 𝔽₁₉×. For q = 9 the elements 2⁸ and 2¹⁷ both have index 8 modulo 9, and their ratio is 2⁹ = −1, a ninth power.

From local powers to a bound for the image

Why do reductions decide whether the ratio β is a qth power in F? Choose x in an algebraic closure with xq = β. At a tested prime choose an integral t whose residue is a nonzero qth root of the reduced β. The product ∏0≤i<q(x − ζit) = xq − tq vanishes upon reduction at a place above that prime. Some factor vanishes. Thus x has the same nonzero residue as an element ζit of F. A Frobenius σ fixes this residue, and σ(x)/x is a qth root of unity reducing to 1. Away from ℓ such a root equals 1. Indeed a nontrivial root would have geometric sum zero, reducing to q = 0 in the residue field. Now a degree-one Chebotarev theorem supplies, outside the finite excluded set, a Frobenius inducing any specified Galois action on x. Its residue field has prime order, so the required surjectivity from 𝒪L′ holds. Every Galois automorphism fixes x. Hence x lies in F, which proves global power detection. By the defining separation of S, the tuple of scaled evaluations at all tested primes is injective on S.

What limits the number of tuples? Lift a degree-m cycle modulo q to an integral chain z. Its boundary is q w, so w gives a class killed by q in integral homology of degree m − 1. This is the Bockstein map. A different lift changes w by a boundary. In one fiber of the map, differences therefore lift to integral cycles. On their scaled evaluations take the stabilized combinations of diagonal copies and ordinary inclusions. Their integral span has rank at most r₂ by the odd-degree rank theorem. In a target killed by q, a rank-r group with finite torsion contributes at most qr times its torsion order. The Bockstein fibers account for the second torsion factor. Writing Tj for the order of integral homology torsion in degree j at GL4e+6(𝒪L′), stability gives

|S| ≤ qr₂ T2e+1 T2e.

The cycles and both torsion groups belong to group homology. The rank estimate below applies to the combinations of cycles selected by block repetition. In the character count a matching qr₂ on the left cancels, leaving the torsion product and the separate kernel loss. The finite relation supplies the filling, and the sum over lines supplies the determinant test. The divisor interpolation explains which determinants must be realized. The lattice construction realizes those determinants. The degree-one Chebotarev theorem supplies the detecting primes.

Why only one real test per complex place survives

In a single Bockstein fiber, the counting proof lifts differences to integral homology in odd degree m = 2e + 1. For a totally complex field L′ with r₂ pairs of complex embeddings, it needs a bound on the number of independent filtered classes. The odd-degree rank theorem gives rank at most r₂ when m < r₂ and the initial matrix size n is at least 2m + 4. The proof uses the homological stability theorem. Over the Dedekind ring 𝒪L′ its stable-range parameter is 2, so enlarging the matrices by identity blocks induces an isomorphism on degree-m integral homology in this range.

Start with a class z0. At step t, take its image under the homomorphism that repeats a matrix in ℓ diagonal blocks, then subtract ℓt+2 times its image under ordinary stabilization to the same size. Call the resulting class zt+1. A linear test of weight j multiplies by ℓj under block repetition and is unchanged by stabilization. After m − 1 steps its value has therefore been multiplied by

∏i=2m(ℓj − ℓi).

Every weight from 2 through m has a zero factor. To see what is left, suppose a real linear combination of the resulting cycles represents a nonzero real homology class. Stability preserves it at a larger matrix size, where a closed cochain detects it. The invariant-form comparison represents that cochain on cycles by integration. In odd degree its evaluation is a sum of the higher-weight tests and one weight-one test τw for each infinite place w. The latter comes from an alternating cyclic trace at that place. Reversing the cycle conjugates the trace. After alternation one of its real and imaginary parts vanishes. If every τw vanished on our combination, the cochain could not detect it. Thus any two cycles with the same test values give the same real homology class. The real homology image is a quotient of the image of the r₂ tests, so its dimension is at most r₂. Independent integral classes stay independent after extension of scalars to ℝ, yielding the rank bound.

Why averaging a differential form preserves its periods here

How can a group cocycle that detects a cycle be replaced by a form invariant under every archimedean matrix? Let m < r₂ be the positive homological degree over the totally complex field L′. Given any starting size, the comparison chooses a size N at least that large. At this one size it applies to every real homogeneous m-cocycle c of Γ = GLN(𝒪L′). The space of integration consists of one positive definite Hermitian matrix per complex place. A bar chain [g₁|…|gm] gives the affine simplex with vertices I, g₁·I, …, (g₁⋯gm)·I, where g·h = (g⁻¹)*hg⁻¹ at each place. Integrating a form ω over these simplices and adding the chain coefficients gives its period ⟨ω,z⟩ on a cycle z.

The partition of unity and Stokes calculation first give a Γ-invariant form with the periods of c. Averaging over central scalars preserves these periods and gives a form ω′ invariant also under those scalars. To compare its values at different points, pull its value at g·I back to the tangent space at I by g. These coefficients are square-integrable on a finite-volume fundamental domain for SLN(𝒪L′) in ∏wSLN(ℂ). Indeed the partition gives a bound by a constant times heightam, and N was chosen to make the moment of order 2am finite. Their normalized Haar mean in the moving frame gives a form ω̄ invariant under all of ∏wGLN(ℂ). To prove that ω̄ represents c, it remains to show that every period of the mean-zero remainder ω₀ = ω′ − ω̄ vanishes.

How does a group cocycle become a differential form?

Let Γ = GLN(𝒪L′) act on the cone of positive Hermitian matrices at the archimedean places. An m-cocycle c assigns a real number to m + 1 group elements. It is invariant when all are left-multiplied by the same element, and its alternating sum over the faces of any tuple of length m + 2 is zero. We want a smooth m-form whose integral on an arithmetic cycle recovers the value of c on that cycle. A partition of unity lets us trade one group argument at a time for a differential.

Write Aγ for the linear action of γ on Hermitian matrices. From a smooth function φ on the cone form the weights ψγ(h) = φ(Aγ⁻¹h). Only finitely many terms occur near any point, and they sum to 1. For a cochain β whose values are forms, let K insert a new first argument and average with these weights. Write δ for the alternating deletion of group arguments and d for exterior differentiation. The construction is

(Kβ)(g₀,…) = ∑γ ψγ β(γ,g₀,…),   η₀ = c,   ηj+1 = d(Kηj).

In Kδβ, deleting the newly inserted γ gives β times ∑ψγ = β. Every other deletion cancels the corresponding term of δKβ. Thus δK + Kδ = 1 in the degrees used here. Starting with δη₀ = 0, induction gives δηj+1 = dδKηj = dηj = 0. Indeed η₀ is constant in the cone variable, and every later ηj is an exterior derivative. After m steps only one group argument remains. The equation δηm = 0 now says its values at any two group elements coincide. This leaves a smooth closed form on the cone. Equivariance of the weights gives arithmetic invariance.

To compare periods, fix the identity matrix I. On a homogeneous tuple (g₀,…,gm), let Wj integrate ηj(g₀,…,gm−j) over the simplex with the last j + 1 vertices Agₘ₋ⱼI, …, AgₘI. Thus W₀ = c. A comparison cochain Bj integrates Kηj in the same way on an input with one fewer group element. In δBj, deleting an early argument invokes δKηj = ηj. The other deletions give the oriented faces of the next simplex. Stokes replaces their sum with the integral of d(Kηj) = ηj+1. Including the orientation sign gives

δBj = Wj + (−1)m−1−jWj+1,   0 ≤ j < m.

Substitute this identity successively for j = 0,…,m−1. The result is c = δb + sWm for an invariant cochain b. The sign starts at 1 and is multiplied at step j by (−1)m−j. Choose ω = sηm. Evaluating δb on a bar chain z gives b evaluated on ∂z. Consequently the periods of ω and c agree on every cycle.

Check the sign in degree one. Let ℤ act on the positive real line by h ↦ 2nh and take c(a,b) = b − a. In the coordinate t = log₂ h, choose a smooth bump θ supported on [−1,1] and positive on (−1,1). Normalize its integer translates to weights ψn(t) = θ(t − n)/∑p θ(t − p). Their weighted mean A(t) = ∑n nψn(t) satisfies A(t + 1) = A(t) + 1. Hence (Kc)(b) = b − A and η₁ = −dA. The sign in the comparison is −1, giving ω = dA. The group element 2 sends h = 1 to h = 4. Their images in the quotient coincide, so the interval from 1 to 4 represents the cycle [2]. Its integral is A(2) − A(0) = 2. This verifies the cocycle construction and its orientation in one dimension.

The arithmetic partition has additional properties. Its generator is unchanged under common positive dilation, so ω already has scalar invariance whenever the scalar moduli agree at all places. Its translated supports have finite overlap, and each weight derivative in the moving frame has norm at most a constant times heighta. At step j + 1 the product rule leaves dψγ wedged with ηj, since dηj = 0. At a point of overlap, translate all active labels on the left by the inverse of one of them. Each resulting label belongs to a fixed finite set. This bounds both the number of terms and the values of c on the relevant tuples, using its invariance. The form therefore grows at most like heightam, with a constant allowed to depend on the cocycle. The construction from the region of bounded lattice minima gives a = 1 for every matrix size N ≥ 1 over the fixed totally complex field. The comparison uses the weaker statement that one a works in every size. For its Stokes input, one obtains the formula on affine simplices by integrating in one coordinate and summing the endpoint faces with alternating signs.

How a compact part of the cone supplies a partition everywhere

Let L be totally complex, Γ = GLN(𝒪L), and h a positive Hermitian form at each infinite place. Write qh(v) for the sum of the local quadratic forms. The minimum λ(h) is the least value on a nonzero integral vector, a squared length. Write λ∨ for the corresponding minimum of the dual form. The partition must work even where one of these minima becomes small. It sends each input equivariantly to a region where both minima are bounded below, normalizes a smooth bump there, and pulls the resulting weights back to the input.

Finding compact representatives. Suppose λ(h), λ∨(h) ≥ c > 0. The transference estimate gives a constant C such that every real vector z has a lattice point v with qh(z−v) ≤ ρ = C/c. The points with qh(v) ≤ 10ρ span LN. To prove this, suppose a nonzero L-linear functional kills them all. Use its coefficients at the infinite places and the inverse matrices of h to choose a real vector z orthogonal to every lattice point in the kernel. Scale it to qh(z) = 4ρ. A lattice point v within squared distance ρ cannot lie in that kernel, since orthogonality would give squared distance at least 4ρ. But the parallelogram identity gives

qh(v) + qh(2z−v) = 2qh(z) + 2qh(z−v) ≤ 10ρ.

This puts v among the short points the functional kills, a contradiction. Take N independent short columns as a matrix A. These columns form a basis over L, but the integral lattice they generate can have index greater than one. Hadamard’s determinant bound at each place and a lower bound for the product of the determinants of h give a uniform bound on |NormL/ℚ(det A)|. Integral changes of coordinates then put A on a finite list of matrices B. For each B the defining conditions qh(v) ≥ c for every nonzero lattice vector and qh(Bj) ≤ 10ρ for every column are closed. They bound all entries of the Gram matrices in those columns and keep the form positive. Each such set is compact, and their finite union K meets every orbit in the region.

How many column matrices are needed to cover the thick part?

Fix a totally complex number field L, rank N ≥ 1 and a common lower bound c > 0 for the primal and dual squared minima. The covering estimate gives a point within squared distance ρ = CT/c of any target. As in the short spanning argument, choose N independent columns in 𝒪LN, each of squared length at most D = 10ρ. Their matrix A is invertible over L. Its determinant can be a nonunit of 𝒪L. To obtain a compact set independent of the input form h, we need only finitely many matrices to stand for all such choices after an integral change of coordinates.

Bound the absolute norm of the determinant. Write r for the number of complex places, e = [L : ℚ] = 2r and d = eN. For each place w put Aw = w(A). Each diagonal entry of the positive column Gram matrix Aw∗hwAw is at most D, since summing these nonnegative local lengths for a given column gives its global squared length. Hadamard’s inequality bounds the determinant by DN. Multiplying over places, the factors |w(det A)|² give the absolute field norm I = |NormL/ℚ(det A)|. Thus I P(h) ≤ DNr, where P(h) = ∏w det hw.

Why the primal minimum bounds the product of determinants from below

Set k = h/c. Its real Gram matrix G in integral coordinates has xᵀGx ≥ 1 on nonzero integer columns, so the integer determinant estimate gives 1 ≤ (4d)d det G. The embedding matrix of an integral basis has squared absolute determinant |ΔL|. Use it on each of the N coordinates. Pairing a complex embedding with its conjugate adds a local Hermitian expression to its conjugate and produces twice its real part. The determinant of the resulting matrix 2G is therefore 2d det G = E P(k)², where E = |ΔL|N.

In this positive-rank setting d ≥ 2 and E ≥ 1. Substitution gives 1 ≤ (2d)dE P(k)² ≤ [E ddP(k)]², because E(d/2)d ≥ 1. Taking a positive square root and using P(k) = c−NrP(h) yields P(h) ≥ cNr/I₀ for I₀ = E dd. The determinant estimate also holds at rank zero, where the empty determinant and the empty products equal one.

1 ≤ I = |NormL/ℚ(det A)| ≤ I₀ (D/c)Nr,   I₀ = |ΔL|Ndd.

Classify enough matrices by a finite residue. This algebraic step works over the integers 𝒪 of any number field of degree e, in every rank. Fix an integer I ≥ 1. For a matrix of determinant norm I, the integer I belongs to the principal ideal generated by det A. Indeed, the absolute norm of the ideal is the order of its additive quotient and kills that quotient. Write I = a det A. Then U = a adj(A) = I A⁻¹ is integral and satisfies AU = UA = I·Id. Record every entry of U modulo I𝒪.

Suppose A′ has the same norm and residue, and write U′ = I A′⁻¹. The difference U−U′ = I X has integral X. Multiplication first on the left by A′ and then, for the inverse, by A gives

g = A′ A⁻¹ = Id + A′ X,   g⁻¹ = A A′⁻¹ = Id − A X,   g A = A′.

Both matrices on the right are integral, so this is a change of rows in GLN(𝒪). Since 𝒪 is free of rank e over ℤ, the quotient 𝒪/I𝒪 has Ie elements and the matrix residue has at most IeN² possibilities. Choose one matrix above each attained residue. Equality of residues suffices to put two matrices in the same orbit, so a single orbit may appear under several residues. For the ceiling J of the norm bound, take the union for 1 ≤ I ≤ J. Its size is at most ∑I=1J IeN² ≤ J1+eN². When J = 0 an empty list suffices.

Recover an integral change of rows over the Gaussian integers

Take L = ℚ(i), N = 2 and A = diag(1 + i, 1). Add (1 + i) times its second row to its first to obtain A′ = [[1 + i, 1 + i], [0, 1]]. Both determinants have norm I = 2. In the ordinary Hermitian form the two squared column lengths change from (2,1) to (2,3). Multiplying both inverses by 2 gives U = diag(1 − i, 2) and U′ = [[1 − i, −2], [0, 2]]. The difference is 2E₁₂, where E₁₂ has its only nonzero entry 1 in position (1,2). The formula above recovers g = Id + (1 + i)E₁₂. There are four residues in ℤ[i]/2ℤ[i], hence at most 4⁴ = 256 matrix residues at this fixed norm.

Each matrix specifies a compact set of forms. For a nonsingular representative B, impose qk(v) ≥ c on every nonzero integral vector and qk(Bⱼ) ≤ D on each column. These inequalities are closed in the real space of Hermitian tuples. The first gives a positive definite real Gram matrix for k/c. Testing it on real coordinates of a vector supported at a single place gives positivity there. The second bounds the entries of Bw∗kwBw in absolute value by 2D, using the sum of the two diagonal entries. Since Bw is invertible, these coordinates recover k by a continuous linear inverse on their image. The closed set is therefore compact. If B = g A, the transformed form satisfies qg·h(Bⱼ) = qh(Aⱼ). The finite union of the compact pieces contains a translate of every h with the two prescribed minima. Each piece can contain continuously many forms.

Dividing by the orbit sum. On a compact neighborhood K′ of K inside the cone, choose a nonnegative smooth bump b supported in K′ and scaled to be at least 1 on K. Form S(k) = ∑γ∈Γ b(γ⁻¹k). Only finitely many terms occur near any positive k. In fact, if a matrix and its translate both lie in a fixed compact set, the columns of γ⁻¹ belong to a fixed finite set of lattice points. Reindexing makes S invariant. Choose a smooth function g with g(s) ≥ ½ everywhere and g(s) = s for s ≥ 1. Then ψ = b/g(S) is smooth, even where S = 0. Whenever an orbit meets K, one bump is at least 1, so its orbit sum is large enough for the exact normalization

∑γ∈Γ ψ(γ⁻¹k) = S(k)/g(S(k)) = 1.

To reach these orbits from any h, first remove its common scale by multiplying it by [∏w(det hw)mult(w)]−1/(N[L:ℚ]). Call the result h₀. Next take a smooth arithmetic-invariant approximate dual minimum μ with λ∨/4 ≤ μ ≤ 4λ∨. The source adds positive semidefinite corrections to μ(h₀)h₀. At each scale s = 4j the correction averages outer products of h0,wvw over short lattice vectors, with smooth cutoff and a factor s−2. The corrected form F(h) has both minima bounded below uniformly in h. Thus the translated weights ψ(γ⁻¹F(h)) sum to one on the whole cone. The pulled-back support can extend towards the cusp. Equivariance and the compact support of ψ still bound the possible relative labels of overlapping translates by a finite set.

How many translates of a smooth weight can meet?

The compact set of representatives K meets the orbits of forms with both squared minima bounded below. A smooth weight around K must give the right total even if several group elements carry a form to the same point. Write Γ = GLN(𝒪L) and let γ act on a form by qγ·h(v) = qh(γ⁻¹v). The weight indexed by γ at h is evaluated at τγh = γ⁻¹·h. The properness and bump statements below hold for every number field L and rank N ≥ 0. The final use of the thick set assumes L totally complex and N ≥ 1.

Count matrices by their columns. For a compact subset Q of the positive cone, let Γ(Q) consist of the γ for which both h and γ·h lie in Q for some h. Fix h₀ ∈ Q. On Q times the unit sphere of archimedean columns, qh₀(v)/qh(v) has a finite upper bound A. Homogeneity gives the same comparison on all columns. Put Bⱼ = maxk∈Q qk(eⱼ). For γ ∈ Γ(Q), its inverse has jth column γ⁻¹eⱼ satisfying

qh₀(γ⁻¹eⱼ) ≤ A qγ·h(eⱼ) ≤ A Bⱼ,   |Γ(Q)| ≤ ∏j #{v ∈ 𝒪LN ∶ qh₀(v) ≤ A Bⱼ}.

Each factor is finite by discreteness of the lattice inside a bounded ellipsoid. All columns together determine γ⁻¹, giving the displayed counting bound. For an empty Q there are no incidences. At rank zero the group is trivial.

Normalize on every orbit meeting the compact set. Choose ε > 0 so the closed ε-neighborhood K′ of K is compact and still in the open positive cone. The smooth support lemma on the ambient real vector space gives 0 ≤ f ≤ 1 with nonzero set exactly the open ε-neighborhood. On nonempty K its minimum m is positive. Put b = f/m, so b ≥ 1 on K. For empty K one may take b = 0 and m = 1. Given another compact B inside the cone, use Q = B ∪ K′. Every label γ with τγh ∈ K′ for some h ∈ B satisfies γ⁻¹ ∈ Γ(Q). Taking B to be a small closed ball about a point of the cone therefore gives the same finite list throughout that ball. The orbit sum S(h) = ∑γ b(τγh) is smooth there. Since τδτγ = τγδ, left multiplication by γ reindexes the sum and makes S invariant.

Let Θ be the smooth transition from zero on (−∞,0] to one on [1,∞). The denominator g(s) = ½ + (s−½)Θ(2s−1) is at least ½ everywhere and equals s for s ≥ 1. Define ψ = b/g(S) on the cone and extend by zero outside it. Every point outside the cone has a neighborhood disjoint from K′, so the extension is smooth. If γ₀·h lies in K, the term labelled γ₀⁻¹ is at least one in the raw sum. Consequently

∑γ∈Γ ψ(τγh) = S(h)/g(S(h)) = 1   whenever Γ·h meets K.

All elements giving the same orbit point contribute separately to S. Their multiplicity is the order of the stabilizer.

Two points of one orbit receive different weights

Take 𝒪 = ℤ[ω] with ω² + ω + 1 = 0. Put h₀ = Id₂, s = [[1,1],[0,1]] and h₁ = s∗s = [[1,1],[1,2]]. Every τγh₀ = γ∗γ has entries in 𝒪. Distinct such matrices differ by at least one in the maximum absolute entry norm, because every nonzero Eisenstein integer has absolute value at least one. Choose two disjoint bumps around h₀ and h₁ inside the cone whose supports meet this orbit only at their respective centers. Give their sum b values 1 and 2 at the centers.

The squared length of a column is the sum of two nonnegative integer norms. A unit column therefore has a single nonzero coordinate, one of the six units. Orthogonality puts the second column on the other axis. The stabilizer U of h₀ has 2·6² = 72 elements. Also γ∗γ = s∗s exactly when γs⁻¹ ∈ U, so the labels giving h₁ form U s. At h₀ there are 144 nonzero terms and S = 72·1 + 72·2 = 216. Each label in U receives 1/216 and each label in U s receives 1/108. The two centers receive total weights ⅓ and ⅔.

Pull back the compactly supported weight. Let F be the smooth equivariant map obtained by normalizing the scale and correcting the two minima. Set φ(h) = ψ(F(h)). Every F(h) meets K up to a translate. Hence ∑γ φ(τγh) = 1 for every positive h. For a compact neighborhood V in the input cone, apply properness to F(V) ∪ K′ to get a finite list on its interior. There is also one finite set of relative labels for the whole cone. Let D be the closure in that cone of {φ ≠ 0}. Continuity gives F(D) ⊆ K′. If the supports with labels γ and η meet, some h has γ⁻¹·h and η⁻¹·h in D. Their images under F are in K′ and differ by the action of η⁻¹γ. This puts η⁻¹γ in the single finite set Γ(K′).

Why this bump also works for the derivative estimate

Say k is δ-close to positive h if |qk(z)−qh(z)| ≤ δqh(z) for all archimedean columns. Polarization on coordinate vectors gives ‖k−h‖ ≤ 2δ‖h‖ in the matrix-entry norm. The smooth compactly supported ψ has an ordinary Lipschitz constant Lψ. Choose R ≥ 0 bounding the norm on K′. If the two values differ, at least one point belongs to K′. For 0 ≤ δ < ¼ the norm estimate then gives ‖h‖ ≤ 2R, so |ψ(k)−ψ(h)| ≤ 4LψRδ. For δ ≥ ¼ the bound 0 ≤ ψ ≤ 2/m supplies the upper bound 16δ/m. Thus Cψ = 16/m + 4LψR works for every δ ≥ 0, including cases where k lies outside the cone. Composing with the relative bounds for the normalization and correction, then differentiating in a moving frame, gives the one-power height bound. The companion finite-overlap assertion controls the labels present in sums of derivatives.

Smooth cutoff thickening in the positive cone, lattice dilation count, and smoothness of the dyadic retraction

Why do the orbit-normalized bump around the compact core K and the dyadic outer-product retraction both define globally smooth objects on the positive-definite cone Pos(L, N)? Three analytic mechanisms govern their local finiteness and regularity. First, Pos(L, N) is an open subset of the finite-dimensional real normed space HS(L, N) of Hermitian matrix tuples, so any compact subset K ⊆ Pos(L, N) sits at a positive metric distance from the boundary of the cone. Smooth support separation on HS(L, N) therefore produces a smooth function whose nonzero locus is an open ε-neighborhood of K with compact closure K′ ⊆ Pos(L, N); dividing by its positive minimum on K yields a smooth bump b ≥ 1 on K whose orbit-normalized weight ψ = b/g(S) is compactly supported and globally Lipschitz. Second, when the squared radius of an integral lattice ellipsoid is dilated from s to αs, placing open qh-balls of squared radius s/4 around the dilated lattice points reduces discrete counting to additive Haar volume comparison on the archimedean space Vℝ: by the quadratic parallelogram inequality, all shifted balls lie inside a single dilated ellipsoid while overlapping centers at any point x ∈ Vℝ inject by subtraction into the undilated lattice ball of squared radius s, yielding a bound independent of both h ∈ Pos(L, N) and s ≥ 0. Third, in the dyadic sum R(h) = μ(h)h + ∑j∈ℤ θ(4jμ(h))T4j(h), the outer cutoff kills large scales 4j ≥ 4/μ(h) while the positive lattice minimum kills small scales 4 · 4j ≤ λ(h) on nonzero integral vectors (and v = 0 contributes the zero outer product), collapsing the infinite series near each base form h0 ∈ Pos(L, N) to a fixed finite sum over scales and lattice vectors.

1. Smooth bump thickening, Haar ball-packing dilation count, and retraction regularity. Let L be an arbitrary number field and N ≥ 0 an integer rank. Write HS(L, N) for the finite-dimensional real normed space of tuples h = (hw)w of N × N complex Hermitian matrices indexed by the infinite places w of L, Pos(L, N) ⊆ HS(L, N) for the open cone of tuples positive-definite at every infinite place, and qh(z) = ∑w Re(zw∗hwzw) on Vℝ = ∏w ℂN of real dimension dℝ = dimℝ Vℝ, with Γ = GLN(𝒪L) acting via qγ·h(z) = qh(γ−1z) and τγh = γ−1·h. Let θ : ℝ → [0, 1] be the Lθ-Lipschitz smooth cutoff of the dual-minimum construction satisfying θ(x) = 1 for x ≤ 1 and θ(x) = 0 for x ≥ 4. For s > 0 and h ∈ Pos(L, N), set Zs(h) = ∑v∈𝒪LN θ(qh(v)/s) ≥ θ(0) = 1 and Ts(h) = (s²Zs(h))−1 ∑v∈𝒪LN θ(qh(v)/s) rk(h, v), where rk(h, v)w = (hwvw)(hwvw)∗. For N ≥ 1 and a smooth Γ-invariant proxy μ : Pos(L, N) → ℝ satisfying cμλ∨(h) ≤ μ(h) ≤ C′μλ∨(h) with cμ > 0 (so μ(h) > 0 on Pos(L, N)), define R(h) = μ(h)h + ∑j∈ℤ θ(4jμ(h))T4j(h).

Proposition (Smooth bump thickening, lattice dilation count, and retraction smoothness). For every number field L:

(i) For every integer rank N ≥ 0 and every compact subset K ⊆ Pos(L, N), there exist ε > 0 whose compact closed metric thickening K′ ⊆ Pos(L, N) equals {x ∈ HS(L, N) : dist(x, K) ≤ ε} when K ≠ ∅ and ∅ when K = ∅, a constant m > 0, and a smooth function b ∈ C∞(HS(L, N), ℝ) supported in K′ with 0 ≤ b ≤ 1/m everywhere and b ≥ 1 on K; every smooth function on HS(L, N) supported in K′—in particular the zero-extended orbit-normalized weight ψ = b/g(S) once local finiteness of S on Pos(L, N) is supplied by column properness—admits a finite global Lipschitz constant Lψ ≥ 0 on HS(L, N).

(ii) For every integer rank N ≥ 0, every dilation parameter α ∈ ℝ, every h ∈ Pos(L, N), and every s ≥ 0,

#{v ∈ 𝒪LN : qh(v) ≤ αs} ≤ Cα #{v ∈ 𝒪LN : qh(v) ≤ s},   Cα = (√(8 max(α, 1) + 2))dℝ.

(iii) Assume N ≥ 1 and let μ : Pos(L, N) → ℝ be a smooth Γ-invariant proxy satisfying cμλ∨(h) ≤ μ(h) ≤ C′μλ∨(h) on Pos(L, N) with cμ > 0. Then μ(h) > 0 on Pos(L, N), and the dyadic retraction R maps Pos(L, N) into Pos(L, N), satisfies R(γ·h) = γ·R(h) for all γ ∈ Γ and qR(h)(z) ≥ μ(h)qh(z) for all z ∈ Vℝ, and belongs to C∞(Pos(L, N), HS(L, N)). Near each h0 ∈ Pos(L, N), there exist a neighborhood U, integers n0, n1 ∈ ℕ, and a finite set F0 ⊂ 𝒪LN (with 0 ∈ F0) such that for all h ∈ Pos(L, N) ∩ U,

R(h) = μ(h)h + ∑j=−n0n1 θ(4jμ(h)) [42j ∑v∈F0 θ(qh(v)/4j)]−1 ∑v∈F0 θ(qh(v)/4j) rk(h, v).

Proof. Since Pos(L, N) is open in the finite-dimensional normed space HS(L, N) and K ⊆ Pos(L, N) is compact, metric separation supplies ε > 0 whose compact closed metric ε-thickening K′ lies inside Pos(L, N), and smooth support separation on HS(L, N) constructs f ∈ C∞(HS(L, N), [0, 1]) whose open support {x : f(x) ≠ 0} equals the open ε-thickening of K inside K′. If K = ∅, then K′ = ∅ and we take b = 0 and m = 1; if K ≠ ∅, compactness of K ⊆ {f > 0} yields m = minx∈K f(x) > 0, so b = f/m ∈ C∞ satisfies 0 ≤ b ≤ 1/m, b ≥ 1 on K, and supp(b) ⊆ K′. Any smooth function on HS(L, N) supported in the compact set K′—including the zero-extended quotient ψ = b/g(S)—has compactly supported continuous derivative and therefore a finite global Lipschitz constant Lψ on HS(L, N).

For the lattice dilation estimate, set ρ = max(α, 1) ≥ 1, so {v ∈ 𝒪LN : qh(v) ≤ αs} ⊆ A := {v ∈ 𝒪LN : qh(v) ≤ ρs}. At s = 0 positive-definiteness of h forces both sets to equal {0} of size 1 ≤ Cα. For s > 0, place around each v ∈ A the open ball Bv = {y ∈ Vℝ : qh(y − v) < s/4}. By the quadratic parallelogram inequality qh(u1) ≤ 2qh(u1 − u2) + 2qh(u2), every x ∈ Bv obeys qh(x) ≤ 2qh(x − v) + 2qh(v) < (8ρ + 2)(s/4), placing ⋃v∈A Bv inside √(8ρ + 2) · B0, while any two centers v, v0 ∈ A with x ∈ Bv ∩ Bv0 satisfy qh(v − v0) ≤ 2qh(x − v0) + 2qh(x − v) < s. Fixing one witness v0 at each x injects {v ∈ A : x ∈ Bv} via v ↦ v − v0 into {w ∈ 𝒪LN : qh(w) ≤ s}, so ∑v∈A 1Bv(x) ≤ #{w ∈ 𝒪LN : qh(w) ≤ s} · 1√(8ρ+2)B0(x). Integrating against additive Haar measure μHaar on Vℝ, using translation invariance μHaar(Bv) = μHaar(B0) ∈ (0, ∞) and scaling μHaar(√(8ρ + 2)B0) = (√(8ρ + 2))dℝ μHaar(B0), and cancelling μHaar(B0) proves (ii). Finally, when N ≥ 1, discreteness of 𝒪LN \ {0} on the positive-definite dual form h∨ gives λ∨(h) > 0 and hence μ(h) ≥ cμλ∨(h) > 0; rk(γ·h, v) = γ·rk(h, γ−1v) and bijection reindexing v ↦ γ−1v give Ts(γ·h) = γ·Ts(h) and R(γ·h) = γ·R(h); positive semidefiniteness qrk(h,v)(z) = ∑w |zw∗hwvw|² ≥ 0 and μ(h) > 0 yield qR(h)(z) ≥ μ(h)qh(z) and R(h) ∈ Pos(L, N); and local truncation to finitely many scales and lattice vectors establishes R ∈ C∞(Pos(L, N), HS(L, N)).

Uniform local truncation of the dyadic retraction to a finite scale and lattice window

Fix N ≥ 1 and h0 ∈ Pos(L, N), so λ(h0) > 0 and μ(h0) ≥ cμλ∨(h0) > 0. Pick n1 ∈ ℕ with 4n1 > 8/μ(h0). Applying local lattice finiteness near h0 at threshold 4 · 4n1 yields a finite subset of 𝒪LN—enlarged by 0 to a finite set F0 ⊂ 𝒪LN—and a neighborhood of h0 on which every v ∉ F0 satisfies qh(v) > 4 · 4n1. Intersecting with the open neighborhood where μ(h) > μ(h0)/2 and where each of the finitely many continuous functions h ↦ qh(v) (v ∈ F0 \ {0}) satisfies qh(v) > λ(h0)/2 produces a neighborhood U of h0. For every integer j > n1 and h ∈ Pos(L, N) ∩ U, 4jμ(h) ≥ 4 · 4n1 · (μ(h0)/2) > 16 > 4, so θ(4jμ(h)) = 0; and for every j ≤ n1 and v ∉ F0, qh(v)/4j > 4 · 4n1−j ≥ 4, so θ(qh(v)/4j) = 0.

At the small-scale end, put m0 = min(λ(h0)/2, 4 · 4n1) > 0. Every nonzero v ∈ 𝒪LN satisfies qh(v) > m0 across Pos(L, N) ∩ U—by the finite-set intersection when v ∈ F0 \ {0}, and by qh(v) > 4 · 4n1 ≥ m0 when v ∉ F0. Choose n0 ∈ ℕ with 4−n0 < m0/4. Then for every integer j < −n0 and every nonzero v ∈ 𝒪LN, qh(v)/4j > 4m0/m0 = 4 so θ(qh(v)/4j) = 0, while at v = 0 one has rk(h, 0) = 0; hence T4j(h) = 0 for all j < −n0. On Pos(L, N) ∩ U, each remaining weight sum Z4j(h) (−n0 ≤ j ≤ n1) equals the finite smooth sum ∑v∈F0 θ(qh(v)/4j) ≥ θ(0) = 1 (since 0 ∈ F0), so division by 42jZ4j(h) ≥ 42j > 0 preserves C∞ regularity.
