For the real alternating form β at the identity, complexifying its multilinear functional produces a matrix T commuting with the unitary tensor powers. Contract its expansion in the Pσ,w with the entries of the Hermitian input matrices Y₁,…,Yq. A term vanishes if σ moves a slot to a different place. Otherwise the indices around each cycle (i₁ … iℓ) sum to tr(Yi₁,w⋯Yiℓ,w) at its common place. Distinct cycles contribute a product. This contraction can vanish even when the place-permutation operator is nonzero.

If the complex coefficient of one product is a + ib, taking its real part gives a times the real part of the trace product minus b times its imaginary part. The archive alternates by a signed sum over the q! input orders. Alternating β itself gives q! β, so the coefficients of the unnormalized alternating generators are a/q! and −b/q!. The cohomological filter then uses the number of cycles as the block weight.

Two slots and one complex place

Take A = [[1,1],[1,0]] and B = [[0,1],[1,3]]. For σ = id the row and column indices agree in each slot, so the contraction gives tr(A)tr(B) = 1·3 = 3. For σ = (12) the contraction pairs Aij with Bji and gives tr(AB) = 2. With d identical diagonal blocks, these become 3d² and 2d. Both expressions are symmetric in the two inputs and vanish upon alternation at this place. In block size N = 1 at one place the identity and swap agree already as operators on a one-dimensional tensor power.

Check the sign and the weight in degree three

At one place take X = [[0,1],[1,0]], Y = [[0,−i],[i,0]] and Z = diag(1,−1), where i² = −1. These three Hermitian matrices anticommute in pairs, and XY = iZ. Thus tr(XYZ) = 2i. Two identical blocks give 24 through the same calculation. These are values on tangent vectors at I. A period on an arithmetic cycle requires integrating the transported tensor over the corresponding simplices.

Why does a filtered cycle stay detectable in a larger matrix group?

Write Γn(R) = GLn(R) and use integral group homology with trivial coefficients. Stabilization sends g to diag(g,1). The proof establishes two one-step bounds in homological degree m. The stable-range parameter s belongs to the ring. A unimodular row of length n + 1 can be shortened whenever n ≥ s, by adding multiples of the last entry to its first n entries while keeping them generators of the unit ideal. For a Dedekind domain the proof takes s = 2.

Hm(Γn(R)) → Hm(Γn+1(R))   is surjective for n ≥ 2m + s + 1, and bijective for n ≥ 2m + s + 2.
Compute the stabilization map from an alternating face map

Fix an ambient size b and put G = Γb(R). An ordered split sequence of length p is a list of vectors and covectors (v₁,λ₁), …, (vp,λp) with λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on these sequences. The group acts on the vectors by g and on the covectors by precomposition with g−1. The differential dp from Cp+1 to Cp deletes one pair with alternating signs. The empty sequence gives C₀ = ℤ.

When p + s ≤ b, the action is transitive. The stabilizer of the last p standard vector–covector pairs is diag(Γb−p,Ip). Fixing both the vectors and the covectors forces the two off-diagonal blocks to vanish. Shapiro’s lemma for this permutation module therefore identifies Hq(G,Cp) with Hq(Γb−p,ℤ). When p + 1 + s ≤ b, both consecutive identifications are isomorphisms. In these coordinates each deletion gives the same stabilization map. A permutation of the final coordinates arranges the remaining pairs in standard order and commutes with Γb−p−1. The sum of p + 1 alternating signs is one for even p and zero for odd p.

Hq(Γb−2)   ⟶0   Hq(Γb−1)   ⟶stab   Hq(Γb).

Set b = n + 1. The integral filling argument shows that cycles on split sequences of length p bound when 2p + s + 1 ≤ b. It gives the exactness of the required part of the sequence of coefficient modules. Group homology need not preserve exactness in each row. For this reason the proof uses induction on the target degree m. In degrees q < m each relevant pair of adjacent maps is a stabilization next to a zero map. Exactness there asks for injectivity of the outgoing stabilization or surjectivity of the incoming one, already known in the corresponding smaller degree and matrix size.

To reach degree m, factor each dp+1 through the kernel of dp. The long exact group homology sequences for these kernels transfer the lower-degree row exactness to surjectivity of Hm(d₀). With one further step of module exactness they give ker Hm(d₀) = im Hm(d₁). The displayed row shows that the latter image is zero. For m ≥ 1, the lower-degree map at p = 2 and q = m − 1 starts at rank n − 2. Surjectivity there requires n − 2 ≥ 2(m − 1) + s + 1, while injectivity requires the right side plus one. The two induction steps check the remaining positions in their respective ranges. Composing the resulting one-step isomorphisms over 𝒪L carries degree-m integral homology unchanged from size n to every size N ≥ n once n ≥ 2m + 4.

A weight-j functional on the resulting cycle is multiplied by (2j − 4)(2j − 8), giving 12, 0 and 0 for j = 1, 2 and 3. This computation specifies the effect on tests without choosing a nonzero class.

The invariant-form comparison supplies a size N at least as large as the final filter level at which closed detecting cochains have invariant-form periods. When does every cycle of ordered split pairs bound?

A split pair in Rn is a vector v with a specified linear functional λ satisfying λ(v) = 1. An ordered list of pairs is split if λi(vj) = δij. Write Cp for the free abelian group on such lists of length p. Its boundary deletes one pair at a time, starting with sign +. Thus a vertex has boundary the empty list, and an edge has boundary its last vertex minus its first. The stability argument needs to know when these signed lists can fill a cycle.

2p + s + 1 ≤ n   ⟹   for every c ∈ Cp with ∂c = 0, some B ∈ Cp+1 satisfies ∂B = c.

This holds for every commutative ring with identity and all nonnegative integers n, p, s satisfying the ring’s stable-range hypothesis at s. That hypothesis says that whenever d ≥ s and the entries of (r₁,…,rd,t) generate the unit ideal, one can find a₁,…,ad so that the entries ri + ait still generate it. Length zero gives surjectivity onto the augmentation group ℤ. For p ≥ 1 the conclusion is vanishing of reduced integral homology in degree p − 1. In particular, length one controls differences of vertices.

Separate the chosen covectors from the auxiliary vectors

A plain unimodular list admits covectors making it split, but leaves the choice open. Introduce chains Da,b on a split list of length a and a plain list of length b. Each covector in the first list must kill every vector in the second. Deleting from the first list defines h and deleting from the second defines v. The deletions commute because their signs count positions in separate lists. Each operator squares to zero.

Fix the split list on the diagonal a + b = p. When a + s ≤ n, a matrix g carries it to the last a standard pairs. Acting by g on vectors and by precomposition with g−1 on covectors preserves all pairings. The proof straightens one pair, then straightens the remaining pairs in its coordinate complement. The auxiliary vectors must now have their last a entries zero. Restricting their witnessing covectors, or extending such covectors by zero, identifies this column with ordinary unimodular lists in Rn−a.

The ordinary-list theorem fills every cycle of length b when b + s ≤ n − a, as required on this diagonal. For s ≥ 1 its proof uses exactness of links in coordinate subspaces and their unions with affine translates. At s = 0, shortening the row (1) forces the zero ring, where prepending zero fills every cycle.

Filling the link of an empty prefix

Let Ln be the span of the first n coordinate vectors (numbered from zero), and let j ≥ n. The permitted letters lie in S = Ln ∪ (eⱼ + Ln). Suppose that, for every unimodular prefix σ, cycles of q further letters in Ln bound when q + s + |σ| ≤ n. We show that a cycle of length p in S, starting with empty prefix, bounds when p + s ≤ n + 1.

First remove letters outside the low slice from the cycle, working from right to left. At the rightmost position still containing an outside letter, group the offending words by their prefix τ ending at that position. For a fixed τ, its tails form a cycle in the low link of τ. Indeed a face obtained by deleting a prefix letter has its last outside letter strictly earlier, so the component of the boundary still beginning with τ sees only tail deletions. If x is the last letter of τ, then xⱼ = 1. Move x to the front for the unimodularity test and replace every other prefix letter u by u − uⱼx. This splits off the summand generated by x. Every low tail letter has coordinate j zero and is fixed. Thus the very same low tails extend a unimodular prefix of length |τ| − 1. Their filling is available since (p − |τ|) + s + (|τ| − 1) = p + s − 1 ≤ n.

Attach each filling after its original prefix with sign (−1)|τ| and subtract its boundary. Its tail faces cancel the offending terms, and its prefix faces have their last outside letter earlier. Iterating leaves a homologous cycle c supported in the low slice. Prepending eⱼ to each term preserves unimodularity because its coordinate splits off and all low letters have zero j-th coordinate. The signed boundary is ∂[eⱼ,c] = c − [eⱼ,∂c] = c. This includes length zero, where ∂[eⱼ] = [ ].

A nonempty prefix in the passage from rank n to rank n + 1

Fix n ≥ s ≥ 1 and j ≥ n + 1. Suppose that links with tail letters in Sₙ = Lₙ ∪ (eⱼ + Lₙ) are exact for every unimodular prefix σ in the range q + s + |σ| ≤ n + 1. For a nonempty unimodular prefix τ we want to fill cycles of length p in its Sn+1-link when p + s + |τ| ≤ n + 2. Choose a letter v of τ and a form f with f(v) = 1. Write h = f − ∑i<n f(eᵢ)δi, where δi reads coordinate i. The first n coordinates of v together with h(v) generate 1. Stable range gives t ∈ Lₙ such that the first n coordinates of w = v + h(v)t generate 1.

The shear x ↦ x + h(x)t carries v to w and has inverse obtained by subtraction, since h(t) = 0. Choose a linear combination λ of the first n coordinate forms with λ(w) = 1 − wₙ. The second shear x ↦ x + λ(x)eₙ is invertible for the same reason. Both maps and their inverses add vectors in Ln+1, so preserve each allowed coset there. They transport the entire link to one in which the chosen prefix letter has vₙ = 1.

For any extension σ in this transported link with |σ| ≤ p, restrict the letters after τσ to Sₙ. These letters have coordinate n zero because j ≥ n + 1. Splitting off v as above fixes each restricted letter and shortens the combined prefix to length |τ| + |σ| − 1. The rank-n hypothesis fills tails of length p − |σ| because the sum in its range is p + s + |τ| − 1 ≤ n + 1. For nonempty σ these fillings move the last outside position to the left by the preceding boundary argument. For empty σ the same bound fills the remaining cycle in Sₙ. This proves the rank step for the whole link.

To see how the induction starts each new rank, first obtain the low-slice conclusion in Ln+1. Use the two slices Lₙ ∪ (eₙ + Lₙ) within it. For an extension σ the smaller-rank affine hypothesis applies directly to the concatenated prefix τσ, since (p − |σ|) + s + |τσ| = p + s + |τ| ≤ n + 1. The same boundary argument fills the full low link. The empty-prefix cone then gives the affine conclusion for the empty prefix at the new rank. For a nonempty prefix use the two shears when n ≥ s and the singleton companion at the first admissible rank. At rank zero with s ≥ 1 the low range is empty, and only the empty-prefix cone can be required.

At the stable-range boundary n = s ≥ 1, a nonempty prefix can consist of a single unimodular vector v. The induction needs a second vector x in a prescribed translate, with two forms dual to the ordered pair (v, x). Its vertex then fills the empty chain.

How does stable range give a companion in the prescribed translate?

Write Ln for the span of the first n coordinate vectors in the module of finitely supported sequences. Fix j ≥ n ≥ s and choose a form f with f(v) = 1. Put aᵢ = f(eᵢ). Remove from f its first n coordinates and its j-th coordinate to obtain φ. With b = φ(v) + aⱼvⱼ, we have 1 = ∑i<n aᵢvᵢ + b. Stable range therefore supplies tᵢ such that the shortened entries vᵢ + tᵢb generate the unit ideal.

Take x = eⱼ − aⱼ∑i<n tᵢeᵢ and v′ = v − vⱼx. By construction x ∈ eⱼ + Ln, its j-th coordinate is one and φ(x) = 0. Each shortened entry is vᵢ′ + tᵢφ(v′), so it belongs to the ideal generated by the coordinates of v′. Those coordinates therefore generate 1. Choose a form h with h(v′) = 1. Writing δj for the j-th coordinate form, set λ = h − h(x)δj and μ = δj − vⱼλ. The first form kills x and takes value one on v′, hence on v. The second kills v and takes value one on x.

For a nonempty prefix τ the range for a tail of length q is q + s + |τ| ≤ n + 1. At n = s this forces |τ| = 1 and q = 0. With τ = [v], the constructed x is a vertex of its link. The augmented boundary is ∂(k[x]) = k[ ] for every integer k.

Over ℤ take n = j = 2 and v = (2,4,3). The coordinate vector e₂ fails because every form vanishing on it takes an even value on v. With f = (−1,0,1) the shortened row (−1,4) gives x = (1,0,1). The two duals are λ = (−1,0,1) and μ = (3,0,−2).

Why does the final auxiliary vector cost one fewer dimension?

Fix a plain list w₁,…,wb with b ≥ 1, and choose duals μj. In this row every split covector kills the wj. To place the split vectors in the opposite kernels as well, inspect a prefix of length t and the tails one may append to it. Replacing each prefix vector x by the vector below preserves its pairings with all split covectors and puts it in every ker μj.

x′ = x − ∑j=1b μj(x)wj,   μi(x′) = 0.

The auxiliary pairs together with the corrected prefix form a split list of length b + t. The admissible tails whose vectors also lie in all the opposite kernels are exactly the tails one can append to this combined list. Straightening it reduces their complex to rank n − b − t. To fill in length a − t, induction on rank requires 2(a − t) + s + 1 ≤ n − b − t. For every 0 ≤ t ≤ a this follows from 2a + b + s + 1 ≤ n. Filling these links moves a cycle into the opposite kernels by successive boundaries. The empty-prefix case then fills it there. On the diagonal a + b = p + 1, the required bound becomes 2p + s + 3 − b ≤ n, which holds for b ≥ 2.

For b = 1 the cycle need only bound in the full split complex. Write its auxiliary vector as u and choose μ(u) = 1. Moving the cycle into ker μ uses only prefixes whose last vector lies outside that kernel, so t ≥ 1. This time 2(p − t) + s + 1 ≤ n − 1 − t already follows at the stated rank. For the resulting cycle c′ = c − ∂B₁ both cross-pairings vanish. Prepending (u,μ) gives a chain with boundary c′ by alternating deletion. Adding B₁ fills the original cycle.

Assemble the individual fillings

Place the original cycle c in Dp,0 with an empty auxiliary list. Both boundaries vanish. The column fillings give vertical lifts. A lift y with vy = c may have a horizontal boundary. Induct on the first index. At index zero the horizontal boundary vanishes. At a positive index, hy has lower first index and is killed by both operators. Induction supplies z′ with vz′ = hy and hz′ = 0. Its second index is now at least two, so the row filling supplies u with hu = z′. The corrected lift satisfies

z = y − vu,   hz = hy − vhu = 0,   vz = c.

In bidegree (p,1), group the finitely many terms of z by their sole auxiliary vector. Each group is a horizontal cycle because h preserves that vector. Their sum after deleting the auxiliary vectors is c, since a singleton has deletion sign +. The preceding cone construction fills each group in the full complex. Summing gives the required integral filling, which supplies the exact sequence used in the stability argument.

Three edges over the field of two elements. In rank two, each of the three nonzero vectors has exactly two possible covectors taking value one on it. A vertex (v,λ) has a unique compatible neighbor. Its vector w is the nonzero element of ker λ, and its covector is uniquely determined by taking value zero on v and one on w. The six vertices therefore form three disjoint edges when directions are forgotten. In particular, A = (e₁,e₁*) and C = (e₁,e₁* + e₂*) are in different components. In rank three, extend these pairs by zero. With U = (e₃,e₃*) the integral boundary of [A,U] + [U,C] is [C] − [A]. Thus one extra coordinate fills this particular cycle. The experiment below also checks all 28 vertices in rank three over 𝔽₂ and finds one connected component. The theorem gives a sufficient rank uniformly over rings of bounded stable range. For a field, one can take s = 1. At length one the theorem guarantees a filling for every cycle from rank four onwards.

Four-transvection simultaneous straightening of a split pair, coset-preserving linear shears, and head-projection unimodularity

Why do the column reduction of the split double complex, the inductive rank step on affine coordinate links, and the head-splitting prefix retraction require three distinct linear-algebraic mechanisms rather than naive Gaussian elimination? Over an arbitrary commutative ring R of stable range at most s, moving a unimodular column vector v ∈ Rn+1 (n ≥ s) to the last standard basis vector en does not automatically carry its chosen dual covector f (f · v = 1) to the last coordinate functional en*: after a product g0 = g3g2g1 of three rank-one transvections shortens the row, sets the last entry of the vector to 1, and clears its first n entries, the contragredient covector f′ = fg0−1 satisfies f′ · en = f · v = 1 while retaining arbitrary entries in coordinates 0, …, n − 1. Because the residual row f′ − en annihilates en, left-multiplying by a fourth rank-one transvection g4 = In+1 + en(f′ − en)T fixes en on column vectors while its contragredient inverse subtracts (f′ · en)(f′ − en) = f′ − en from f′, straightening vector and covector simultaneously inside GLn+1(R). Second, inside the finitely supported sequence module M∞ = ⨁k≥0 R ek, normalizing a prefix letter within Ln+1 ∪ An+1,j requires invertible shears ψ(x) = x + h(x)t that preserve both the low coordinate subspace and every affine coset; choosing t inside the low subspace with h(t) = 0 confines the displacement ±h(x)t to coordinates below the cutoff for both ψ and ψ−1. Third, once a head vector u ∈ M satisfies φ(u) = 1, testing whether a prepended list [u] ++ l belongs to the unimodular set 𝒰(M) reduces to unimodularity of the projected tail P(l) under P(x) = x − φ(x)u by lifting any dual forms Hk on P(l) along P and correcting φ by −∑k φ(xk)(Hk ∘ P).

1. Simultaneous split-pair straightening, coset-preserving shears, and head-projection splitting. Let R be a commutative ring with identity 1. On Rm (m ∈ ℕ, with coordinates indexed by 0, …, m − 1), identify row covectors with elements of Rm via the standard dot product b · a = ∑k=0m−1 bkak (so on Rn+1 the last standard basis vector en also represents the last coordinate functional en*(x) = en · x = xn), and for a, b ∈ Rm set Ta,b = Im + abT. Say that R has stable range at most s ∈ ℕ if for every integer d ≥ s and every tuple (r0, …, rd−1, rd) ∈ Rd+1 generating the unit ideal R, there exist t0, …, td−1 ∈ R such that (r0 + t0rd, …, rd−1 + td−1rd) ∈ Rd generates R. Let M∞ = ⨁k≥0 R ek denote the module of finitely supported R-sequences, with low coordinate span Ln = spanR{e0, …, en−1} = {x ∈ M∞ : xk = 0 for all k ≥ n} and affine translate An,j = ej + Ln = {x ∈ M∞ : x − ej ∈ Ln} (n, j ∈ ℕ). For any R-module M, write 𝒰(M) for the set of ordered lists l = [x0, …, xq−1] (q ∈ ℕ) in M admitting simultaneous dual functionals F0, …, Fq−1 ∈ HomR(M, R) with Fi(xj) = δi,j (0 ≤ i, j < q).

Proposition (Four-transvection split straightening, coset-preserving shears, and head-projection unimodularity).

(i) For every m ∈ ℕ and all a, b ∈ Rm with b · a = 0, one has (abT)² = 0 and Ta,b ∈ GLm(R) with inverse Ta,b−1 = Im − abT, satisfying Ta,bx = x + (b · x)a and rTa,b−1 = r − (r · a)b for all x, r ∈ Rm. Whenever R has stable range at most s ∈ ℕ, n ∈ ℕ satisfies s ≤ n, and v, f ∈ Rn+1 satisfy f · v = 1, there exists a product g = g4g3g2g1 ∈ GLn+1(R) of four rank-one transvections such that

Ta,bx = x + (b · x)a,   rTa,b−1 = r − (r · a)b,   gv = en,   fg−1 = en.

(ii) For every n ∈ ℕ, every h ∈ HomR(M∞, R), and every t ∈ Ln with h(t) = 0, the map ψ(x) = x + h(x)t is an R-linear automorphism of M∞ with inverse ψ−1(x) = x − h(x)t satisfying ψ(x) ∈ Ln ⟺ x ∈ Ln and ψ(x) ∈ An,j ⟺ x ∈ An,j for all x ∈ M∞ and j ∈ ℕ.

(iii) For every R-module M, every φ ∈ HomR(M, R), every u ∈ M with φ(u) = 1, and every ordered list l = [x0, …, xq−1] (q ∈ ℕ) in M, the projection P(x) = x − φ(x)u and entrywise projected list P(l) = [P(x0), …, P(xq−1)] satisfy

P(x) = x − φ(x)u,   P(u) = 0,   [u] ++ l ∈ 𝒰(M)   ⟺   P(l) ∈ 𝒰(M).

Proof. For (i), when b · a = 0, associativity gives (abT)² = a(bTa)bT = (b · a)(abT) = 0, so (Im + abT)(Im − abT) = Im = (Im − abT)(Im + abT), and direct multiplication yields Ta,bx = x + (b · x)a and rTa,b−1 = r − (r · a)b for all x, r ∈ Rm. Now assume s ≤ n and f · v = ∑k=0n fkvk = 1. Because (v0, …, vn−1, vn) generates R and n ≥ s, stable range provides t0, …, tn−1 ∈ R and coefficients c0, …, cn−1 ∈ R such that ∑i=0n−1 ci(vi + tivn) = 1. Put a = (t0, …, tn−1, 0) ∈ Rn+1 and c′ = (c0, …, cn−1, 0) ∈ Rn+1. First, since en · a = 0, setting g1 = Ta,en gives w = g1v = v + vna with wi = vi + tivn for 0 ≤ i < n, whence c′ · w = 1. Second, since ((1 − wn)c′) · en = 0, setting g2 = Ten,(1−wn)c′ gives u = g2w = w + (1 − wn)(c′ · w)en with last coordinate un = wn + (1 − wn) = 1. Third, since en · (en − u) = 1 − un = 0, setting g3 = Ten−u,en gives g3u = u + un(en − u) = en. With g0 = g3g2g1 ∈ GLn+1(R), we have g0v = en, so f′ = fg0−1 satisfies f′n = f′ · (g0v) = f · v = 1. Fourth, since (f′ − en) · en = f′n − 1 = 0, setting g4 = Ten,f′−en and g = g4g0 ∈ GLn+1(R) yields gv = g4en = en + ((f′ − en) · en)en = en and fg−1 = f′g4−1 = f′ − (f′ · en)(f′ − en) = en.

For (ii), R-linearity of h makes ψ and ψ−1(x) = x − h(x)t R-linear, and h(t) = 0 gives ψ−1(ψ(x)) = x + h(x)t − (h(x) + h(x)h(t))t = x and ψ(ψ−1(x)) = x. Since t ∈ Ln and Ln is an R-submodule, h(x)t ∈ Ln for every x ∈ M∞; hence ψ(x) = x + h(x)t lies in Ln if and only if x ∈ Ln, and ψ(x) − ej = (x − ej) + h(x)t lies in Ln if and only if x − ej ∈ Ln.

For (iii), note that P ∈ HomR(M, M) satisfies P(u) = u − φ(u)u = 0. If [u] ++ l ∈ 𝒰(M) has duals F0, F1, …, Fq ∈ HomR(M, R), then Fi+1(u) = 0 for each 0 ≤ i < q, so Fi+1(P(xj)) = Fi+1(xj) − φ(xj)Fi+1(u) = δi,j, witnessing P(l) ∈ 𝒰(M). Conversely, if H0, …, Hq−1 ∈ HomR(M, R) satisfy Hi(P(xj)) = δi,j, define F0 = φ − ∑k=0q−1 φ(xk)(Hk ∘ P) and Fi+1 = Hi ∘ P (0 ≤ i < q); then P(u) = 0 gives F0(u) = 1 and Fi+1(u) = 0, while for 0 ≤ j < q one has F0(xj) = φ(xj) − φ(xj) = 0 and Fi+1(xj) = δi,j, witnessing [u] ++ l ∈ 𝒰(M).

Nilpotent outer-product square, contragredient row action, coset coordinate invariance, and Kronecker-delta verification of lifted duals

In coordinates on Rm, the outer product N = abT has (i, j)-entry aibj, so ((abT)²)i,j = ∑k=0m−1 aibkakbj = (b · a)aibj = 0 when b · a = 0. For x, r ∈ Rm, commutativity of R gives (Ta,bx)i = xi + ∑j=0m−1 aibjxj = xi + (b · x)ai and (rTa,b−1)j = rj − ∑i=0m−1 riaibj = rj − (r · a)bj. Moreover, for any g ∈ GLn+1(R), (fg−1) · (gv) = f · (g−1gv) = f · v, justifying f′n = f′ · en = (fg0−1) · (g0v) = 1 at the fourth step.

In M∞, since t ∈ Ln satisfies tk = 0 for every index k ≥ n, every x ∈ M∞ obeys (ψ(x))k = xk + h(x)tk = xk and (ψ(x) − ej)k = (x − ej)k for all k ≥ n, immediately giving ψ(x) ∈ Ln ⟺ x ∈ Ln and ψ(x) ∈ An,j ⟺ x ∈ An,j. Finally, on the indexed list z = [u, x0, …, xq−1] of length q + 1, checking all index pairs (μ, ν) ∈ {0, …, q}² splits into four cases: (0, 0) gives F0(u) = φ(u) − ∑k=0q−1 φ(xk)Hk(0) = 1; (0, j + 1) gives F0(xj) = φ(xj) − ∑k=0q−1 φ(xk)δk,j = 0; (i + 1, 0) gives Fi+1(u) = Hi(0) = 0; and (i + 1, j + 1) gives Fi+1(xj) = Hi(P(xj)) = δi,j = δi+1,j+1.

Prefix-concatenation boundary Leibniz rule, prepending cone homotopy, and equivariant transport of link exactness

Why can the right-to-left prefix retraction, the row-kernel retraction, and the inductive rank step attach local tail fillings after an arbitrary prefix τ without recomputing alternating deletion signs across the entire word? In the free abelian chain group ℤ[List(V)] generated by basis elements ⟨l⟩ for ordered lists l over an alphabet V, deleting the i-th entry of a concatenated list τ ++ w partitions at the prefix length |τ|: indices 0 ≤ i < |τ| delete inside τ while keeping the tail w intact, whereas indices i = |τ| + j delete the j-th entry of w with shifted sign (−1)|τ|+j, yielding the graded Leibniz formula ∂(τ ++ c) = ((∂⟨τ⟩) ++ c) + (−1)|τ|(τ ++ ∂c). When τ = [x] is a single letter, its augmented boundary is ∂⟨[x]⟩ = ⟨[]⟩, so the prepending operator κx(⟨l⟩) = ⟨[x] ++ l⟩ satisfies the contracting cone identity ∂ ∘ κx = id − κx ∘ ∂, which both fills cycles in coneable links and proves ∂² = 0 by induction on list length. Moreover, because face deletion depends solely on list indices, any injective alphabet map e : V → W induces chain isomorphisms Cp(F) ≅ Cp(e*(F)), identifying finite-rank unimodular sequences 𝒰m in Rm with the empty-prefix low-coordinate link in M∞ and pulling link exactness back along coset-preserving linear automorphisms.

1. Prefix boundary calculus, injective alphabet functoriality, and linear-equivalence link pullback. For any set V, let List(V) denote the set of finite ordered lists l = [x0, …, xm−1] of length |l| = m (with empty list [], concatenation τ ++ w, and i-th face deletion l(i) = [x0, …, x̂i, …, xm−1] omitting entry i for 0 ≤ i < m), and let ℤ[List(V)] be the free abelian group of finite ℤ-linear combinations of basis generators ⟨l⟩ (l ∈ List(V)), equipped with the augmented alternating face-deletion boundary ∂⟨[]⟩ = 0 and ∂⟨l⟩ = ∑i=0m−1 (−1)i⟨l(i)⟩ for m ≥ 1 (so ∂⟨[x]⟩ = ⟨[]⟩). For F ⊆ List(V) and p ∈ ℕ, put Cp(F) = ℤ[{⟨l⟩ : l ∈ F, |l| = p}], say that F is exact at length p if every c ∈ Cp(F) with ∂c = 0 equals ∂B for some B ∈ Cp+1(F), and for X ⊆ V and τ ∈ List(V) define linkX(F, τ) = {w ∈ List(V) : (∀ u ∈ w, u ∈ X) and τ ++ w ∈ F}. For an injective map e : V → W, write e*([x0, …, xm−1]) = [e(x0), …, e(xm−1)], e*(⟨l⟩) = ⟨e*(l)⟩, and e*(F) = {e*(l) : l ∈ F}. Over a commutative ring R with identity, set 𝒰m = 𝒰(Rm)—identifying HomR(Rm, R) with row covectors g ∈ Rm via v ↦ g · v—and let embm : Rm ↪ M∞ embed Rm onto the first m coordinates Lm ⊆ M∞.

Proposition (Graded prefix Leibniz rule, cone identity ∂² = 0, and equivariant link exactness transport).

(i) For every prefix τ ∈ List(V), every letter x ∈ V, and every chain c = ∑w aw⟨w⟩ ∈ ℤ[List(V)], writing τ ++ c = ∑w aw⟨τ ++ w⟩, (∂⟨τ⟩) ++ c = ∑w aw((∂⟨τ⟩) ++ ⟨w⟩) (where ⟨σ⟩ ++ ⟨w⟩ = ⟨σ ++ w⟩ extends ℤ-linearly in σ), and κx(c) = [x] ++ c, one has

∂(τ ++ c) = ((∂⟨τ⟩) ++ c) + (−1)|τ|(τ ++ ∂c),   ∂(κx(c)) = c − κx(∂c),   ∂(∂c) = 0.

(ii) For every injective map e : V → W, its linear extension e* : ℤ[List(V)] → ℤ[List(W)] is injective, satisfies ∂ ∘ e* = e* ∘ ∂, and restricts for each F ⊆ List(V) and p ∈ ℕ to a bijection Cp(F) ≅ Cp(e*(F)), so e*(F) is exact at length p if and only if F is exact at length p. Moreover, for all m, q ∈ ℕ,

embm*(𝒰m) = linkLm(𝒰(M∞), []),   (ψ−1)*(linkX(𝒰(M), ψ*(τ))) = linkX(𝒰(M), τ),

so exactness of linkLm(𝒰(M∞), []) at length q implies exactness of 𝒰m at length q.

(iii) In the second identity above, for every R-module M, subset X ⊆ M, prefix τ ∈ List(M), length p ∈ ℕ, and R-linear automorphism ψ : M ≅R M satisfying ψ(y) ∈ X ⟺ y ∈ X for all y ∈ M, exactness of linkX(𝒰(M), ψ*(τ)) at length p implies exactness of linkX(𝒰(M), τ) at length p. In particular, when R has stable range at most s ∈ ℕ, s ≤ n, j ≥ n + 1, τ ∈ 𝒰(M∞) is nonempty, and linkLn ∪ An,k(𝒰(M∞), σ) is exact at length q for every k ≥ n, σ ∈ 𝒰(M∞), and q ∈ ℕ with q + s + |σ| ≤ n + 1, the link linkLn+1 ∪ An+1,j(𝒰(M∞), τ) is exact at every length p satisfying p + s + |τ| ≤ n + 2.

Proof. For (i), on any basis generator ⟨w⟩, splitting the deletion indices 0 ≤ i < |τ| + |w| of τ ++ w into 0 ≤ i < |τ| (deleting entry i inside τ before appending w) and i = |τ| + j with 0 ≤ j < |w| (preserving τ and deleting entry j inside w with sign (−1)|τ|+j) gives ∂⟨τ ++ w⟩ = ((∂⟨τ⟩) ++ ⟨w⟩) + (−1)|τ|(τ ++ ∂⟨w⟩); extending linearly over c = ∑w aw⟨w⟩ yields the Leibniz rule. Taking τ = [x] (|τ| = 1, ∂⟨[x]⟩ = ⟨[]⟩, ⟨[]⟩ ++ c = c) gives ∂(κx(c)) = c − κx(∂c). On basis generators ⟨l⟩, induction on |l| gives ∂(∂⟨[]⟩) = 0 and, assuming ∂(∂⟨l⟩) = 0, ∂(∂⟨[x] ++ l⟩) = ∂(⟨l⟩ − κx(∂⟨l⟩)) = ∂⟨l⟩ − (∂⟨l⟩ − κx(∂(∂⟨l⟩))) = 0, whence ∂(∂c) = 0 by linearity.

For (ii), entrywise application of an injection e : V → W is injective on List(V), preserves length, and commutes with omitting the i-th entry, so e* is injective on ℤ[List(V)], satisfies ∂ ∘ e* = e* ∘ ∂, and maps Cp(F) bijectively onto Cp(e*(F)), giving the exactness equivalence. Writing πm : M∞ → Rm for projection onto the first m coordinates (πm ∘ embm = idRm), extending dual covectors gi ∈ Rm to x ↦ gi · πm(x) on M∞ shows embm*(𝒰m) ⊆ linkLm(𝒰(M∞), []), while restricting duals Fi on M∞ to Fi ∘ embm on any list in Lm = embm(Rm) proves equality; transport along embm then gives exactness of 𝒰m.

For (iii), an R-linear automorphism ψ : M ≅R M preserves 𝒰(M) in both directions (transporting duals by precomposition with ψ−1 or ψ) and preserves X under both ψ and ψ−1, so w ∈ linkX(𝒰(M), ψ*(τ)) holds if and only if (ψ−1)*(w) ∈ linkX(𝒰(M), τ); injective transport along ψ−1 transfers exactness at length p. When s ≤ n, j ≥ n + 1, and τ = [u] ++ τ0 ∈ 𝒰(M∞) has 0-th dual f (f(u) = 1), setting h1 = f − ∑i=0n−1 f(ei)ei* gives ∑i=0n−1 f(ei)ui + h1(u) = 1, so stable range provides t ∈ Ln ⊆ Ln+1 (h1(t) = 0) and h2 = ∑i=0n−1 ciei* (h2(en) = 0) whose two shears ψ1(x) = x + h1(x)t and ψ2(x) = x + h2(x)en from the coset-preserving shear proposition compose to ψ = ψ2 ∘ ψ1 preserving X = Ln+1 ∪ An+1,j with u′n = (ψ(u))n = 1. On τ′ = ψ*(τ) = [u′] ++ τ′0, every word in Sn = Ln ∪ An,j has n-th coordinate 0 (as j ≥ n + 1) and is fixed by P(y) = y − ynu′, so head-projection unimodularity identifies each restricted link of τ′ ++ τ1 (|τ1| ≤ p) in Sn with linkSn(𝒰(M∞), P(τ′0 ++ τ1)), which is exact at length p − |τ1| by the rank-n hypothesis at k = j; right-to-left prefix retraction via (i) fills every p-cycle of linkX(𝒰(M∞), τ′), and pullback along ψ concludes.

Deletion-index splitting across concatenated words, dual restriction, and self-contained two-shear prefix retraction

Let τ = [t0, …, tr−1] and w = [y0, …, yq−1]. When r = 0, τ = [], ∂⟨[]⟩ = 0, and (−1)0 = 1, so both sides of ∂⟨τ ++ w⟩ = ((∂⟨τ⟩) ++ ⟨w⟩) + (−1)|τ|(τ ++ ∂⟨w⟩) equal ∂⟨w⟩. When r ≥ 1 and q = 0, w = [], ∂⟨[]⟩ = 0, and appending [] is the identity on lists, so both sides equal ∂⟨τ⟩. When r ≥ 1 and q ≥ 1, deleting entry i ∈ {0, …, r + q − 1} of [t0, …, tr−1, y0, …, yq−1] yields τ(i) ++ w for 0 ≤ i < r (including r = 1, where τ(0) = [] and ∂⟨[t0]⟩ = ⟨[]⟩) and yields τ ++ w(j) for i = r + j (0 ≤ j < q) with sign (−1)r+j = (−1)r(−1)j. Summing over i proves ∂⟨τ ++ w⟩ = ((∂⟨τ⟩) ++ ⟨w⟩) + (−1)r(τ ++ ∂⟨w⟩).

In the coordinate-subspace identification, if w = [x0, …, xq−1] ∈ linkLm(𝒰(M∞), []), each xa ∈ Lm has support in {0, …, m − 1} and therefore satisfies embm(πm(xa)) = xa; if F0, …, Fq−1 ∈ HomR(M∞, R) satisfy Fi(xa) = δi,a, then the row covectors gi = (Fi(e0), …, Fi(em−1)) ∈ Rm satisfy gi · πm(xa) = Fi(xa) = δi,a, showing [πm(x0), …, πm(xq−1)] ∈ 𝒰m and w ∈ embm*(𝒰m). Finally, in the rank step of (iii), stable range on (u0, …, un−1, h1(u)) gives t0, …, tn−1, c0, …, cn−1 ∈ R with ∑i=0n−1 ci(ui + tih1(u)) = 1 − un, so u″ = ψ1(u) satisfies u″n = un and h2(u″) = 1 − un, hence (ψ2(u″))n = 1. Putting F′ = linkX(𝒰(M∞), τ′) and Sn = Ln ∪ An,j, for any τ1 ∈ F′ with |τ1| ≤ p, applying P(y) = y − en*(y)u′ to [u′] ++ (τ′0 ++ τ1 ++ w) fixes every w in Sn and shows linkSn(F′, τ1) = linkSn(𝒰(M∞), P(τ′0 ++ τ1)), exact at length p − |τ1| since (p − |τ1|) + s + (|τ| + |τ1| − 1) = p + s + |τ| − 1 ≤ n + 1. Inducting downward on m = p, …, 0 over cycles c ∈ Cp(F′) whose entries at indices ≥ m lie in Sn, grouping terms at step m + 1 → m with entry m outside Sn by their length-(m + 1) prefix τ1 writes c = c0 + ∑τ1 (τ1 ++ zτ1) where prefix deletions shift entry m to index m − 1 so ∂c = 0 forces ∂zτ1 = 0; choosing ∂Bτ1 = zτ1 in Cp−m(linkSn(F′, τ1)) and subtracting ∂(∑τ1 (−1)m+1(τ1 ++ Bτ1)) via (i) moves all offending entries below index m, until at m = 0 (τ1 = []) exactness of linkSn(F′, []) bounds the retracted cycle in Cp+1(F′).

Finite-support fiber decomposition of vertical and horizontal double-complex slices and chain isomorphism to the permutation representation complex

Why does exactness of each nonempty column or row fiber immediately force vertical or horizontal exactness across the entire pair-sequence double complex Da,b(𝒟) in the double-complex zigzag, and how does untyped exactness of split-pair lists transfer to the typed GLn(R)-permutation complex in the homological stability argument? Every double chain x ∈ Da,b(𝒟) has finite support in List(V) × List(W), so projecting supp(x) onto its first coordinate visits only finitely many prefixes l ∈ T1 ⊂ List(V) of length a. Because the vertical boundary ∂v acts purely on the second factor while leaving l fixed, the vertical boundaries of distinct l-slices occupy pairwise disjoint fibers {l} × List(W); a double chain is therefore ∂v-closed if and only if each finite slice gl is closed in its column fiber Col𝒟(l), and summing finite fillings yl over l ∈ T1 stays finitely supported in Da,b+1(𝒟). Symmetrically, currying along the finite second-coordinate support T2 ⊂ List(W) converts row-fiber exactness into horizontal fillings for ∂h. Finally, the group-homology spectral sequence acts on the typed free abelian modules ℤ[𝒮n,p] generated by split lists of fixed length p, whereas the double-complex retraction operates inside the single untyped chain group ℤ[List(Rn × Rn)]; because the linear extension Φp = ηp* of subtype inclusion ηp is injective with image Cp(𝒮n) and intertwines the representation face differential dp with ∂, untyped exactness at length 0 gives surjectivity onto ℤ[𝒮n,0] ≅ ℤ and untyped exactness at length p + 1 gives ker(dp) = im(dp+1) (consumed downstream in the range s + 1 ≤ n and 2(p + 1) + s + 1 ≤ n once the untyped split-sequence exactness bound is established).

1. Fiberwise double-complex slice exactness and typed split-simplex chain isomorphism. Let V and W be sets with augmented sequence boundaries ∂V on ℤ[List(V)] and ∂W on ℤ[List(W)]. For any relation 𝒟 ⊆ List(V) × List(W) and integers a, b ∈ ℕ, let Da,b(𝒟) ⊆ ℤ[List(V) × List(W)] denote the subgroup of finite ℤ-linear combinations x = ∑(l,w) x(l, w)⟨(l, w)⟩ supported on pairs (l, w) ∈ 𝒟 with |l| = a and |w| = b, with horizontal differential ∂h(⟨(l, w)⟩) = ∑i=0|l|−1 (−1)i⟨(l(i), w)⟩ and vertical differential ∂v(⟨(l, w)⟩) = ∑k=0|w|−1 (−1)k⟨(l, w(k))⟩ (written h and v in the split double complex), column fibers Col𝒟(l) = {w ∈ List(W) : (l, w) ∈ 𝒟}, and row fibers Row𝒟(w) = {l ∈ List(V) : (l, w) ∈ 𝒟}. Over a commutative ring R with identity and n ∈ ℕ, let 𝒮n ⊆ List(Rn × Rn) be the set of split lists [(v0, λ0), …, (vp−1, λp−1)] satisfying λi · vj = δi,j (0 ≤ i, j < p), and for each p ∈ ℕ set 𝒮n,p = {l ∈ 𝒮n : |l| = p} with inclusion ηp : 𝒮n,p ↪ List(Rn × Rn), ℤ-linear extension Φp : ℤ[𝒮n,p] → ℤ[List(Rn × Rn)] sending ⟨σ⟩ to ⟨ηp(σ)⟩, and alternating face differential dp : ℤ[𝒮n,p+1] → ℤ[𝒮n,p] sending ⟨σ⟩ to ∑i=0p (−1)i⟨∂i(σ)⟩, where ∂i(σ) ∈ 𝒮n,p deletes the i-th pair of σ.

Proposition (Double-complex column and row slice exactness and typed split-chain isomorphism).

(i) Let 𝒟 ⊆ List(V) × List(W) and a, b ∈ ℕ. For any x ∈ Da,b(𝒟), setting T1 = {l ∈ List(V) : ∃ w, x(l, w) ≠ 0}, T2 = {w ∈ List(W) : ∃ l, x(l, w) ≠ 0}, gl = ∑w x(l, w)⟨w⟩, ιl(⟨w⟩) = ⟨(l, w)⟩, pw(x) = ∑l x(l, w)⟨l⟩, and jw(⟨l⟩) = ⟨(l, w)⟩ yields

x = ∑l∈T1 ιl(gl) = ∑w∈T2 jw(pw(x)),   ∂v(ιl(gl)) = ιl(∂Wgl),   ∂h(jw(pw(x))) = jw(∂Vpw(x)).

If Col𝒟(l) is exact at length b for every l ∈ List(V) with |l| = a and Col𝒟(l) ≠ ∅, then every x ∈ Da,b(𝒟) with ∂vx = 0 equals ∂vy for some y ∈ Da,b+1(𝒟). Symmetrically, if Row𝒟(w) is exact at length a for every w ∈ List(W) with |w| = b and Row𝒟(w) ≠ ∅, then every x ∈ Da,b(𝒟) with ∂hx = 0 equals ∂hy for some y ∈ Da+1,b(𝒟).

(ii) For all n, p ∈ ℕ, Φp is injective with image Cp(𝒮n), satisfies Φp(dp(c)) = ∂(Φp+1(c)) for all c ∈ ℤ[𝒮n,p+1], and satisfies dp(dp+1(c′)) = 0 for all c′ ∈ ℤ[𝒮n,p+2]. Exactness of 𝒮n at length 0 implies surjectivity of d0 : ℤ[𝒮n,1] → ℤ[𝒮n,0], and exactness of 𝒮n at length p + 1 implies ker(dp) = im(dp+1) in

Φp(ℤ[𝒮n,p]) = Cp(𝒮n),   Φp(dp(c)) = ∂(Φp+1(c)),   ⋯ ⟶ ℤ[𝒮n,2] ⟶d1 ℤ[𝒮n,1] ⟶d0 ℤ[𝒮n,0] ⟶ 0.

Proof. For (i), let x ∈ Da,b(𝒟) satisfy ∂vx = 0. Finiteness of supp(x) makes T1 finite, and every l ∈ T1 satisfies |l| = a, Col𝒟(l) ≠ ∅, and gl ∈ Cb(Col𝒟(l)), with x = ∑l∈T1 ιl(gl). On basis generators, ∂v(ιl(⟨w⟩)) = ∂v(⟨(l, w)⟩) = ιl(∂W⟨w⟩), so 0 = ∂vx = ∑l∈T1 ιl(∂Wgl). Because supp(ιl(∂Wgl)) ⊆ {l} × List(W) are pairwise disjoint across distinct l ∈ T1, ∂Wgl = 0 for every l ∈ T1. Choosing yl ∈ Cb+1(Col𝒟(l)) with ∂Wyl = gl and setting y = ∑l∈T1 ιl(yl) ∈ Da,b+1(𝒟) gives ∂vy = ∑l∈T1 ιl(∂Wyl) = x. Exchanging the two coordinates over the finite set T2 with ∂h(jw(c)) = jw(∂Vc) proves the horizontal claim.

For (ii), injectivity of ηp makes Φp injective with image ℤ[{⟨l⟩ : l ∈ 𝒮n, |l| = p}] = Cp(𝒮n). For each σ ∈ 𝒮n,p+1, ηp(∂i(σ)) deletes the i-th entry of ηp+1(σ) (0 ≤ i ≤ p), giving Φp(dp(⟨σ⟩)) = ∂(Φp+1(⟨σ⟩)) and hence Φp(dp(c)) = ∂(Φp+1(c)) by linearity. Using ∂(∂u) = 0 from the prepending cone identity gives Φp(dp(dp+1(c′))) = ∂(∂(Φp+2(c′))) = 0, so dp(dp+1(c′)) = 0 by injectivity of Φp, which in particular implies im(dp+1) ⊆ ker(dp). Finally, for c0 ∈ ℤ[𝒮n,0], Φ0(c0) ∈ C0(𝒮n) = ℤ[⟨[]⟩] satisfies ∂(Φ0(c0)) = 0, so exactness at length 0 yields B = Φ1(B0) ∈ C1(𝒮n) with Φ0(d0(B0)) = ∂B = Φ0(c0), hence d0(B0) = c0; and for c0 ∈ ker(dp) ⊆ ℤ[𝒮n,p+1], ∂(Φp+1(c0)) = Φp(dp(c0)) = 0, so exactness at length p + 1 yields B = Φp+2(B0) ∈ Cp+2(𝒮n) with Φp+1(dp+1(B0)) = ∂B = Φp+1(c0), hence dp+1(B0) = c0 and ker(dp) = im(dp+1).

Disjoint support evaluation on double-complex fibers, horizontal row symmetry, and basis-simplex verification of the face differential

For fixed l ∈ List(V) and any chain c ∈ ℤ[List(W)], evaluating ιl(c) at (l′, u) ∈ List(V) × List(W) gives c(u) when l′ = l and 0 when l′ ≠ l. Moreover, each yl ∈ Cb+1(Col𝒟(l)) is supported on lists w′ ∈ Col𝒟(l) of length b + 1, so every pair in supp(ιl(yl)) has the form (l, w′) ∈ 𝒟 with |l| = a and |w′| = b + 1, confirming y = ∑l∈T1 ιl(yl) ∈ Da,b+1(𝒟) because Da,b+1(𝒟) is closed under finite sums.

In the horizontal mirror, for fixed w ∈ List(W) and c ∈ ℤ[List(V)], (jw(c))(u, w′) equals c(u) when w′ = w and 0 when w′ ≠ w, and ∂h(jw(⟨l⟩)) = ∑i=0|l|−1 (−1)i⟨(l(i), w)⟩ = jw(∂V⟨l⟩); evaluating ∂hx = ∑w∈T2 jw(∂Vpw(x)) = 0 at (u, w0) gives (∂Vpw0(x))(u) = 0 for each w0 ∈ T2, and summing jw(zw) over zw ∈ Ca+1(Row𝒟(w)) produces y ∈ Da+1,b(𝒟) with ∂hy = x. Finally, for any σ = [(v0, λ0), …, (vp, λp)] ∈ 𝒮n,p+1, its length is p + 1 ≥ 1 and ∂i(σ) omits the i-th pair while preserving λa · vb = δa,b on the remaining p pairs, so Φp(dp(⟨σ⟩)) = ∑i=0p (−1)i⟨ηp(∂i(σ))⟩ = ∂(⟨ηp+1(σ)⟩).

What the detecting cycles can miss

The cycle bound controls the image of a twisted norm. Here is how much of the arithmetic count that image can miss. Keep the enlarged field L′ fixed, with r₂ complex places. At depth ν the cyclic layer F/L′ has generator γ and degree n = ℓν−c. Write q = ℓν, a = (1 + ℓc)e and f = vℓ(e) for the positive twist e. Write 𝓧 for the group of equivariant characters at this depth. Each element assigns a value φ(P) in ℤ/q to each prime ideal, vanishes on principal divisors when extended additively, and satisfies φ(γ−1P) = aφ(P). Define C by quotienting the ideal class group of F by the image of γ−1 − a. Each φ descends to C and is recovered from its values on primes. Its target is an ℓ-group, so there are at most |C|ℓ such characters, where |·|ℓ means the ℓ-part of a finite group order.

Where the matching power of q comes from. Write E for the integral units 𝒪F× modulo roots of unity and the image of γ−1 − a, using additive notation. The finite group W in the norm construction satisfies |W| = |E| |C|. Indeed, its map to the class group has unit kernel E and image the kernel of γ−1 − a on that group. A finite group endomorphism has kernel and cokernel of equal order. To compute |E|, take logarithms of units at the infinite places and add one constant coordinate direction to complete the unit lattice. Above each complex place of L′ the action permutes n places in a cycle. On this block the absolute determinant of the permutation minus a times the identity is an − 1. The extra constant direction contributes a − 1. Thus |E|(a − 1) = (an − 1)r₂.

The valuation formula vℓ((1 + ℓc)h − 1) = c + vℓ(h) holds for positive h, with c ≥ 1 and c ≥ 2 when ℓ = 2. Apply it with h = e and h = en. The unit identity gives |E|ℓ ℓc+f = ℓ(ν+f)r₂ ≥ qr₂. The second valuation also shows that the exact valuation of (an − 1)/q is f. For example, at ℓ = 3, c = 2, e = 3 and ν = 3 we have a = 1000 and n = 3. The number 1000³ − 1 has 3-adic valuation 4. Dividing by 27 leaves valuation 1. Increasing ν by one also increases the numerator’s valuation by one.

Why the kernel cost stays bounded. Write N for the twisted norm, additively, and δ = γ−1 − a. Expanding the geometric sum gives δN = Nδ = (1 − an)γ−1. If ℓbN(y) is a q-multiple modulo roots of unity, applying δ and dividing by q in the torsion-free quotient shows that ℓb(an − 1)/q kills the class of y in W. On its ℓ-primary part the prime-to-ℓ factor is invertible. The kernel there is killed by ℓb+f. Each multiplication by ℓ on W[ℓj] has image in W[ℓj−1] and kernel of size at most |W[ℓ]|. It remains to count just the elements killed by ℓ.

Those elements inject into invariant classes represented by α with all valuations divisible by ℓ. If ρ generates the roots of unity in F, their invariance gives γα/α = vℓρt, 0 ≤ t < ℓ. For each t the field norm of v has at most ℓ possible values, since its ℓth power is Norm(ρ)−t. Equal pairs (t, Norm(v)) give a norm-one ratio of the two v’s. Hilbert’s Theorem 90 then lets the ratio of the two α’s descend to the base field modulo ℓth powers. Its valuations away from ℓ remain divisible by ℓ because the layer is unramified there. The base-field classes with this property have at most ℓ2D+⌊log₂ h⌋ elements, where D = [L′:ℚ] and h is its class number. The three contributions come from units modulo ℓth powers, ℓ-torsion ideal classes, and the valuations modulo ℓ at primes over ℓ. The ≤ ℓ² choices of the pair thus give |W[ℓ]| ≤ ℓg for g = 2D + ⌊log₂ h⌋ + 2.

|𝓧| qr₂ ≤ B ℓX,   X = (b + f)g + c + f.

Here B bounds the image seen by the detecting cycles. The kernel costs ℓ(b+f)g and the unit comparison costs ℓc+f. In the application B = qr₂T2e+1T2e, so cancelling the positive common factor leaves |𝓧| ≤ T2e+1T2eℓX. The base field, twist, and b were fixed before ν. This bound therefore applies at every allowed depth ν ≥ c.

Where the exponent 150 comes from

The torsion proof uses an exact complex with bounds on the numbers of orbits and on stabilizers. In degree j ≤ 2e + 1 and rank ≤ 4e + 6 it proves log Tj ≤ K24(e,n′,Δ′). Set u = 2en′ and Y = log(2Δ′). The class-number estimate and the bounds on b, c and f give X log ℓ ≤ u⁹Y. Taking logs in the character bound gives two contributions at most exp(u24Y) and the polynomial term. For u ≥ 2 and Y ≥ ½ the numerical comparison bounds their sum by exp(u26Y). Now put x = 2en. The layer estimates give u ≤ x⁵ and Y ≤ x¹¹ log(2Δ). Hence s(L) log ℓ ≤ K141(e,n,Δ), since 5 · 26 + 11 = 141.

How an integral boundary matrix bounds torsion

The character count above uses the orders of the torsion subgroups of two integral homology groups. A torsion class is killed by a nonzero integer. An infinite free summand in homology can therefore coexist with the finite quantity we need to bound. Start with a free lattice E = ℤr, with r ≤ A, and any set of integral relation vectors. Write Λ for their integer span. Suppose each relation has sum of absolute coordinates at most b, where b ≥ 1. The bound used in the proof is

|tors(E/Λ)| ≤ bA.

If we have r independent relation vectors, put them in a square matrix V. The sublattice they generate has index |det V|. Expanding the determinant as a signed sum over permutations and taking absolute values gives a sum of products. Allowing every choice of one column for each row only increases this sum, and the enlarged sum factors as ∏i ∑j |Vij|. This proves the bound br. Additional relations give a quotient of this finite group.

Suppose instead that the relation vectors span only a proper rational subspace. Choose a maximal independent subset and complete it to a rational basis using standard unit vectors. Let K be the integer span of that completed list. Its determinant still has absolute value at most br, since every added vector has length one. To compare torsion, choose a lift in E for each torsion class in E/Λ and reduce its lift modulo K. If two images coincide, the difference x of their lifts lies in K. Their difference class is torsion, so some nonzero multiple of x belongs to Λ. Consequently x lies in the rational span of the original relations. In the completed basis every coefficient of an added vector must then vanish. Because x belongs to K, the remaining coefficients are integers. Thus x is an integer combination of selected relations and the two classes were equal. This injects the set of torsion classes into the finite set E/K.

For example, impose the three relations (2,0,0), (0,2,0), (1,1,0) in ℤ³. The third coordinate stays free. In the first two coordinates a vector is a relation exactly when the coordinates have the same parity. Hence the torsion subgroup has order two. Choosing the first two relations and the third unit vector gives det V = 4. The general bound gives 2³ = 8. The three numbers measure respectively the actual torsion, the index for this completed list, and the estimate using the common row bound.

The extra cost in positive homological degree

Let a group G permute the simplex basis in each degree and commute with each face map. Suppose the augmented complex is exact through degree m. An orbit identifies simplices related by the action. A stabilizer fixes a specified simplex. Suppose there are at most A orbits per degree up to m and every corresponding stabilizer has order at most s ≥ 1. A boundary in degree m + 1 is an alternating sum of m + 2 faces. After identifying generators in the same orbit, coordinates add and the sum of their absolute values can only decrease. In degree zero the coefficient module at the end of the induction is generally a kernel. Identifying g x with x presents the coinvariants of that module. It gives the determinant factor (m + 2)A.

For positive degree, take the short exact sequence given by the first permutation module, its augmentation and its kernel. The connecting map in the long exact sequence compares the desired torsion with the torsion one degree lower for that kernel and the finite homology of the permutation module. For a single orbit the latter is the homology of the stabilizer by Shapiro’s lemma. A group of order h has hj bar generators in degree j > 0, and the two equivariant coefficient maps show that multiplication by h kills its positive-degree homology. The cycles form a subgroup of a free abelian group with that many generators, hence the homology has order at most hhʲ. Combining the orbits costs at most sA sʲ. Repeating the exact-sequence comparison for j = m, …, 1 gives

|tors Hm(G,ℤ)| ≤ (m + 2)A sm A sᵐ.

The last exponent uses ∑j=1m sj ≤ m sm. This part needs the orbit and stabilizer estimates, exactness of the complex, the long exact sequence, Shapiro’s lemma and annihilation of finite-group homology. Each supplies a distinct input.

For G = GLN(𝒪L) with L totally complex of degree n, the complex of ordered faces is exact, with an orbit bound A and the stabilizer bound s = 3nN². With N ≤ 4e + 6, 1 ≤ N and m ≤ 2e + 1 for e ≥ 1, substitution into the logarithm of the displayed bound gives the witness 24 in K24. The later character count and the change of field turn this into 5(max(24,9) + 2) + 11 = 141. In the character count the torsion estimate is applied over the enlarged field L′. The last numerical step expresses its degree and discriminant in terms of those of the original L.

Why the order of a stabilizer kills positive-degree homology

Suppose a group G acts transitively on a nonempty set X of faces. Choose a face x and write S for its stabilizer. The module ℤ[X] consists of finite integral sums of faces, with G permuting their labels. To compute its group homology we can keep just x and the group that fixes it.

Shapiro’s lemma for homology. For a subgroup S of G, a left ℤ[S]-module M, and any degree j ≥ 0, there is a natural isomorphism

Hj(G, ℤ[G] ⊗ℤ[S] M) ≅ Hj(S, M).

One proof starts with a free resolution of the trivial right ℤ[G]-module ℤ. On restriction to S it is still a free resolution, since the elements of each coset gS give a copy of the regular right module ℤ[S] in ℤ[G]. Tensoring that resolution over ℤ[G] with the induced module on the left of the formula gives, by associativity of tensor product, the same chain complex as tensoring it over ℤ[S] with M. For trivial M = ℤ, the induced module identifies with ℤ[X] by g ⊗ 1 ↦ [gx]. Indeed gx = g′x exactly when gS = g′S. C. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, lemma 6.3.2 and corollary 6.3.3[256].

Now suppose S is finite of order h. Give ℤ the trivial S-action and ℤ[S] the left regular action. Define two coefficient maps

ℤ → ℤ[S] → ℤ,   1 ↦ ∑t∈S[t],   [t] ↦ 1.

Left multiplication permutes the summands of the first image, and the second map sums coefficients. Both maps therefore respect the action. Their composite multiplies by h. Applying homology in degree j gives maps in the same order. On a representative chain their composite multiplies each coefficient by h, so it also multiplies the homology class by h. But the middle group is Hj(S, ℤ[S]) ≅ Hj({1}, ℤ) by Shapiro applied to the regular orbit. For j > 0 this group vanishes, since ℤ itself is a free resolution of length zero over the trivial group. Thus h kills every class in Hj(S, ℤ). In degree zero the middle group is ℤ. All basis elements [t] become equal in the coinvariants, so the first map multiplies by h and the second sends their common class to 1. The composite on H0(S, ℤ) = ℤ is still multiplication by h.

How many classes can one orbit contribute?

In positive degree j, the integral bar chain group with trivial coefficients has one generator for each ordered j-tuple of elements of S, including tuples with identity entries. Its rank is hj. The cycles form a subgroup of this free abelian group, hence are free of some rank r ≤ hj. One can see the rank bound by projecting onto the first coordinate. The image is cyclic, and the kernel lies in a free abelian group with one fewer coordinate. A lift of a generator of a nonzero image extends a basis of that kernel. The images of the r basis cycles generate homology. Since h kills each image, every class can be written with all coefficients between 0 and h − 1. This gives

|Hj(S, ℤ)| ≤ hr ≤ hhj.

Suppose now X has at most A orbits and every stabilizer is finite of order at most s, with s ≥ 1. Splitting a sum of faces by orbit splits ℤ[X] as a finite direct sum of permutation modules. The bar differential preserves these summands, so their homology groups also form a direct sum. Shapiro and the one-orbit bound give each summand order at most ssj. Multiplying these orders gives |Hj(G, ℤ[X])| ≤ sA sj. For X empty the group is zero and its order is one. This is the factor used once at each positive degree of the homology bound for the face complex. Weibel, §§6.5.1–6.5.4, the bar resolution[257].

A stabilizer of order two. Let S = {1, t} with t² = 1. Its free resolution has one copy of ℤ[S] in each degree. The differential is multiplication by t − 1 in odd degrees and by 1 + t in positive even degrees. To check exactness, write an element as a + bt. The first multiplier kills exactly the multiples of 1 + t, and the second kills exactly the multiples of t − 1. The augmentation also has kernel generated by t − 1. Tensor with the trivial module ℤ. The two differentials become 0 and 2, giving H1 ≅ ℤ/2 and H2 = 0. The actual orders are 2 and 1, within the respective one-orbit bounds 4 and 16. Weibel, calculation 6.2.1 and theorem 6.2.2[258].

How a stabilizer bound enters the next homological degree

Let ⋯ → C1 → C0 → M → 0 be a complex of integral G-modules, where Cp = ℤ[Xp] and G permutes the basis of faces. Fix j ≥ 1. Assume the complex is exact at M and at C0, …, Cj. Suppose each Xp up to degree j has at most A orbits and stabilizers of order at most s ≥ 1. Put K = ker(C0 → M). Exactness identifies K with the image of C1 → C0. Thus 0 → K → C0 → M → 0 is short exact. The tail ⋯ → C2 → C1 → K → 0 gives the complex for the next step. Its last map is the same boundary with its target restricted to its image, so its kernel is still the image of C2.

The connecting map. Apply the long exact homology sequence to the short exact sequence of coefficients. Indeed the bar resolution is free in each degree, so tensoring it with the three modules preserves exactness degree by degree. The resulting homology sequence has the following segment, exact at its middle term.

Hj(G, C0) → Hj(G, M) →δ Hj−1(G, K).

To see the degree drop, lift a cycle with coefficients in M to a chain with coefficients in C0. Its boundary maps to zero in the chains with coefficients in M, hence has coefficients in K. The class of this boundary is δ of the original class. Changing the lift adds a boundary with coefficients in K. If the original cycle changes by a boundary, lift a chain that produces that boundary and add its boundary to the old lift. Taking the boundary again gives zero for the added term. If δ vanishes, subtract a chain with coefficients in K whose boundary is that of the lift. The corrected lift is a cycle, which explains exactness at the middle term. Weibel, theorem 1.3.1, the long exact homology sequence[259].

In an exact segment U → V → W of abelian groups, suppose U is finite and the torsion subgroup of W is finite. The homomorphism tors V → tors W has kernel contained in the image of U, and its image lies in tors W. Counting a kernel and its cosets gives |tors V| ≤ |U| · |tors W|. The distinction matters even for the familiar exact sequence 0 → ℤ →×n ℤ → ℤ/n → 0, with n > 1. Its last three terms are ℤ → ℤ/n → 0. Both outer torsion subgroups have order one, yet the middle torsion subgroup has order n.

The permutation-module estimate bounds the whole group on the left of the homology sequence, so the comparison becomes

|tors Hj(G, M)| ≤ sA sj · |tors Hj−1(G, K)|.

If each basis boundary Cj+1 → Cj has sum of absolute coefficients at most b ≥ 1, this same boundary remains at the top of every shortened complex. At degree zero the integral presentation of the coinvariants therefore contributes at most bA. Unwinding the inequality supplies one power of s for each positive degree, with total exponent A(s + ⋯ + sj). Since each of the j summands is at most sj, the product is at most bA sj A sj. For the face complex take M = ℤ with trivial action, and b = j + 2 because a basis element in degree j + 1 has that many face terms. This recovers the stated torsion bound.

An exact complex for the arithmetic group

The degree shift requires an augmented complex that is exact over the integers. For the group of invertible integral matrices we will build it from Hermitian forms on the embedded lattice. Two questions govern the construction. Which ordered tuples share a supporting functional, and how can a cycle of such tuples be filled?

Why do the lattice inequalities force positive definiteness?

In the count of frames on a common face, the only initial constraint on the Hermitian forms is a lower bound on lattice vectors. Let L be the totally complex number field, let N ≥ 1, and put d = [L∶ℚ]N. Choose one embedding σw in each complex conjugate pair. For a family of Hermitian matrices hw indexed by these places, set qh(y) = ∑w σw(y)*hwσw(y), where * denotes conjugate transpose. Every summand is real. Suppose qh(y) ≥ 1 for all nonzero y ∈ 𝒪LN. An integral basis of 𝒪L in each coordinate identifies these vectors with ℤd. Denote by G the real symmetric matrix of their quadratic form in this basis. We claim

G is positive definite,   1 ≤ (4d)d det G.

First, nonnegativity on all integer points implies nonnegativity on rational points by clearing denominators and using homogeneity of degree two. Density and continuity give nonnegativity on ℝd. Strict positivity on rational points alone could leave an irrational null direction. The uniform lower bound of one rules this out, as the following volume calculation shows.

For ε > 0, put Gε = G+εI. It is positive definite and still takes value at least one on each nonzero integral vector. Write Gε = BtB using its positive square root. The lattice Bℤd has covolume |det B|. Set t = |det B|1/d. The symmetric cube [−2t,2t]d has volume 4d|det B|, strictly greater than the Minkowski threshold 2d|det B|. It therefore contains some Bc with 0 ≠ c ∈ ℤd. Its squared Euclidean length is at most 4dt² and at least one. Raising to the power d gives 1 ≤ (4d)d det Gε. The determinant is a polynomial in ε, so the same inequality holds at ε = 0. The nonnegative eigenvalues of G have positive product and hence are all positive. Sutherland, Theorem 14.13, Minkowski’s lattice point theorem[63].

This also gives positivity at each individual place. The real coordinates in the integral basis parameterize the entire product ∏w ℂN as a real vector space. Indeed the matrix of all embeddings of the basis is invertible by its nonzero discriminant. Solving for a tuple whose entries at conjugate embeddings are conjugate gives real coefficients, by uniqueness of the solution. In particular any nonzero z at one chosen place, with zeros elsewhere, comes from a nonzero real coordinate vector. Its value for G is z*hwz > 0. Every hw is therefore positive definite. Sutherland, Proposition 12.6, the embedding matrix and the discriminant[260].

Where does the discriminant enter the frame bound?

Write D = |disc L|, m = [L∶ℚ] and P = ∏w det hw. The factors of P are positive by the real Gram estimate. To compute their product from G, take an integral basis b₁,…,bₘ and form T = (σ(bⱼ))σ,j using all embeddings. The matrix of traces TrL/ℚ(bᵢbⱼ) is TtT, so its determinant gives (det T)² = disc L, and |det T|² = D.

Apply T separately to each of the N coordinates, and group the output by embedding. Call the resulting square matrix U. Reordering the coordinates leaves |det U|² = DN. In this output space form a block diagonal matrix H with hw at the chosen embedding and its conjugate, equivalently its transpose, at the conjugate embedding. An entry of U*HU is a sum over all embeddings. The two summands for a conjugate pair add to twice the real part of the chosen summand, precisely that pair’s contribution to 2G. Thus U*HU = 2G. The two blocks in each conjugate pair have the same real determinant, so det H = P². Taking determinants now gives

2d det G = DN P²,   1 ≤ DN dd P.

For the inequality, substitute the identity in 1 ≤ (4d)ddet G. The right side becomes (2d)dDNP². Because d ≥ 2 and D ≥ 1, this is at most (ddDNP)². Taking the positive square root proves the assertion. Now let the columns of an integral matrix A be independent common minimal vectors. Their values for qh are one. Hence each diagonal entry of each pulled-back form σw(A)*hwσw(A) is at most one. Hadamard’s determinant inequality bounds its determinant by their product, hence by one. Multiplying over the places gives |NormL/ℚ(det A)|P ≤ 1. The preceding lower bound for P therefore bounds the index |NormL/ℚ(det A)| by DNdd in the count of common frames. Writing J = DNdd, the same calculation gives a lower bound at each place. The product of the pulled-back determinants is at least P ≥ 1/J, since the nonzero integral determinant has absolute norm at least one. Every factor is at most one, so each individual determinant is at least 1/J. This is the bound used in the coordinate estimate. Hadamard’s inequality here follows by writing the positive matrix as a Gram matrix and orthogonalizing the vectors that it represents. Each projected length is at most the original vector length.

For a check with a nonreal matrix entry, take L = ℚ(i), N = 2 and h with diagonal entries 1 and upper-right entry i/2. Its eigenvalues are ½ and 3/2. On a Gaussian integer vector (a+bi,c+ei) it takes the integer value a²+b²+c²+e²−ae+bc, so every nonzero vector satisfies the bound of one. With the integral basis (1,i), the real Gram matrix separates into the (a,e) and (b,c) blocks, both of determinant ¾. Thus det G = 9/16. Here d = 4, D = 4 and P = ¾, giving 2⁴ · 9/16 = 9 = 4² · (¾)².

Which Hermitian forms can a positive functional see?

The torsion estimate uses a complex of ordered vertices. Its boundary deletes one vertex at a time. To use the complex we must prove that every integral cycle in it bounds. We start by finding the geometric object that records which tuples are allowed.

Let F be totally complex and take one complex embedding from each conjugate pair. A point h in our real vector space is a tuple of Hermitian matrices of size N ≥ 1. Each nonzero vector y in 𝒪FN gives a real linear functional on that space, namely the sum qy(h) of its Hermitian values over the chosen embeddings. Write P for the closed convex set on which all these functionals are at least one. A form is a vertex when the equalities qy(h) = 1 determine it uniquely. Equivalently, the only variation annihilated by every active functional is zero.

The embedded integer vectors form a full real lattice. A sufficiently large multiple of the identity form therefore belongs to P. The real Gram bound makes every member positive definite at each place. In a neighborhood of any such form the least eigenvalues stay above a common positive constant c. An equality qy = 1 there forces the squared Euclidean norm of the embedded vector to be at most 1/c. Only finitely many lattice vectors occur in that ball. All other inequalities stay strict throughout the neighborhood.

Let T be the closed cone of tuples of positive semidefinite matrices and let X consist of all linear functionals strictly positive on its nonzero elements. The sum of the traces belongs to X since a nonzero positive semidefinite matrix has a positive eigenvalue. For a vertex v the normal cone collects the functionals minimized at that vertex.

Aᵥ = {ℓ : ℓ(v) ≤ ℓ(h) for every h ∈ P}.

Each cone is closed and convex because it is an intersection of closed half-spaces. To see that the cones cover X, fix ℓ ∈ X. On the unit vectors of T, compactness gives ℓ a strictly positive minimum. Thus bounded upper levels of ℓ on P are compact. The minimum on P is attained, and its minimizers form a compact convex set. Choose a minimizer of maximal squared Euclidean norm in that set. Strict convexity of the squared norm prevents this point from being the midpoint of two distinct minimizers. If some nonzero direction killed all its active functionals, small displacements in both directions would be feasible. Indeed only the finite list above can become active nearby. The two displaced values of ℓ average to the minimum and so both attain it. This contradicts the midpoint property. The chosen minimizer is a vertex.

Only finitely many cones can meet the convex hull of a finite set of functionals ℓ₁,…,ℓs in X. Fix any h₀ ∈ P. If a convex combination of the ℓᵢ is minimized at v, at least one ℓᵢ satisfies ℓᵢ(v) ≤ ℓᵢ(h₀). Those finitely many compact sublevels contain only finitely many vertices. A finite neighborhood cover gives a finite pool of possible active inequalities, and their active subset determines each vertex uniquely.

For a two-dimensional example, impose h₁ ≥ 1, h₂ ≥ 1 and h₁+h₂ ≥ 3. A positive functional with equal coefficients is minimized along the segment from (1,2) to (2,1). Both endpoints belong to its minimizing face. A slight increase in the coefficient of h₁ selects (1,2) alone. The shared supporting functional lets the ordered pair of endpoints appear in the complex.

How does cutting a convex set help fill a cycle?

Given closed convex sets Aᵢ covering a nonempty convex set X, keep an ordered tuple of labels whenever the corresponding sets share a point of X. This collection is the nerve of the cover. Deleting a label keeps the same witness. A chain of degree p is a finite integer sum of such tuples of length p+1. Labels can repeat. The boundary of a tuple is the alternating sum over deletions. Deleting two different positions in the two possible orders produces opposite signs, so the boundary applied twice is zero. In degree zero, summing the coefficients defines the augmentation to ℤ.

Consider first a nonempty compact convex portion K that meets finitely many cover sets. Suppose that all the sets meeting K contain one common point in K. Choose one of their labels a. Prepending a to each tuple defines an integral operator s. Deleting its newly prepended entry returns the original tuple, and every other deletion has the opposite sign from the corresponding term in s∂. Hence ∂s+s∂ is the identity, including the augmentation if s sends the empty tuple to [a]. A cycle z is filled by sz.

In the general compact case, count the unordered subsets of active labels that have a common witness in K, including the empty subset. This finite count controls an induction even though tuples may have repeated entries and arbitrarily large length. Choose a realized subset Σ of largest cardinality. Unless all active labels have a common witness, some active label i is outside Σ. There is no point witnessing Σ together with i. The witnesses of Σ form a nonempty compact convex set, disjoint from the nonempty compact convex set K ∩ Aᵢ. Separate them by a hyperplane, with i strictly on the left and Σ strictly on the right. In Euclidean coordinates the midpoint hyperplane perpendicular to a shortest segment between the two compact sets works. Varying either endpoint toward another point of its set cannot shorten the segment, which puts the entire set on its own side. Boyd and Vandenberghe, §2.5.1, pp. 46–47[261].

Each closed half of K and the slice on the hyperplane has fewer realized subsets. The left half loses Σ, the right half loses {i}, and the slice loses both. Each is nonempty since K contains the segment joining the opposite witnesses. The nerve on K is the union of the two half nerves. Their intersection is the nerve of the slice. Indeed a tuple witnessed on both sides is witnessed on the joining segment, at the point where it crosses the hyperplane, since every set named by the tuple is convex.

To join the fillings, split an integral cycle as z = u+v with chains in the two halves. The boundary b = ∂u = −∂v belongs to their intersection. Exactness there gives a chain e with ∂e = b. Now u−e and v+e are cycles in the two halves, so the induction fills them. Their fillings add to a filling of z. For zero-dimensional cycles b is an integer and multiplying a slice vertex by b gives a chain of augmentation b. This proves

∂(U+V) = (u−e) + (v+e) = z.

Why does the arithmetic face complex give an exact sequence?

On [0,4] take the closed intervals A = [0,1], B = [1,3], C = [3,4]. There is no common point of all three, and no edge [A,C]. Cut at 2. Only B meets the slice. The cycle [C]−[A] splits into −[A] on the left and [C] on the right. The two augmentations are −1 and 1. Use −[B] on the slice to correct them. The corrected cycles [B]−[A] and [C]−[B] are the boundaries of [A,B] and [B,C]. Their sum cancels the artificial vertex in the boundary. At the contacts 1 and 3 the cut still gives the union and intersection identities. One half then keeps all the faces. Every cut strictly between 1 and 3 separates the chosen witness sets, reducing the face count on both sides.

Return to the normal cones of the Hermitian vertices. The parameter space X of positive functionals can be unbounded. A cycle has finite support, so choose one witness in X for each tuple that occurs and include one fixed point of X. Their convex hull K lies in X and is compact, being the image of a finite-dimensional closed simplex under the convex-combination map. By the finite-cone property only finitely many normal cones meet K. They cover it. Every tuple in the cycle already occurs in its nerve, and the compact filling argument supplies a finite integral chain with that boundary. Its witnesses in K are also witnesses in X.

⋯ → ℤ[ordered triples] → ℤ[ordered pairs] → ℤ[vertices] → ℤ → 0.

Here ℤ[ ] means finite integer combinations of the allowed tuples. The augmentation from ℤ[vertices] to ℤ sends each vertex to 1 and is onto because the cover contains a vertex. In every preceding degree the alternating deletion rule puts every boundary in the kernel. The filling puts every kernel element in the image. An integral change of lattice basis permutes the vertices and carries a common supporting functional to its pullback. This commutes with deletion at each position. We have therefore constructed the exact complex of permutation modules needed in the group homology bound. The face orbits and stabilizers are counted separately. Exactness here is asserted before identifying equivalent faces under the group action.

How many faces can an arithmetic group have up to symmetry?

In the homology inequality, A bounds the number of face orbits and s bounds the order of the subgroup fixing any one face. A face in this chain model is an ordered tuple of vertices, with repetitions allowed. Two such tuples represent one orbit if the same group element moves every entry of the first tuple to the corresponding entry of the second. Here the group is G = GLN(𝒪F), with F a totally complex number field, n = [F : ℚ], D = |disc F|, N ≥ 1 and d = nN. Thus d is the integer rank of the vector lattice 𝒪FN. We will count orbits in each face degree p ≥ 0.

Find a frame shared by the whole face

For each infinite place of F take a Hermitian form on ℂN. Their values on the images of a lattice vector y add to a real number qh(y). Impose qh(y) ≥ 1 for every nonzero y. A vector is minimal for h when equality holds. A vertex is a feasible family h uniquely determined by its equalities. A degree-p face in the complex is an ordered list of p + 1 such vertices at which one supporting linear functional attains its minimum. That functional is strictly positive on nonzero positive semidefinite families. The definition allows repeated vertices.

The common minimal vectors of a face span FN. To see why, average the vertices. At the average a lattice inequality is tight exactly when it is tight at every vertex. If the common minimal vectors missed a direction, a nonzero F-linear functional λ would vanish on their span. The family of rank-one forms obtained from |λ|² at all embeddings is positive semidefinite and nonzero. A sufficiently small subtraction of this family from the average preserves the tight constraints. Local finiteness of the inequalities keeps the others feasible. The supporting functional would strictly decrease below its minimum. Thus we can choose N independent common minimal columns and place them in a matrix A. They form a basis over F. Its integral determinant can be a nonunit. The determinant estimate gives

r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| ≤ J,   J = DNdd.

For this last inequality pull back each local form by A. The pulled-back determinants have product at most one by the diagonal bounds and Hadamard’s inequality. Their product is r times the product of the original determinants, for which the geometric lower bound is 1/J.

One congruence count for the frame

Fix its positive integer r. Over F put B = rA−1. Why does this have integral entries? The principal ideal (det A) has norm r and contains the integer r. Hence r/det A lies in 𝒪F, and multiplying the integral adjugate of A by that element gives B. Reduce its entries modulo r𝒪F. Suppose a second frame A′ has the same norm and its matrix B′ has the same residue list. Write B − B′ = rX with X integral. Over the field this gives

A′A−1 = 1 + A′X,   AA′−1 = 1 − AX.

Both matrices are integral and they are inverses. The first therefore belongs to G and takes A to A′ by left multiplication. An integral basis identifies 𝒪F/r𝒪F as an additive group with (ℤ/rℤ)n. The list of N² entries has at most rnN² = rdN values. Choosing one frame for each attained list covers every orbit. Summing the bound for r = 1,…,J costs at most J1+dN.

Example. In ℤ[i] take the one-column matrices A = 1 + i and A′ = 1 − i. Both norms are 2. The scaled inverses are B = 1 − i and B′ = 1 + i, so X = −i. The formula gives g = −i, and multiplication by this Gaussian unit sends 1 + i to 1 − i. This tests the congruence argument for frames of bounded determinant norm.

How many vertices can share a chosen frame?

Fix a representative A. A nearby vector is one that can be minimal for some feasible form making every column of A minimal. The coordinate estimate gives |σ((By)j)| ≤ R = NNJ² at every embedding. Since AB = r·1, the vector By determines y. Each of its coordinates has at most (2R + 1)n possibilities. Indeed, if two such algebraic integers differ by (2R + 1)x, every conjugate of x has absolute value at most 2R/(2R + 1) < 1. A nonzero algebraic integer has nonzero integer norm, ruling this out. The residue count thus bounds the number of nearby vectors by M = (2R + 1)d. The coordinate estimate on the scaled inverse, separation by conjugate size, counting all coordinates. The column replacement argument below derives the coordinate bound at each embedding.

The equations qh(y) = 1 are linear in the unknown coefficients of h. At a vertex, at most dN independent equations suffice to determine it. Their vectors lie in the nearby set. A set of at most dN vectors drawn from M choices can be recorded as a list of length dN by sorting it and padding with a blank. Hence this frame admits at most (M + 1)dN vertices. Each entry of an ordered tuple can use any of these in an upper bound. Together with the frame count this gives the orbit bound

Ap = J1+dN(M + 1)dN(p+1) ≤ (2Dd)12(p+1)d³N.

This count allows lists that fail the common-support condition, which only enlarges the bound. Formally choose a frame and a translated tuple for each orbit. Equal choices of frame and entries give the same tuple, hence the same orbit.

How a determinant bounds one coordinate

A vector can have small energy and large coordinates if the form measuring its energy is nearly singular. The determinant measures the loss we must allow here. Let G be a positive semidefinite Hermitian N × N matrix with every diagonal entry at most 1. If a complex column c has energy c*Gc ≤ 1, then for each coordinate a,

|det G| · |ca| ≤ N! ≤ NN.

Write ⟨x,y⟩ = x*Gy. Positivity gives |⟨x,y⟩|² ≤ ⟨x,x⟩⟨y,y⟩. Indeed, subtracting ⟨x,y⟩x/⟨x,x⟩ from y leaves a vector of nonnegative energy. If x has zero energy, the energy of y + tx can stay nonnegative for all complex t only if ⟨x,y⟩ = 0. Apply the inequality first to two coordinate vectors and then to a coordinate vector and c. It gives |Gij| ≤ 1 and |(Gc)i| ≤ 1.

Replace column a of G by Gc. This new column is the sum of the original columns weighted by the coordinates of c. Expand the determinant in that column. Every term except the ath has a repeated column, so the determinant equals ca det G. Each entry of the new matrix has absolute value at most 1. Its determinant is a signed sum of N! products, each of absolute value at most 1. This proves the bound even when G is singular. To bound |ca| itself we now need a positive lower bound for the determinant. Gilbert Strang, MIT 18.06, Lecture 20, Cramer’s rule[262].

Why the integral coordinates lie in one box

Fix a nonsingular integral frame A over the totally complex field F. A vector y is nearby if one feasible family of forms h makes both y and every column of A minimal. Each y may have its own family. Set r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| and use the integral matrix B = rA−1. For n = [F : ℚ], d = nN, D = |disc F| and J = DNdd, every such y satisfies

|σw((By)a)| ≤ R,   R = NNJ²,

for every coordinate a and one embedding σw in each complex conjugate pair. Its conjugate gives the same absolute value. To see the bound, let Hw be the local matrix of the chosen family and put Aw = σw(A), Gw = Aw*HwAw. The diagonal entries of Gw are nonnegative. For each column their sum over the places is the energy of that column, exactly 1. Thus each diagonal entry is at most 1. The frame estimate, using the discriminant bound, gives both 1 ≤ r ≤ J and det Gw ≥ 1/J at every place.

Let cw = σw(By)/r. Since AB = rI, multiplying cw by Aw recovers σw(y). The resulting local energies cw*Gwcw are nonnegative and sum to the energy of y, exactly 1. Apply the preceding coordinate estimate at each place. Dividing by det Gw costs at most one factor J. Multiplying by r to recover the integral coordinate costs at most another. This gives the stated R. The map y ↦ By is injective, because multiplying its output by A recovers ry. The count of nearby vectors can therefore count integral columns in this fixed box.

A minimal Gaussian vector with a denominator in frame coordinates

Over ℤ[i] take the form q(u,v) = |u + (1 + i)v/2|² + |v|²/2. Every nonzero integral pair has energy at least 1. If v = 0 this follows from |u| ≥ 1. If |v|² ≥ 2 the second term suffices. For a Gaussian unit v, the real and imaginary parts of (1 + i)v/2 are both half-integers, so the first term is at least 1/2.

Take frame columns (1,0) and (−i,1 + i). They are orthogonal for this form and each has energy 1, so their Gram matrix is the identity. Their determinant is 1 + i and r = 2. The vector y = (0,1) also has energy 1. Solving Ac = y gives c = ((1 + i)/2,(1 − i)/2), of squared length 1. Multiplication by r gives the integral column By = (1 + i,1 − i). Multiplying that column by A gives (0,2), as required.
