How can the error shrink with the exceptional main term?

Write d = log m, L = log U, and φ = φ(m). When an exceptional pair exists, set η = min{1, (1−β)d} and s = χ(a) ∈ {−1,1}. In its absence take η = 1, s = 0 and β = 1. The difficulty occurs at s = 1. As β approaches one, both the expected number of primes and the permissible error in this class shrink. We need the same factor η in two estimates.

Lower bound for the corrected main term. Suppose U ≥ 16 and L ≥ d. Then B ≥ P, where

P = Uη/(2φL).

Indeed β ≥ ½ and Uβ ≥ 2. If s ≤ 0, integrating 1/log t from U/2 to U already gives φB ≥ U/(2L). If s = 1, integrate from Uβ to U. Throughout this interval 1/log t ≥ 1/L. Its length is U[1−exp(−(1−β)L)] ≥ Uη/2. Here (1−β)L ≥ η and 1−exp(−η) ≥ η/2 for 0 ≤ η ≤ 1, by concavity and the endpoint values. This gives the bound for both signs.

The corresponding saving in the error. Let Ψ(t) sum log p for each prime power pk ≤ t congruent to a modulo m. Its model is F(t) = (t − s tβ/β)/φ. The analytic input, obtained by summing the errors for Dirichlet characters and applying their orthogonality, gives constants A, c > 0 such that

|Ψ(t) − F(t)| ≤ A tη[exp(−c log t/d) + exp(−c√(log t))]/φ.

This holds for 8 ∣ m, gcd(a,m) = 1 and log t ≥ C d log(d+2) with an absolute C large enough. To see where η enters for large moduli, recall that the contribution from a zero ρ, after dividing the weighted explicit formula by t, contains tRe ρ−1. A very close exceptional zero forces the remaining zeros farther to the left by the Deuring–Heilbronn theorem. The density estimate at this modulus counts zeros separated in height for each character. A local count restores their multiplicities. Once the weighted bound is available, partial summation converts it to a prime count. After the exceptional zero has been set aside, these two inputs bound the relevant weighted zero sum by a constant times η dN exp(−c′ log t/d) for fixed N and c′ > 0. The remaining power of d can be paid for explicitly. Once log t ≥ (2N/c′)d log(d+2), we have dN exp(−c′ log t/(2d)) ≤ 1. Half the exponential decay and the whole factor η survive. When d is at most a fixed small multiple of √(log t), the small-modulus argument recovers η while summing the character errors. The explicit formula, zero-density and repulsion estimates are the deeper analytic inputs to this step. A published zero-density theorem incorporating repulsion is given by Thorner and Zaman, Refinements to the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions, Theorem 2.1[263].

Classical zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function, regional logarithmic-derivative bound, and square-root exponential remainder for the smoothed prime sum

Why does a positivity inequality among three values of −ζ′/ζ push the zeros of ζ a distance of order 1/log(|t| + 2) to the left of the line Re s = 1, and why is this distance exactly what turns a contour shift into the saving exp(−c√(log y)) used in the square-root exponential estimate for one character? For σ > 1 the series −ζ′(s)/ζ(s) = ∑ Λ(n)n−s has nonnegative coefficients, and 3 + 4 cos θ + cos 2θ = 2(1 + cos θ)2 ≥ 0, so 3 Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ) + 4 Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + it) + Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + 2it) is never negative. Just to the right of 1, the first term is about 1/(σ − 1) because of the pole; a zero β + it with β close to 1 makes the second term contain −1/(σ − β); and the third term is only of size log(|t| + 2), because the pole is far away. Four copies of 1/(σ − β) outweigh three copies of 1/(σ − 1) as soon as σ − β < (4/3)(σ − 1), and the terms of size log(|t| + 2) cost only a fixed fraction of 1/(σ − 1) once σ − 1 is a small multiple of 1/log(|t| + 2); this balance produces the region. Both local statements, the term −1/(σ − β) and the bound of size log(|t| + 2), come from the disk lemma for logarithmic derivatives on disks of radius 1/2, where ζ grows at most polynomially. Once the zeros are excluded from Re s ≥ 1 − c/log(|Im s| + 2), the same lemma bounds ζ′/ζ + 1/(s − 1) by a constant times (log(|Im s| + 2))2 throughout the region. The smoothed prime sum S(y) is a Perron integral of −(ζ′(w)/ζ(w))yw/(w(w − 1)) along a vertical line to the right of 1; moving that line to Re w = 1 − c/log(T + 2) crosses only the double pole at w = 1, whose residue y log y − (1 + γ)y is the main term, and with T = exp(c√(log y)/4) every remaining piece is y times a negative exponential in √(log y).

1. Zeta zero-free region, regional logarithmic-derivative bound, and the smoothed zeta prime sum. Let ζ be the Riemann zeta function, with its simple pole at s = 1, let Λ be the von Mangoldt function and γ Euler’s constant, and write ζ′ for the complex derivative. For real x put

S(x) = ∑1≤n≤⌊x⌋ Λ(n)(x/n − 1),   G(x) = S(x) − x log x + (1 + γ)x,   Fy(w) = −(ζ′(w)/ζ(w)) yw/(w(w − 1)),

the last for real y > 0 and complex w. For real x0, x1, y0, y1, the counterclockwise boundary integral of a function g over the rectangle [x0, x1] × [y0, y1] is ∫x0x1 g(x + iy0) dx − ∫x0x1 g(x + iy1) dx + i∫y0y1 g(x1 + iy) dy − i∫y0y1 g(x0 + iy) dy.

Proposition (Classical zero-free region, regional logarithmic-derivative bound, and smoothed prime number theorem for ζ).

(i) There is c0 > 0, and (ii) there are c1 > 0 and a real constant C1, such that for every complex s ≠ 1

ζ(s) ≠ 0   (Re s ≥ 1 − c0/log(|Im s| + 2)),   |ζ′(s)/ζ(s) + 1/(s − 1)| ≤ C1(log(|Im s| + 2))2   (Re s ≥ 1 − c1/log(|Im s| + 2)),   s ≠ 1.

(iii) There are c > 0 and a real constant K such that

|G(y)| = |S(y) − y log y + (1 + γ)y| ≤ K y exp(−c√(log y))   for every real y ≥ 2.

Proof. For (i), let C ≥ 0 be the right-of-one constant, so that |ζ′(s)/ζ(s)| ≤ 1/(Re s − 1) + C whenever Re s > 1 (see the details below), and put t0 = max(3, exp(3C)). Let ζ(β + it) = 0 with β, t real and |t| ≥ t0, and write ℓ = log(|t| + 2). Then ℓ > 1 because |t| + 2 ≥ 5 > e, and 3C ≤ ℓ because |t| ≥ exp(3C). Test at σ = 1 + (1/10000)/ℓ, so that 1 < σ ≤ 2 and 1/(σ − 1) = 10000ℓ. For τ ∈ {t, 2t} we have |τ| ≥ 3, so the closed disk of radius 1/2 about σ + iτ stays away from the pole; ζ is analytic there and satisfies |ζ(w)| ≤ M|ζ(σ + iτ)| with M = (|t| + 2)10, hence log M = 10ℓ. The disk lemma of the local zero expansion with radius 1/2 lists the zeros ρ of ζ within 1/6 of σ + iτ with multiplicities m(ρ) ≥ 1 and writes ζ′/ζ(σ + iτ) = ∑ m(ρ)/(σ + iτ − ρ) + E with |E| ≤ 72 log M/(1/2) = 144 log M = 1440ℓ. Since ζ has no zeros in Re s > 1, every listed zero has Re ρ < σ, so every Re(m(ρ)/(σ + iτ − ρ)) is nonnegative, and taking real parts gives Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + iτ) ≤ 1440ℓ − Sτ with Sτ = ∑ m(ρ) Re(1/(σ + iτ − ρ)) ≥ 0. If σ − β ≤ 1/6, the zero β + it is listed for τ = t and contributes m(β + it)/(σ − β) ≥ 1/(σ − β) to St. Inserting these bounds and Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ) ≤ |ζ′(σ)/ζ(σ)| ≤ 10000ℓ + C into the 3–4–1 inequality gives

0 ≤ 3 Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ) + 4 Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + it) + Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + 2it) ≤ 3(10000ℓ + C) + 4(1440ℓ − 1/(σ − β)) + 1440ℓ,

that is, 4/(σ − β) ≤ 37200ℓ + 3C ≤ 37201ℓ. Hence σ − β ≥ 4/(37201ℓ) > (21/200000)/ℓ and β < 1 + (1/10000)/ℓ − (21/200000)/ℓ = 1 − (1/200000)/ℓ. If instead σ − β > 1/6, then β < 1 + 1/10000 − 1/6 < 1 − 1/200000 < 1 − (1/200000)/ℓ directly. So every zero β + it with |t| ≥ t0 satisfies β < 1 − (1/200000)/log(|t| + 2). Below that height, compactness supplies c2 > 0 such that ζ(s) ≠ 0 whenever |Im s| ≤ t0, Re s ≥ 1 − c2 and s ≠ 1. Put c0 = min(1/200000, c2 log 2). Because log(|Im s| + 2) ≥ log 2, the region of (i) lies in Re s ≥ 1 − c2 where |Im s| ≤ t0, and in Re s ≥ 1 − (1/200000)/log(|Im s| + 2) where |Im s| > t0; in both cases ζ(s) ≠ 0.

For (ii), keep CR = C from (i), and let cS > 0 and CS be the bounded-height constants for the height e24: |ζ′(s)/ζ(s) + 1/(s − 1)| ≤ CS whenever s ≠ 1, |Im s| ≤ e24 and 1 − cS ≤ Re s ≤ 3. Put c1 = min(c0/4, 1, cS log 2) and C1 = (1441 + 60/c0) + (4 + 4CR) + 4|CS|. Fix s = σ + it ≠ 1 in the region of (ii) and set ℓ = log(|t| + 2) ≥ log 2 > 1/2, so that ℓ2 > 1/4. If σ > 1 + 1/ℓ, then |ζ′(s)/ζ(s)| ≤ 1/(σ − 1) + CR and |1/(s − 1)| ≤ 1/(σ − 1) with 1/(σ − 1) < ℓ, so the sum is at most 2ℓ + CR ≤ (4 + 4CR)ℓ2. If σ ≤ 1 + 1/ℓ and ℓ < 24, then |t| < e24, σ < 3 and c1/ℓ ≤ cS, so the bounded-height estimate gives at most CS ≤ 4|CS|ℓ2. The decisive regime is σ ≤ 1 + 1/ℓ with ℓ ≥ 24. Centre the disk lemma at z0 = 1 + 1/ℓ + it with radius 1/2 and M = (|t| + 2)10, as in (i). The zeros within 1/6 of z0 have total multiplicity at most 10ℓ/log 2 ≤ 15ℓ, and because 1 − 1/ℓ ≤ 1 − c1/ℓ ≤ σ ≤ 1 + 1/ℓ, the point s lies within 2/ℓ ≤ 1/12 of z0, where the remainder is at most 1440ℓ. Each listed zero ρ has |Im ρ| + 2 ≤ (|t| + 2)2, so (i) forces Re ρ < 1 − c0/(2ℓ), while σ ≥ 1 − (c0/4)/ℓ; thus Re(s − ρ) > c0/(4ℓ), and the zero sum has absolute value at most 15ℓ · 4ℓ/c0 = (60/c0)ℓ2. Finally |Im s| ≥ 1, so |1/(s − 1)| ≤ 1, and the three contributions add up to at most 1440ℓ + (60/c0)ℓ2 + 1 ≤ (1441 + 60/c0)ℓ2. In every regime the bound is at most C1ℓ2, since the three summands of C1 are nonnegative.

For (iii), put D = max(C1, 0), c = min(c0, c1, 1/2), and for y ≥ 2 write s = √(log y), so that log y = s2. Suppose first that s ≥ 8/c, so s ≥ 16. Choose the height T = exp(cs/4) and put L = log(T + 2), σ0 = 1 + 1/log y and σ1 = 1 − c/L; then 1/2 ≤ σ1 < 1 < σ0, yσ0 = ey, L ≤ s/4 and L/c ≤ s/2. Because c ≤ c0 and |Im w| ≤ T on the closed rectangle [σ1, σ0] × [−T, T], part (i) shows ζ(w) ≠ 0 for every w ≠ 1 in it. The Perron formula writes 2πS(y) as the integral of Fy(σ0 + iu) over all real u; split it into V0, over |u| ≤ T, and the tail E, over |u| > T. Inside the rectangle the only singularity of Fy is the double pole at w = 1, where Fy(w) = y/(w − 1)2 + R/(w − 1) + (analytic) with R = y log y − (1 + γ)y, so its counterclockwise boundary integral equals 2πi R. Writing H− and H+ for the integrals along the bottom and top edges and V1 for the integral of Fy(σ1 + iu) over |u| ≤ T, this reads H− − H+ + i V0 − i V1 = 2πi R. Since G(y) = S(y) − R,

2πG(y) = E + i(H− − H+) + V1,   2π|G(y)| ≤ |E| + |H−| + |H+| + |V1|.

On the right line, |Fy(σ0 + iu)| ≤ (log y + CR)ey/u2 for |u| ≥ T, so |E| ≤ 2(log y + CR)ey/T ≤ 2π(log y + CR)ey/T. On the horizontal edges, (ii) gives |Fy| ≤ (DL2 + 1)ey/T2, along edges of length σ0 − σ1 ≤ 2. On the shifted line, (ii) gives |Fy(σ1 + iu)| ≤ (DL2 + L/c)yσ1(2L/c) over a segment of length 2T, and yσ1 = y exp(−cs2/L) with cs2/L ≥ 4cs because L ≤ s/4. This is the point of the choice of T: the tail and the horizontal edges cost 1/T = exp(−cs/4), while the shifted line gains a factor exp(−cs2/L) that beats its length 2T. Collecting the four estimates with |G(y)| ≤ 2π|G(y)|, log y + CR ≤ (1 + CR)s3, L ≤ s/4 and L/c ≤ s/2 gives |G(y)| ≤ (2πe(1 + CR) + 4e(D + 1) + 4(D + 1))s3y exp(−cs/4), and s3exp(−cs/8) ≤ 6(8/c)3 turns this into |G(y)| ≤ Ay exp(−(c/8)√(log y)) with A = (2πe(1 + CR) + 4e(D + 1) + 4(D + 1)) · 6(8/c)3. If instead s < 8/c, then log y ≤ (8/c)2, y ≤ exp((8/c)2) and exp(−(c/8)s) ≥ e−1, so the trivial bound |G(y)| ≤ y(y log y + log y + 2) gives the same shape with B = (exp((8/c)2)(8/c)2 + (8/c)2 + 2)e. Hence (iii) holds with exponent c/8 and constant max(A, B).

Right-of-one, growth and reciprocal bounds for zeta, compactness at bounded height, the 3–4–1 coefficients, the growth ratio on disks of radius one half, Perron inversion, and the rectangle residue at the double pole

For σ > 1 and real y, the real part of the n-th term of −ζ′/ζ(σ + iy) = ∑ Λ(n)n−σ−iy is a cos(y log n) with a = Λ(n)n−σ ≥ 0. With θ = t log n and cos 2θ = 2cos2θ − 1, the n-th term of the 3–4–1 combination is 3a + 4a cos θ + a cos 2θ = 2a(1 + cos θ)2 ≥ 0, and summing over n proves the inequality used in (i). For the right-of-one bound, let λ(σ) = ∑ Λ(n)n−σ = −ζ′(σ)/ζ(σ), a nonincreasing function of σ > 1 with |ζ′(s)/ζ(s)| ≤ λ(Re s). Near the pole, ζ′(σ)/ζ(σ) + 1/(σ − 1) stays bounded, say by B, for real 1 < σ < 1 + ε. If 1 < Re s < 1 + ε/2, then λ(Re s) ≤ B + 1/(Re s − 1); if Re s ≥ 1 + ε/2, then λ(Re s) ≤ λ(1 + ε/2). So C = max(B, 0, λ(1 + ε/2)) works.

For Re s = σ > 0 and s ≠ 1, the telescoping identity (s − 1)ζ(s) = s − D(s) holds with D(s) = ∑n≥0 [(n + 1)1−s − (n + 2)1−s − (s − 1)(n + 2)−s]. The n-th term equals (s − 1)∫n+1n+2 (x−s − (n + 2)−s) dx, whose absolute value is at most |s − 1||s|(n + 1)−σ−1, and the comparison σ(x + 1)−σ−1 ≤ x−σ − (x + 1)−σ for x ≥ 1 telescopes to ∑n≥0 (n + 1)−σ−1 ≤ 1 + 1/σ. Thus |D(s)| ≤ |s − 1||s|(1 + 1/σ) and |ζ(s)| ≤ |s|/|s − 1| + |s|(1 + 1/σ) ≤ 1 + 1/|s − 1| + |s|(1 + 1/Re s). For Re s > 1, 1/ζ(s) = ∑ μ(n)n−s with |μ(n)| ≤ 1, and the integral comparison ∑n≥1 n−σ ≤ 1 + ∫1∞ x−σ dx gives |ζ(s)|−1 ≤ σ/(σ − 1).

At bounded height, fix T. The set of s such that s = 1 or ζ(s) ≠ 0 is open, because ζ is continuous away from 1 and |ζ| tends to infinity at the simple pole; it contains the compact segment {1 + iy : |y| ≤ T}, since ζ has no zeros on Re s = 1, so it contains a uniform thickening of radius c > 0 of that segment. Points with |Im s| ≤ T and Re s ≥ 1 − c lie either in that thickening or in Re s > 1, where ζ has no zeros. In the same way, ζ1(s) = (s − 1)ζ(s) is entire and has no zeros on the compact rectangle [1, 3] × [−T, T] (ζ has no zeros there and ζ1(1) = 1), hence none on [1 − δ/2, 3] × [−T, T] for some δ > 0; on that rectangle ζ′/ζ + 1/(s − 1) = ζ1′/ζ1 away from 1, and ζ1′/ζ1 is continuous, hence bounded. This gives the constants cS = δ/2 and CS used in (ii).

For the growth ratio, let 1 < σ ≤ 2, T ≥ 3 and 3 ≤ |τ| ≤ 2T. On the closed disk of radius 1/2 about σ + iτ we have Re w ≥ 1/2, |w − 1| ≥ 1 and |w| ≤ 2T + 5/2, so the growth bound gives |ζ(w)| ≤ 2 + 3(2T + 5/2) ≤ 6(T + 2), while the reciprocal bound gives |ζ(σ + iτ)| ≥ (σ − 1)/σ ≥ (σ − 1)/2. If moreover 2/(σ − 1) ≤ 20000(T + 2), then |ζ(w)| ≤ 120000(T + 2)2|ζ(σ + iτ)| ≤ (T + 2)10|ζ(σ + iτ)|, since T + 2 ≥ 5 and 58 > 120000. With T = |t|, the condition holds for σ = 1 + (1/10000)/ℓ in (i), where 2/(σ − 1) = 20000ℓ, and for σ = 1 + 1/ℓ in (ii), where 2/(σ − 1) = 2ℓ.

For the Perron formula, fix y ≥ 1 and σ0 > 1. For Re w > 1 and each n ≥ 1, ∫n∞ (x/n − 1)x−w−1 dx = n−w/(w(w − 1)), so ∫0∞ S(x)x−w−1 dx = −ζ′(w)/(ζ(w)w(w − 1)). Since |w(w − 1)| ≥ min((σ0 − 1)2, 1)(1 + u2) on w = σ0 + iu, the integrand u ↦ Fy(σ0 + iu) is integrable, and Mellin inversion at the continuity point y of S gives S(y) = (1/2π)∫ Fy(σ0 + iu) du. Mellin transform and inversion, DLMF §1.14(iv)[264].

For the residue, if g(w) = G0(w) + a/(w − p)2 + b/(w − p) for w ≠ p, with G0 analytic on an open set containing the closed rectangle and p strictly inside, then the boundary integral of G0 vanishes by the Cauchy–Goursat theorem, the term a/(w − p)2 has the primitive −a/(w − p) and contributes 0, and the simple pole contributes 2πib. For Fy, write −ζ′/ζ = −ζ1′/ζ1 + 1/(w − 1), so that Fy(w) = H(w)/(w − 1)2 with H(w) = (1 − (w − 1)ζ1′(w)/ζ1(w))yw/w, analytic near 1. Then H(1) = y, and the expansion ζ(w) = 1/(w − 1) + γ + O(w − 1) gives ζ1′(1)/ζ1(1) = γ, hence H′(1) = −γy + (y log y − y) = y log y − (1 + γ)y. Subtracting y/(w − 1)2 + H′(1)/(w − 1) leaves a removable singularity, so for y > 0, 0 < σ1 < 1 < σ0, T > 0 and ζ zero-free on the closed rectangle apart from 1, the boundary integral of Fy over [σ1, σ0] × [−T, T] is 2πi(y log y − (1 + γ)y). Laurent expansion of ζ at 1, DLMF (25.2.4)[265].

Finally, for y ≥ 1 each of the at most y terms Λ(n)(y/n − 1) of S(y) lies in [0, y log y], so 0 ≤ S(y) ≤ y2 log y, and γ < 1 gives |G(y)| ≤ y2 log y + y log y + 2y = y(y log y + log y + 2).

Twisted Möbius inverse bound, uniform right-of-one logarithmic derivative, and local zero sum with derivative-witnessed multiplicities at 11/10 + it

Why does the zero-free region for Dirichlet L-functions need a second local expansion, now centred at 11/10 + it with outer radius 3/5, when the local Dirichlet expansion already expands −L′/L about 101/100 + it, and why must the multiplicities now carry a derivative witness? The 3–4–1 argument evaluates Dχ = −L′/L on the segment 1 < σ ≤ 6/5 at one height t, and needs every zero within 1/5 of 11/10 + it, in particular every zero β + it with 9/10 ≤ β < 1, to appear in the subtracted sum with weight at least 1/(σ − β). A zero disk of radius 1/5 requires the disk lemma on radius 3/5, three times larger, and the expansion is then valid on radius 1/10, which covers exactly the segment |σ − 11/10| ≤ 1/10. The mechanism is that of the local Dirichlet expansion: a lower bound at the centre from the twisted Möbius series, polynomial growth from partial summation, and the disk lemma for logarithmic derivatives; only the constants change, to |L(11/10 + it, χ)| ≥ 1/11, the growth ratio M = 22C1q(|t| + 2) and the remainder 72 log M/(3/5) = 120 log M. What is new is that the multiplicities are tied to the derivative: m(ρ) ≥ 2 when f′(ρ) = 0 and m(ρ) = 1 when f′(ρ) ≠ 0. A zero at which L′ also vanishes is therefore counted at least twice in the subtracted sum, which is how the same-character small-height estimate concludes that a surviving zero is simple.

1. Twisted Dirichlet series bounds and the derivative-witnessed disk lemma. Let q ≥ 1 be an integer, χ a Dirichlet character modulo q with L-function L(s, χ) (entire when χ is nonprincipal), μ the Möbius function, and put

Dχ(s) = −L′(s, χ)/L(s, χ),   σ = Re s.

Let CR ≥ 0 be the right-of-one constant for ζ from the zeta zero-free region. Let C be a constant such that |L(s, χ)| ≤ Cq(1 + |s|) for every q ≥ 1, every nonprincipal χ modulo q and every s with Re s ≥ 1/2, as provided by partial summation in the local Dirichlet expansion, and put C1 = max(C, 1) and C0 = 120(1 + log(22C1)/log 2).

Proposition (Twisted inverse and right-of-one bounds, derivative-witnessed multiplicities, and the local zero sum at 11/10 + it).

(i) For every q ≥ 1, every χ modulo q and every s with Re s > 1, |L(s, χ)|−1 ≤ σ/(σ − 1) and |Dχ(s)| ≤ 1/(σ − 1) + CR.

(ii) Let r > 0, M ≥ 1, and let f be complex differentiable on the closed disk of centre z0 and radius r, with f(z0) ≠ 0 and |f(z)| ≤ M|f(z0)| on that disk. Then the zeros of f in the closed disk of radius r/3 form a finite set Z with multiplicities m(ρ) ≥ 1 satisfying the two conclusions of the disk bound, namely ∑ρ∈Z m(ρ) ≤ log M/log 2 and |f′(z)/f(z) − ∑ρ∈Z m(ρ)/(z − ρ)| ≤ 72 log M/r whenever |z − z0| ≤ r/6 and f(z) ≠ 0, and moreover, for every ρ ∈ Z,

f′(ρ) = 0   ⟹   m(ρ) ≥ 2,   f′(ρ) ≠ 0   ⟹   m(ρ) = 1.

(iii) For every q ≥ 1, every nonprincipal χ modulo q and every real t, the zeros of L(·, χ) in the closed disk of centre 11/10 + it and radius 1/5 form a finite set Z with multiplicities m(ρ) ≥ 1, m(ρ) ≥ 2 whenever L′(ρ, χ) = 0, and

Re Dχ(σ + it) ≤ C0 log(q(|t| + 2)) − ∑ρ∈Z m(ρ) Re(1/(σ + it − ρ))   for every 1 < σ ≤ 6/5.

Proof. For (i), when σ > 1 the product of L(s, χ) with the twisted Möbius series ∑ χ(n)μ(n)n−s equals 1, and |χ(n)μ(n)| ≤ 1, so |L(s, χ)|−1 ≤ ∑n≥1 n−σ ≤ σ/(σ − 1). Likewise Dχ(s) = ∑ χ(n)Λ(n)n−s, so |Dχ(s)| ≤ ∑ Λ(n)n−σ = |ζ′(σ)/ζ(σ)| ≤ 1/(σ − 1) + CR by the zeta bound at the real point σ. Only |χ(n)| ≤ 1 enters, which is why the constant is the one for ζ, uniformly in q and χ.

For (ii), the disk lemma factors f(w) = ∏ρ∈Z (w − ρ)m(ρ) h(w) on the disk of radius r, with h complex differentiable there and zero-free on radius r/3; the count and the remainder are obtained exactly as in the disk bound, the remainder from the bound 24 log M/(r/3) = 72 log M/r for the logarithmic derivative of h on radius r/6. Fix ρ ∈ Z. Near ρ, f(w) = (w − ρ)m(ρ)k(w) with k(w) = ∏ρ′∈Z, ρ′≠ρ (w − ρ′)m(ρ′) h(w), and k(ρ) ≠ 0 because the other zeros are distinct from ρ and h(ρ) ≠ 0. Writing (w − ρ)mk(w) = (w − ρ) · (w − ρ)m−1k(w), the product rule gives f′(ρ) = [(w − ρ)m−1k(w)]w=ρ, which equals k(ρ) ≠ 0 when m = 1 and 0 when m ≥ 2. Hence f′(ρ) = 0 forces m(ρ) ≥ 2, and f′(ρ) ≠ 0 forces m(ρ) = 1.

For (iii), fix q, a nonprincipal χ and t, and put z0 = 11/10 + it, r = 3/5. The closed disk of radius 3/5 about z0 lies in Re z ≥ 1/2 and satisfies |z| ≤ 11/10 + |t| + 3/5, so 1 + |z| ≤ 2(|t| + 2) and |L(z, χ)| ≤ C1q(1 + |z|) ≤ 2C1q(|t| + 2). At the centre, (i) with σ = 11/10 gives |L(z0, χ)|−1 ≤ (11/10)/(1/10) = 11, so L(z0, χ) ≠ 0 and |L(z0, χ)| ≥ 1/11. Therefore |L(z, χ)| ≤ M|L(z0, χ)| on the disk with M = 22C1q(|t| + 2) ≥ 1, since M/11 = 2C1q(|t| + 2). Part (ii) with r = 3/5 produces Z, the zeros within (3/5)/3 = 1/5 of z0, with m(ρ) ≥ 1 and m(ρ) ≥ 2 whenever L′(ρ, χ) = 0, together with |L′/L(s, χ) − ∑ m(ρ)/(s − ρ)| ≤ 72 log M/(3/5) = 120 log M whenever |s − z0| ≤ (3/5)/6 = 1/10 and L(s, χ) ≠ 0. For 1 < σ ≤ 6/5 the point s = σ + it has |s − z0| = |σ − 11/10| ≤ 1/10, and L(s, χ) ≠ 0 since Re s > 1. Taking real parts,

Re Dχ(s) = −Re(L′/L(s, χ) − ∑ m(ρ)/(s − ρ)) − ∑ m(ρ) Re(1/(s − ρ)) ≤ 120 log M − ∑ρ∈Z m(ρ) Re(1/(s − ρ)).

Finally log M = log(22C1) + log(q(|t| + 2)) with log(22C1) ≥ 0 and log(q(|t| + 2)) ≥ log 2, so log(22C1) ≤ (log(22C1)/log 2) log(q(|t| + 2)), hence 120 log M ≤ C0 log(q(|t| + 2)).

Twisted Möbius and von Mangoldt series, the integral comparison for the zeta series, and the disk geometry at 11/10 + it compared with 101/100 + it

For σ > 1 the series ∑ χ(n)n−s and ∑ χ(n)μ(n)n−s converge absolutely, and since χ is completely multiplicative their Dirichlet convolution has coefficients χ(n)∑d∣n μ(d), which is 1 at n = 1 and 0 otherwise; this is the identity L(s, χ) · ∑ χ(n)μ(n)n−s = 1. Termwise, |χ(n)μ(n)n−s| ≤ n−σ, and comparing the decreasing function x−σ with its integral gives ∑n≥1 n−σ ≤ 1 + ∫1∞ x−σ dx = 1 + 1/(σ − 1) = σ/(σ − 1). Twisting the identity Λ ∗ 1 = log by the completely multiplicative χ gives (χΛ) ∗ χ = χ log, that is Dχ(s)L(s, χ) = −L′(s, χ), so Dχ(s) = ∑ χ(n)Λ(n)n−s for σ > 1, dominated termwise by Λ(n)n−σ, whose sum is −ζ′(σ)/ζ(σ) = |ζ′(σ)/ζ(σ)|.

In the disk geometry, |z0| ≤ 11/10 + |t|, so every z within 3/5 of z0 has 1 + |z| ≤ 1 + 11/10 + 3/5 + |t| ≤ 2(|t| + 2), and Re z ≥ 11/10 − 3/5 = 1/2. The real part of a finite sum ∑ m(ρ)/(s − ρ) is ∑ m(ρ) Re(1/(s − ρ)). For a nonprincipal character every zero has Re ρ < 1, because L(s, χ) has no zeros in Re s ≥ 1, so each Re(1/(σ + it − ρ)) with σ > 1 is positive and the subtracted sum in (iii) is nonnegative. Compared with the local Dirichlet expansion, whose centre 101/100 + it and outer radius 2/5 give the centre bound 1/101, the remainder 72 log B/(2/5) = 180 log B, and an inner expansion disk reaching into the critical strip to Re s = 101/100 − 1/15 = 283/300 < 1, moving the centre to 11/10 + it with outer radius 3/5 yields 1/11 and 120 log M, while the inner expansion disk |s − (11/10 + it)| ≤ 1/10 reaches left only to Re s = 1 (covering 1 < σ ≤ 6/5).

For example, take f(w) = w2(w − 1/10) on the closed disk of centre 1/5 and radius 3/4. Then f(1/5) = 1/250 ≠ 0, both zeros 0 and 1/10 lie within 1/4 of the centre, and f′(w) = 2w(w − 1/10) + w2 gives f′(0) = 0 and f′(1/10) = 1/100 ≠ 0. The derivative test therefore assigns multiplicity at least 2 to 0 and exactly 1 to 1/10, matching the analytic orders 2 and 1.

Principal-character reduction, uniform principal logarithmic-derivative bound, 3–4–1 character positivity, and exclusion of nonreal and large-height real zeros near Re s = 1

Why do the zeros of L(s, χ) avoid the region Re s ≥ 1 − c/log(q(|Im s| + 2)) for every nonreal χ, and for every real χ as soon as |Im s| is not too small, while a real zero of a real character can survive close to 1? The 3–4–1 positivity of the zeta argument has a character analogue. With a = Λ(n)n−σ and w = χ(n)n−it at a unit n, where |w| = 1, one has 3a + 4a Re w + a Re w2 = 2a(1 + Re w)2 ≥ 0, so 3 Re D1q(σ) + 4 Re Dχ(σ + it) + Re Dχ2(σ + 2it) ≥ 0. The first term carries the pole of the principal L-function, about 1/(σ − 1), and a zero β + it of L(·, χ) makes the second term contain −1/(σ − β) through the local zero sum. The third term decides the outcome. If χ2 is nonprincipal, L(·, χ2) has no pole, its own local zero sum bounds the third term by a multiple of log(q(|t| + 2)), and the contradiction goes through at every height. If χ is real, then χ2 = 1q is principal, and the third term contains the pole term Re(1/(σ − 1 + 2it)) = (σ − 1)/((σ − 1)2 + 4t2), which is close to 1/(σ − 1) when |t| is small compared with σ − 1, and then no contradiction arises; but once |t| ≥ δ/log(q(|t| + 2)) and σ − 1 is a small multiple a of 1/log(q(|t| + 2)) with a ≤ δ/2, this pole term is at most 1/16 of 1/(σ − 1), and the argument closes again. The principal character itself is reduced to ζ through L(s, 1q) = ∏p∣q(1 − p−s)ζ(s).

1. Principal reduction, character positivity, and the two exclusions. Keep q ≥ 1, the characters χ, χ1, χ2 modulo q, the principal character 1q, and Dχ = −L′/L from the local zero sum. For c > 0 say that s lies in the region of width c at modulus q if Re s ≥ 1 − c/log(q(|Im s| + 2)). Let CR ≥ 0 be the right-of-one constant and C0 the constant of the local zero sum, let Cζ denote the constant C1 of the regional bound for ζ, and put K3 = ∑ Λ(n)n−6/5, Kζ = 840 + |Cζ| log 4 + |K3| and CP = Kζ + 1.

Proposition (Principal reduction, principal bound, character positivity, and nonreal and large-height exclusions).

(i) For every q ≥ 1 and every s with Re s > 0 and s ≠ 1, L(s, 1q) = 0 implies ζ(s) = 0.

(ii) For every q ≥ 1, every real t and every 1 < σ ≤ 2, Re D1q(σ + it) ≤ Re(1/(σ − 1 + it)) + CP log(q(|t| + 2)).

(iii) For every q ≥ 1 and σ > 1, all characters χ modulo q and all real t,

0 ≤ 3 Re D1q(σ) + 4 Re Dχ(σ + it) + Re Dχ2(σ + 2it),

while 0 ≤ Re D1q(σ) + Re Dχ(σ) whenever χ2 = 1q, and 0 ≤ Re D1q(σ) + Re Dχ1(σ) + Re Dχ2(σ) + Re Dχ1χ2(σ) whenever χ12 = χ22 = 1q.

(iv) There is c > 0 such that L(s, χ) ≠ 0 for every q ≥ 1, every χ modulo q with χ2 ≠ 1q, and every s in the region of width c at modulus q.

(v) For every δ > 0 there is c > 0 such that L(s, χ) ≠ 0 for every q ≥ 1, every χ modulo q with χ2 = 1q and χ ≠ 1q, and every s in the region of width c at modulus q with |Im s| ≥ δ/log(q(|Im s| + 2)).

Proof. For (iii), let σ > 1. For every character ψ modulo q and real u, Dψ(σ + iu) = ∑ ψ(n)Λ(n)n−σ−iu, with n-th term aψ(n)n−iu and a = Λ(n)n−σ ≥ 0. When gcd(n, q) > 1 every character modulo q vanishes at n. At a unit n, put w = χ(n)n−it, so |w| = 1 and χ2(n)n−2it = w2; since Re w2 = 2(Re w)2 − 1, the real part of the n-th term of the first combination is a(3 + 4 Re w + 2(Re w)2 − 1) = 2a(1 + Re w)2 ≥ 0. When χ2 = 1q, χ(n) = ±1 on units and the n-th term of the second combination is a(1 + χ(n)) ≥ 0; when χ12 = χ22 = 1q, the n-th term of the third is a(1 + χ1(n))(1 + χ2(n)) ≥ 0, which is the four-character identity. Summing the nonnegative real parts over n proves (iii).

For (i), the factorization L(s, 1q) = ∏p∣q(1 − p−s)ζ(s) holds for s ≠ 1, and when Re s > 0 no factor vanishes, because |p−s| = p−Re s < 1. For (ii), the same factorization for Re s > 1 gives Re D1q(s) ≤ Re(−ζ′/ζ)(s) + log q, since each Euler factor changes the logarithmic derivative by at most log p and ∑p∣q log p ≤ log q. It therefore suffices to show Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + it) ≤ Re(1/(σ − 1 + it)) + Kζ log(|t| + 2) for 1 < σ ≤ 2, because Kζ ≥ 0, log q ≥ 0 and log(q(|t| + 2)) = log q + log(|t| + 2) then yield the constant CP = Kζ + 1. The decisive regime is |t| > 2 with σ ≤ 6/5. Apply the disk lemma to ζ at z0 = 11/10 + it with radius 3/5. On that disk Re z ≥ 1/2, |z − 1| ≥ 1 and |z| ≤ |t| + 3, so the growth bound gives |ζ(z)| ≤ 6(|t| + 2), while the reciprocal bound at Re z0 = 11/10 gives |ζ(z0)| ≥ 1/11; hence M = 66(|t| + 2). Since every zero of ζ has real part less than σ, the subtracted zero sum is nonnegative, and Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + it) ≤ 120 log M. As |t| + 2 ≥ 4 and 46 > 66, log M ≤ 7 log(|t| + 2), so Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + it) ≤ 840 log(|t| + 2), to which the nonnegative term Re(1/(σ − 1 + it)) may be added. The two other regimes, |t| ≤ 2 and |t| > 2 with σ > 6/5, cost |Cζ| log 4 and |K3| (see the details below).

For (iv), put K = |C0|, A = 6K + 5CR + 1, δ = min(1/10, 1/(2A)) and c = δ/8. Suppose χ2 ≠ 1q, so χ ≠ 1q, and L(s, χ) = 0 with β = Re s ≥ 1 − c/ℓ, where ℓ = log(q(|Im s| + 2)) ≥ log 2 > 0.69. Then β < 1, and δ/(8ℓ) ≤ 1/10 gives β ≥ 9/10. Test at σ = 1 + δ/ℓ, so 1 < σ ≤ 6/5, and write u = 1/δ, so 1/(σ − 1) = ℓu. By (i) of the local zero sum, Re D1q(σ) ≤ ℓu + CR. At height Im s, the zero s lies within 1/5 of 11/10 + i Im s, so it belongs to Z and contributes m(s)/(σ − β) ≥ 1/(σ − β) to the subtracted sum, whose other terms are nonnegative; since σ − β ≤ δ/ℓ + δ/(8ℓ) = (9/8)(δ/ℓ), this gives Re Dχ(σ + i Im s) ≤ Kℓ − (8/9)ℓu. As χ2 is nonprincipal, the local zero sum for χ2 at height 2 Im s, with its nonnegative subtracted sum, gives Re Dχ2(σ + 2i Im s) ≤ K log(q(2|Im s| + 2)) ≤ 2Kℓ. Positivity (iii) at t = Im s then yields

0 ≤ 3(ℓu + CR) + 4(Kℓ − (8/9)ℓu) + 2Kℓ = 6Kℓ + 3CR − (5/9)ℓu.

But u ≥ 2A gives ℓu ≥ 12Kℓ + 10CRℓ + 2ℓ, and ℓ > 0.69 gives 3CR ≤ 5CRℓ, so (5/9)ℓu ≥ (20/3)Kℓ + (50/9)CRℓ + (10/9)ℓ > 6Kℓ + 3CR, a contradiction.

For (v), fix δ > 0 and put K = 4 max(C0, 0) + 2 max(CP, 0) + 6CR, a = min(δ/2, 1/10, 1/(4K + 1)) and c = a/8; then Ka ≤ 1/4 and a2/(4δ2) ≤ 1/16. Suppose χ2 = 1q, χ ≠ 1q, L(s, χ) = 0, and write t = Im s and L = log(q(|t| + 2)) > 1/2, with δ/L ≤ |t| and β = Re s ≥ 1 − a/(8L). Test at σ = 1 + a/L ≤ 6/5. As in (iv), σ − β ≤ (9/8)(a/L), the zero s belongs to the local zero set at height t, and Re Dχ(σ + it) ≤ C0L − (8/9)(L/a); also Re D1q(σ) ≤ L/a + CR. Because χ2 = 1q, the third term of (iii) is Re D1q(σ + 2it), which (ii) bounds by (σ − 1)/((σ − 1)2 + 4t2) + CP log(q(2|t| + 2)). Here t2 ≥ δ2/L2 gives (σ − 1)/((σ − 1)2 + 4t2) ≤ (a/L)/(4δ2/L2) = (a2/(4δ2))(L/a) ≤ (1/16)(L/a), and CP log(q(2|t| + 2)) ≤ 2 max(CP, 0)L. With 3CR ≤ 6CRL and 4C0L ≤ 4 max(C0, 0)L, the terms without the factor L/a add up to at most KL ≤ (1/4)(L/a), and positivity (iii) gives

0 ≤ 3(L/a + CR) + 4(C0L − (8/9)(L/a)) + (1/16)(L/a) + 2 max(CP, 0)L ≤ (3 − 32/9 + 1/16 + 1/4)(L/a) = −(35/144)(L/a) < 0,

a contradiction. With the zeta region, statement (i) excludes zeros of the principal character in a region of the same shape, (iv) excludes nonreal characters, and (v) excludes real characters at height at least δ/log(q(|Im s| + 2)). Real characters below that height are treated in the same-character small-height estimate, which combines all of these into one region containing at most one character–zero pair, real and simple.

Euler-factor logarithmic derivatives, the two outer regimes of the principal bound, the doubling inequality for log(q(|t| + 2)), and positivity of the zero terms

For a prime p and Re s > 1, the logarithmic derivative of 1 − p−s is log p · p−s/(1 − p−s), of absolute value at most log p · p−σ/(1 − p−σ) ≤ log p, since p−σ ≤ 1/2. Differentiating log L(s, 1q) = ∑p∣q log(1 − p−s) + log ζ(s) gives D1q(s) = −ζ′(s)/ζ(s) − ∑p∣q log p · p−s/(1 − p−s), and ∑p∣q log p is the logarithm of the product of the distinct prime divisors of q, at most log q.

In the principal bound, if |t| ≤ 2 then every s = σ + it with σ > 1 lies in the region of the regional bound for ζ, so Re(−ζ′/ζ)(s) = Re(1/(s − 1)) − Re(ζ′/ζ(s) + 1/(s − 1)) ≤ Re(1/(σ − 1 + it)) + Cζ(log(|t| + 2))2, and (log(|t| + 2))2 ≤ log 4 · log(|t| + 2). If |t| > 2 and σ > 6/5, then Re(−ζ′/ζ)(s) ≤ ∑ Λ(n)n−σ ≤ K3 ≤ |K3| log(|t| + 2), because log(|t| + 2) ≥ 1, and Re(1/(σ − 1 + it)) ≥ 0 may again be added. In the middle regime the disk bound for ζ on |z − (11/10 + it)| ≤ 3/5 uses |Im z| ≥ |t| − 3/5 > 1 for |z − 1| ≥ 1, and 1 + 1/|z − 1| + |z|(1 + 1/Re z) ≤ 2 + 3(|t| + 3) ≤ 6(|t| + 2) for the growth bound; the point σ + it lies within (3/5)/6 = 1/10 of the centre, and 72 log M/(3/5) = 120 log M.

For any real y, q(2|y| + 2) ≤ (q(|y| + 2))2, so log(q(2|y| + 2)) ≤ 2 log(q(|y| + 2)), and log(q(|y| + 2)) ≥ log 2 because q(|y| + 2) ≥ 2. For real x, y not both zero, Re(1/(x + iy)) = x/(x2 + y2). If χ ≠ 1q, L(ρ, χ) = 0 and σ > 1, then Re ρ < 1 < σ, so Re(1/(σ + it − ρ)) = (σ − Re ρ)/|σ + it − ρ|2 > 0; this is the positivity of every term of the subtracted sums used in (iv) and (v). For the disk membership in (iv), 9/10 ≤ β < 1 gives |s − (11/10 + i Im s)| = 11/10 − β ≤ 1/5; in (v), a/(8L) ≤ 1/40 gives 1 − 1/40 ≤ β < 1 and the same conclusion.

Four-character product, entire continuation, near-one upper bound, alternating Taylor series at s = 2, and the Estermann key inequality

Why does a Taylor expansion around s = 2 of a product of four L-functions force a quantitative lower bound on Re F(σ) for σ just below 1, supplying the engine behind Siegel’s lower bound and the exceptional-zero gap? For two real quadratic nonprincipal characters χ1 modulo q1 and χ2 modulo q2 whose induced product ψ modulo q1q2 is nonprincipal, the four-factor product F(s) = ζ(s) L(s, χ1) L(s, χ2) L(s, ψ) has nonnegative Dirichlet coefficients an ≥ 0 with a1 = 1, and only a single simple pole at s = 1, of residue λ = L(1, χ1) L(1, χ2) L(1, ψ). Subtracting λ/(s − 1) produces an entire function G(s). Because an ≥ 0, the derivatives of F at s = 2 alternate in sign with βn = ((−1)n/n!) F(n)(2) ≥ 0 and β0 = F(2) ≥ 1, while the derivatives of 1/(s − 1) at 2 are (−1)nn!. Expanding G(σ) about 2 in powers of x = 2 − σ ∈ (1, 9/8] therefore writes the first M Taylor terms as ∑n<M xnβn − λ(xM − 1)/(x − 1). When λ/(σ − 1) = −λ/(x − 1) is added back to recover F(σ), the pole term +λ/(x − 1) cancels identically, leaving a nonnegative sum at least 1, a negative residue penalty −|λ|(2 − σ)M/(1 − σ), and a Cauchy tail bounded via polynomial growth on the circle |s − 2| = 3/2 (from the zeta growth estimate and the partial-summation bound for nonprincipal characters). Choosing M of size log(q1q2)/log(4/3) cuts the tail below 1/2 and turns (2 − σ)M into a constant times (q1q2)K(1−σ).

1. Four-character product, near-one upper bound, and Estermann’s Taylor lower bound. Let q1, q2 ≥ 1 be positive integers and let χ1 modulo q1, χ2 modulo q2 be Dirichlet characters. Say that a character ψ modulo q1q2 is the product character of χ1 and χ2 if ψ(n) = χ1(n)χ2(n) for every natural number n. Define for complex s

F(s) = ζ(s) L(s, χ1) L(s, χ2) L(s, ψ),   λ = L(1, χ1) L(1, χ2) L(1, ψ),   G(s) = F(s) − λ/(s − 1),

with G(1) defined by removable continuation whenever χ1, χ2, ψ are nonprincipal. Write CG for a constant such that |L(s, χ)| ≤ CG q(1 + |s|) for every nonprincipal χ modulo q ≥ 1 and Re s ≥ 1/2 (from the local Dirichlet expansion), and set Cg = 14(9|CG|/2)3, CL = 38 e3/2, c0 = |Cg| + 54|CL|3 + 1, ℓ = log(4/3), K = 3/ℓ, and CB = e2 exp(log(8c0)/(8ℓ)).

Proposition (Four-character product properties, near-one upper bound, and the Estermann key inequality).

(i) Whenever χ12 = 1, χ22 = 1, and ψ is the product character of χ1 and χ2, there exists a sequence of real numbers an ≥ 0 with a1 = 1 and abscissa of absolute convergence at most 1 such that F(s) = ∑n≥1 an n−s for all Re s > 1. Whenever χ1, χ2, ψ are nonprincipal, G extends to an entire function on ℂ and satisfies |F(s)| ≤ Cg (q1q2)3 on the circle |s − 2| = 3/2.

(ii) For every q ≥ 1, every nonprincipal character χ modulo q, and every complex w satisfying Re w ≥ 1 − 3/(2 log(3q)), Re w ≥ 1/4, and |w| ≤ 2,

|L(w, χ)| ≤ 38 e3/2 log(3q),   and in particular   |L(1, χ)| ≤ 38 e3/2 log(3q).

(iii) For all q1, q2 ≥ 1, all real quadratic nonprincipal characters χ1 modulo q1 and χ2 modulo q2 with nonprincipal product character ψ modulo q1q2, and every real σ ∈ [7/8, 1),

1/2 − CB |λ| (q1q2)K(1−σ) / (1 − σ) ≤ Re F(σ).

Proof. Taking parts (i) and (ii) from the details below, we prove (iii) in two steps. First let F, G, λ be any functions satisfying F(s) = ∑n≥1 an n−s for Re s > 1 (with an ≥ 0, a1 = 1, abscissa at most 1), G entire, F(s) = G(s) + λ/(s − 1) for s ≠ 1, and |G(s)| ≤ B on the circle |s − 2| = 3/2. Since 1 < 2, every term of F(2) = ∑n≥1 an n−2 is nonnegative and the n = 1 term equals 1, so F(2) ≥ 1. Differentiating termwise at s = 2 gives (−1)nF(n)(2) = ∑k≥1 ak (log k)n k−2 ≥ 0, so βn = ((−1)n/n!) F(n)(2) ≥ 0 for every n ≥ 0, with β0 = F(2) ≥ 1. On the other hand, differentiating (s − 1)−1 n times at s = 2 yields (−1)nn!, so G(n)(2) = F(n)(2) − λ(−1)nn!. Now fix σ ∈ [7/8, 1), set x = 2 − σ ∈ (1, 9/8], and let M ≥ 1 be an integer. Because G is entire, its Taylor series at 2 converges at σ: G(σ) = ∑n=0M−1 tn + ∑k=0∞ tk+M, where tn = (n!)−1(σ − 2)nG(n)(2) = xnβn − λxn. Summing the geometric series for n < M gives ∑n=0M−1 tn = ∑n=0M−1 xnβn − λ(xM − 1)/(x − 1). Since σ − 1 = −(x − 1), adding λ/(σ − 1) cancels +λ/(x − 1) and yields F(σ) = ∑n=0M−1 xnβn − λxM/(x − 1) + ∑k=0∞ tk+M. Every term xnβn is real and nonnegative, so the finite sum has real part at least β0 ≥ 1. By Cauchy’s estimate on |s − 2| = 3/2, |G(m)(2)| ≤ m! B/(3/2)m, whence |tm| ≤ B (x/(3/2))m ≤ B(3/4)m because x ≤ 9/8 gives x/(3/2) ≤ 3/4. Summing the geometric tail gives |∑k=0∞ tk+M| ≤ B(3/4)M/(1 − 3/4) = 4B(3/4)M. Taking real parts with x − 1 = 1 − σ yields

1 − |λ| (2 − σ)M / (1 − σ) − 4B(3/4)M ≤ Re F(σ).

Second, specialize to F and G from (i). For each nonprincipal character of modulus q, part (ii) and log(3q) ≤ 3q give |L(1, χ)| ≤ |CL| · 3q, so |λ| ≤ 27|CL|3(q1q2)2. On the circle |s − 2| = 3/2 we have |s − 1| ≥ 1/2, so |λ/(s − 1)| ≤ 2|λ| ≤ 54|CL|3(q1q2)2, and combining with |F(s)| ≤ Cg(q1q2)3 gives |G(s)| ≤ B := c0(q1q2)3 (for a general growth exponent Kg this uses K′ = max(Kg, 2), which equals 3 here). Since 8B ≥ 8 ≥ 1, take the truncation order M = ⌈log(8B)/ℓ⌉ + 1 ≥ 1. Then Mℓ ≥ log(8B), so (4/3)M ≥ 8B and 4B(3/4)M ≤ 1/2; moreover M ≤ 2 + log(8B)/ℓ. Using 2 − σ = 1 + (1 − σ) ≤ e1−σ and 0 < 1 − σ ≤ 1/8,

(2 − σ)M ≤ eM(1−σ) ≤ e2 exp((log(8c0) + 3 log(q1q2))(1 − σ)/ℓ) ≤ e2 exp(log(8c0)/(8ℓ)) (q1q2)(3/ℓ)(1−σ) = CB (q1q2)K(1−σ).

Substituting 4B(3/4)M ≤ 1/2 and this bound on (2 − σ)M into the truncated Taylor lower bound gives (iii).

Prime-power convolution nonnegativity, entire pole removal, circle growth on |s − 2| = 3/2, and the near-one bound via summation by parts

For Dirichlet series nonnegativity in (i), put f = (1 ∗ χ1) ∗ (χ2 ∗ ψ), a multiplicative arithmetic function with f(1) = 1 whose Dirichlet series for Re s > 1 equals (ζ(s)L(s, χ1))(L(s, χ2)L(s, ψ)) = F(s). Because f is multiplicative, it suffices to show f(pk) ≥ 0 for every prime p and k ≥ 0. Since χ12 = 1, the values of χ1(p) lie in {0, 1, −1}, so (1 ∗ χ1)(pj) = ∑i=0j χ1(p)i is always nonnegative (equal to 1, j + 1, or (1 + (−1)j)/2). Using ψ(n) = χ1(n)χ2(n) and complete multiplicativity of χ2, we have (χ2 ∗ ψ)(n) = χ2(n)(1 ∗ χ1)(n). If χ2(p) ∈ {0, 1}, then (χ2 ∗ ψ)(pj) ≥ 0 for all j, so the divisor convolution f(pk) is a sum of products of nonnegative terms. If χ2(p) = −1 and χ1(p) ∈ {0, 1}, swapping the symmetric roles of χ1 and χ2 reduces to the preceding case. In the last case χ1(p) = χ2(p) = −1, (1 ∗ χ1)(pj) vanishes for odd j and equals 1 for even j, so (−1)j(1 ∗ χ1)(pj) = (1 ∗ χ1)(pj) ≥ 0 for every j. For example, at p2 with χ1(p) = χ2(p) = −1, both factors take values (1, 0, 1) at (1, p, p2), giving f(p2) = 1·1 + 0·0 + 1·1 = 2 ≥ 0.

For entire continuation in (i), let ζ0(s) = ζ(s) − 1/(s − 1) for s ≠ 1 and ζ0(1) = γ; because ζ(s) − 1/(s − 1) → γ as s → 1, ζ0 is entire. Writing P(s) = L(s, χ1)L(s, χ2)L(s, ψ), which is entire since χ1, χ2, ψ are nonprincipal and satisfies P(1) = λ, the divided difference Q(s) = (P(s) − P(1))/(s − 1) (with Q(1) = P′(1)) is entire, and G(s) = ζ0(s)P(s) + Q(s) is entire with G(s) + λ/(s − 1) = (ζ(s) − 1/(s − 1))P(s) + (P(s) − λ)/(s − 1) + λ/(s − 1) = F(s) for all s ≠ 1.

For circle growth in (i), any s with |s − 2| = 3/2 satisfies Re s ≥ 2 − 3/2 = 1/2, |s| ≤ 2 + 3/2 = 7/2, and |s − 1| ≥ |s − 2| − 1 = 1/2. The zeta growth bound of the zeta zero-free region gives |ζ(s)| ≤ 1 + 1/|s − 1| + |s|(1 + 1/Re s) ≤ 1 + 2 + (7/2)·3 = 27/2 ≤ 14. The polynomial growth bound for each nonprincipal L-function gives |L(s, χ)| ≤ |CG| q(1 + 7/2) = (9/2)|CG| q; bounding q1, q2 ≤ q1q2 and multiplying all four factors gives |F(s)| ≤ 14(9|CG|/2)3(q1q2)3.

For the near-one bound (ii), a nonprincipal character modulo q cannot exist for q = 1 or q = 2 (whose unit groups are trivial), so q ≥ 3 and log(3q) ≥ log 9 > 2 (as e < 2.72 gives e2 < 9). Whenever 1 ≤ x ≤ 3q and t ≤ 3/(2 log(3q)), we have xt = exp(t log x) ≤ e3/2. Hence for every integer 1 ≤ n ≤ q and Re w ≥ 1 − 3/(2 log(3q)), n−Re w = n1−Re wn−1 ≤ e3/2/n, and summing over 1 ≤ n ≤ q gives |∑n=1q χ(n)n−w| ≤ e3/2Hq ≤ e3/2(1 + log q) ≤ e3/2(1 + log(3q)). Writing Aχ(M) = ∑n=1M χ(n), complete periodicity over a full period of length q gives |∑n=0M χ(n)| ≤ q, hence |Aχ(M)| ≤ q + 1 for every M. Summation by parts at q splits L(w, χ) into the partial sum through q, the boundary term −Aχ(q)(q + 1)−w, and the tail ∑n≥q+1 Aχ(n)(n−w − (n + 1)−w). Because 1 ≤ q + 1 ≤ 3q, we have (q + 1)(q + 1)−Re w = (q + 1)1−Re w ≤ e3/2, bounding the boundary term by e3/2. With |w| ≤ 2 and Re w ≥ 1/4 we have |w|/Re w ≤ 8, so the tail bound (q + 1)(|w|/Re w)(q + 1)−Re w is at most 8 e3/2. Summing all three parts gives |L(w, χ)| ≤ e3/2(10 + log(3q)) ≤ 38 e3/2 log(3q) since log(3q) ≥ 2. Evaluating at w = 1 (where Re 1 = 1 ≥ 1 − 3/(2 log(3q)) and ≥ 1/4, and |1| = 1 ≤ 2) gives the specialization for L(1, χ). Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, DLMF §1.9(iii)[266].

Character existence, real-line sign control, same-character Euler-factor comparison, and Estermann–Landau deduction of Siegel’s lower bound

Why does the Estermann–Landau proof of Siegel’s theorem produce a lower bound |L(1, χ)| ≥ c(ε) q−ε for every ε > 0 while refusing to compute c(ε) explicitly, and how do both branches of the alternative collapse into a single inequality? Given ε > 0 and the exponent K ≥ 0 from the Estermann key inequality, fix the threshold σ0 = max(7/8, 1 − ε/(2(K + 1))) < 1, so that K(1 − σ) ≤ ε/2 throughout [σ0, 1). Either some real nonprincipal character χ1 modulo q1 has a real zero β ∈ [σ0, 1), or none does. In Case 1, fix such a pair (χ1, β) depending only on ε; then for every real nonprincipal χ modulo q and induced product ψ modulo q1q, the four-factor product F(β) vanishes identically because L(β, χ1) = 0, so Re F(β) ≤ 0. In Case 2, no real nonprincipal character vanishes on [σ0, 1); fix any concrete real nonprincipal character χ1 (namely the quadratic character χ4 modulo 4) and evaluate at σ = σ0 itself. Since L(·, ·) tends to 1 at +∞ and is real on the real axis, having no zeros on [σ0, ∞) forces L(σ0, χ1), L(σ0, χ), and L(σ0, ψ) (when ψ ≠ 1) all to be strictly positive, whereas ζ(σ0) < 0 on (0, 1); hence Re F(σ0) < 0 ≤ 0 directly, with no limit σ → 1− needed. Thus both cases supply a fixed pair (χ1, σ) with Re F(σ) ≤ 0 whenever ψ ≠ 1. Plugging Re F(σ) ≤ 0 into the Estermann key inequality yields 1/2 ≤ CB |L(1, χ1)| |L(1, χ)| |L(1, ψ)| (q1q)K(1−σ)/(1 − σ), bounding |L(1, χ)| from below by c q−ε; and in the degenerate case ψ = 1, χ1 and χ agree on all integers coprime to q1q, so comparing their Euler factors at s = 1 bounds |L(1, χ)| directly from |L(1, χ1)| > 0.

1. Auxiliary character existence, real-line signs, level comparison, and Siegel’s theorem. Keep the constants CB, K ≥ 0, and CL from the Estermann key inequality, and write ω(n) for the number of distinct prime divisors of a positive integer n.

Proposition (Character existence, real-line signs, Euler-factor level comparison, and Siegel’s lower bound).

(i) For every pair of moduli q1, q2 ≥ 1 and Dirichlet characters χ1 modulo q1, χ2 modulo q2, there exists a product character ψ modulo q1q2 satisfying ψ(n) = χ1(n)χ2(n) for all n; moreover there exists a real nonprincipal Dirichlet character, namely the quadratic character χ4 modulo 4.

(ii) For every real σ ∈ (0, 1), ζ(σ) is real and strictly negative: Im ζ(σ) = 0 and Re ζ(σ) < 0. For every q ≥ 1, every real nonprincipal χ modulo q, and every real σ0 such that L(σ, χ) ≠ 0 for all σ ≥ σ0, one has Im L(σ, χ) = 0 and Re L(σ, χ) > 0 for all σ ≥ σ0.

(iii) Whenever q1, q ≥ 1 and nonprincipal characters χ1 modulo q1 and χ modulo q satisfy χ1(n) = χ(n) for every natural number n coprime to q1q,

|L(1, χ1)| ≤ (ω(q1q) + 1)2 |L(1, χ)|.

(iv) For every ε > 0 there exists c > 0 such that for every q ≥ 1 and every real quadratic nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ modulo q (χ2 = 1, χ ≠ 1),

c q−ε ≤ |L(1, χ)|.

Proof. Taking (i)–(iii) from the details below, we first prove the unified product-character implication: fix ε > 0, a real nonprincipal character χ1 modulo q1 ≥ 1, and σ ∈ [7/8, 1) with K(1 − σ) ≤ ε/2, and suppose that Re F(σ) ≤ 0 for every q ≥ 1, every real nonprincipal χ modulo q, and every nonprincipal product character ψ modulo q1q of χ1 and χ. Since χ1 ≠ 1, L(1, χ1) ≠ 0, so |L(1, χ1)| > 0. Put A = |CL| + 1 > 0, D = (2/(ε log 2) + 1)2 > 0, Pc = (3q1)ε > 0, and

c = min((1 − σ)/(2 max(CB, 1) |L(1, χ1)| A (2/ε) Pc),   |L(1, χ1)|/(D Pc)) > 0.

Given any q ≥ 1 and any real nonprincipal χ modulo q, part (i) yields a product character ψ modulo q1q of χ1 and χ. We must show c ≤ |L(1, χ)| qε.

If ψ = 1, then for every n coprime to q1q we have χ1(n)χ(n) = ψ(n) = 1 and χ(n)2 = 1, so χ1(n) = χ(n). Part (iii) gives |L(1, χ1)| ≤ (ω(q1q) + 1)2 |L(1, χ)|. Because 2ω(n) ≤ ∏p∣n p ≤ n for any positive integer n, taking logarithms and using log n ≤ nε/2/(ε/2) gives ω(n) ≤ (2/(ε log 2))nε/2, hence (ω(n) + 1)2 ≤ D nε. Applying this at n = q1q with (q1q)ε ≤ (3q1)ε qε = Pc qε yields |L(1, χ1)| ≤ D Pc |L(1, χ)| qε, so c ≤ |L(1, χ1)|/(D Pc) ≤ |L(1, χ)| qε.

If ψ ≠ 1, then the hypothesis Re F(σ) ≤ 0 and the Estermann key inequality yield (1 − σ)/2 ≤ CB |L(1, χ1)| |L(1, χ)| |L(1, ψ)| (q1q)K(1−σ). Set M = (3q1q)ε/2, so M2 = (3q1)ε qε = Pc qε. By the upper bound at s = 1 from the near-one estimate and log(3q1q) ≤ (3q1q)ε/2/(ε/2), we have |L(1, ψ)| ≤ A (2/ε) M. Meanwhile K(1 − σ) ≤ ε/2 gives (q1q)K(1−σ) ≤ (q1q)ε/2 ≤ M. Combining with CB ≤ max(CB, 1) yields (1 − σ)/2 ≤ max(CB, 1) |L(1, χ1)| A (2/ε) Pc |L(1, χ)| qε, hence c ≤ |L(1, χ)| qε.

Now deduce (iv). Given ε > 0, set σ0 = max(7/8, 1 − ε/(2(K + 1))); then 7/8 ≤ σ0 < 1, and every σ ∈ [σ0, 1) satisfies K(1 − σ) ≤ (K + 1)(1 − σ) ≤ ε/2. Split into two cases:

Case 1: There exist q1 ≥ 1, a real nonprincipal character χ1 modulo q1, and β ∈ [σ0, 1) with L(β, χ1) = 0. Then for every real nonprincipal χ and nonprincipal product character ψ, F(β) = ζ(β) L(β, χ1) L(β, χ) L(β, ψ) = 0, so Re F(β) = 0 ≤ 0. The unified implication at (χ1, β) gives (iv).

Case 2: No real nonprincipal character has a real zero in [σ0, 1). Choose the real nonprincipal character χ1 = χ4 modulo q1 = 4 from (i). Since no nonprincipal Dirichlet L-function vanishes in Re s ≥ 1, every real nonprincipal character is zero-free on [σ0, ∞). By (ii), for every real nonprincipal χ modulo q and every nonprincipal product character ψ modulo q1q (which also satisfies ψ2 = 1), the values L(σ0, χ1), L(σ0, χ), and L(σ0, ψ) are all real and strictly positive, whereas ζ(σ0) is real and strictly negative. Their product F(σ0) is therefore real and strictly negative, so Re F(σ0) < 0 ≤ 0. The unified implication at (χ1, σ0) again yields (iv).

Change-of-level product character, real-line negativity of ζ, Schwarz conjugation and positivity of L, and the Euler-factor induction

For (i), inducing χ1 modulo q1 and χ2 modulo q2 to the common modulus q1q2 and multiplying gives a Dirichlet character ψ modulo q1q2; on integers coprime to q1q2 each induced factor equals χi(n), while if gcd(n, q1q2) > 1 then either gcd(n, q1) > 1 or gcd(n, q2) > 1, so both sides vanish. For the concrete real nonprincipal character, χ4(1) = 1, χ4(3) = −1, and χ4(0) = χ4(2) = 0 satisfies χ42 = 1 and χ4(3) = −1 ≠ 1.

For the first half of (ii), recall from the zeta zero-free region that (s − 1)ζ(s) = s − D(s) for Re s > 0, where D(s) = ∑n≥0 dn(s) and dn(s) = (s − 1)∫n+1n+2 (x−s − (n + 2)−s) dx. For real σ ∈ (0, 1), the function x ↦ x−σ is decreasing on [n + 1, n + 2], so each integral rn = ∫n+1n+2 (x−σ − (n + 2)−σ) dx is real and nonnegative, with ∑n≥0 rn convergent because ∑n≥0 |dn(σ)| converges. Dividing (σ − 1)ζ(σ) = σ − (σ − 1)∑n≥0 rn by σ − 1 ≠ 0 gives ζ(σ) = σ/(σ − 1) − ∑n≥0 rn, which is real and strictly negative because σ/(σ − 1) < 0 and ∑n≥0 rn ≥ 0.

For the second half of (ii), a character with χ2 = 1 takes values in {0, 1, −1} ⊂ ℝ, so for Re z > 1 the termwise Dirichlet series satisfies L(z, χ) = L(z̄, χ)̄ (the complex conjugate of the value at the conjugate point z̄). Both sides are entire functions of z when χ ≠ 1, so by the identity theorem this conjugation symmetry holds for every s ∈ ℂ; in particular, L(σ, χ) is real for every real σ. Moreover, as real σ → +∞, the Dirichlet series converges to its n = 1 term χ(1) = 1, so Re L(x, χ) > 0 for all sufficiently large x. If Re L(σ, χ) ≤ 0 for some σ ≥ σ0, the intermediate value theorem on [σ, x] would produce a real point in [σ0, x] where Re L and Im L both vanish, contradicting the hypothesis.

For (iii), inducing χ1 and χ to modulus q1q produces the same character modulo q1q because they agree on all units modulo q1q. The change-of-level identity at s = 1 gives L(1, χ1) ∏p∣q1q (1 − χ1(p)p−1) = L(1, χ) ∏p∣q1q (1 − χ(p)p−1). Since |χ1(p)p−1| ≤ 1/p and |χ(p)p−1| ≤ 1/p, taking absolute values gives |L(1, χ1)| ∏p∣q1q (1 − 1/p) ≤ |L(1, χ)| ∏p∣q1q (1 + 1/p). For any finite set S of integers ≥ 2, induction on the maximum element a of S shows ∏p∈S (1 − 1/p) ≥ 1/(|S| + 1): with s = S \ {a} ⊆ [2, a − 1], we have |s| + 2 ≤ a, so (1 − 1/a)/(|s| + 1) − 1/(|s| + 2) = (a − |s| − 2)/(a(|s| + 1)(|s| + 2)) ≥ 0. Since (1 + 1/p)(1 − 1/p) = 1 − 1/p2 ≤ 1 for every p ∈ S, we also have ∏p∈S (1 + 1/p) ≤ (∏p∈S (1 − 1/p))−1 ≤ |S| + 1. Applying both inequalities to the set of prime factors of q1q (of cardinality ω(q1q)) yields |L(1, χ1)| ≤ (ω(q1q) + 1)2 |L(1, χ)|. For example, on S = {2, 3, 5} (|S| = 3), ∏(1 − 1/p) = (1/2)(2/3)(4/5) = 4/15 ≥ 1/4 and ∏(1 + 1/p) = (3/2)(4/3)(6/5) = 12/5 ≤ 4, so the ratio is 9 ≤ 16 = (3 + 1)2. (A parallel rearrangement using log(2N0) = log 2 + log N0 ≤ (2N0)ε/2/(ε/2) also bounds (ω(N0) + 1)2 by (4/(ε log 2)2) 2ε q1ε qε for N0 = q1q.)

Cauchy first-derivative bound near s = 1 and deduction of the exceptional-zero gap

How does Siegel’s lower bound |L(1, χ)| ≥ c0 q−ε/3 exclude real zeros β of L(s, χ) within distance c q−ε of 1, supplying the gap 1 − β ≥ c q−ε invoked in the exceptional denominator test, the small-modulus relative error, power-sum repulsion, and the relative progression count? If β is a real zero very close to 1, say β > 1 − 1/log(3q), then L(1, χ) = L(1, χ) − L(β, χ) is bounded in absolute value by (1 − β) times the maximum of |L′(σ, χ)| over [β, 1]. Because the near-one estimate holds throughout Re w ≥ 1 − 3/(2 log(3q)) (including Re w > 1 on the right half of a circle centred at σ ≤ 1), placing a Cauchy circle of radius 1/(2 log(3q)) around any real σ ∈ [1 − 1/log(3q), 1] divides the bound 38 e3/2 log(3q) by 1/(2 log(3q)) to give |L′(σ, χ)| ≤ 76 e3/2 (log(3q))2 (the same circle derivative bound also enters the positive prime moment). Absorbing each factor of log(3q) into qε/3 turns |L(1, χ)| ≥ c0 q−ε/3 into 1 − β ≥ c q−ε.

1. Near-one Cauchy derivative estimate and the exceptional-zero gap. Write CD = 76 e3/2. For a given ε > 0, let c0 > 0 be the constant from Siegel’s lower bound at exponent ε/3, put Kε = log 3 + 3/ε and MD = max(CD, 1), and set c = min(1/Kε, c0/(MD Kε2)) > 0.

Proposition (Near-one first-derivative bound and exceptional-zero repulsion gap).

(i) For every q ≥ 1, every nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ modulo q, and every real σ ∈ [1 − 1/log(3q), 1],

|L′(σ, χ)| ≤ 76 e3/2 (log(3q))2.

(ii) For every ε > 0 there exists c > 0 (explicitly the constant above) such that for every q ≥ 1, every real quadratic nonprincipal character χ modulo q (χ2 = 1, χ ≠ 1), and every real β with L(β, χ) = 0,

β ≤ 1 − c q−ε.

Proof. For (i), fix q ≥ 1, a nonprincipal χ modulo q, and σ ∈ [1 − 1/log(3q), 1]. Because χ ≠ 1 we have q ≥ 3 and log(3q) ≥ 2, so 1/log(3q) ≤ 1/2 and the Cauchy radius ρ = 1/(2 log(3q)) satisfies 0 < ρ ≤ 1/4. Take any complex z on the circle |z − σ| = ρ. Then |Re z − σ| ≤ ρ, so Re z ≥ σ − ρ ≥ 1 − 1/log(3q) − 1/(2 log(3q)) = 1 − 3/(2 log(3q)), and also Re z ≥ 1 − 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4; moreover, σ ≥ 1 − 1/2 > 0 and σ ≤ 1 give |z| ≤ |z − σ| + |σ| ≤ 1/4 + 1 < 2. Thus the near-one bound applies to every point on the circle |z − σ| = ρ, giving |L(z, χ)| ≤ 38 e3/2 log(3q). Because L(·, χ) is entire, Cauchy’s derivative estimate on that circle yields

|L′(σ, χ)| ≤ (38 e3/2 log(3q)) / (1/(2 log(3q))) = 76 e3/2 (log(3q))2.

For (ii), fix ε > 0, let q ≥ 1 and χ modulo q be real and nonprincipal, and suppose L(β, χ) = 0 for a real β. Since a nonprincipal L-function has no zeros in Re s ≥ 1, we have β < 1. Set u = qε/3 ≥ 1, so that q−ε/3 = u−1 and q−ε = (u3)−1. From log(3q) = log 3 + log q ≤ (log 3)u + u/(ε/3) = Kε u, consider two cases:

If β ≤ 1 − 1/log(3q), then c ≤ 1/Kε and u ≤ u3 give c log(3q) ≤ (1/Kε)(Kε u) = u ≤ u3, so c q−ε = c / u3 ≤ 1/log(3q) ≤ 1 − β.

If instead β > 1 − 1/log(3q), then every t ∈ [β, 1] lies in [1 − 1/log(3q), 1], where (i) bounds |L′(t, χ)| by CD (log(3q))2 ≤ MD (Kε u)2. Applying the mean-value inequality to the smooth map t ↦ L(t, χ) on [β, 1] with L(β, χ) = 0, and combining with Siegel’s lower bound |L(1, χ)| ≥ c0 u−1, gives

c0 u−1 ≤ |L(1, χ) − L(β, χ)| ≤ MD (Kε u)2 (1 − β).

Multiplying by u yields c0 ≤ MD Kε2 u3 (1 − β), whence c q−ε = c / u3 ≤ (c0/(MD Kε2)) / u3 ≤ 1 − β. In both cases β ≤ 1 − c q−ε.

Logarithmic absorption log(3q) ≤ (log 3 + 3/ε) qε/3 and the power-splitting identity

For any δ > 0 and real x ≥ 1, the elementary inequality log x ≤ xδ/δ (from y ≤ ey applied to y = δ log x) and 1 ≤ xδ give log(3x) = log 3 + log x ≤ (log 3)xδ + xδ/δ = (log 3 + 1/δ)xδ. Taking δ = ε/3 gives log(3q) ≤ Kε qε/3 for every q ≥ 1. Moreover, for any x > 0 and integer k ≥ 1, (xε/k)k = xε, so x−ε = ((xε/k)k)−1; taking k = 3 splits the exponent ε evenly into one factor q−ε/3 for Siegel’s lower bound on |L(1, χ)| and two factors qε/3 for (log(3q))2 in the derivative estimate. For any nonprincipal character χ modulo q, both q = 1 and q = 2 have a single unit modulo q (the class 1), so every character modulo 1 or 2 is principal; hence q ≥ 3 and log(3q) ≥ log 9 > 2 automatically.

How does the square-root exponential arise for one character?

Write d = log m, s = √(log y), and ψχ(y) = ∑n≤y Λ(n)χ(n). In the small-modulus range, d is at most a fixed small multiple of s. Take cZ to be the smaller of 1/20 and a positive constant provided by the ordinary zero-free-region theorem. Its region is Re z ≥ 1 − cZ/log(m(|Im z| + 2)), with 0 < cZ ≤ 1/20. Let Bχ consist of the zeros of L(·,χ) in this region. Across the characters of this modulus there is at most one such zero. If present, it is simple, real, and belongs to a nonprincipal quadratic character. The product over all characters is what makes uniqueness simultaneous. See Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Theorem 12.3[267]. There are constants c, C > 0 such that for y ≥ 2 and d ≤ cs,

|ψχ(y) − 𝟙χ principaly + ∑β∈Bχ yβ/β| ≤ Cy exp(−cs).

For a nonprincipal χ, smooth by weighting Λ(n)χ(n) with y/n − 1 for n ≤ y. Denote this sum by S(y). The contour formula for it has a linear term D(1)y, where D = −L′/L, and a term −yβ/[β(β − 1)] for each β in the region. To see the rate of decay of the remainder, take height T = exp(cZs/2) and put J = log(m(T + 2)). For d ≤ cZs/4 we have J ≤ 3cZs/4 + 2. The shifted line can be chosen with real part σ ≤ 1 − cZ/(4J). Truncation and the shifted line together cost at most a constant times (s + 2)³(y/T + Tyσ). For sufficiently large s, J ≤ s/4, so Tyσ ≤ y exp(−cZs/2). Absorbing the cubic factor and increasing the constant on bounded s gives a remainder of order y exp(−cZs/4).

To undo the smoothing take u = y(1 + h). The expression [yS(u) − uS(y)]/(u − y) gives weight one to n ≤ y, and a weight between zero and one to the at most yh + 1 integers in (y,u]. This costs at most (yh + 1)log u. The linear term cancels. The difference of the β term is −yβ/β with error at most 2yh, uniformly up to β = 1 from below. Indeed the difference quotient for S(x)/x averages xβ−2 over [y,u], with a factor −yu/β. The relative factor multiplying −yβ/β lies between (1 + h)β−1 and 1 + h, hence within h of 1 since ½ ≤ β < 1. The two contour remainders, after differencing, are of order y exp(−cZs/4)/h. These competing errors explain why the width of the averaging interval matters.

For the principal character, the unrestricted smoothed zeta sum has main term x log x − (1 + γ)x, where γ is Euler’s constant, and error of order x exp(−cζ√(log x)). This zeta estimate also follows from the ordinary prime number theorem. If ψ(t) = t + E(t), partial summation gives S(x) = x ∫1x ψ(t)dt/t². The bound |E(t)| ≪ t exp(−b√(log t)) makes ∫x∞ |E(t)|dt/t² exponentially small in √(log x), after decreasing b. Its constant ∫1∞ E(t)dt/t² equals −1 − γ. Indeed −ζ′(w)/[wζ(w)] − 1/(w − 1) is the integral of E(t)t−w−1 for real w > 1. Taking w down to 1 in the integral and the Laurent expansion gives the constant. See Koukoulopoulos, proof of Theorem 8.1[267] and DLMF (25.2.4)[265].

The difference of the principal main term gives y(1 + h)log(1 + h)/h, between y and y(1 + h). Remove the powers of primes dividing m. At each exponent their weights sum to at most log m, and there are at most log y/log 2 exponents. Now put c₀ = min(1, cζ, cZ/4) and h = exp(−c₀s/2). Both h and exp(−c₀s)/h equal exp(−c₀s/2). The logarithms in the short interval and the deleted prime powers fit within Cy exp(−c₀s/4) when d ≤ c₀s/4. This proves the displayed estimate with c = c₀/4. The large-modulus formula below uses the same elementary weights with a different contour and a longer list of zeros.

Where does the exceptional factor come from at small modulus?

Suppose 8 divides m. The progression theorem chooses one pair (χ₁,β) for the entire modulus when there is a nonprincipal quadratic character with a real zero 1 − 1/(8d) < β < 1. It chooses the pair in the ordinary zero-free region first if one exists. This rule makes the main term the same in both modulus ranges. For a single character let Mχ(y) be y if χ is principal and zero otherwise, with yβ/β subtracted if χ = χ₁. Put η = min(1,(1 − β)d) if a pair was chosen and η = 1 otherwise.

Set cA = min(c/4,cZ) and assume d ≤ cAs. If a selected β lies in the region, the character bound already contains its contribution. If the selected β lies outside, the regional list for χ₁ is empty. The additional term in Mχ₁ has modulus at most 2y exp(−s/2). Indeed β ≥ ½, and 1 − β > cZ/log(2m) ≥ cZ/(2d) ≥ 1/(2s). Since log y = s², this is precisely the loss in the exponent of yβ. If no pair exists every regional list is empty.

Summing the absolute errors over the φ(m) ≤ m characters costs one factor of m. To retain η, use the exceptional-zero bound η ≥ b/m for a fixed b > 0. This is the exponent-one case of Siegel’s lower bound. For a real primitive character of conductor f and a real zero β near 1 one has 1 − β ≥ bεf−ε. A character modulo m is induced from conductor f ≤ m, and its additional Euler factors have no zeros of positive real part. The factor d in η is at least log 8. Thus introducing η costs at most one further factor m/b. But m² ≤ exp(2cAs), with 2cA ≤ c/2 and 2cA ≤ 1/10. Both exponentials survive. See Kedlaya, Notes on analytic number theory, Theorem 10.9[268].

∑χ mod m |ψχ(y) − Mχ(y)| ≤ [(C + 2)/b] yη exp(−c′s),   c′ = min(c/2, 2/5).

For a reduced class a, multiply each error by the conjugate of χ(a), whose modulus is one, and divide the sum by φ(m). Character orthogonality gives the small-modulus contribution to the weighted progression estimate. The error still falls with η in a class where the exceptional term subtracts from the main term. See DLMF §27.8, Dirichlet characters and orthogonality[269].

Check the loss from primes dividing the modulus

For m = 8 and y = 16, the unrestricted count includes 2, 4, 8 and 16. Each contributes log 2, so passing to the principal character removes exactly 4 log 2. The general bound counts four possible exponents, with allowance log 8 at each. This checks the correction to the principal sum independently of any exceptional zero.

Why does repelling the other zeros save the exceptional factor?

Fix the modulus m, with 8 ∣ m, and put d = log m, Y = log t. In the large-modulus part of the progression estimate, the explicit formula is truncated at T₀ = m12. Its finite zero lists satisfy 1 − κ < Re ρ < 1 and |Im ρ| ≤ T₀ + 1, with a fixed positive κ ≤ 1/20 chosen within the range of the repulsion theorem. Put H = log(m(T₀ + 3)), so d ≤ H ≤ 14d. For a listed zero set v = H(1 − Re ρ). Its weight in the error after division by t is exp(−vY/H). We sum over all characters modulo this one modulus, counting multiplicities and subtracting the one exceptional occurrence if it is present in the lists. Call the sum W. When the exceptional zero occurs, its multiplicity is at least one. Removing one copy leaves every remaining weight nonnegative.

Why does a smoothed prime sum produce this list of zeros?

Fix a modulus m ≥ 3, a Dirichlet character χ modulo m, a height T ≥ 2 and a strip width 0 < κ ≤ 1/20. The sharp sum we seek is ψχ(y) = ∑n≤y Λ(n)χ(n), where Λ equals log p on positive powers of a prime p and vanishes elsewhere. Start with the continuous weight y/n − 1 on 1 ≤ n ≤ y, zero beyond that range. Call the weighted sum Sχ(y).

For Re s > 1, integrating (x − 1)x−s−1 from 1 to infinity gives 1/[s(s − 1)]. Mellin inversion recovers the weight at x = y/n. Multiplying by Λ(n)χ(n) and summing gives Perron’s integral for Sχ(y), with integrand (−L′/L)(s,χ)ys/[s(s − 1)]. On the initial vertical line Re s = 1 + 1/log y the Dirichlet series converges absolutely and the kernel decays quadratically with height. Mellin inversion, DLMF 2.5.2[270].

Move this line left to σ₁ between 1 − κ and 1 − 3κ/4 and truncate at a height T′ between T and T + 1. The left side and both heights are fixed before y varies. The right side moves with y but stays to the right of 1. All enclosed zeros therefore stay in the same list at both arguments of the difference. The local expansion of the logarithmic derivative bounds the number of zeros, counted with multiplicities, in the strip Re ρ ≥ 9/10, |Im ρ − t| ≤ 1 by C log(m(|t| + 2)). Adding these estimates along the strip bounds the number of zeros up to T + 3 by a constant times (T + 1)log(m(T + 2)). Exclude short intervals around their real parts and absolute ordinates when choosing the sides. Their total length leaves room for a clearance of at least κ/[C(T + 1)log(m(T + 2))].

Write Zχ for the zeros strictly inside the resulting rectangle and aρ for their orders of vanishing. Every listed zero satisfies 1 − κ < Re ρ < 1 and |Im ρ| ≤ T + 1. Every zero with Re ρ ≥ 1 − κ/2 and |Im ρ| ≤ T is included. Between those two boundaries the list may depend on the chosen rectangle. At a zero of order aρ, −L′/L has residue −aρ. To read the term at 1, put Fχ(s) = (s − 1)L(s,χ) with its value continued at 1 for the principal character, and Fχ = L(·,χ) otherwise. Then Fχ(1) ≠ 0. Put Kχ = −F′χ(1)/Fχ(1). The residue at 1 contributes yKχ. For the principal character there is also the double pole from the kernel times 1/(s − 1). Differentiating ys/s at 1 gives y(log y − 1). The residue theorem equates the sum of these contributions to the integral around the rectangle. Dividing by y gives the following identity for every y ≥ 2. Residue theorem, DLMF 1.10.8[271].

Sχ(y)/y = Kχ + 𝟙χ principal(log y − 1) − ∑ρ∈Zχ aρyρ−1/[ρ(ρ − 1)] + Rχ(y),
|Rχ(y)| ≤ C[(mT)Cy−κ/2 + (log y)(log(mT))²/T].

Here C depends only on κ. On the three new sides the local logarithmic-derivative estimate costs a factor of at most a constant depending on κ times T(log(mT))², apart from the known principal pole. Each horizontal segment gains T′−2 from the kernel. The omitted tails of the original line gain 1/T′ after integrating the inverse square. These give the second error. The left side has length 2T′, and after division by y it contains yσ₁−1 ≤ y−3κ/4. Its cost fits inside a constant times (mT)⁴y−κ/2. Enlarging C gives the displayed bound. The same local counts give the multiplicity estimate used in the count of zero strips.

How much of a logarithmic derivative comes from nearby zeros?

A zero of order a gives a term a/(s−ρ) in f′/f. To move a contour near many zeros, we need to bound both their total multiplicity and the part of the derivative left after removing them. Both follow from the same comparison of the size of f at the centre of a disk with its size on the boundary.

Local zero expansion. Let f be analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed disk of centre z₀ and radius r > 0. Suppose f(z₀) ≠ 0 and |f(z)| ≤ B|f(z₀)| throughout the disk, with B ≥ 1. Let Z consist of all zeros at distance at most r/3 from the centre. Write aρ for the order at ρ and N for the sum of these orders. At every s within r/6 of the centre where f(s) ≠ 0,

N ≤ log B / log 2,   |f′(s)/f(s) − ∑ρ∈Z aρ/(s−ρ)| ≤ 72 log B / r.

The zeros in the smaller closed disk are finite, since an accumulation point there would force f to vanish identically. Divide f by the polynomial P(z) = ∏(z−ρ)aρ. At each zero its Taylor expansion shows that the quotient g extends holomorphically with a nonzero value. At the centre, |P(z₀)| ≤ (r/3)N. On the outer circle each zero is at least 2r/3 away. There |P| ≥ (2r/3)N, hence |g| ≤ B 2−N|g(z₀)|. The maximum-modulus principle carries this inequality back to the centre. Cancelling |g(z₀)| gives 2N ≤ B. Maximum-modulus principle, DLMF §1.10(v)[272].

On the disk of radius r/3 the quotient is zero-free. Choose the analytic logarithm H of g/g(z₀) with H(z₀) = 0. Its real part is at most log B by the preceding bound. The Borel–Carathéodory inequality gives |H| ≤ 6 log B on the disk of radius r/4, since 2(r/4)/(r/3−r/4) = 6. For |s−z₀| ≤ r/6, the circle of radius r/12 about s stays in that disk. Cauchy’s estimate bounds |H′(s)| by 72 log B/r. Since f′/f = P′/P + H′, this is exactly the remainder in the displayed formula. Siu, the Borel–Carathéodory theorem[273] · Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, DLMF §1.9(iii)[266].

For example, take f(z) = exp(z)(z−1/9)² on the unit disk about zero. At the centre f′/f = −17. The zero contributes 2/(0−1/9) = −18, and the remaining 1 is the logarithmic derivative of the exponential. Counting the zero once would leave an extra pole in the remainder.

Which disk controls a Dirichlet character at height t?

Fix an integer m ≥ 3, any Dirichlet character χ modulo m, and any real t. Set z₀ = 101/100 + it and r = 2/5. For the principal character take F(s) = (s−1)L(s,χ), continued at 1. For the other characters take F = L(·,χ). All these functions are analytic on the outer disk. For σ = Re s > 1 the Euler product gives |1/L(s,χ)| ≤ ζ(σ) ≤ 1 + 1/(σ−1), the last inequality by comparison with an integral. Hence |L(z₀,χ)| ≥ 1/101. In the principal case |z₀−1| ≥ 1/100. The uniform centre bound is therefore |F(z₀)| ≥ 1/10100. Dirichlet series, analytic continuation and Euler products, DLMF §25.15(i)[274].

The whole disk lies in σ ≥ 1/2. For a nonprincipal character the complete period sums to zero, so |∑n≤xχ(n)| ≤ m. Partial summation expresses L(s,χ) as s times the integral of this partial sum against x−s−1 on [1,∞), giving |L| ≤ 2m|s|. For the principal character the finite factors ∏p∣m(1−p−s) have product of absolute values at most ∏p∣mp ≤ m. Applying the same partial summation to the integer count ⌊x⌋ = x−{x} gives ζ(s) = s/(s−1) − s∫₁∞ {x}x−s−1 dx. The integral is bounded by 1/σ. After removing the pole we obtain |F(s)| ≤ C₀m(1+|s|)² with an absolute constant C₀ ≥ 1.

Since |s| ≤ |t|+2 on this disk, the preceding lemma applies with B = 10100C₀m(|t|+3)². Its logarithm is at most a fixed multiple of log(m(|t|+2)). Thus the disk of radius 2/15 contains at most that order of zeros, with multiplicity. For |s−z₀| ≤ 1/15, s ≠ 1 and F(s) ≠ 0, the sign needed in the contour integral is

−L′(s,χ)/L(s,χ) = 𝟙χ principal/(s−1) − ∑|ρ−z₀|≤2/15, F(ρ)=0 aρ/(s−ρ) + E(s),   |E(s)| ≤ 180 log B.

If the contour stays at distance at least δ from each listed zero, the pole sum costs at most N/δ. In the smoothed progression formula, only zeros with real part at least 9/10 need to be avoided. The contour has real part at least 19/20, so all other zeros are already at least 1/20 away. To the right of 107/100 the absolutely convergent series for −L′/L supplies a uniform bound.

To count the zeros in the window |Im ρ−t| ≤ 1 and 9/10 ≤ Re ρ < 1, take the fifteen centres with real part 101/100 and heights t+k/7 for −7 ≤ k ≤ 7. Choose the nearest of these heights to Im ρ. Its vertical distance is at most 1/14 and the horizontal distance is at most 11/100. Since (11/100)²+(1/14)² < (2/15)², the zero belongs to one of the counting disks. Summing the fifteen disk bounds counts every zero at least as many times as its multiplicity. Their heights differ from t by at most one, so the window count is still bounded by a constant times log(m(|t|+2)). This gives the short-interval multiplicity count. The power-sum argument uses the disk lemma with centre 26/25 + it and radius 12/25, then differentiates the analytic remainder by Cauchy’s formula.

How does the difference recover the sharp prime count?

Choose 0 < δ ≤ ½, put u = (1 + δ)y and b = yu/(u − y) = y(1 + δ)/δ. Multiply the difference Sχ(u)/u − Sχ(y)/y by b. For every n ≤ y, the two weights differ by 1/y − 1/u = 1/b. Thus these terms contribute exactly ψχ(y). An integer in (y,u] contributes with weight b(1/n − 1/u) between zero and one. Their total in absolute value is at most (δy + 1)log(2y).

Check the weights at 4, 5 and 6

Take the principal character modulo 3, y = 4 and u = 6. Then b = 12. Every integer up to 4 has weight one in the scaled difference. Only 2 and 4 contribute, giving 2 log 2. At 5 the weight is 12(1/5 − 1/6) = 2/5. At 6 it is zero. The difference equals 2 log 2 + (2/5)log 5, so its entire discrepancy from ψχ(4) comes from the short interval.

Counting a strip with multiplicities. The two finite-sum detectors prove a fixed-modulus density theorem. It bounds the number of distinct pairs (χ,ρ) with ½ ≤ σ ≤ Re ρ, |Im ρ| ≤ T, and ordinates at least one apart for each individual χ. Its bound is C(mT)24(1−σ)(log(mT))10, for m ≥ 3 and T ≥ 2. At height T = T₀ + 3 and in a strip j < v ≤ j + 1, take σ = max(½, 1 − (j + 1)/H). The bound for separated pairs becomes C exp(24(j + 1))H10.

What does a zero force a finite sum to do?

Fix a modulus m ≥ 3 and a height T ≥ 2. We count pairs (χ,ρ) with χ a character modulo m, L(ρ,χ) = 0, σ ≤ Re ρ < 1 and |Im ρ| ≤ T. Assume ¾ ≤ σ < 1. Two distinct zeros of the same character in this list must have ordinates at least one apart. The strip argument explains how to put the multiplicities back afterwards. The problem here is to bound the number of these separated pairs.

Take q = ⌈mT⌉, V = q³, J = 8(⌊log₂ q⌋ + 1), and N = 2J. Thus q⁸ ≤ N ≤ 256q⁸. For a character χ let PN(s) = ∑n≤N χ(n)n−s. Multiply it by MV(s) = ∑d≤V μ(d)χ(d)d−s. Here μ is the Möbius function. It is zero on integers divisible by a prime square and equals (−1)k on a product of k distinct primes.

In the product the coefficient of χ(n)n−s is bN(n) = ∑dk=n, d≤V, k≤N μ(d). This equals 1 at n = 1. For 1 < n ≤ V every divisor occurs, and their Möbius sum is ∏p∣n(1 − 1) = 0. The product is consequently 1 + DN, where the remainder runs over V < n ≤ VN. Partition it into J sums on doubling intervals. With U = V2j their common form is

BN,U(χ,ρ) = ∑U<n≤2U bN(n)χ(n)n−ρ.

Nonprincipal detector. At a zero of a nonprincipal character, |PN(ρ)| ≤ 8qN−Re ρ. Indeed, complete periods of χ sum to zero, so partial sums on every interval are bounded by 2(m + 1). Partial summation of the tail of the L-series bounds it by 2(m + 1)(1 + |ρ|/Re ρ)N−Re ρ, and 1 + |ρ|/Re ρ ≤ 3T. These bounded partial sums give locally uniform convergence on Re s > 0, so the series there agrees with the continued L-function. Since L(ρ,χ) vanishes, the finite sum equals the negative of the tail. Also |MV(ρ)| ≤ V. Thus |1 + DN| ≤ 8q · q−6 · q³ = 8/q² ≤ ½. The remainder must have absolute value at least ½. At least one of its J blocks therefore has absolute value ≥ 1/(2J).

Check the cancellation before grouping the blocks

Use small cutoffs V = 3 and N = 4 just to check the coefficients. At n = 2 and 3 they are 1 − 1 = 0. At n = 6 the admissible pairs (d,k) are (2,3) and (3,2). Each contributes −1, so the coefficient is −2. The cutoff has removed the pairs (1,6) and (6,1) that would complete the divisor sum. These surviving coefficients are exactly what the detector measures.

How is the principal character detected?

A zero of the principal character in Re ρ > 0 is a zero of ζ, since the removed Euler factors 1 − p−ρ are nonzero there. In this paragraph use the character of modulus one in P, M and D. The alternating sum up to 2N is P2N(ρ) − zPN(ρ) with z = 21−ρ. Its infinite sum is (1 − z)ζ(ρ) = 0. At s = 1 the factor 1 − 21−s cancels the simple pole of ζ and the alternating sum is log 2. The zeros used in the detector satisfy Re ρ < 1. Alternating signs have bounded partial sums, giving the tail bound 4(1 + |ρ|/Re ρ)N−Re ρ. Multiplying by the same Möbius sum as before gives

1 − z = (P2N − zPN)MV − D2N + zDN.

The first term on the right has absolute value at most 12/q². A principal zero cannot be the exceptional zero in the Dirichlet zero-free region. Hence 1 − Re ρ > c₀/(2 log q) for its fixed constant c₀ > 0, using m(|Im ρ| + 2) ≤ q². By the reverse triangle inequality, |1 − z| ≥ 21−Re ρ − 1 ≥ (1 − Re ρ)/2. For sufficiently large q we also have 12/q² ≤ c₀/(8 log q). Since |z| ≤ 2, at least one of |DN| and |D2N| exceeds c₀/(24 log q). Breaking that remainder into at most J + 1 blocks detects the zero at threshold c₀/[24(J + 1) log q]. This extra log q is the price of the principal character.

How many separated zeros can one block detect?

Fix a block (U,2U] and its truncation N or 2N. Let R be the number of pairs it detects at threshold θ. Split each coefficient vector into a common vector b(n) = bN′(n)n−σ and a row with entries χ(n)n−(ρ−σ), where N′ is this block’s truncation. Write LU = 1 + log(2U). The squared norm of the common vector is at most A = 2U1−2σLU³. In fact |bN′(n)| is at most the number of divisors of n. To sum the squares of these divisor counts up to x, count pairs of divisors a,b of the same multiple. There are at most x/lcm(a,b) such multiples. Writing a = gu, b = gv with gcd(u,v) = 1 and bounding each harmonic sum by 1 + log x gives a total at most x(1 + log x)³.

Form the Gram matrix of the rows. In a row belonging to χ, pairing with a different character gives a nonprincipal character sum with bounded partial sums. Its absolute contribution per pair is at most K = 8(m + 1)(2 + 2T) by partial summation. For two rows with the same χ, the product character is principal. Summing its mean by integration gives an additional contribution of at most 4U/|Im ρ − Im ρ′| for unequal ordinates. This is where separation matters. On either side of one ordinate, the kth nearest ordinate is at distance at least k. The reciprocal distances sum to at most 2(1 + log(2T + 1)). For example, for ordinates −2, 0, 1, 3 of one character, the reciprocal distances from 0 sum to ½ + 1 + ⅓ = 11/6. A second character may also have an ordinate at 0 because its pairing uses the nonprincipal character sum. The diagonal is bounded by U. Including all errors, the sum of the absolute values in each row is at most UG + RK with G = 9 + 8 log(2T + 1).

A Hermitian matrix has operator norm bounded by its largest absolute row sum, as follows by applying 2|xy| ≤ |x|² + |y|² to each term of its quadratic form. Applied to this Gram matrix, the squared block values sum to at most A(UG + RK). Each of the R selected values has squared absolute value at least θ². For sufficiently large q, AK ≤ θ²/2. Indeed, U ≥ q³ and σ ≥ ¾ give U1−2σ ≤ q−3/2, while K is at most a constant times q. The resulting q−1/2 pays for all logarithms, including those in θ. Moving the term ARK to the left gives

Rθ² ≤ A(UG + RK),   R ≤ 4U2−2σLU³G/θ².

For sufficiently large q every block used here has 2U ≤ 2VN ≤ 512q11 ≤ q12. Hence U2−2σ ≤ q24(1−σ). To count all the zeros, sum the bound over the possible blocks. There are at most a constant times log q. This last sum costs one logarithm, LU³ costs three, and G costs one. The inverse squared threshold costs two more logarithms for nonprincipal characters and four for the principal one. Their totals are seven and nine. Since mT ≤ q ≤ 2mT, both contributions are bounded by a fixed constant times (mT)24(1−σ)(log(mT))10. For ½ ≤ σ < ¾, the simple bound m(2T + 1) already fits under this estimate, and a larger constant covers bounded q. This proves the fixed-modulus density input used to count the zero strips.

How far to the left must a remaining zero lie?

The zero-free region has a constant cZ > 0. Any zero in the region Re ρ ≥ 1 − cZ/log(m(|Im ρ| + 2)) is the unique simple exceptional zero for the corresponding family, and its occurrence is subtracted from W. The zeros still to be bounded thus satisfy v ≥ cZ. If an exceptional pair (χ₁,β) exists, then β < 1 gives δ = 1 − β > 0 and 0 < η = min(1,δd) ≤ 1. Otherwise set η = 1.

Repulsion estimate. There are fixed positive c₀, c₁, c₂ and an exponent N = 3 such that if δH < c₁, each other zero in the indicated height range with Re ρ ≥ 1 − c₀ satisfies

v ≥ c₂ log(c₁/(δHN)).
