How does a real zero push other zeros away from 1?

Let χ₁ be a nonprincipal quadratic character modulo m with a real zero β. Let ρ be a zero belonging to a character χ of the same modulus. Write λ = 1 − β, Δ = 1 − Re ρ, γ = Im ρ and H = log(mT). Assume m ≥ 3, T ≥ 2 and |γ| ≤ T. The pair (χ,ρ) must differ from (χ₁,β). In particular this includes another zero of χ₁ itself. There are fixed positive constants c₀, c₁, c₂ such that if 0 < λ < c₁/H and Δ ≤ c₀, then

ΔH ≥ c₂K,   K = log(c₁/(λH³)).

Taking T = T₀ + 3 gives the strip coordinate v = ΔH used above. The exponent N in the strip bound can therefore be taken to be 3. The cube specifies when the logarithm helps. It is positive precisely when λH³ < c₁. At fixed height and modulus, decreasing λ by a factor of e⁴ raises the asserted lower bound for Δ by 4c₂/H. The ordinary zero-free region already gives ΔH ≥ cZ/2 for a distinct pair. We use that bound when K is bounded. For large K, the additional information comes from the derivatives of four logarithmic derivatives of L-functions.

The same primes control two heights. Write Dψ = −L′(s,ψ)/L(s,ψ). Evaluate the pair for the principal character and χ₁ at s₀ = 1 + Δ, and the pair for χ and χχ₁ at s₁ = 1 + Δ + iγ. In the sum of their signed derivatives of order j − 1, the real contribution of an integer n coprime to m contains the factor (1 + χ₁(n))(1 + Re(χ(n)n−iγ)). Both brackets are nonnegative. The other weights are Λ(n)(log n)j−1n−1−Δ/(j − 1)!, where Λ(pk) = log p for prime powers and is zero elsewhere. Integers sharing a factor with m contribute zero. The triangle inequality also bounds the absolute value of the shifted derivative pair by the nonnegative unshifted one, denoted Pj−1 after division by the factorial and multiplication by (−1)j−1.

Near s₁, list the zeros of the two shifted factors within distance 4/25 of 26/25 + iγ, counting multiplicity. Write wa = s₁ − ρa. Remove one copy of β if its character is χ₁ and it occurs in the disk. The target zero remains and contributes wa = 2Δ. Every listed zero has real part below 1, so Re wa ≥ Δ. The disk factorization and Cauchy’s estimate for the logarithmic derivative, after separating the zeros and the possible principal pole, expresses its normalized derivative as a pole term minus a sum of inverse powers of these distances, with error bounded by CH25j. A pole at 1 paired with a zero at β contributes at most jλ/Δj+1, by integrating the derivative of (s − x)−j from x = β to 1. If β falls outside the shifted disk, the unpaired shifted pole is at distance at least ⅛ and its cost fits in the error. At the real point the other first inverse powers have nonnegative real part and can be dropped from the upper estimate. Together these give

Re ∑a 1/wa ≤ 2λ/Δ² + 25CFH,
|∑a wa−j| ≤ Pj−1 + 2jλ/Δj+1 + CFH25j   (j ≥ 1).
Where the three powers of the logarithm enter

Set ℓ = log(3m). The prime estimate at 1 + Δ uses the nonnegative divisor coefficients ∑b∣n χ₁(b). For 1 ≤ y ≤ x, their sum with weights 1/n on (y,x] is at most |L(1,χ₁)| log(x/y) + Cm(1 + log y)/√y. The positive prime moment estimate uses |L(1,χ₁)| ≤ Cλℓ² to give

Pj−1 ≤ CPλℓ²(j + 1)²/Δj+1 + (CPℓ)j/(j − 1)! + CP(j + 1)ℓ²/(mΔj).

Multiply through by Δj. The first term now contains λℓ²/Δ. Since ℓ ≤ 2H and 1/Δ ≤ 2H/cZ, this costs a constant times λH³. For the last term use the exceptional-zero lower bound λ ≥ cS/√m and ℓ² ≤ 32√m. This gives ℓ²/m ≤ 32λ/cS. The middle term will decay once the order j is large enough compared with Δℓ.

How does a real zero control the mass of prime powers?

Fix a nonprincipal quadratic character χ₁ modulo m ≥ 3. At the real point σ > 1, the sum −L′(σ,χ₀)/L(σ,χ₀) − L′(σ,χ₁)/L(σ,χ₁), where χ₀ is the principal character, has coefficient Λ(n)(χ₀(n) + χ₁(n)). It is nonnegative. We want to keep track of its size on entire intervals. For this purpose introduce the divisor sum r(n) = ∑b∣n χ₁(b), the coefficient of ζ(s)L(s,χ₁). The Dirichlet convolution formula gives this identity and the multiplicativity of r. See DLMF (27.5.1)[275].

For n = ph, r(n) = 1 + χ₁(p) + ⋯ + χ₁(p)h. It equals h + 1 when χ₁(p) = 1. When χ₁(p) = −1 it alternates between zero for odd h and one for even h. At a prime dividing m it equals one, while both characters evaluated at ph vanish for h ≥ 1. These three cases prove 0 ≤ Λ(n)(χ₀(n) + χ₁(n)) ≤ 2(log n)r(n). For other positive n, Λ(n) = 0 and r(n) ≥ 0 by multiplicativity.

∑y<n≤x r(n)/n ≤ |L(1,χ₁)| log(x/y) + 400m(1 + log y)/√y   (1 ≤ y ≤ x).

The divisor sum over an interval. Write F(N) = ∑n≤N r(n)/n. Each pair ab ≤ N contributes χ₁(b)/(ab). Choose U = ⌊√N⌋. For b ≤ U the inner sum over a is the harmonic number of index ⌊N/b⌋, within 2b/N of log N + γ − log b. For b > U, sum first over b at each a. Every full period of χ₁ sums to zero. Partial summation therefore bounds the tail of ∑χ₁(b)/b beyond U by 4(m + 1)/U. This controls the inner sums and also allows the truncated sum in the main term to be replaced by L(1,χ₁). These estimates give

F(N) = (log N + γ)L(1,χ₁) − T(U) + R(N),
T(U) = ∑b≤U χ₁(b)(log b)/b,   |R(N)| ≤ 26(m + 1)(1 + log N)/√N.

Subtract this identity at N₀ = ⌊y⌋ and N₁ = ⌊x⌋. The constant γ cancels. For V ≥ U ≥ 1, another partial summation against the bounded character sums gives |T(V) − T(U)| ≤ 4(m + 1)(1 + log(U + 1))/(U + 1). Thus both endpoint errors and this difference cost at most 86(m + 1)(1 + log N₀)/√N₀. Replacing the integer endpoints by x and y uses log(y/N₀) ≤ 2/y, √y ≤ 2√N₀ and |L(1,χ₁)| ≤ 5(m + 1). This yields the displayed interval bound, even at y = 1. A related hyperbola estimate for the same divisor sum appears in Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Exercise 12.3(b)[267].

Which prime powers survive for the quadratic character modulo 3?

The character has χ₁(2) = −1 and χ₁(7) = 1. At 2 and 4 the divisor sums are 0 and 1, and the prime coefficients are 0 and 2 log 2. At 7 the divisor sum is 2 and the prime coefficient is 2 log 7. At 3 the divisor sum is 1 but the prime coefficient is zero. Thus the divisor sum can count more mass while still detecting the cancellation at 2.

Why do three different terms appear in the prime moment?

Suppose χ₁ has a real zero 1 − 1/ℓ ≤ β < 1, with ℓ = log(3m). Put λ = 1 − β, a = σ − 1, and assume 0 < a ≤ 1. For an integer k ≥ 0, differentiating the absolutely convergent series k times multiplies each term by (−log n)k. After changing sign by (−1)k and dividing by k!, we obtain the positive moment

Pk = (1/k!) ∑n≥1 (log n)k Λ(n)(χ₀(n) + χ₁(n))/n1+a.

The first term comes from small integers. Set v₀ = ⌈8 log m⌉ ≤ 9ℓ. Up to exp(v₀) the character coefficient is at most two. The elementary Mertens bound ∑n≤z Λ(n)/n ≤ CT log z gives a contribution at most 2CTv₀k+1/k!. To verify the Mertens bound, put ψ(z) = ∑n≤z Λ(n). Each prime power in (N,2N] contributes log p to the logarithm of the central binomial coefficient, since the corresponding floor difference in the factorials is one and all other floor differences are nonnegative. Hence ψ(2N) − ψ(N) ≤ log((2N)!/(N!)²) ≤ 2N log 2. Summing over powers of two and rounding z up to the next power gives ψ(z) ≤ 4(log 2)z. Partial summation bounds ψ(z)/z + ∫1z ψ(t)dt/t² by 4(log 2)(1 + log z), at most CT log z when z ≥ 2.

For the rest, group the integers by v < log n ≤ v + 1, v an integer ≥ v₀. The bound on the prime coefficient spends one extra power of log n. Together with n−a ≤ exp(−av), this leaves a weight Wv = (v + 1)k+1exp(−av). Set A = |L(1,χ₁)|. The interval estimate bounds the block’s contribution before division by k! by 2Wv[A + 400m(v + 1)exp(−v/2)].

For the term with A, sum the weights. If p = k + 1, split a as pa/(p + 1) + a/(p + 1). Bound the polynomial against the first exponential using tp ≤ p!exp(t). Summing the remaining geometric series gives ∑v≥v₀ Wv ≤ 2e²(p + 1)p!/ap+1. Here the real zero enters.

Throughout [β,1] the bound |L′(t,χ₁)| ≤ CDℓ² follows from Cauchy’s estimate on a circle of radius 1/(2ℓ), where |L| ≤ 38e3/2ℓ. To check this circle bound, a point w on any of the circles satisfies Re w ≥ 1 − 3/(2ℓ), Re w ≥ ¼ and |w| ≤ 2, since ℓ ≥ log 9 > 2. Through n = m, the Dirichlet series is bounded by e3/2∑n≤m 1/n ≤ e3/2(1 + ℓ). For the remainder, the character sums are bounded by m + 1. Summation by parts at m bounds the endpoint and tail by (1 + |w|/Re w)(m + 1)1−Re w ≤ 9e3/2. Adding gives the stated circle bound, and Cauchy’s estimate divides it by the radius. Integrating from the zero to 1 gives A ≤ CDλℓ². The circle estimate uses Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, DLMF (1.9.31)[276].

For the error in the block mass, take the supremum of Wv, at most e · p!/ap by the same exponential-series inequality. The remaining sum of (v + 1)exp(−v/2) is at most 20exp(−v₀/4), by comparing it with the geometric series 4exp(−v/4). The choice v₀ ≥ 8 log m now gives m exp(−v₀/4) ≤ 1/m. Dividing the three bounds by k! where needed, and allowing ℓ² ≥ 1 in the last term, gives an absolute C with

Pk ≤ Cλℓ²(k + 2)²/ak+2 + (Cℓ)k+1/k! + C(k + 2)ℓ²/(mak+1).

The three terms record respectively the value at 1, the small integers, and the error in the large blocks. In the zero moment comparison, substitute k = j − 1 and a = Δ. Multiplication by Δj leaves just one inverse power of Δ in the first term. This is where the extra height logarithm enters.

Why must one of the power sums be large?

Set ua = Δ/wa. One value equals ½. Also |ua|² ≤ Re ua, since Re wa ≥ Δ. By the first-moment estimate the sum S of these real parts is at most 2λ/Δ + 25CFΔH. Suppose, seeking a contradiction, that ΔH < c₂K. Choosing c₁ small relative to the ordinary gap ensures 2λ/Δ ≤ 1. We can then make S ≤ 1 + κK for a fixed small κ by choosing c₂ small enough.

Keep the n indices with |ua| ≥ ε, where r = 16e² and ε = 1/r. The index with value ½ survives and nε² ≤ S. At order j ≥ 2 the discarded terms have total absolute value at most εj−2S. Thus even a large list of tiny terms has a controlled contribution. Divide the retained values by their largest modulus, which is at least ½, to obtain n numbers za of modulus at most one with maximum modulus one.

Turán’s power-sum bound. For any such list and any integer h ≥ 0, some integer j between h + 1 and h + n satisfies |∑ zaj| ≥ [n/(1600(h + n))]n. For instance, (1 + i)/2 and (1 − i)/2 both satisfy the disk inequality for u. Their squares sum to zero and their fourth powers sum to −½. The modulus and the freedom to choose the order both matter.

Take α = 1/(2 log r) and h = ⌈αK⌉. Since nε² ≤ 1 + κK, choosing κ small gives αK < j ≤ 2αK + j₀ and n log 1600 ≤ j + a fixed constant. In Turán’s bound, (1 + h/n)n ≤ eh. Restoring the largest modulus costs at most a factor 2j. With h ≤ j, the resulting lower bound for the retained sum is at least (2e²)−j/E₀ for a fixed E₀. Add back the discarded tail to obtain

(8/r)j/E₀ ≤ |∑a uaj| + εj−2S.

The upper bound for the same expression decays faster. The terms involving the real zero are at most C(j + 1)²λH³. For the factorial term, j! ≥ (j/e)j, and Δℓ ≤ 2c₂K allows us to arrange eCPΔℓ/j ≤ 1/r. The Cauchy remainder is (25CFΔH)(25Δ)j−1. Its first factor is at most κK and the fixed strip width c₀ ensures 25Δ ≤ 1/r. The discarded tail obeys the same geometric estimate because S ≤ 1 + κK. Finally λH³ = c₁e−K ≤ c₁rj₀r−j by the upper bound for j. Hence the right side is at most G(j + 1)²r−j for a fixed G. Comparing gives 8j ≤ E₀G(j + 1)², impossible for large K since j > αK. The ordinary gap covers the bounded values of K after decreasing c₂. This proves the logarithmic repulsion used in the zero-strip sum.

How does a weighted error give a relative error for the number of primes?

Enlarge the range constant so that the weighted estimate holds throughout √U ≤ t ≤ U and L ≥ 16d. There log t ≥ L/2. Put c₃ = min(c/2, c²/2), R = exp(−c₃L/d) + exp(−√(c₃L)), and D = AηR/φ. We now have |Ψ(t) − F(t)| ≤ Dt on the whole upper interval.

Partial summation removes the logarithmic weights. The endpoint error is at most DU/L. The integral of the error over the upper interval is at most ∫√UU D dt/(log t)² ≤ 4DU/L². Applying the same integration to F gives the corrected logarithmic integrals, since F′(t) = (1−s tβ−1)/φ. On the lower interval [2,√U], Chebyshev’s bound gives 0 ≤ Ψ(t) ≤ 6t. The model satisfies |F(t)| ≤ 3t, because φ ≥ 1, |s| ≤ 1, tβ ≤ t and 1/β ≤ 2. Since log t ≥ log 2 > 1/2, the absolute value of the integrand (Ψ(t) − F(t))/(t(log t)²) is at most 36. The lower integral therefore costs at most 36(√U − 2). Its two boundary corrections are F(2)/log 2 and s li(2β)/φ. The first has absolute value at most 12. For the second, √2 ≤ 2β ≤ 2, and 1/log t ≤ 2/log 2 < 4 on [√2,2], an interval of length less than one. The total cost of the lower integral and both corrections is thus at most 40√U. The resulting sum still counts pk with weight 1/k. For k ≥ 2 the base prime is at most √U and there are at most L/log 2 possible exponents, so their contribution is at most 4√UL. Combining these bounds gives

|π(U;m,a) − B| ≤ 5DU/L + 44√UL.

The first term is 10A R P. To compare the second with P, the exceptional-zero bound at exponent one gives η ≥ c₁/m for some c₁ > 0, and φ ≤ m. Thus 44√UL/P ≤ (88/c₁)L² exp(2d−L/2). Now 2d ≤ L/8 and L² ≤ 64 exp(L/4), so the last bound is at most (5632/c₁)exp(−L/8). The inequality √(c₃L) ≤ 2c₃ + L/8 makes this at most (5632 exp(2c₃)/c₁)R. Since P ≤ B, both errors are now bounded by a fixed constant times R B. This is the relative estimate required for the candidate count.

Check the size of the subtracting interval

To test the inequality numerically, take m = 16, U = 1616 and a trial value 1−β = 1/(128 log 16). These values illustrate the integral bound without requiring an exceptional zero at that modulus. Then η = 1/128, (1−β)L = 1/8, and (U−Uβ)/U = 1−exp(−1/8) ≈ 0.1175. The proof retains η/2 = 1/256 of U, enough to compare with an error that also contains η.

Removing failed twists

First remove primes for which some such character has a zero in the box of height H. Choose one offending character for each removed prime. Its conductor determines the prime uniquely. Indeed if fp = f′p′, primality forces p to divide f′ or p′. The first possibility contradicts 0 < f′ ≤ F < p, so p = p′. The zero-density theorem bounds the number of offending primitive characters by C H1/4. Dividing by the number of candidates makes the loss tend to zero.

#primes removed / |P| ≤ C(FU)1/4/U9/10 ≤ C U−21/40.

Thus the same exclusion works for every member of Ξ. The fixed exponent 1/4 counts characters admitting a zero in this particular rectangle.

How can one count characters whose L-function has a zero?

Write Q for the height H of the box in the preceding prime selection. Consider all primitive characters of conductor at most Q that have at least one zero ρ with Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. The number of these characters is at most CQ1/4 for every real Q ≥ 3 and a single absolute constant C. One zero, chosen separately for each character, suffices. The argument turns it into a large finite sum on one interval, then bounds how many characters can give large sums on the same interval.

Detecting one zero. For large Q take X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋ + 1) and N = 2J. Here Y is the length of an auxiliary sum within this proof. Multiply the first N terms of L(s,χ), denoted P(s), by M(s) = ∑d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−s, summing over positive integers. The Möbius function μ is zero on multiples of squares of primes. On a product of k distinct primes it is (−1)k, including μ(1) = 1. In the product the coefficient multiplying χ(n)n−s is

a(n) = ∑db=n, 1≤d≤Y, 1≤b≤N μ(d).

For 2 ≤ n ≤ Y every divisor occurs, since Y ≤ N. The sum is zero by expanding (1−1)k over the distinct prime divisors. At n = 1 it is one. Thus PM = 1 + D, where D uses only Y < n ≤ YN. For a short calculation set Y = 3 and N = 4. At 6 only (2,3) and (3,2) qualify, so a(6) = −2. At 4 only (1,4) and (2,2) occur, and their contributions cancel. Truncating the product can leave either outcome beyond the initial range.

Why must at least one block be large at a zero?

For a primitive character of conductor q > 1, complete periods of χ sum to zero. The remainder estimate by partial summation gives, at the chosen zero with σ = Re ρ, |P(ρ)| ≤ 2(q+1)(1+|ρ|/σ)N−σ. Every term of the second polynomial has modulus at most one, so |M(ρ)| ≤ Y. When Q ≥ 20 we have q+1 ≤ 2X and 1+|ρ|/σ ≤ 3X. Also N ≥ X⁸ and σ > 15/16, so Nσ ≥ X⁷√X ≥ 4X⁷. Multiplication by Y = X⁴ gives |PM| ≤ 3/X ≤ 1/2. Since PM = 1 + D, the reverse triangle inequality forces |D| ≥ 1/2. Split (Y,YN] into J successive blocks (U,2U] with U = Y2j. At least one block sum has modulus ≥ 1/(2J).

How many characters can select the same block?

Write σ₀ = 399/400. Suppose T characters selected one block (U, 2U]. Place their values in rows vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀), and put b(n) = a(n)n−σ₀. Multiplying each row by this same column gives its selected large block. The squared norm of a row is at most U. For two different rows the character χψ̄ at their common product modulus is nonprincipal: equality of the induced characters would identify their conductors and then the original primitive characters. Complete periods of this product sum to zero, so its partial sums have modulus at most the product of the conductors, at most Q². Partial summation against the complex power gives the bound 2Q²(1+|w|) for the inner product, with w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀). Each of these nonprincipal zeros has real part below 1, and the two imaginary parts have absolute values at most Q. Thus the inner product has modulus at most 8Q³.

The number of divisors of n bounds |a(n)| and is at most a constant times n1/400. Squaring after multiplying by n−σ₀ and summing the U terms gives ∑|b(n)|² ≤ C U−99/100 ≤ C U−197/200. The matrix of row inner products has absolute row sums at most U + 8TQ³. This bounds its operator norm: in its quadratic form use 2|xᵢxⱼ| ≤ |xᵢ|² + |xⱼ|² and the symmetry of the absolute entries. Applying the bound to the rectangular matrix and the column b gives

T/(4J²) ≤ ∑χ |∑n b(n)vχ(n)|² ≤ (U + 8TQ³)C U−197/200.

Since U ≥ Q⁴, the coefficient of T on the right is at most 8CQ−47/50. Above a single threshold independent of the characters, this is at most 1/(8J²), so we can subtract it and obtain T ≤ 8CJ²U3/200. Summing over the J blocks gives at most 8CJ³(YN)3/200. Here YN ≤ 2²⁰Q¹² and, eventually, J³ ≤ Q7/100. The exponents add to 12·3/200 + 7/100 = 1/4. The only primitive character of conductor one costs at most one further character. For bounded Q, the finite number of characters below the fixed threshold can be absorbed into the same absolute constant. In the prime selection we apply this bound at Q = FU, where U again denotes the upper limit on candidate primes.

How accurately does a finite character sum approximate the value at a zero?

Let χ be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo q. Write A(n) = ∑1≤k≤n χ(k) and PN(s) = ∑1≤n≤N χ(n)n−s. A complete period of χ sums to zero. Deleting whole periods bounds |A(n)| uniformly, and we may take B = q+1. For any complex s with σ = Re s > 0, put f(x) = x−s on the positive real axis. The point of using the partial sums A(n) is that the differences of f are absolutely summable throughout this half-plane.

Indeed, integrate f′(x) = −s x−s−1 from n to n+1, and take absolute values inside the integral. This gives |f(n)−f(n+1)| ≤ (|s|/σ)(n−σ−(n+1)−σ). Moreover, on any compact subset with σ ≥ σ₁ > 0 and |s| ≤ K, the difference is at most K n−σ₁−1. Thus G(s) = ∑n≥1 A(n)(f(n)−f(n+1)) converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function there. For finite N, replacing χ(n) by A(n)−A(n−1) gives

PN(s) = ∑1≤n≤N A(n)(f(n)−f(n+1)) + A(N)f(N+1).

The last term tends to zero. For σ > 1, the limit on the left is the absolutely convergent Dirichlet series for L(s,χ). By uniqueness of analytic continuation G therefore gives L throughout σ > 0. Subtracting the displayed identity from G leaves the sum of differences beginning at N+1, followed by minus A(N)f(N+1). In the bound for the sum, the consecutive differences of n−σ telescope to (N+1)−σ. The boundary term costs B(N+1)−σ. Hence for all integers N ≥ 1,

|L(s,χ)−PN(s)| ≤ B(1+|s|/σ)(N+1)−σ ≤ 2B(1+|s|/σ)N−σ.

The second, deliberately weaker bound is the one used in the detector. It applies at a zero even on the left of the line of absolute convergence. One can see the boundary term already with the quadratic character modulo 4, s = 1 and N = 2. Here A(1) = A(2) = 1, so the first two differences give (1−1/2)+(1/2−1/3) = 2/3. The boundary term is +1/3 in the finite identity, giving P₂(1) = 1. Kiran Kedlaya, Notes on analytic number theory, Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.5 and equation (3.2.3)[277].

Why are there exactly J possible blocks?

Fix Q ≥ 20 and a primitive character of conductor 1 < q ≤ Q. It is nonprincipal because the principal character is induced from conductor one. Take a zero ρ with σ = Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. For this step the lower bound on σ suffices. Put X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋+1) and N = 2J. The number 2⌊log₂ X⌋+1 is strictly larger than X, including when X is a power of two. Its eighth power is N, so N ≥ X⁸ ≥ Y.

At ρ the remainder bounds |PN(ρ)|. Since |ρ| ≤ σ+Q and σ > 1/2, we have 1+|ρ|/σ ≤ 2+2Q ≤ 3X. Also q+1 ≤ 2X. The weaker inequality σ ≥ 15/16 already gives Nσ ≥ X15/2 = X⁷√X ≥ 4X⁷. The other factor in the detector is MY(ρ) = ∑1≤d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−ρ. Each summand has modulus at most one, so |MY(ρ)| ≤ Y. All four estimates hold simultaneously for every allowed character and zero. Multiplying them gives

|PN(ρ)MY(ρ)| ≤ 2(2X)(3X) X⁴/(4X⁷) = 3/X ≤ 1/2.

By the finite Möbius product identity, the same product is 1+D, where D sums the coefficients a(n)χ(n)n−ρ over Y < n ≤ YN. The reverse triangle inequality gives |D| ≥ 1/2. Partition these integers with endpoints Y, 2Y, 4Y, …, Y2J = YN. There are J+1 endpoints and exactly J intervals. For index j = 0,…,J−1, write Bⱼ(ρ) for the sum on (Y2j, Y2j+1]. The first integer included is Y+1. Each internal endpoint belongs to the earlier interval, and the last interval includes YN. Thus

1/2 ≤ |D| ≤ ∑j=0J−1|Bⱼ(ρ)| ≤ J max0≤j<J|Bⱼ(ρ)|.

For the small product example Y = 3, N = 4 = 2², the two intervals are (3,6] and (6,12]. The coefficient a(6) = −2 belongs entirely to the first block, and a(12) = −1 belongs to the second. In the zero count, each character supplies at least one block of modulus ≥ 1/(2J), with equality allowed. Choosing one such index per character produces the families in the block mean-square estimate. That estimate also needs Re ρ < 1. The Euler product excludes zeros with Re ρ > 1, and the classical nonvanishing theorem excludes the whole line Re ρ = 1 for a nonprincipal character, including the real point ρ = 1. Every chosen zero of conductor greater than one therefore lies strictly to the left of that line. Kedlaya, equation (3.2.1) and Theorems 3.8, 3.10 and 3.11[277].

How do two different characters interact in the same detector block?

Fix a real Q ≥ 3. Take a finite set S of distinct primitive Dirichlet characters of conductors at most Q. For each χ choose one complex point ρχ with σ₀ = 399/400 < Re ρχ < 1 and |Im ρχ| ≤ Q. The zero detector assigns one such zero and one block to each selected character of conductor greater than one when Q ≥ 20. For the mean square itself the points may be anywhere in that strip, even at the same height. Fix a positive integer U and use the same U integers U < n ≤ 2U for every row. Set vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀). For any complex coefficients b(n), the block mean square satisfies

∑χ∈S |∑U<n≤2U b(n)vχ(n)|² ≤ (U + 8|S|Q³) ∑U<n≤2U|b(n)|².

Write Gχψ = ∑ vχ(n) conj(vψ(n)). The diagonal is at most U since each term is at most one. For χ ≠ ψ let m be the product of their conductors. The sequence ξ(n) = χ(n) conj(ψ(n)) is a character modulo m. On units it is the quotient of the two induced characters. On a nonunit at least one factor vanishes. If ξ were principal, the two induced characters would agree on every unit. Uniqueness of the primitive character inducing a given character would force χ = ψ. A complete period of ξ therefore sums to zero. Multiplication of the unit classes by some a with ξ(a) ≠ 1 leaves the sum unchanged and multiplies it by ξ(a). Deleting complete periods gives |A(r)| ≤ m for A(r) = ∑0≤n<r ξ(n). Andrew Sutherland, Theorem 18.13 and Corollary 18.15[278].

The complex weights vary across the block. Put w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀), so 0 < Re w < 1 and |Im w| ≤ 2Q. For f(x) = x−w, the derivative has modulus |w|x−Re w−1 ≤ |w|/U throughout the block. Substituting ξ(n) = A(n+1)−A(n) and shifting the second sum leaves endpoint terms f(2U)A(2U+1)−f(U+1)A(U+1), followed by −∑U<n<2U (f(n+1)−f(n))A(n+1). Each endpoint costs at most m and the full difference sum costs at most m|w|. Hence |Gχψ| ≤ 2m(1+|w|) ≤ 8Q³, using m ≤ Q² and |w| ≤ 1+2Q.

It remains to pass from pairwise comparisons to the sum of squares. Write V for the row matrix and Δ = U + 8|S|Q³. Every absolute row sum of G = VV∗ is ≤ Δ, and the same holds for columns by Hermitian symmetry. For any vector z, bound each term in z∗Gz by |Gχψ| (|zχ|²+|zψ|²)/2. Summing gives ‖V∗z‖² ≤ Δ‖z‖². Take z = Vb. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖z‖² = |⟨V∗z,b⟩| ≤ √Δ ‖z‖ ‖b‖. For z ≠ 0 division and squaring give the stated inequality. For z = 0 it already holds.

For a small check of that matrix argument, use the unweighted quadratic characters modulo 3 and 4 on the integers 5, 6, 7, 8. Their rows are (−1,0,1,−1) and (1,0,−1,0). The off-diagonal entry equals −2 even though the complete product period of length 12 sums to zero. The diagonal entries are 3 and 2, so one may take Δ = 5. Against b = (1,0,−1,0) the row outputs are −2 and 2. Their squared sum 8 is bounded by 5‖b‖² = 10. This example checks the finite matrix inequality for arbitrary coefficients.

Why can the bound contain the number of characters on both sides?

The detector uses a common coefficient a(n) = ∑ μ(d) over de = n, 1 ≤ d ≤ Y and 1 ≤ e ≤ N. Put b(n) = a(n)n−σ₀. Then b(n)vχ(n) = a(n)χ(n)n−ρχ, exactly the term evaluated at the chosen point. Each divisor of n contributes at most one in modulus, so |a(n)| ≤ τ(n), the number of its positive divisors.

Here is a uniform constant for that coefficient bound. For ε = 1/400 let K = ⌈21/ε⌉, A = max(1,1/(ε log 2)) and D = AK. If p ≥ K, a prime power pk has k+1 ≤ 2k ≤ pεk divisors. For p < K, the inequality 1+x ≤ exp(x) gives k+1 ≤ A(1+εk log 2) ≤ A pεk. Multiplying over the prime powers in n costs at most K factors A, since only primes smaller than K need one. Thus τ(n) ≤ D n1/400. This deliberately coarse constant is independent of Y,N,U and of the family of characters.

Now |b(n)| ≤ D U−199/200 on the block. There are exactly U integers in it, giving ∑|b(n)|² ≤ D²U−99/100 ≤ C U−197/200 with C = D². Suppose every character in S selected this block among J ≥ 1 candidates. Each output then has modulus at least 1/(2J). If T = |S|, the mean square gives

T/(4J²) ≤ C U3/200 + T · 8CQ³U−197/200.

The second term can use at most half the left side once 8CQ³U−197/200 ≤ 1/(8J²). Under exactly this hypothesis we can subtract it to obtain T ≤ 8CJ²U3/200. For the selected windows X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋+1), N = 2J and U = Y2j with 0 ≤ j < J. Since U ≥ Q⁴, the coefficient of T on the right is at most 8CQ−47/50 for every block. The factor J² grows only as the square of a logarithm. Consequently there is one threshold Q₀ ≥ 20 depending only on C above which subtraction is valid for all those windows. The sum over the selected blocks then gives the exponent 1/4, with one additional character allowed for conductor one. The bounded range of smaller heights is covered by counting all characters with conductor below the fixed threshold.

Unit-step complex-power integral bound and Hermitian Gram expansion of the dual column norm

Why do the off-diagonal twist estimate and the finite block mean-square inequality require both a slit-plane integral representation over unit steps and an explicit adjoint Gram expansion? Two elementary mechanisms convert pairwise character cancellation on a dyadic block (U, 2U] into a simultaneous mean-square bound across a finite family S. First, when summation by parts separates the bounded character partial sums from the complex weights n−z (Re z > 0), the discrete difference (n + 1)−z − n−z cannot be estimated by the real mean-value theorem alone because Im z may have modulus up to 2Q; instead, for any x > 0 the real segment [x, x + 1] lies strictly inside the open slit plane ℂ \ (−∞, 0], so integrating the holomorphic derivative −z t−z−1 and bounding |t−z−1| = t−Re z − 1 at the left endpoint x yields |x−z − (x + 1)−z| ≤ |z|x−Re z − 1, which is at most |z|/U for every integer n ≥ U ≥ 1. Second, passing from pairwise row correlations Gi,j = ∑n∈I vi(n) conj(vj(n)) to the squared row-output sum ∑i∈S |si|² requires no spectral decomposition: pairing the coefficient vector b with the dual column w(n) = ∑i∈S conj(si)vi(n) rewrites ∑i∈S |si|² as ∑n∈I b(n)w(n), and expanding ∑n∈I |w(n)|² into ∑i,j∈S conj(si)sjGi,j lets Hermitian symmetry |Gj,i| = |Gi,j| and 2|si||sj| ≤ |si|² + |sj|² collapse all off-diagonal couplings into the single row-sum budget Δ.

1. Slit-plane unit-step difference and finite Hermitian duality. Let x > 0 be a real number and let z ∈ ℂ, with complex powers defined by the principal branch on ℂ \ (−∞, 0]. Independently, let S and I be arbitrary finite index sets, let b : I → ℂ be a complex coefficient vector, and let v : S × I → ℂ, (i, n) ↦ vi(n), be a finite complex array. Define the row outputs si = ∑n∈I b(n)vi(n) for i ∈ S, the dual column w(n) = ∑i∈S conj(si)vi(n) for n ∈ I, and the Gram entries Gi,j = ∑n∈I vi(n) conj(vj(n)) for i, j ∈ S, and suppose Δ ≥ 0 is a real constant satisfying ∑j∈S |Gi,j| ≤ Δ for every i ∈ S (specialized in the block mean-square sieve to I = (U, 2U] ∩ ℕ and Δ = U + 8|S|Q³).

Proposition (Unit-step complex-power bound and finite Hermitian duality inequality).

(i) For every real x > 0, every z ∈ ℂ satisfies |∫xx+1 t−z−1 dt| ≤ ∫xx+1 t−Re z − 1 dt; whenever z ≠ 0, the real-variable map t ↦ t−z is continuously differentiable on [x, x + 1] with derivative −z t−z−1 and satisfies the integral identity below; and whenever Re z > 0, it satisfies the left-endpoint bound:

x−z − (x + 1)−z = z ∫xx+1 t−z−1 dt,   |x−z − (x + 1)−z| ≤ |z| x−Re z − 1.

In particular, for every integer U ≥ 1 and every integer n ≥ U, whenever Re z > 0 one has |(n + 1)−z − n−z| ≤ |z|/U.

(ii) For any finite index sets S and I and any Δ ≥ 0 with ∑j∈S |Gi,j| ≤ Δ for all i ∈ S, the Gram entries satisfy Gj,i = conj(Gi,j) and |Gj,i| = |Gi,j| for all i, j ∈ S, and the dual column norm and row outputs obey

∑n∈I |w(n)|² = ∑i∈S ∑j∈S conj(si) sj Gi,j ≤ Δ ∑i∈S |si|²,   ∑i∈S |si|² ≤ Δ ∑n∈I |b(n)|².

Proof. For (i), every t ∈ [x, x + 1] satisfies t ≥ x > 0, so its complex embedding has positive real part and lies in ℂ \ (−∞, 0]; for every z ∈ ℂ, |t−z−1| = t−Re z − 1 gives |∫xx+1 t−z−1 dt| ≤ ∫xx+1 t−Re z − 1 dt, and when z ≠ 0 the map t ↦ t−z has continuous derivative −z t−z−1; compare the partial-summation tail derivative. The fundamental theorem of calculus on [x, x + 1] gives (x + 1)−z − x−z = ∫xx+1 (−z t−z−1) dt, and negating both sides yields the integral identity. When Re z > 0 (hence z ≠ 0 and −Re z − 1 < 0), taking complex moduli gives |x−z − (x + 1)−z| ≤ |z| ∫xx+1 t−Re z − 1 dt ≤ |z|x−Re z − 1 since t−Re z − 1 ≤ x−Re z − 1 across [x, x + 1]. When n ≥ U ≥ 1 are integers, setting x = n ≥ U ≥ 1 gives n−Re z − 1 ≤ n−1 ≤ U−1 because Re z > 0, proving |(n + 1)−z − n−z| ≤ |z|/U (applied in particular to integers n > U at z = (ρχ − σ0) + conj(ρψ − σ0) on (U, 2U]).

For (ii), interchanging summation over i ∈ S and n ∈ I gives ∑i∈S |si|² = ∑i∈S si conj(si) = ∑n∈I b(n)w(n). Taking moduli and applying the finite Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on I yields (∑i∈S |si|²)² ≤ (∑n∈I |b(n)||w(n)|)² ≤ (∑n∈I |b(n)|²)(∑n∈I |w(n)|²). Expanding |w(n)|² = w(n) conj(w(n)) and interchanging summation over n ∈ I with i, j ∈ S gives ∑n∈I |w(n)|² = ∑i∈S ∑j∈S conj(si)sjGi,j ≤ ∑i∈S ∑j∈S |si||sj||Gi,j|. Using 2|si||sj| ≤ |si|² + |sj|² together with |Gj,i| = |Gi,j| reduces the double sum to ∑i∈S |si|² ∑j∈S |Gi,j| ≤ Δ ∑i∈S |si|². Substituting this bound gives (∑i∈S |si|²)² ≤ Δ (∑n∈I |b(n)|²)(∑i∈S |si|²); if ∑i∈S |si|² = 0 then 0 ≤ Δ ∑n∈I |b(n)|² holds since Δ ≥ 0, and if ∑i∈S |si|² > 0 then dividing both sides by that positive factor yields ∑i∈S |si|² ≤ Δ ∑n∈I |b(n)|².

Hermitian conjugation of the Gram matrix, Fubini interchange, and symmetric quadratic collapse

On [x, x + 1] with x > 0, every point satisfies t ≥ x > 0, so |t−z−1| = tRe(−z−1) = t−Re z − 1 is continuous and integrable on [x, x + 1]. Because Re z > 0 implies −Re z − 1 < 0, monotonicity of real powers with nonpositive exponent on (0, ∞) gives t−Re z − 1 ≤ x−Re z − 1 for all t ∈ [x, x + 1], whence ∫xx+1 t−Re z − 1 dt ≤ ((x + 1) − x)x−Re z − 1 = x−Re z − 1.

In the finite matrix identity, termwise complex conjugation over n ∈ I gives conj(Gi,j) = ∑n∈I conj(vi(n))vj(n) = ∑n∈I vj(n) conj(vi(n)) = Gj,i, so |Gj,i| = |conj(Gi,j)| = |Gi,j|. Next, for each n ∈ I, |w(n)|² = (∑i∈S conj(si)vi(n))(∑j∈S sj conj(vj(n))) = ∑i∈S ∑j∈S conj(si)sjvi(n) conj(vj(n)); summing over n ∈ I, interchanging the outer sum over n with the double sum over i, j ∈ S, and factoring conj(si)sj out of ∑n∈I vi(n) conj(vj(n)) produces ∑i∈S ∑j∈S conj(si)sjGi,j. Finally, since (|si| − |sj|)² ≥ 0 gives |si||sj| ≤ (|si|² + |sj|²)/2 and |Gi,j| ≥ 0, splitting the double sum yields ∑i∈S ∑j∈S |si||sj||Gi,j| ≤ (1/2) ∑i∈S |si|² ∑j∈S |Gi,j| + (1/2) ∑j∈S |sj|² ∑i∈S |Gi,j|. Substituting |Gi,j| = |Gj,i| into the second sum and exchanging the dummy indices (i, j) identifies the two halves, giving ∑i∈S |si|² ∑j∈S |Gi,j| ≤ ∑i∈S |si|² · Δ = Δ ∑i∈S |si|².

Prime-power divisor majorant, dyadic coefficient-square monotone bound, and explicit binary-logarithm absorption thresholds

Why does a single explicit constant C = A2K dominate the squared Möbius-convolution weights on every dyadic block (U, 2U], and why can one threshold Q0 ≥ 20 simultaneously validate both the off-diagonal subtraction condition and the final Q1/4 zero-density bound? Two quantitative trade-offs drive these estimates. First, comparing the divisor product τ(n) = ∏p|n (vp(n) + 1) against nε = ∏p|n (pε)vp(n) for any ε > 0, every prime factor large enough that pε ≥ 2 already satisfies k + 1 ≤ 2k ≤ (pε)k with prefactor 1; only primes below the finite cutoff K = ⌈21/ε⌉ require a compensating factor, and for each such prime p ≥ 2 the linear-to-exponential bound k + 1 ≤ A exp(εk log 2) ≤ A(pε)k with A = max(1, 1/(ε log 2)) costs at most one factor A across at most K primes, yielding τ(n) ≤ AKnε. Second, on the dyadic detector windows X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log2 X⌋ + 1), and N = 2J, the number of blocks grows only logarithmically (J ≤ 32 log Q for Q ≥ 20): on the shortest block U ≥ Y ≥ Q⁴, the power saving Q³U−197/200 ≤ Q−47/50 overwhelms 64C J², while at the terminal scale Y N ≤ 220Q12 the exponent (Y N)3/200 ≤ 23/10Q9/50 leaves Q7/100 to absorb J³.

1. Prime-power divisor bound, dyadic square sum, and simultaneous window thresholds. For any real exponent ε > 0, define A = max(1, 1/(ε log 2)) ≥ 1, K = ⌈21/ε⌉ ∈ ℕ, and D = AK ≥ 1, writing τ(n) for the number of positive divisors of an integer n ≥ 1 and vp(n) for the exponent of each prime divisor p of n. For nonnegative integer cutoffs Y, N ≥ 0, recall from the finite Möbius product the truncated convolution coefficient a(n) = ∑d e=n, 1≤d≤Y, 1≤e≤N μ(d) (which vanishes when Y = 0 or N = 0), set σ0 = 399/400 and b(n) = a(n)n−σ0, and specialize the divisor parameters to ε = 1/400 with C = D² = A2K. For any real box height Q, set X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log2 X⌋ + 1), N = 2J, and dyadic block scales U = Y2j for 0 ≤ j < J.

Proposition (Uniform divisor majorant, dyadic square sum, and simultaneous window absorption).

(i) For every real ε > 0 and every integer n ≥ 1, τ(n) ≤ D nε with D = max(1, 1/(ε log 2))⌈21/ε⌉. For all integers Y, N ≥ 0, the truncated convolution satisfies |a(n)| ≤ τ(n) for all n ≥ 1; for all integers Y, N ≥ 1, a(1) = 1, and whenever 1 ≤ Y ≤ N, R ≥ Y N, q ≥ 1, χ is a Dirichlet character modulo q, and s ∈ ℂ, one has (∑1≤e≤N χ(e)e−s)(∑1≤d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−s) = 1 + ∑Y<n≤R a(n)χ(n)n−s. At ε = 1/400 and σ0 = 399/400, with C = D², all integers Y, N ≥ 0 and U ≥ 1 satisfy

τ(n) ≤ D nε,   ∑U<n≤2U |b(n)|² ≤ C U−99/100 ≤ C U−197/200.

(ii) For every real constant C ≥ 0 (in particular C = D² above), there exist a threshold Q0 ≥ 20 and a constant C1 = 1 + 8C · 10485763/200 > 0 (1048576 = 220) such that for every real Q ≥ Q0, the cutoffs X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log2 X⌋ + 1), and N = 2J satisfy J ≤ 32 log Q, Y N ≤ 1048576 Q12, and simultaneously for all integers 0 ≤ j < J with U = Y2j,

8C Q³ U−197/200 ≤ 1/(8J²),   1 + J · 8J² C (Y N)3/200 ≤ C1 Q1/4.

Proof. For (i), let ε > 0. For any real α > 0 and k ∈ ℕ, since 1 ≤ max(1, 1/α) and 1 ≤ max(1, 1/α)α, one has k + 1 ≤ max(1, 1/α)(1 + αk) ≤ max(1, 1/α) exp(αk). Setting α = ε log 2 > 0 and taking any integer p ≥ 2 (so log 2 ≤ log p) gives k + 1 ≤ A exp(εk log p) = A(pε)k. Whenever a base satisfies pε ≥ 2, induction on k ∈ ℕ gives k + 1 ≤ (pε)k without prefactor (1 ≤ 1 at k = 0, and k + 2 ≤ 2(k + 1) ≤ pε(pε)k = (pε)k+1 for k ≥ 0). Writing any integer n ≥ 1 in prime powers gives τ(n) = ∏p|n (vp(n) + 1) and nε = ∏p|n (pε)vp(n). Every prime divisor p ≥ K = ⌈21/ε⌉ satisfies p ≥ 21/ε and hence pε ≥ 2, contributing vp(n) + 1 ≤ (pε)vp(n), while each prime divisor p < K satisfies p ≥ 2 and contributes vp(n) + 1 ≤ A(pε)vp(n). Because {p | n : p < K} ⊆ {0, 1, …, K − 1} has cardinality at most K and A ≥ 1, multiplying over all prime factors of n yields τ(n) ≤ AKnε = D nε.

For any integers Y, N ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1, each summand |μ(d)| ≤ 1 in a(n) corresponds via (d, e) ↦ d to a distinct positive divisor of n, so |a(n)| ≤ τ(n). When Y, N ≥ 1, the support of a(1) in [1, Y] × [1, N] is the singleton {(1, 1)}, so a(1) = μ(1) = 1; when 1 ≤ Y ≤ N and R ≥ Y N, fiberwise regrouping of (d, e) ∈ [1, Y] × [1, N] by the product d e = n ∈ [1, R] = {1} ⊔ [2, Y] ⊔ (Y, R] combines a(1)χ(1)1−s = 1 with a(n) = 0 on 2 ≤ n ≤ Y from the full-divisor Möbius cancellation to give 1 + ∑Y<n≤R a(n)χ(n)n−s. Fixing ε = 1/400 and σ0 = 399/400, for all Y, N ≥ 0 and U ≥ 1 every integer n ∈ (U, 2U] satisfies n ≥ U > 0 and |b(n)| = |a(n)|n−399/400 ≤ D n1/400n−399/400 = D n−199/200 ≤ D U−199/200. Squaring and summing over the 2U − U = U integers in (U, 2U] gives ∑U<n≤2U |b(n)|² ≤ U(D U−199/200)² = C U−99/100 ≤ C U−197/200 since U ≥ 1 and −99/100 ≤ −197/200.

For (ii), because (log Q)³ = o(Q7/100) and (log Q)² = o(Q47/50) as Q → ∞, there exists Q1 above which (log Q)³ ≤ 2−15Q7/100 (215 = 32768) and (log Q)² ≤ [65536(C + 1)]−1Q47/50 (216 = 65536); put Q0 = max(20, Q1) ≥ 20. For every Q ≥ Q0, Q ≥ 20 > exp(1) gives log Q ≥ 1 and Q ≤ X = ⌈Q⌉ ≤ 2Q. From 2⌊log2 X⌋ ≤ X ≤ 2Q and log 2 > 2/3, taking logarithms yields ⌊log2 X⌋ ≤ 3 log Q and hence J = 8(⌊log2 X⌋ + 1) ≤ 8(3 log Q + log Q) = 32 log Q. Consequently, every block U = Y2j ≥ X⁴ ≥ Q⁴ (0 ≤ j < J) obeys Q³U−197/200 ≤ Q−47/50 while 64C J² ≤ 65536C(log Q)² ≤ [C/(C + 1)]Q47/50 ≤ Q47/50, giving 8C Q³U−197/200 ≤ 1/(8J²) in the block subtraction budget. Finally, 2J = (2⌊log2 X⌋ + 1)⁸ ≤ 256X⁸ and X ≤ 2Q yield Y N = X⁴2J ≤ 256(2Q)12 = 1048576Q12, so (Y N)3/200 ≤ 10485763/200Q9/50 and J³ ≤ 32768(log Q)³ ≤ Q7/100; using 7/100 + 9/50 = 1/4 and 1 ≤ Q1/4 (Q ≥ 20) gives 1 + J · 8J²C(Y N)3/200 ≤ C1Q1/4 for the assembled zero-density count.

Real-power prime-factorization identity, binary-logarithm ceiling arithmetic, and dyadic exponent bookkeeping

For any integer n ≥ 1, canonical factorization gives n = ∏p|n pvp(n) over the finite set of prime divisors of n. Because every factor pvp(n) is strictly positive in ℝ, repeated application of (u v)ε = uεvε over that finite product, followed by (pvp(n))ε = (pε)vp(n) for p > 0, establishes nε = ∏p|n (pε)vp(n). Partitioning the prime divisors of n at K = ⌈21/ε⌉ gives τ(n) ≤ (∏p|n, p<K A(pε)vp(n))(∏p|n, p≥K (pε)vp(n)) = A#{p|n : p<K}nε ≤ AKnε because #{p | n : p < K} ≤ #{0, 1, …, K − 1} = K and A ≥ 1.

For the binary-logarithm bound when Q ≥ Q0 ≥ 20, we have 20 ≤ Q ≤ X = ⌈Q⌉ < Q + 1 ≤ 2Q and log Q ≥ log 20 > 1 ≥ log 2. Since X ≥ 1, the integer binary logarithm satisfies 2⌊log2 X⌋ ≤ X ≤ 2Q, so ⌊log2 X⌋ log 2 ≤ log(2Q) = log Q + log 2 ≤ 2 log Q. Because 2³ = 8 > exp(2) gives 3 log 2 > 2, we obtain (2/3)⌊log2 X⌋ ≤ ⌊log2 X⌋ log 2 ≤ 2 log Q, hence ⌊log2 X⌋ ≤ 3 log Q; combining with 1 ≤ log Q yields J = 8(⌊log2 X⌋ + 1) ≤ 8(3 log Q + log Q) = 32 log Q (and J ≥ 8 > 0). For each 0 ≤ j < J, U = X⁴2j ≥ Q⁴ > 0 implies U−197/200 ≤ (Q⁴)−197/200 = Q−197/50, so 8C Q³U−197/200 ≤ 8C Q3 − 197/50 = 8C Q−47/50; meanwhile 64C J² ≤ 64C(1024(log Q)²) = 65536C(log Q)² ≤ [C/(C + 1)]Q47/50 ≤ Q47/50 (as C ≥ 0), and dividing by 8J²Q47/50 > 0 gives 8C Q³U−197/200 ≤ 1/(8J²). Finally, 2⌊log2 X⌋ + 1 = 2 · 2⌊log2 X⌋ ≤ 2X implies N = 2J = (2⌊log2 X⌋ + 1)⁸ ≤ 256X⁸, so Y N ≤ 256X12 ≤ 256(2Q)12 = 1048576Q12; raising to 3/200 gives (Y N)3/200 ≤ 10485763/200Q9/50, multiplying by 8C J³ ≤ 8C · 32768(log Q)³ ≤ 8C Q7/100 gives 8C J³(Y N)3/200 ≤ 8C · 10485763/200Q1/4, and adding 1 ≤ Q1/4 completes the bound.

The second reason for failure is a large prime sum. Fix ξ, put Z = (YA)400, and write Sp(y) for the finite sum of Λ(n) min(1,y/n) ξ(n)(n/p) over 1 ≤ n ≤ Z. Here Λ is the von Mangoldt function. The mean-square estimate at a fixed y gives ∑p∈P|Sp(y)|² ≤ C y log y |P|. At a fixed height the estimate holds for any one coefficient sequence of absolute value at most one shared by all primes. To allow the witnessing height to vary with the prime, we also need control of the derivative. To see why, the right derivative of the weight is 1/n for n > y and zero otherwise. Thus y S′p(y) is the same sum with ξ(n) replaced by ξ(n)1n>y. At each fixed integration height these coefficients are common to all primes. The mean-square estimate also gives ∑|S′p(y)|² ≤ C log y |P|/y.

Why averaging the square over primes saves a power of the height

Choose 0 < ε ≤ 1, K ≥ 1 and a sufficiently large Y. Set Z = (YK)400. Fix one height y ∈ [Y,YK] and one complex sequence |κ(n)| ≤ 1 for the entire progression P of primes √U < q ≤ U, q ≡ a mod m. With N = ⌊Z⌋ and cn = Λ(n) min(1,y/n), expand the square of Sq = ∑n≤N cnκ(n)(n/q). Each ordered pair (n,n′) contributes a coefficient cncn′κ(n)κ(n′) times a sum of quadratic symbols. We can take the absolute value of each such sum after summing over q. This order retains cancellation among primes.

For a product nn′, let s be the product of primes outside m whose exponent in nn′ is odd. For an admitted progression and sufficiently large Y, its lower cutoff √U is at least N² and hence every q exceeds N², so a square factor has symbol +1. The primes dividing m contribute a fixed sign on the progression. Indeed, 8 divides m, which fixes the symbol of 2 and the sign in quadratic reciprocity. For odd primes dividing m it also fixes the residue of q modulo that prime. Hence for a sign σ depending on the pair and the progression,

(n/q)(n′/q) = σ(q/s),   σ ∈ {−1,+1}.

For example, 53 and 101 are both 5 modulo 24. The pair (4,3) has s = 1 even though 12 is not a square. Its symbol is −1 at both primes. For (3,5) the symbol is −(q/5), giving +1 at 53 and −1 at 101. These two terms cancel exactly. The example illustrates the correlation on two primes.

Why should ∑q∈P(q/s) be small for s > 1? Split the progression into reduced classes b mod ms above a. Their ordinary prime-counting main terms cancel because the nontrivial character (b/s) sums to zero. A real zero β of a quadratic character χ can add a term proportional to ∑b(b/s)χ(b). Multiplying every class by a unit u ≡ 1 mod m permutes the sum. If χ(u) differs from (u/s), this multiplies it by −1, forcing it to vanish. If the characters agree on these units, the logarithmic integral li(Uβ) is small enough unless β > 1 − c₀/log(mY800K). The near-one uniqueness theorem makes any two such near-one characters agree on common units. Distinct squarefree s would give different symbols on one of those units. The Chinese remainder theorem lets us choose a nonresidue at one prime dividing just one of them and 1 at every other prime involved, as well as modulo m. Thus at most one integer s★ escapes the bound |∑(q/s)| ≤ η|P|, η = Y−(K+1). It is chosen for the progression before y and κ.

Why only one quadratic twist can keep a near-one zero

In the fixed-height mean square, the prime number theorem for a residue class modulo M can contribute a term involving li(Uβ). Here β is a real zero of a nonprincipal quadratic Dirichlet character. Two such terms at different moduli might both be large. To compare them, the proof first puts both characters at the same modulus. The analytic reason this works, as in the 3–4–1 positivity for characters, is that two nearby zeros would force a sum of four logarithmic derivatives to be negative, while every coefficient in its Dirichlet series is nonnegative.

Fix a positive modulus Q and two distinct nonprincipal characters χ₁, χ₂ with χ₁² = χ₂² = 1. Their product is nonprincipal because each character is its own inverse. Write Dψ(σ) = Re(−L′(σ,ψ)/L(σ,ψ)). At a real σ > 1, this is an absolutely convergent sum with coefficients Λ(n) Re ψ(n), where Λ is the von Mangoldt function. On units modulo Q, χ₁ and χ₂ take the values ±1. At every nonunit all four characters, including the principal character 1 modulo Q, vanish. Consequently

D₁ + Dχ₁ + Dχ₂ + Dχ₁χ₂ = ∑(n,Q)=1 Λ(n) (1+χ₁(n))(1+χ₂(n))/nσ ≥ 0.

Each unit has a multiplier of 0 or 4. Suppose both characters have real zeros β₁, β₂ near 1. Put ℓ = log(2Q). In the interval 1 < σ ≤ 6/5 the expansion over zeros in the closed disk of radius 1/5 about 11/10 bounds Dχ by Cℓ minus a sum of Re(1/(σ−ρ)), counted with multiplicity. Every summand is positive since Re ρ < 1. A real zero β in [9/10,1) thus subtracts at least 1/(σ−β). The product character contributes at most Cℓ, and the principal character contributes at most 1/(σ−1)+C′, with C′ ≥ 0. Both constants are uniform in Q.

Set H = 3|C| + 2C′ + 1, e = 1/(20Hℓ), and test at σ = 1+2e. Since ℓ ≥ log 2 > 1/2, we have e ≤ 1/10. If β₁, β₂ ≥ 1−e, each contributes at least 1/(3e). The upper bound for the same four-term sum is then

3Cℓ + C′ + 1/(2e) − 2/(3e) ≤ (H−1)ℓ − (10/3)Hℓ < 0.

This contradiction excludes two distinct characters. A single zero is compatible with the calculation: the pole allowance 1/(2e) exceeds the one guaranteed subtraction 1/(3e).

A second estimate handles two zeros of the same real character at small imaginary part. At its test point σ = 1+1/T, the local sum over zeros is strictly less than 8T/5, and each zero in the restricted region contributes at least 4T/5. Two distinct zeros or one zero of multiplicity at least two exceed the available bound. A nonreal zero would occur with its complex conjugate, so a surviving zero is real and simple. Combining these estimates with the exclusions for the principal character, nonreal characters and larger imaginary parts produces an absolute c > 0. For every Q ≥ 1 the closed region Re z ≥ 1−c/log(Q(|Im z|+2)) contains at most one character–zero pair, with the pole of the principal character excluded.

Now take levels M₁, M₂ ≤ D with D ≥ 3 and induce both characters to Q = M₁M₂. The change-of-level formula preserves a zero by multiplying its L-value by Euler factors. Since log(2Q) ≤ 3 log D, any two real zeros above 1−c/(3 log D) lie in the same region. Their induced characters must agree on every common unit. For example, take m = 8 and squarefree denominators 3 and 5. At the levels 24 and 40, the common unit 41 is 1 modulo 8, but (41/3) = −1 and (41/5) = +1. Thus characters agreeing there with the respective quadratic symbols cannot both have such a zero. The example uses no assumption that either zero exists.

Fix 0 < ε ≤ 1 and K ≥ 1. For every sufficiently large Y and every admitted progression with modulus m, take D = mY800K and c₀ = c/3. A denominator s can produce an uncontrolled contribution only if the progression formula at ms supplies a pair with 1−β < c₀/log D and its character agrees with (·/s) on units congruent to 1 modulo m. For a misaligned character the weighted sum of its main terms vanishes. For an aligned character with 1−β ≥ c₀/log D, the ratio li(Uβ)/li(U) is at most 4 log U exp(−c₀ log U/log D), small enough at the common threshold for Y. At most one odd squarefree s > 1 coprime to m, s ≤ Y800K, can survive both tests. The proof chooses it (or 0 if none) before the height y and coefficients κ. Its pairs are included in the quadratic estimate. A separate use of Siegel’s lower bound gives 1−β ≥ c₁/m at the original modulus and supplies the lower bound on the number of primes.

The remaining task is to count the pairs where cancellation can fail. Since Λ vanishes off prime powers, each index has the form pj. It contributes the single prime p to the parity calculation when p ∤ m and j is odd, and contributes nothing otherwise. Let R be the total weight of indices contributing nothing, sp the total weight of all powers of p, B a common upper bound on sp, and T the total weight. All weights in these definitions are cn, for 1 ≤ n ≤ N.

  • For s = 1 the two indices either contribute nothing or contribute the same prime twice. Their weight is at most R² + ∑psp².
  • If s★ is a prime r, the source covers same-base pairs by sr². For distinct bases, one index contributes r and the other contributes nothing, costing at most 2srR in the two orders. If s★ is composite, only a product of two distinct primes p, r can occur, at cost ≤ 2spsr. Thus 2B² + 2BR covers either case.
  • Every other pair with s > 1 costs at most η|P| times its weight. Summing all positive weights gives an upper bound η|P|T².
∑q∈P|Sq|² ≤ |P| [∑psp² + R² + 2B² + 2BR + ηT²].

Put w = Yε/5. The modulus condition requires each prime divisor of m to be at most w or greater than Z. Among these divisors only the first group can contribute to R, with at most w bases of weight ≤ B each. Every other index in R is a square. The squares have total weight bounded by a constant times √y by summing Λ(j) min(1,y/j²). Consequently R ≤ C₁(√y + w log y) ≤ 5C₁√y. The other estimates are B = C₂ log y, ∑psp² ≤ C₃y log y, and T ≤ C₄y log Z. For large Y, (log Z)² ≤ Y, and y ≤ YK gives ηT² ≤ C₄²y. The displayed bound is therefore ≤ C y log y |P| with one absolute C. Once ε and K are fixed, the threshold for Y works for every admitted progression satisfying this prime-divisor condition, every y ∈ [Y,YK] and every common κ. The separate argument for heights chosen by individual primes uses this conclusion twice, for the sum and for its derivative.

For each prime choose any witnessing yp in a block [V,2V] inside the interval, truncating the final block at YA. Integrate the derivative from V and use Cauchy–Schwarz. The resulting sum of |Sp(yp)|² is at most 4CV log(2V) |P|. Each prime violating |Sp(yp)| ≤ yp1/2+τ/2 contributes at least V1+2τ/4. For τ > 0 the bad fraction is at most (32C/τ)V−τ. Summing over V = 2jY costs the finite factor (1 − 2−τ)−1. Now allocate η/[2(R+1)] of the candidates to each character’s failure set and η/2 to the zero-density exceptions. Beyond a common threshold their union contains at most η|P|. The explicit formula for a surviving twist writes its centered sum as the negative finite sum minus a tail. The contour estimate in its zero-free box bounds this tail contribution by the remaining half of y1/2+τ.

How the finite prime sum controls the centered ramp

The prime-selection argument has found a prime p for which the finite sums are small throughout the required interval. There is still a term to estimate for its twist χ(n) = ξ(n)(n/p). Write an = Λ(n)χ(n) and D(s) = −L′(s,χ)/L(s,χ). For a height y and a cutoff Z ≥ y > 0, set

R(y) = ∑1≤n≤y an(y/n − 1),   SZ(y) = ∑1≤n≤Z an min(1,y/n),   PZ = ∑1≤n≤Z an/n.

For n ≤ y, subtracting 1 from y/n gives the ramp weight. For y < n ≤ Z, the two weights in yPZ − SZ(y) cancel. Hence the centered ramp satisfies an exact identity, with a tail that is a single complex number for the whole interval.

Gχ(y) = R(y) − yD(1) = −SZ(y) − y[D(1) − PZ].

How close is the finite slope PZ to D(1)? Measure the same increment ΔR = R(Z + h) − R(Z) in two ways. First, every term already present at Z advances by exactly han/n. The new terms have Z < n ≤ Z + h. For Z ≥ 1 and h > 0, there are at most h + 1 of them, each with ramp weight ≤ h/Z and |an| ≤ log(Z + h). Thus |ΔR − hPZ| ≤ h(h + 1) log(Z + h)/Z.

A prime power entering the ramp. Take the nontrivial character modulo 3, with values 1, −1, 0 on residues 1, 2, 0. From Z = 7/2 to Z + h = 5, the old slope is PZ = −log(2)/2. The ramp goes from −(3/4)log 2 to −(5/4)log 2, so ΔR − hPZ = (1/4)log 2. The entire correction comes from 4 = 2², since χ(4) = 1 and 5/4 − 1 = 1/4. The new prime 5 has weight zero at the endpoint. This calculation checks the finite difference for arbitrary cutoffs.

The same increment from a contour. Suppose χ is nonprincipal of modulus N ≤ Q, with Q ≥ 2, and L(s,χ) has no zero for Re s > 1 − 1/400 and |Im s| ≤ Q. For u ≥ 1, Perron inversion writes R(u) as the integral of D(s)us/[s(s−1)] on Re s = 2, with measure ds/(2πi). Move the segment of height |Im s| ≤ T = Q/2 to σ = 1 − 1/400 + δ, where 0 < δ ≤ 1/800. The rectangle lies inside the zero-free box and stays to the right of 0. Its only possible pole is at 1. Multiplication by s−1 leaves D(s)us/s, whose value there is uD(1). At u = Z + h and u = Z, subtracting these residues gives hD(1).

Put h = ηZ with 0 < η ≤ 1. On the left edge, differentiate us with respect to the positive variable u. This gives |(Z + h)s − Zs| ≤ |s|ηZσ. The factor |s| cancels one denominator. Integrating 1/|s−1| over the segment costs at most 4 log(1 + 800T). The other logarithm comes from |D(s)| ≤ Cδ log Q on the smaller box Re s ≥ σ, |Im s| ≤ Q − 1. In the local formula for L′/L, the nearby zeros stay at least δ away and their total multiplicity is bounded by a constant times log Q. On the two horizontal sides the denominator has size at least T². On the unshifted right tails the integrand decays as 1/|Im s|². Together these give a constant Aδ independent of χ, Z, η and Q.

|ΔR − hD(1)| ≤ Aδ log Q [(log Q)ηZσ + Z²/Q].

Why use the 400th power? Fix 0 < ε ≤ 1/4, K ≥ 1 and τ > 0. For sufficiently large Y, the selection stage has Yε/6 ≤ log Q ≤ Yε/4. Choose x = YK, the largest required height, and set Z = x400, η = x−2, h = x398, δ = ε/(1600K). Subtract the errors ΔR − hPZ and ΔR − hD(1). Their difference is h[D(1) − PZ], whose size is bounded by the sum of the two errors’ absolute values. Multiply by x/h. The left-edge term now contains xZσ−1 = x400δ = Yε/4. Thus the width 1/400 of the zero-free strip pays for the entire factor x. The resulting upper bound for x|D(1) − PZ| has three terms.

  • Aδ(log Q)²Yε/4 ≤ AδY3ε/4, eventually at most Yε/3.
  • Aδ(log Q)x403/Q ≤ AδY404K exp(−Yε/6), eventually at most 1/3.
  • (x398 + 1) log(Z + h)/x399 ≤ 802 for x ≥ 3, since Z + h ≤ x401, log x ≤ x, and x398 + 1 ≤ 2x398. Eventually 802 ≤ Yε/3.

One bound now covers every y ∈ [Y,x]. Since y ≤ x, the tail in the centered ramp is at most Yε. For Y ≥ 16 this is at most y1/2+τ/2. The surviving prime already satisfies |SZ(y)| ≤ y1/2+τ/2 throughout the interval, by the exclusion of large finite sums. Adding gives |Gχ(y)| ≤ y1/2+τ. The selection applies this calculation to the full primitive twist with Q = FU, the product of the base conductor bound and the prime cutoff. Every prime passing the two tests thus supplies a centered estimate at every required height.

8.29Making both choices at the same threshold

Take τ = ε/2, η = 1/2 and work at base modulus N₀ = 8M. In the first progression take U = exp z, F = N₀ and the primitive characters inducing the characters modulo N₀. At least half of a nonempty set of primes survives. Choose any surviving q. For the second progression take U = exp z′, F = N₀ exp z, and the primitive characters inducing ξ and ξ(·/q) for all ξ modulo N₀. Whatever q was chosen, this family has at most twice the number of characters modulo N₀. The second-stage theorem verifies the modulus and conductor bounds uniformly in q. In particular q > (YA)400 for large Y, while the other odd prime factors of B are at most z. At least half of this second nonempty set also survives. The two thresholds were fixed before choosing either prime.

The first selection controls the twist by q alone. The second controls the twist by d and the twist by both primes. For a real base character of conductor dividing 8M, change of level places it in the same family, hence the same rectangle excludes all zeros for the induced primitive character, with height 8M exp(z + jz′) if j records the presence of d. For a base character modulo M these estimates bound the centered sum by y1/2+ε/2. The logarithmic derivative at one satisfies the sharper bound 4 log y. The source first proves 1000 log log H + C from the zero-free box and then uses log H ≤ 3Yε/5(log Y)². The leading coefficient in units of log Y is at most 1000/(5 · 52) = 50/13 < 4, so the log log Y and constant terms fit in the remaining margin for large Y. The proof inputs at this point are the relative prime-number theorem in progressions with its exceptional-zero bound, primitive-character zero density, the quadratic-twist mean-square theorem and the contour tail estimates.

Norm primes in short intervals without an ineffective constant

Why can both the dyadic selection of the two auxiliary primes g0, g1 and the selection of every word’s level prime Tu inside a narrow multiplicative window of relative width 1/(fk) proceed unconditionally, without introducing any ineffective Siegel constant? In an arbitrary rational residue class modulo a large integer, a real Dirichlet character can carry an exceptional zero whose distance from s = 1 is controlled only ineffectively once the exponent drops below one. Here, however, the global lattice construction does not ask for primes in a general rational progression. Instead it seeks rational primes p = ππ̄ that split in the fixed imaginary quadratic field K = ℚ(√(−d)) (with d prime, d ≡ 3 modulo 4 and d ≥ 100) and admit a factor π ≡ 1 modulo M𝒪K. Such primes are governed by the ray class group G of K modulo M𝒪K. For any real character χ of G, the Dedekind–ray-class product series formed by convolving the trivial character with χ has nonnegative Dirichlet coefficients. Testing that series near s = 1 against a nonnegative Bessel-type smoothing kernel yields an effective polynomial lower bound at s = 1 in the conductor scale B = 4dM², and hence an effective zero repulsion away from s = 1.

Theorem (Short-interval norm primes). There exist absolute constants A > 0, c > 0 and c′ > 0 with the following property. Let d be a prime satisfying d ≡ 3 modulo 4 and d ≥ 100, let M ≥ 3 be an integer, put B = 4dM², and let X ≥ 1 and h be real numbers satisfying log B ≤ c√(log X) and exp(−c√(log X)) ≤ h ≤ 1. Then the short interval (X, X(1 + h)] satisfies

#{p ∈ (X, X(1 + h)] ∩ ℕ : p prime, ∃ A0, B0 ∈ ℤ, A0² + dB0² = 4p, M ∣ B0, 2M ∣ A0 − 2 − B0} ≥ c′hX / ((4dM²)A log X).

Proof. Since d ≡ 3 modulo 4, we have −d ≡ 1 modulo 4 and the ring of integers of K = ℚ(√(−d)) is 𝒪K = ℤ[(1 + √(−d))/2]. A rational prime p admits integers A0, B0 satisfying 4p = A0² + dB0², M ∣ B0 and 2M ∣ A0 − 2 − B0 if and only if p = ππ̄ for some algebraic integer π ∈ 𝒪K with π − 1 ∈ M𝒪K. Such a prime is necessarily coprime to M and splits in K into principal-ray-class prime ideals belonging to the trivial class of the ray class group G of K modulo M𝒪K. Injecting G into Cl(𝒪K) × (𝒪K/M𝒪K) and applying Minkowski’s discriminant bound hK ≤ |ΔK| = d ≤ 4d bounds the group order by |G| ≤ hKM² ≤ 4dM² = B, while d ≥ 100 > 3 (so 𝒪K× = {±1}) and M ≥ 3 make generators congruent to 1 modulo M𝒪K unique and give each ray class ideal-count density 2π/(√d M²).

By finite abelian character orthogonality on G, the von Mangoldt prime-power weight restricted to the trivial ray class over (X, X(1 + h)] is the average (1/|G|)∑χ∈Ĝ [ψ(X(1 + h); χ) − ψ(X; χ)] of the ray-class Chebyshev differences. Four analytic properties of the ray-class L-functions L(s, χ) at parameter B = 4dM² control this character sum:

  • Across all χ ∈ Ĝ, L(s, χ) obeys a standard logarithmic zero-free region in terms of B and |Im s|, up to possible real zeros near s = 1.
  • Across the entire dual group Ĝ, at most one real character can vanish in that real exceptional segment, and any such exceptional zero β is unique and simple.
  • For every real character χ ∈ Ĝ, nonnegativity of the quadratic Dirichlet convolution coefficients paired with a positive Bessel-type smoothing kernel produces an effective polynomial lower bound at s = 1, forcing any real exceptional zero β to satisfy 1 − β ≥ δ, where δ = c9/BA1 for explicit constants 0 < c9 ≤ 1 and A1 > 0.
  • The truncated Perron explicit formula on (X, X(1 + h)] extracts the pole contribution hX from the principal character, bounds the magnitude of the optional exceptional-zero term by at most hX(1 − δ/2), and—for sufficiently small c > 0 under log B ≤ c√(log X) and exp(−c√(log X)) ≤ h ≤ 1—bounds the sum of the contour-truncation and zero-sum errors over all |G| ≤ B characters by at most hXδ/4.

Combining the three contributions in the character sum leaves at least hX − hX(1 − δ/2) − hXδ/4 = hXδ/4. Dividing by |G| ≤ B bounds the trivial-class prime-power weight on (X, X(1 + h)] below by hXδ/(4B) = c9hX/(4BA1+1). Subtracting higher prime powers costs O(√X), which is absorbed into half of this main term on the admitted range of B and h. Each surviving prime p ∈ (X, X(1 + h)] splits into at most two prime ideals of K and therefore contributes at most 2 log(X(1 + h)) ≤ 4 log X to the weighted sum. Dividing by 4 log X and setting A = A1 + 1 yields at least c′hX/((4dM²)A log X) norm primes in (X, X(1 + h)].

Quadratic congruence equivalence and prime-power absorption

Write an arbitrary element of 𝒪K = ℤ[(1 + √(−d))/2] as π = u + v(1 + √(−d))/2 with u, v ∈ ℤ, and set A0 = 2u + v and B0 = v. Then 4ππ̄ = (2u + v)² + dv² = A0² + dB0², and conversely any integers A0, B0 solving A0² + dB0² = 4p have the same parity because d is odd, so u = (A0 − B0)/2 and v = B0 are integers defining π ∈ 𝒪K of norm p. Moreover, π − 1 = (u − 1) + v(1 + √(−d))/2 belongs to M𝒪K if and only if M divides both v = B0 and u − 1 = (A0 − 2 − B0)/2, which is equivalent to M ∣ B0 and 2M ∣ A0 − 2 − B0. If a prime ℓ divided both p and M, then π ≡ 1 modulo ℓ𝒪K would force p = ππ̄ ≡ 1 modulo ℓ, a contradiction; hence p is coprime to M.

For the prime-power tail and logarithmic divisor, note that d ≥ 100 and M ≥ 3 give B = 4dM² ≥ 3600, so taking c small enough in log B ≤ c√(log X) forces X ≥ 2 and keeps hB−AX1/2 ≥ exp(−(1 + A)c√(log X) + (1/2) log X) arbitrarily large, absorbing the O(√X) contribution of prime squares and higher powers into half of c9hX/(4BA). Finally, since h ≤ 1 and X ≥ 2, we have X(1 + h) ≤ 2X ≤ X², whence 2 log(X(1 + h)) ≤ 4 log X.

Specializing the theorem to relative width h = 1 on a dyadic interval (Y, 2Y] with log(4dM²) ≤ c√(log Y) absorbs the denominator (4dM²)A log Y into Y1/10 for all sufficiently large Y, producing at least Y9/10 split norm-one primes in (Y, 2Y]. Applied on the global route at base conductor N = QS · q · d (for the positive host integer QS), rank 1 ≤ r ≤ x⁵ (with 1 ≤ k ≤ r) and dyadic scale Y = (kb)⁸, where b = exp(L) and L = xε, at most (3r + 1)(1 + 2r²(Y3/4 + 1)) ≤ 20r³Y3/4 < Y9/10 candidates in [Y, 2Y] can share an exceptional cyclotomic prime divisor through exponent r; this extracts two distinct auxiliary primes g0 ≠ g1 in [(kb)⁸, 2(kb)⁸] with disjoint exceptional divisor sets, each represented by an element of 𝒪K congruent to 1 modulo N𝒪K and satisfying log gi ≤ 9L once 2(kb)⁸ ≤ b⁹.

Continuation, zero-free region and Landau–Page uniqueness without a functional equation

Why can the analytic properties of the ray-class L-functions invoked in the short-interval norm-prime theorem above—holomorphic continuation into the critical strip, nonvanishing and logarithmic differentiation on Re s > 1, the classical logarithmic zero-free region, and Landau–Page uniqueness of at most one real exceptional zero—be established without proving a Hecke functional equation, root numbers, or gamma factors, and even without factoring the series into an Euler product? Two elementary mechanisms replace both. First, subtracting the linear main term from the ideal-counting sum in each ray class leaves a square-root remainder O(√x), so Mellin integration by parts continues (s − 1)𝟏χ=1L(s, χ) holomorphically to Re s > 1/2 with quadratic polynomial growth in ‖s‖; on concentric discs centered at 5/4 + it, that polynomial bound suffices for Jensen’s zero count and the Borel–Carathéodory logarithmic-derivative expansion. Second, the group-ring convolution identity (a log) = λ ∗ a integrates on Re s > 1 to express each L-series directly as an exponential of prime-power weights, and nonnegativity of the class weights λ(g, n) ≥ 0 supplies both a uniform lower bound at 5/4 + it and the trigonometric and four-character positivity inequalities that repel zeros from Re s = 1.

To state all three analytic inputs uniformly, let G be a finite abelian group written additively with identity 0 ∈ G and character group Ĝ = Hom(G, ℂ×), where χ = 1 denotes the trivial character χ(g) = 1 and (χψ)(g) = χ(g)ψ(g). Fix a scale parameter B ≥ 4 and a local class density κ ∈ [1/B, 4] (denoting here the ideal-count density per class of G, distinct from the global relative-error parameter of Chapters 2, 7 and 9) with |G| ≤ B, together with two nonnegative sequences a, λ : G × ℕ → ℝ≥0 satisfying five axioms:

|∑1≤n≤x a(g, n) − κx| ≤ 10√x  (x ≥ 1),   |∑n≥1 a(g, n) e−tn − κ/t| ≤ B10t  (0 < t ≤ 1),   a(g, n) log n = ∑h∈G ∑pq=n λ(h, p)a(g − h, q),

supplemented by the normalization a(g, 0) = 0 for all g ∈ G, a(0, 1) = 1 and a(g, 1) = 0 for g ≠ 0, the von Mangoldt dominance ∑g∈G λ(g, n) ≤ 2Λ(n) for all n ≥ 0, and real-character convolution positivity: for every real character χ ∈ Ĝ (meaning χ² = 1) and every n ≥ 0, the Dirichlet convolution of b1(p) = ∑g∈G a(g, p) with bχ(q) = ∑g∈G (Re χ(g))a(g, q) satisfies ∑pq=n b1(p)bχ(q) ≥ 0 and ∑pq=n² b1(p)bχ(q) ≥ b1(n). The ray class group G of K = ℚ(√(−d)) modulo M𝒪K (for prime d ≡ 3 modulo 4 with d ≥ 100 and integer M ≥ 3) satisfies all five axioms at B = 4dM² ≥ 3600 and κ = 2π/(√d M²) ∈ [1/B, 4], with a(g, n) and λ(g, n) counting integral ideals and prime-power ideals of norm n coprime to M in class g, and quadratic convolution positivity coming from the nonnegative Euler-factor coefficients of ζK(s)L(s, χ). For each χ ∈ Ĝ, define the twisted coefficients aχ(n) = ∑g∈G χ(g)a(g, n) and λχ(n) = ∑g∈G χ(g)λ(g, n), the Chebyshev sum ψ(χ, u) = ∑1≤n≤u λχ(n), the residue ρχ = κ|G| when χ = 1 and ρχ = 0 when χ ≠ 1, the Mellin remainder integral M(χ, s) = ∫₁∞ (∑1≤n≤x aχ(n) − ρχx)x−s−1 dx, the regularized continuation F(χ, s) = ρχs + (s − 1)sM(χ, s) when χ = 1 and F(χ, s) = sM(χ, s) when χ ≠ 1, and the conductor-height weight ℓ(t) = log(B(|t| + 2)) > 2.

Theorem (Analytic continuation, zero-free region and Landau–Page uniqueness). For every finite-group L-family as above and every χ ∈ Ĝ, the function F(χ, s) is holomorphic on Re s > 1/2, agrees with (s − 1)𝟏χ=1 ∑n≥1 aχ(n)n−s on Re s > 1, satisfies ‖F(χ, s)‖ ≤ 300B(‖s‖ + 1)² on Re s ≥ 11/20, obeys Schwarz symmetry F(χ, s̄) = conj(F(χ, s)) whenever χ² = 1, and on Re s > 1 satisfies F(χ, s) ≠ 0 together with −F′(χ, s)/F(χ, s) + 𝟏χ=1/(s − 1) = ∑n≥1 λχ(n)n−s. Moreover, there exist absolute constants c₁ > 0 and c₂ > 0 such that across every finite-group L-family:

Re s ≥ 3/4,   F(χ, s) = 0,   (χ² ≠ 1 or Im s ≠ 0)  ⇒  Re s < 1 − c₁ / ℓ(Im s),

and whenever χ, ψ ∈ Ĝ satisfy χ² = ψ² = 1 and β, β′ ∈ ℝ satisfy β, β′ ≥ max(3/4, 1 − c₂/ℓ(0)) with F(χ, β) = F(ψ, β′) = 0, one has χ = ψ, β = β′, and F′(χ, β) ≠ 0.

Proof. By character orthogonality ∑g∈G χ(g) equals |G| when χ = 1 and 0 when χ ≠ 1, so summing the counting bound over g ∈ G gives ‖∑1≤n≤x aχ(n) − ρχx‖ ≤ 10|G|√x ≤ 10B√x for all x ≥ 1. Hence M(χ, s) converges holomorphically on Re s > 1/2 and satisfies ‖M(χ, s)‖ ≤ 10B ∫₁∞ x−11/20−1/2 dx = 200B on Re s ≥ 11/20. Abelian summation on Re s > 1 identifies F(χ, s) = (s − 1)𝟏χ=1L(aχ, s), while ρ1 = κ|G| ≤ 4B gives ‖F(χ, s)‖ ≤ 4B‖s‖ + 200B‖s‖(‖s‖ + 1) ≤ 300B(‖s‖ + 1)² on Re s ≥ 11/20; when χ² = 1, every value χ(g) lies in {±1} ⊂ ℝ, so aχ(n) ∈ ℝ and F(χ, s̄) = conj(F(χ, s)). Next, multiplying the convolution axiom by χ(g) = χ(h)χ(g − h) and summing over g ∈ G yields (aχ log) = λχ ∗ aχ with aχ(1) = χ(0)a(0, 1) = 1 and ‖λχ(n)‖ ≤ ∑g∈G λ(g, n) ≤ 2Λ(n). On Re s = σ > 1, this Dirichlet convolution identifies L(aχ, s) = exp(∑n≥2 (λχ(n)/log n)n−s); comparing the real part of the exponent with R = ∑n≥2 (Λ(n)/log n)n−σ = log ζ(σ) ≤ log(σ/(σ − 1)) gives ‖L(aχ, s)‖ ≥ e−2R ≥ ((σ − 1)/σ)² > 0, whence F(χ, s) ≠ 0 and −F′(χ, s)/F(χ, s) + 𝟏χ=1/(s − 1) = L(λχ, s).

For any real height t, the closed disc B̄(c, 7/10) around c = 5/4 + it lies inside {Re w ≥ 11/20}, where ‖F(χ, w)‖ ≤ 300B(‖w‖ + 1)², while at the center c one has ‖F(χ, c)‖ ≥ |c − 1|𝟏χ=1((5/4 − 1)/(5/4))² ≥ 1/100. Dividing out the finite Blaschke product of zeros on the concentric subdisc ‖w − c‖ ≤ 3/5 (relative radius 6/7 < 1) and applying Borel–Carathéodory and Cauchy’s derivative estimate on ‖s − c‖ ≤ 1/2 (relative radius 5/7 < 6/7) yields an absolute constant C > 0 such that F(χ, ·) has at most Cℓ(t) zeros w (counted with multiplicity) in ‖w − c‖ ≤ 3/5, and for every s in ‖s − c‖ ≤ 1/2 away from those zeros, ‖F′(χ, s)/F(χ, s) − ∑‖w−c‖≤3/5 ordw(F(χ, ·))/(s − w)‖ ≤ Cℓ(t). Because every remaining zero w satisfies Re w ≤ 1 < σ for σ ∈ (1, 5/4], its neglected partial-fraction term has positive real part, so Re L(λψ, σ + it) ≤ 𝟏ψ=1 Re(1/(σ − 1 + it)) − ∑w∈S Re(1/(σ + it − w)) + Cℓ(t) for any subset S of zeros (with multiplicity) in ‖w − (5/4 + it)‖ ≤ 3/5. Meanwhile, nonnegativity λ(g, n) ≥ 0 gives four inequalities for σ > 1 and t ∈ ℝ: (i) 3 Re L(λ₁, σ) + 4 Re L(λχ, σ + it) + Re L(λχ², σ + 2it) ≥ 0 from 3 + 4 Re z + Re(z²) = 2(1 + Re z)² ≥ 0 on |z| = 1; (ii) Re L(λ₁, σ) ≥ 0; and for real characters χ² = ψ² = 1, (iii) Re L(λ₁ + λχ, σ) ≥ 0 and (iv) Re L(λ₁ + λχ + λψ + λχψ, σ) ≥ 0 from 1 + χ(g) ≥ 0 and (1 + χ(g))(1 + ψ(g)) ≥ 0. Testing (ii) (when χ = 1) or (iii) (when χ ≠ 1) at σ = 1 + 60ε when χ² = 1 and 0 < (Im s)² < (30ε)² (pairing s with its distinct conjugate zero s̄), testing (i) at σ = 1 + 6ε in all remaining cases of the zero-free region, and testing (ii)–(iv) at σ = 1 + 2c₂/ℓ(0) for two real zeros or a multiple real zero near 1 completes both claims.

Euler-product-free exponential identity, conjugate-zero pairing and four-character Landau–Page test

On Re s > 1, define G(s) = ∑n≥2 (λχ(n)/log n)n−s, which converges absolutely with G′(s) = −L(λχ, s) because ‖λχ(n)‖ ≤ 2Λ(n). Termwise differentiation and Dirichlet multiplication give (d/ds)[L(aχ, s) exp(−G(s))] = [−L(aχ log, s) + L(λχ, s)L(aχ, s)] exp(−G(s)) = 0 since aχ log = λχ ∗ aχ. As Re s → +∞ along the real axis, L(aχ, s) → aχ(1) = 1 and G(s) → 0, so L(aχ, s) = exp(G(s)) everywhere on Re s > 1.

Suppose now that F(χ, s) = 0 with s = 1 − δ + iγ, Re s ≥ 3/4, and either χ² ≠ 1 or γ ≠ 0. Nonvanishing on Re s > 1 gives δ ≥ 0, and if δ > 1/400 then δ > (1/800)/ℓ(γ) because ℓ(γ) > 2. Assume 0 ≤ δ ≤ 1/400 and fix any ε ∈ (0, 1/400] with δ ≤ ε. If χ² = 1 and 0 < γ² < (30ε)², Schwarz symmetry gives the distinct zero s̄ = 1 − δ − iγ, and both s, s̄ lie inside B̄(5/4, 3/5) because (1/4 + δ)² + γ² ≤ (101/400)² + (3/40)² < (3/5)². Evaluating 0 ≤ Re L(λ₁, 1 + 60ε) (when χ = 1) or 0 ≤ Re L(λ₁, 1 + 60ε) + Re L(λχ, 1 + 60ε) (when χ ≠ 1) yields 2(60ε + δ)/((60ε + δ)² + γ²) ≤ 1/(60ε) + 2Cℓ(0); since (60ε + δ)² + γ² < (61ε)² + (30ε)² = 4621ε² and 120/4621 − 1/60 = 2579/277260 > 1/108, we obtain 1/(108ε) ≤ 2Cℓ(0) ≤ 2Cℓ(γ). Otherwise either χ² ≠ 1 or γ² ≥ (30ε)², and applying 3 Re L(λ₁, 1 + 6ε) + 4 Re L(λχ, 1 + 6ε + iγ) + Re L(λχ², 1 + 6ε + 2iγ) ≥ 0 bounds the first pole by 3/(6ε) = (1/2)/ε, subtracts at least 4/(6ε + δ) ≥ (4/7)/ε from the zero s, while on |γ| ≥ 30ε any pole at s = 1 in the second term (when χ = 1) satisfies 4 Re(1/(6ε + iγ)) = 24ε/(36ε² + γ²) ≤ 24ε/(936ε²) = 4/(156ε) and any pole in the third term (when χ² = 1) satisfies Re(1/(6ε + 2iγ)) = 6ε/(36ε² + 4γ²) ≤ 6ε/(3636ε²) < 1/(156ε). Because ℓ(2γ) ≤ 2ℓ(γ), collecting errors gives (1/14 − 5/156)/ε = (43/1092)/ε ≤ 9Cℓ(γ), so 1/ε ≤ 300Cℓ(γ) in both cases; letting ε ↓ δ rules out δ = 0 and gives δ ≥ 1/(300Cℓ(γ)) > c₁/ℓ(γ) for c₁ = 1/(1200C + 800).

For Landau–Page uniqueness, set c₂ = 1/(100(C + 1)) and σ = 1 + 2c₂/ℓ(0) ∈ (1, 5/4]. Every real zero x ∈ [1 − c₂/ℓ(0), 1] lies in B̄(5/4, 3/5) and contributes ordx/(σ − x) ≥ ordx · ℓ(0)/(3c₂), while the pole at 1 of L(λ₁, σ) contributes ℓ(0)/(2c₂). If χ = ψ and either β ≠ β′ or ordβ(F(χ, ·)) ≥ 2, the real-zero multiplicity is at least 2, so testing Re L(λ₁, σ) ≥ 0 (when χ = 1) or Re L(λ₁ + λχ, σ) ≥ 0 (when χ ≠ 1) yields 2ℓ(0)/(3c₂) ≤ ℓ(0)/(2c₂) + 2Cℓ(0), contradicting 1/(6c₂) > 2C. Siegel-free polynomial repulsion at s = 1 via the positive Bessel kernel

Why does a real ray-class character χ of an imaginary quadratic field escape Siegel’s ineffectivity at s = 1, whereas an arbitrary real Dirichlet character modulo q admits only an ineffective lower bound L(1, χ) ≫ q−ε? Because the Dirichlet convolution b1 ∗ bχ of the total norm-counting sequence b1(n) = ∑g∈G a(g, n) with a real ray-class character sequence bχ(n) = aχ(n) has nonnegative coefficients for every n ≥ 1 and equals 1 at n = 1. Instead of meromorphically continuing the product L-function across the critical strip via a functional equation, one pairs the two Laplace transforms θ1(v/w) and θχ(w) against the scale-invariant measure dw/w on (0, ∞). Termwise change of variables turns every product exp(−vm/w − qw) into the positive modified Bessel integral W(vmq), bounding the paired integral uniformly below by W(1) > 0 for all 0 < v ≤ 1, while isolating the polar main term ρ1w/v of θ1(v/w) at an explicit polynomial scale v ≍ B−44 forces F(χ, 1) ≥ c₃/B45; Cauchy’s derivative estimate near s = 1 then converts that value bound into a completely effective polynomial zero repulsion 1 − β ≥ c₄/B46.

Theorem (Effective lower bound at s = 1 and real-zero repulsion). There exist absolute constants c₃ > 0 and 0 < c₄ ≤ 1 such that for every finite-group L-family (with scale B ≥ 4, class density κ ∈ [1/B, 4], and |G| ≤ B), every real character χ ∈ Ĝ satisfying χ² = 1, and every real zero β ≥ 3/4 of F(χ, ·),

‖F(χ, 1)‖ ≥ c₃ / B45,   1 − β ≥ c₄ / B46.

Proof. When χ = 1, evaluating F(1, s) = ρ1s + (s − 1)sM(1, s) at s = 1 gives F(1, 1) = κ|G| ≥ 1/B ≥ 1/B45 because B ≥ 4 and |G| ≥ 1. Suppose now that χ ≠ 1 with χ² = 1, so χ(g) = Re χ(g) ∈ {±1}, bχ(n) = aχ(n) ∈ ℝ, and |bχ(n)| ≤ b1(n). Form the Laplace series θ1(t) = ∑n≥1 b1(n)e−tn and θχ(t) = ∑n≥1 bχ(n)e−tn for t > 0. Summing the small-t Laplace axiom over |G| ≤ B classes for 0 < t ≤ 1 and applying partial summation from the counting bound for t ≥ 1 gives an absolute constant C₀ > 0 such that |θ1(t) − ρ1/t| ≤ C₀B11 min(t, 1/t) and |θχ(t)| ≤ C₀B11 min(t, 1/t) for all t > 0, with |θχ(t)| ≤ C₀Be−t/2 on t ≥ 1 and ∫₀∞ θχ(w) dw = F(χ, 1) ∈ ℝ.

Define the positive Bessel kernel W(y) = ∫₀∞ exp(−y/w − w) dw/w for y > 0, which is strictly positive, decreasing in y, satisfies W(y) ≤ 12/y³ via e−y/w ≤ 6(w/y)³, and takes a positive value w₀ = W(1) > 0 at y = 1. For any 0 < v ≤ 1, substituting w = u/q in each term (m, q) expands ∫₀∞ θ1(v/w)θχ(w) dw/w = ∑n≥1 (b1 ∗ bχ)(n)W(vn). By real-character convolution positivity, (b1 ∗ bχ)(n) ≥ 0 for all n ≥ 1, while the normalization axiom gives b1(1) = bχ(1) = 1 and hence (b1 ∗ bχ)(1) = 1. Dropping all terms n ≥ 2 and using monotonicity W(v) ≥ W(1) = w₀ yields w₀ ≤ ∫₀∞ θ1(v/w)θχ(w) dw/w. Conversely, splitting θ1(v/w) = ρ1w/v + (θ1(v/w) − ρ1w/v) and bounding |θ1(u) − ρ1/u| ≤ E√u (since min(u, 1/u) ≤ √u) and |θχ(w)| ≤ E min(w, 1/w) with E = C₀B11 gives w₀ ≤ (ρ1/v)F(χ, 1) + E²√v K, where K = ∫₀∞ min(w, 1/w)w−3/2 dw = 8/3. Choosing v = s₀² with s₀ = δ₀/B22 and δ₀ = min(1, w₀/(2C₀²K)) > 0 makes 0 < v ≤ B−44 < 1 and E²√v K = C₀²Kδ₀ ≤ w₀/2, leaving w₀/2 ≤ (ρ1/s₀²)F(χ, 1) ≤ (4B/s₀²)|F(χ, 1)| (since ρ1 = κ|G| ≤ 4B), and hence |F(χ, 1)| ≥ (w₀δ₀²/8)/B45. Setting c₃ = min(1, w₀δ₀²/8) covers both χ = 1 and χ ≠ 1.

Finally, let β ≥ 3/4 be any real zero of F(χ, ·). Nonvanishing on Re s > 1 from the continuation theorem above forces β ∈ [3/4, 1] ⊂ B̄(1, 1/4). For every z ∈ B̄(1, 1/4), the closed disc B̄(z, 1/10) lies inside {Re w ≥ 13/20 ≥ 11/20, ‖w‖ ≤ 27/20}, where (‖w‖ + 1)² ≤ (47/20)² < 6 and ‖F(χ, w)‖ ≤ 1800B; Cauchy’s derivative inequality on radius 1/10 therefore bounds ‖F′(χ, z)‖ ≤ 18000B on [β, 1]. By the mean-value inequality, c₃/B45 ≤ ‖F(χ, 1) − F(χ, β)‖ ≤ 18000B(1 − β), proving 1 − β ≥ c₄/B46 with c₄ = min(1, c₃/18000) ∈ (0, 1], which supplies the effective parameter δ = c₄/B46 used in the short-interval count.

Write Aχ(x) = ∑1≤n≤x aχ(n), so Aχ(x) = 0 for x < 1 and ‖Aχ(x) − ρχx‖ ≤ 10B√x for x ≥ 1; in particular ‖Aχ(x)‖ ≤ 4Bx + 10B√x ≤ 14Bx for x ≥ 1. When 0 < t ≤ 1, summing the second axiom over g ∈ G with χ(g) gives ‖θχ(t) − ρχ/t‖ ≤ |G|B10t ≤ B11t.

For χ ≠ 1 (so ρχ = 0), the bounds |θχ(t)| ≤ C₀B11t on (0, 1] and |θχ(t)| ≤ C₀Be−t/2 on [1, ∞) make θχ integrable on (0, ∞). Fix c₀ ∈ (0, 1/20]. For a character χ ∈ Ĝ, say that a finite set Z ⊂ ℝ is a c₀-admissible exceptional zero set for χ when |Z| ≤ 1, every β ∈ Z satisfies 1 − c₀/ℓ(0) ≤ β < 1, F(χ, β) = 0 and F′(χ, β) ≠ 0, and every zero w ∈ ℂ of F(χ, ·) satisfying Re w ≥ 1 − c₀/ℓ(Im w) belongs to Z. By the zero-free region and Landau–Page theorem, choosing c₀ = min(c₁, c₂, 1/20) equips every χ ∈ Ĝ with such a set Z (empty unless χ² = 1 and F(χ, ·) vanishes on [1 − c₀/ℓ(0), 1), and across all χ ∈ Ĝ at most one character has Z ≠ ∅).

Theorem (Explicit formula with an optional exceptional zero). For every c₀ ∈ (0, 1/20], there exist constants c > 0 and C > 0 (depending only on c₀) such that for every finite-group L-family (with scale B ≥ 4), every χ ∈ Ĝ, every c₀-admissible exceptional zero set Z ⊂ ℝ for χ, and every real u ≥ 2 satisfying log B ≤ √(log u),

Substituting L(λχ, s) = −F′(χ, s)/F(χ, s) + 𝟏χ=1/(s − 1) and shifting across [σ₁, σ₀] × [−T, T] extracts 𝟏χ=1u at s = 1 and −uβ/β whenever β ∈ Z ∩ (σ₁, 1) (while if β ∈ Z satisfies β < σ₁, then β ≤ 1 − 2d makes |uβ/β| ≤ 2u1−2d directly). Truncated Perron kernel estimate, height comparison and short-interval assembly

For any sequence c(n) with ‖c(n)‖ ≤ 2Λ(n), σ₀ = 1 + 1/log u (giving uσ₀ = eu) and 2 ≤ T ≤ u, interchange the finite integral with L(c, s) = ∑n≥1 c(n)n−s along s = σ₀ + it using the standard truncated Perron bound |(1/(2πi)) ∫σ₀−iTσ₀+iT (u/n)s ds/s − 𝟏n≤u| ≤ C₀(u/n)σ₀ min(1, 1/(T|log(u/n)|)) (with the n = u term bounded by C₀). Proposition (Unconditional word-level prime selection and window bounds). Fix 0 < ε < 1/52, cs > 0 and CY > 0 (with CY = 9 on the global route).
