Suppose that the integers m and f, k ≥ 1 satisfy m ≥ x1/3 and 1 ≤ V = fk ≤ x12. For any word u with D★ > 0, du★ > 0, Γ > 1 and csmL ≤ log Tu*, where Xu = (D★/du★)1/(fk) and Tu* = XuΓ−2/(fk), all sufficiently large x ≥ x0 admit a rational prime Tu ∈ (Tu*, (1 + 1/(fk))Tu*] ⊆ [Tu*, (1 + 1/(fk))Tu*], distinct from any two pre-assigned host primes strictly below X′ = exp(xε/3), satisfying Tu ≡ 1 modulo QS · q · d together with an algebraic integer πu ∈ 𝒪E ∩ K of the host CM field E ⊇ K such that πuπ̄u = Tu and πu − 1 ∈ N(g0g1)²𝒪E. Moreover, for Γ ≥ 1, every prime Tu ∈ [Tu*, (1 + 1/(fk))Tu*] satisfies

du★ Tufk ≤ (exp(1)/Γ²) D★,   log Xu − 2 log Γ / (fk) ≤ log Tu ≤ log Tu* + 1 ≤ log Xu + 1.

Proof. Since d divides N and gi ≥ 1, the combined modulus M = N(g0g1)² satisfies M ≥ N ≥ d ≥ 100 ≥ 3 and 4dM² ≤ 4N³(g0g1)⁴. Taking logarithms gives log(4dM²) ≤ log 4 + 3 log N + 4(log g0 + log g1) ≤ log 4 + 9xε/5(log x)² + 8CYxε. On the other hand, csmL ≤ log Tu* and m ≥ x1/3 imply log Tu* ≥ csx1/3+ε, whence √(log Tu*) ≥ √cs x1/6+ε/2. Because 0 < ε < 1/52, the exponent 1/6 + ε/2 strictly exceeds both ε and ε/5. Above a threshold x0 independent of u, we therefore have Tu* ≥ 1, log(4dM²) ≤ c√(log Tu*), and log(fk) ≤ 12 log x ≤ c√(log Tu*), the last inequality placing h = 1/(fk) inside [exp(−c√(log Tu*)), 1].

The short-interval norm-prime theorem applied to (d, M, Tu*, 1/(fk)) now furnishes a prime Tu ∈ (Tu*, (1 + 1/(fk))Tu*] ⊆ [Tu*, (1 + 1/(fk))Tu*] and an element πu ∈ 𝒪K with πuπ̄u = Tu and πu − 1 ∈ M𝒪K. Since K ⊆ E has ring of integers 𝒪K ⊆ 𝒪E ∩ K and complex conjugation on E restricts to quadratic conjugation on K, we obtain πu ∈ 𝒪E ∩ K and πu − 1 ∈ M𝒪E = N(g0g1)²𝒪E. Expanding Tu − 1 = πuπ̄u − 1 shows that M divides Tu − 1 in ℤ, whence Tu ≡ 1 modulo QS · q · d because N = QS · q · d divides M. Once x ≥ max(2, cs−4), we have csm ≥ csx1/4 ≥ 1 and xε/3 ≤ xε = L ≤ csmL, so both pre-assigned host primes lie strictly below X′ = exp(xε/3) ≤ exp(csmL) ≤ Tu* ≤ Tu.

Rational congruence descent and the three window inequalities

Since πu − 1 ∈ M𝒪K and quadratic conjugation preserves M𝒪K, we also have π̄u − 1 ∈ M𝒪K. Consequently

(Tu − 1)/M = (πu − 1)(π̄u − 1)/M + (πu + π̄u − 2)/M ∈ ℚ ∩ 𝒪K = ℤ,

because ℤ is integrally closed in ℚ. Thus M divides Tu − 1 as rational integers, and in particular QS · q · d = N divides Tu − 1.

For the three quantitative estimates on [Tu*, (1 + 1/(fk))Tu*], the definitions Xufk = D★/du★ and Tu* = XuΓ−2/(fk) give (Tu*)fk = D★/(du★Γ²). Using 1 + t ≤ exp(t) at t = 1/(fk) yields (1 + 1/(fk))fk ≤ exp(1), so du★Tufk ≤ du★(1 + 1/(fk))fk(Tu*)fk ≤ (exp(1)/Γ²)D★; when the ramified column dimension satisfies d0(D, u) = du★(Tuk − 1)f ≤ du★Tufk, this gives d0(D, u) ≤ (exp(1)/Γ²)D★ = D★ exp(1 − 2 log Γ), and hence d0(D, u) ≤ D★ exp(−2Cm⁵fL) whenever 1 + 2Cm⁵fL ≤ 2 log Γ. Taking logarithms of Tu ≥ Tu* gives log Tu ≥ log Xu − 2 log Γ/(fk) (losing at most 2 whenever log Γ/(fk) ≤ 1), while Tu ≤ (1 + 1/(fk))Tu* and log(1 + 1/(fk)) ≤ 1/(fk) ≤ 1 give log Tu ≤ log Tu* + 1 ≤ log Xu + 1 because Γ ≥ 1 makes −2 log Γ/(fk) ≤ 0.

8.30How an interval with exponent two gives one with exponent three halves

Here a change of scale serves two constraints at once. Fix the character ψ, 0 < ε < 1/52 and a scale multiplier c ≥ 1. In addition to the cohomological window, assume the prime-pair theorem. It supplies primes meeting the size and divisibility requirements, coprime to the character modulus. For the indicated nontrivial quadratic twists it also supplies centered-sum and logarithmic-derivative bounds, and for the indicated real characters a zero-free rectangle. These are stronger assumptions than prime existence alone.

At input scale Y0 the primes satisfy q ≡ 3 mod 8 and d ≡ 7 mod 16. Put A = Y0ε/5. Then A/2 < log q ≤ A and ½A(log Y0)² < log d ≤ A(log Y0)². The integer d + 1 is divisible by q and by every odd prime ≤ A. The auxiliary field is selected by the fixed subgroup described above.

Write r = 2 + 8ε and b = c1/r. Choose the tower exponent function e using the fact that some power of two lies between z and 2z for z ≥ 1. Apply the cohomological window theorem to this function, obtaining J and a threshold. To place the output interval beyond a prescribed lower bound, choose X so large that X1/J exceeds that lower bound, the prime-pair threshold, b³ and b400. Choose the primes at X1/J, then take the cohomological window [W, W²] with W ≥ X1/J and W² ≤ X.

Set Z = bW. Since W ≥ b³, Z3/2 ≤ W². For every x ∈ [Z, Z3/2] set x′ = x/b. Both x′ and x are in [W, W²]. Evaluating the page rule at x′ gives xr ≤ c2e(x′) ≤ 2xr. Evaluating the cohomological bound at that same x′ supplies its field at exactly that same tower level. Since x′ ≥ b400, we have

x400 = b400(x′)400 ≤ (x′)401,   exp((x′)ε/2) ≤ exp(xε/2).

All summands in the cohomological sum are nonnegative. Shortening the twist range and increasing the allowed upper bound therefore gives the cohomological bound at the rescaled window. The loss of one power from 401 to 400 pays for rescaling. Within a chosen window the primes can stay fixed, while the tower index depends on the point of evaluation.

8.31From finite subsets of primes to a series

The arithmetic comparison eventually needs a summable sequence of nonnegative terms. Choose the algebraic closure and local data attached to the arithmetic datum. Finiteness of each module length ensures conversion from extended natural numbers to integers recovers its value. For each prime the arithmetic contribution is bounded by its logarithm times the sum of these lengths in the specified range. All finite subsums are bounded by the same B. Their supremum is therefore finite, and equals the sum of the full nonnegative series. This is the use of the universal quantifier over finite sets of primes. The conclusion also includes the finiteness assertion on the relevant twists.

Why is an exponential bound small enough for a final estimate near √x? At the same scale x the weight in a single arithmetic measurement is b = exp(xε). The cohomological series has sum at most exp(xε/2) = √b. Since b ≥ 1, it fits within the allowance b in the finite-place lattice estimate. This is a bound on one input to the measurement. Only after the arithmetic comparisons are added does the proof divide the error by the total weight to bound the centered prime sum.

Turning this bound into the final divisible-lattice estimate also requires rank equalities, the local-to-global normalization and common family parameters. The preceding sections explain how the tower bounds, degree-two estimate and signed character counts apply to the same pair and field. The two-stage prime selection supplies the smoothed-sum and zero-free conditions for the same pair. The remaining interfaces there are the underlying progression, zero-density, mean-square and contour estimates.
